How high or low a sound is. It depends on how fast the sound vibrates: faster is higher.
Orchestras tune to the pitch A4 = 440 vibrations per second.
One musical sound with a fixed pitch. The seven natural notes are C D E F G A B (Do Re Mi Fa Sol La Si), then they repeat higher.
Middle C (C4) is the C closest to the middle of the piano.
A line of single notes, one after another, that forms a recognizable tune.
The melody is the part of a song you hum afterwards.
Absolute pitch is naming a note with no reference. Relative pitch is hearing notes in relation to each other — a skill anyone can train.
Relative pitch tells you a melody went up a fifth; absolute pitch tells you it started on A.
A tiny unit of pitch: 100 cents make one half step. Tuners show how many cents you are sharp or flat.
Here: A in tune, then the same A 25 cents sharp.
Singing notes on the syllables Do Re Mi Fa Sol La Si. In "movable Do", Do is always the home note of the key; in "fixed Do", Do is always C.
In G major with movable Do, G is Do and D is Sol.
Hearing music clearly in your head with no sound playing — the basis of sight-singing and playing by ear.
Keep the tune going through the silence, then check: does your next note match?
The set of notes a piece uses, organized around one home note. "In G major" means G is home and the notes are those of the G major scale.
A song in G major uses G A B C D E F♯ and ends on G.
The notes of a key played in order, step by step, from the home note up to the next one.
The C major scale: C D E F G A B C — only white keys.
Degree 1 of the key: the note where the music feels at rest and finished.
In C major the tonic is C; most songs in C end on it.
A note’s number in the key, counted from the home note: 1 is home, and the scale runs 1 to 7.
In C major, E is degree 3 and G is degree 5; in G major, those numbers belong to B and D.
Degree 7 of a major scale, a half step below home. It leans strongly up into the tonic.
In C major the leading tone is B; stop on it and you can feel C coming.
The two main colors of chords and keys. Major usually sounds bright; minor sounds darker. The difference is the third: a half step lower in minor.
C major is C E G; C minor is C E♭ G — one note apart.
A major key and a minor key that share exactly the same notes. The relative minor starts on degree 6 of the major.
C major and A minor are relatives: both use only the white keys.
The basic minor scale: degrees 3, 6 and 7 are a half step lower than in major.
C natural minor: C D E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C.
Natural minor with degree 7 raised a half step, so the scale gets a leading tone and a major V chord.
In A harmonic minor, G♯ makes E major, so E → Am closes firmly.
Minor with both 6 and 7 raised — a minor scale that is major from degree 3 upward. In jazz it is used the same both ways.
C melodic minor: C D E♭ F G A B C. Classical tradition comes down as natural minor.
A five-note scale with no half steps, so almost any order of its notes sounds good.
The black keys of the piano alone form a pentatonic scale. C major pentatonic: C D E G A.
The minor pentatonic plus one extra "blue note", the lowered 5, which gives blues and rock their bite.
C blues scale: C E♭ F F♯ G B♭ C — F♯ is the blue note.
Moving by half steps, using all 12 notes. A chromatic note is one from outside the key.
"Flight of the Bumblebee" (Rimsky-Korsakov) races up and down in chromatic lines.
A scale heard from a different home note. Playing the white keys from D to D gives Dorian, from E Phrygian, and so on — each with its own color.
The seven modes of the white keys: Ionian (C), Dorian (D), Phrygian (E), Lydian (F), Mixolydian (G), Aeolian (A), Locrian (B).
A minor mode with a raised 6. It sounds minor but warmer and less sad.
"Scarborough Fair" is a well-known Dorian melody. C Dorian: C D E♭ F G A B♭ C.
A minor mode with a lowered 2: the half step just above home gives it a dark, Spanish flavor.
Flamenco guitar lives on Phrygian moves like F → E over E. C Phrygian: C D♭ E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C.
A major mode with a raised 4. It sounds bright, floating and a little magical.
The Simpsons theme is a famous Lydian tune. C Lydian: C D E F♯ G A B C.
A major mode with a lowered 7. Common in rock, folk and blues: major, but relaxed instead of pushing home.
The chords D – C – G over a home of D are a typical Mixolydian riff. C Mixolydian: C D E F G A B♭ C.
The darkest mode: lowered 2 and lowered 5, so its home chord is diminished and never feels settled.
Rarely the home of a whole song; it appears in some metal riffs. C Locrian: C D♭ E♭ F G♭ A♭ B♭ C.
The distance between two notes, named by counting letter names (a third, a fifth) and measured exactly in half steps.
C to E is a third (4 half steps); C to G is a fifth (7 half steps).
The smallest step in Western music: from one piano key to the very next, black or white. Also called a semitone or minor second.
E–F and B–C are half steps with no black key between; the "Jaws" theme rocks between two notes a half step apart.
Two half steps: from one key to the one after next. Also called a whole tone or major second.
C–D and F–G are whole steps; "Happy Birthday" climbs a whole step on its third note.
A skip of one scale note. A minor third is 3 half steps, a major third 4 — the interval that decides if a chord is minor or major.
C–E♭ is a minor third, C–E a major third.
Five half steps, like Sol up to Do. Open and solid, it often launches a melody.
"Amazing Grace" and "Here Comes the Bride" both open with a fourth up.
Six half steps — exactly half an octave. Tense and restless; it is the clash inside every dominant seventh chord.
"Maria" from West Side Story leaps a tritone on its first two notes; in G7, B and F form a tritone.
Seven half steps, like Do up to Sol. The most stable interval after the octave — strong, open and hollow.
"Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star" jumps a fifth on its third note; rock power chords are just root + fifth.
A minor sixth is 8 half steps, a major sixth 9. Wide and singing, often warm and nostalgic.
"My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean" opens with a major sixth up.
A minor seventh is 10 half steps, a major seventh 11 — one half step short of the octave. Both want to move on.
"Somewhere" from West Side Story opens with a minor seventh up.
Twelve half steps: the same note name, higher or lower. The higher note vibrates exactly twice as fast.
"Over the Rainbow" opens with an octave leap; men and women singing "together" are usually an octave apart.
Any interval wider than an octave: an octave plus a smaller interval. A ninth is an octave plus a second.
C4 up to D5 is a ninth; C4 up to E5 is a tenth.
Consonant intervals sound stable and blended; dissonant ones clash and create tension that wants to move.
C + G is consonant; C + C♯ is dissonant.
A sharp raises a note a half step, a flat lowers it a half step. A natural sign ♮ cancels either.
F♯ and G♭ are the same piano key — two names for one sound.
Moving a whole piece up or down by the same interval, so it keeps its shape in a new key.
Moving "Happy Birthday" from C to F so it fits your voice.
Three or more notes sounding together. Chords are usually built by stacking thirds.
C major: C E G. Under a song, a guitarist strums chords while the singer carries the melody.
A three-note chord: root, third and fifth. There are four kinds: major, minor, diminished and augmented.
In C major the triads on 1, 4 and 5 — C, F and G — are all major.
The note a chord is built on and named after. It stays the root even when another note is in the bass.
In C–E–G the root is C; in Am (A–C–E) it is A.
A triad of two minor thirds: root, minor third, lowered fifth. Tense and unstable. Add another minor third and you get a diminished seventh.
B diminished (B D F) is the chord on degree 7 of C major; written B° or Bdim.
A triad of two major thirds: root, major third, raised fifth. Dreamy and suspended, it often leads somewhere new.
C augmented: C E G♯, written C+ or Caug.
A chord whose third is replaced by the 4 (sus4) or the 2 (sus2). Neither major nor minor, it hangs in the air.
Csus4 (C F G) → C (C E G): the 4 slips down to the 3.
A triad with one extra color note but no seventh, written "add" plus the number.
Cadd9 = C E G + D; a favorite of acoustic guitarists.
A chord with a chosen bass note, written chord/bass. Often used to make the bass line walk smoothly.
C – G/B – Am: G/B is a G chord with B in the bass, so the bass steps C, B, A.
A chord with a note other than the root in the bass. Third in the bass = first inversion; fifth in the bass = second inversion.
C/E is C major in first inversion; C/G is second inversion.
A triad plus a seventh above the root: four notes. The main types are maj7, dominant 7, m7, half-diminished (m7♭5) and diminished 7.
Cmaj7 = C E G B; C7 = C E G B♭; Cm7 = C E♭ G B♭.
Notes stacked above the seventh — 9, 11 and 13 — that add color without changing the chord’s job.
Cmaj9 = Cmaj7 + D; G13 = G7 with E on top.
A major chord on the lowered 2 (D♭ in C), usually in first inversion just before the dominant. Dark and dramatic.
In C minor: D♭/F → G → Cm.
A chord with the lowered 6 in the bass and the raised 4 above it; the two spread outward onto the dominant, an octave apart.
In C: A♭ in the bass and F♯ above move out to G and G (the Italian sixth).
How the notes of a chord are arranged: which note is on top, how close together, and in which octave.
C E G packed together, or C G E spread over two octaves — the same chord, two voicings.
The notes of a chord played one after another instead of together.
C–E–G–C picked one string at a time, as in many guitar ballads.
The job a chord does in a key. Tonic (I) is rest, subdominant (IV, ii) moves away, dominant (V) builds tension that pulls home.
In C: C is tonic, F subdominant, G dominant — C F G C is the whole story in four chords.
The chord on degree 5. With its seventh (V7) it holds the leading tone and a tritone, so it pulls strongly to the tonic.
In C major the dominant is G (G7 = G B D F).
Music builds tension with dissonance or distance from home, then resolves it by moving to a stable sound.
G7 → C: the tense B–F inside G7 settles onto C–E.
The chords that close a phrase — musical punctuation. Some end like a full stop, others like a comma or a surprise.
A phrase ending V → I sounds finished; one ending on V sounds like a question.
Dominant to tonic: the strongest, most final ending. With the tonic on top of the last chord it is called "perfect".
G7 → C at the end of countless songs and classical pieces in C.
Subdominant to tonic: a softer, gentler close than V → I.
The "Amen" at the end of a hymn is a plagal cadence, IV → I.
A phrase that stops on the dominant. It sounds open, like a comma or a question waiting for an answer.
C – F – G, then pause: the next phrase usually answers with a full cadence.
The dominant sets up the tonic, but the music turns to vi instead — a surprise that keeps the piece going.
G7 → Am instead of G7 → C.
A series of chords in order — the harmonic skeleton of a song, usually written as Roman numerals so it works in any key.
I–V–vi–IV (in C: C G Am F) underlies a huge number of pop songs.
A dominant chord borrowed to point at a chord other than the tonic: "V of" that chord, for a moment of extra pull.
In C major, D7 → G: D7 is V/V, "five of five".
Changing key in the middle of a piece, so a new note becomes home.
A pop song that lifts its last chorus up a half step has modulated.
A chord taken from the parallel key — usually from minor into major — for a moment of shadow. Also called modal interchange.
In C major, F → Fm → C: the F minor is borrowed from C minor.
How each note of one chord moves to the next chord. Good voice leading keeps common notes and moves the others by the smallest step.
C → F: C stays, E rises to F, G rises to A.
Two or more independent melodies played at once that still fit together — often moving in opposite directions.
Bach’s two-part inventions: one melody in each hand, equally important.
A bass line with numbers under it that show the intervals to play above each bass note — the Baroque chord chart.
A "6" under E means play a sixth and a third above it: C and G, so a C chord in first inversion.
The lowest note or part in the music. It anchors the harmony: what you hear in the bass shapes how the chord sounds.
A bass player often plays the root of each chord on beat 1.
Notes sounding together and how chords follow each other — the vertical side of music, under or around the melody.
A second singer a third below the melody is singing harmony.
The steady pulse under the music — what you tap your foot to. Beats are grouped into bars.
The drummer’s "1, 2, 3, 4" before a song sets the beat.
How fast the beat goes, measured in beats per minute (BPM).
60 BPM is one beat per second; a brisk march is about 120.
The pattern of long and short sounds and silences placed over the beat.
Clap a well-known song without singing — many people can still name it from the rhythm.
A group of beats between two bar lines. The time signature says how many beats each bar holds.
In 4/4, each bar holds four beats: 1 2 3 4 | 1 2 3 4.
Two stacked numbers at the start of the music: the top says how many beats per bar, the bottom which note value gets one beat.
3/4 = three quarter-note beats per bar, the waltz; 4/4 = four, most pop and rock.
Beat 1 of the bar, the strongest. A conductor’s baton drops on it — hence the name.
In a waltz you feel the downbeat: ONE two three, ONE two three.
Accents on beats 2 and 4 instead of 1 and 3 — the snare-drum pulse of rock, pop and soul.
Clap on 2 and 4 with almost any rock song.
The big drum on the floor, played with the foot pedal. It gives the groove its low thump, usually on beats 1 and 3 in rock.
Rock beat: kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4.
Two cymbals on a stand, closed by a foot pedal. Struck with a stick it keeps the time; closed by the foot alone it clicks on 2 and 4.
Eighth notes on the closed hi-hat over the rock beat.
A short break from the groove, often at the end of a phrase, that leads back to beat 1 of the next section.
Three bars of groove, then a one-beat fill on the snare and toms, and a crash on 1.
Splitting each beat into smaller equal parts — two eighths, four sixteenths — to place notes precisely.
Count "1 & 2 &" for eighths, "1 e & a" for sixteenths.
Three equal notes in the time normally taken by two — the beat split into three instead of two.
Say "tri-o-la" on each beat: three even syllables per click.
Accenting a weak part of the beat — often a note on the "&" held over the next beat — so the rhythm pushes against the pulse.
"eighth – quarter – eighth": the long note starts between beats. Funk, reggae and Latin music are full of it.
Playing pairs of eighth notes long–short instead of even, giving a lilting feel.
Jazz and shuffle blues swing their eighths: "doo-ba doo-ba".
A meter whose beats split into three, not two. 6/8 has two big beats, each made of three eighths.
Count 6/8 as ONE-two-three FOUR-five-six — two beats, not six.
A meter with an uneven number of beats per bar, like 5/4 or 7/8, felt as groups of 2 and 3.
"Take Five" (Dave Brubeck Quartet) is in 5/4; 7/8 is common in Balkan music, counted 2+2+3.
Two different even pulses at the same time, such as 3 against 2, meeting again on beat 1.
3 against 2: one hand taps three times while the other taps twice in the same span. Common in West African drumming.
One or more notes before the first full bar, leading into the downbeat.
"Happy Birthday" begins with a pickup: the first two short notes come before beat 1.
How loud or soft the music is. Written in Italian: p (piano) soft, mf medium, f (forte) loud.
The same phrase played pp, then ff, can feel like a secret and then a shout.
Gradually getting louder (crescendo, <) or softer (diminuendo or decrescendo, >).
A drum roll that swells into a big chorus is a crescendo.
Smooth and connected: each note joins the next with no gap. Marked with a curved slur.
A lullaby is sung legato; on a violin, several notes in one bow stroke.
Short and detached: each note is cut off, leaving a little silence. Marked with a dot above or below the note.
Here the same five notes: first staccato, then legato.
A musical sentence: a group of notes that feels complete, often 2 or 4 bars, ending in a cadence.
The first line of a folk song, sung in one breath, is usually one phrase.
A short, recognizable idea — a few notes or a rhythm — that is repeated and developed through a piece.
Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony opens with a four-note motif: short-short-short-long.
A tune stated twice (A A), a contrasting section (B, the bridge), then the tune again (A) — usually 8 bars each, 32 in all.
"Over the Rainbow" and many jazz standards are 32-bar AABA songs.
The two main sections of a song. Verses change their words and tell the story; the chorus returns with the same words and the hook.
The chorus is usually higher, louder and fuller than the verse.
A contrasting section that brings fresh material — new chords, often a new key area — before the familiar part returns.
In AABA the B is the bridge; in pop it often comes once, before the last chorus.
Three parts: a first section, a contrasting middle, and a return of the first.
A minuet with trio (minuet – trio – minuet) is in ternary form.
A form where the main theme keeps coming back between different episodes: A B A C A.
Beethoven’s "Für Elise" is a rondo: its famous opening returns between two contrasting sections.
The classic blues form: twelve bars on I, IV and V, usually all dominant sevenths, repeated over and over.
How the layers of music combine: one line alone (monophony), a melody with chords (homophony), or several independent lines (polyphony).
A solo singer is monophonic; a singer with guitar is homophonic; a Bach fugue is polyphonic.
One long note (or fifth) held under the music. Against it, every melody note’s color becomes easy to hear.
Bagpipes and the Indian tanpura play a constant drone.
What makes two sounds of the same pitch and loudness different — why a flute and a violin never sound alike.
The same A (440 Hz) as a pure sine tone, then on piano.
Fainter higher pitches that sound inside every musical note. Their mix is what gives each instrument its timbre.
Above low C: C, G, C, E, G… — the harmonic series. Touch a guitar string lightly at fret 12 to hear one alone.
How many times per second a sound vibrates, in hertz (Hz). Double the frequency and you are an octave higher.
A4 is 440 Hz, A5 is 880 Hz; the low hum of mains power is 50 or 60 Hz.
Turning chosen frequency ranges up or down to shape a sound: more weight in the lows, less harshness in the mids, more air on top.
Cutting below about 100 Hz on a vocal removes rumble; a gentle boost near 10 kHz adds air.
Removes everything beyond a cut-off frequency. A high-pass removes the lows (thin sound); a low-pass removes the highs (muffled sound).
A low-pass on the whole band gives the "music from the next room" effect common in dance-music build-ups.
The tail of reflections a room adds after a sound. A short tail suggests a small room; a long one, a hall or cathedral.
Clap in a tiled bathroom, then in a carpeted bedroom: that difference is reverb.
Automatically turning down the loudest moments so the level is more even; the whole track can then be turned up and sounds denser.
Pop vocals are compressed so quiet words are not lost under the band.
Placing a sound between the left and right speakers. Best heard on headphones.
A rhythm guitar panned left and a second one panned right make room for the vocal in the middle.
How wide a sound spreads between the speakers: mono sits as a point in the middle, a wide sound fills the space.
Here the same loop in mono, then wide. Use headphones.
All the notes a voice or instrument can produce, from its lowest to its highest.
A tenor usually sings from about C3 to C5; a soprano from about C4 to C6.
A region of the range — low, middle or high — each with its own color.
The same tune in a low register sounds dark; in a high register, bright.
Chest voice is the full, speech-like sound of the low range; head voice is the lighter, ringing sound up high. Mix voice blends the two.
Speak "hey" normally (chest), then call "whoo-hoo" like an owl (head).
The zone where the voice shifts from chest to head. Untrained, it cracks or strains; trained, it passes smoothly.
Many male voices meet it around E4–G4; slide up slowly through it on "ng" or a lip trill.
A slight, regular wave in pitch on a held note — about five to seven waves a second — that makes it sound alive.
A plain held note, then a pitch that wavers around it. Singers and violinists add vibrato on long notes.
Controlling the outflow of air with the body — not the throat — so the tone stays steady and in tune.
Sing one long note on "ss" or "oo" for 15 seconds without it wobbling or going flat.
How a sung note begins. Breathy onset leaks air first; hard (glottal) onset starts with a click; balanced onset starts air and tone together.
Say "ha" (breathy), "uh-oh" (hard), then sing a clean "ah" (balanced).
The metal strips on a guitar neck. Each fret raises the string by one half step; fret 12 is the octave.
Low E string: open = E, fret 1 = F, fret 3 = G, fret 5 = A.
A clamp across all strings at one fret. It raises the pitch, so the same chord shapes sound in a higher key.
An open G shape with a capo on fret 2 sounds as A major.
Five open-chord shapes — C, A, G, E, D — that slide up the neck. Linked together, they map every chord and scale across the fretboard.
The open E shape, barred at fret 5, is an A chord.
The right pedal of a piano: while it is down, notes keep ringing after you lift your fingers.
The same arpeggio dry, then with the pedal down. Lift and press again at each chord change.
Minor 7 on 2, dominant 7 on 5, major 7 on 1: the most common progression in jazz, used to arrive in any key.
In C: Dm7 – G7 – Cmaj7. "Autumn Leaves" is built almost entirely from ii–V–Is.
A jazz voicing of just root, 3 and 7 — the notes that define the chord’s quality — leaving room for the melody and the bass.
Dm7 (D F C) → G7 (G F B) → Cmaj7 (C E B): the 3s and 7s move by a half step or stay.
The 3rd and 7th of a chord: they decide its quality, and from chord to chord they move by a half step or stay. Not the leading tone, which is degree 7 of the key.
Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7: C falls to B and stays; F stays and falls to E.
A bass line with one note on every beat, walking through the chords: chord tones on the strong beats, a step or a half step into the next root.
Over C7 to F7: C, E, G, F♯ — and F arrives on beat 1.
The written melody with chord symbols above it: the map a band plays a tune from. Each player builds a part from it.
C | Am | Dm7 G7 | C — four bars of a lead sheet.
Reaching a target note from both sides: a note above it, a note below it, then the target itself on the beat. A basic bebop move.
To land on E: F, then D♯, then E.
Replacing a dominant 7 with the dominant 7 a tritone away. Both share the same tritone, so the pull is the same but the bass slides by a half step.
Dm7 – D♭7 – Cmaj7: D♭7 replaces G7; both contain F and B (C♭).
Pianist Barry Harris’s system: a major 6 chord and the diminished 7 chord a half step below alternate along an eight-note scale.
C6 (C E G A) and B°7 (B D F G♯), on the scale C D E F G G♯ A B.
The melodic mode system of Arabic, Turkish and related music: a scale built from small segments (ajnas), plus typical paths and an emotional character.
Maqam Rast on C: C D E𝄳 F G A B𝄳 C — E and B are a quarter tone low.
A building block of a maqam: three to five notes with a set pattern of steps. Plural: ajnas.
Jins Hijaz on D: D E♭ F♯ G — the wide step in the middle gives its famous color.
Half of a half step (50 cents) — a note between two piano keys, essential in many maqamat.
E♭, then E half-flat, then E: the middle one is the "neutral third" of maqam Rast.
A rhythmic cycle in Arabic music, built from low "dum" and high "tak" strokes on the drum.
Maqsum: dum-tak, -tak, dum, -tak — one of the most common rhythms in Egyptian and Arabic pop.
The five horizontal lines music is written on. Higher on the staff means higher in pitch.
In treble clef the lines, bottom to top, are E G B D F.
The sign at the start of the staff that fixes which line is which note. Treble (G) clef for high parts, bass (F) clef for low parts.
The treble clef curls around the G line; the bass clef’s two dots surround the F line.
The sharps or flats at the start of each line, applying to those notes throughout. They tell you the key.
One sharp (F♯) means G major or E minor; one flat (B♭) means F major or D minor.
A sharp, flat or natural written before a single note, outside the key signature. It lasts until the end of the bar.
F, then F♯ with a sharp sign, then F again after a natural sign ♮.
A short extra line above or below the staff for notes that do not fit on the five lines.
Middle C sits on one ledger line below the treble staff; A5 on one above.
How long a written note lasts. Each value is half the one before: whole, half, quarter, eighth, sixteenth.
In 4/4: whole = 4 beats, half = 2, quarter = 1, eighth = ½. A dot adds half the value again.
The thick line joining the stems of eighth notes or shorter, so a beat’s worth of notes is read as one group.
Two eighths share one beam; four sixteenths share two.
A written silence with an exact length; every note value has a matching rest.
Here: note, quarter rest, note, quarter rest — the silences are counted just like notes.
The same rhythm can start on a different beat of the bar. Moving it (displacement) changes how it feels, even though the pattern is identical.
Hi {name}! This is the Charleston: a long note, then a quick one, on the first beats of the bar. Count one, two, three, four with the clicks.
Now the very same pattern starts one beat later, on beat two. Nothing else changed — but it suddenly feels pushed and jazzy.
Musicians call this displacement: moving a rhythm in time, the way transposing moves a melody in pitch. You can move it by a beat, or by just half a beat.
A trick: keep counting the beat out loud, and say "now" where the pattern starts. The count stays put; only the pattern slides along it.
Your turn! Hear how far a pattern moved, pick the moved one on paper, then tap it yourself starting on beat two.

Rhythmic displacement moves a whole pattern to a new place in the bar. Every note length and every gap stays the same; only its position against the beat changes. Here is the Charleston from beat one, then the same figure from beat three.

Why it feels different: in 4/4, beat one is the strongest, beat three next, two and four weaker, and the "and"s between the beats weaker still. A note on a weak spot pulls against the beat — that pull is syncopation. Listen: hits on one and three, then on the "and"s after them.
A shift of half a beat is the most dramatic: every note leaves the beat and lands on an "and". The shape is identical, but now it floats between the clicks.

To hear a displacement, keep counting and ask two questions. Does the first note land on a number or on an "and"? Which number is nearest? This Charleston starts on the "and" of two: it moved by a beat and a half.
To play it, fix your foot on the beat first. Clap the pattern from beat one, then from two, then from the "and" of one, without letting the foot move. Start slowly; the foot is your anchor.

The common mistake: when a pattern is shifted, the ear quietly moves beat one to its first note, and the shift disappears. If a displaced pattern suddenly sounds normal, check your count against the accented click — that is still beat one.

In real music displacement is everywhere. Jazz pianists comp with the Charleston and shifted copies of it, so the chords never fall in the same place twice. Rock and funk riffs often start on the "and" of four, just before the bar line, which makes them push forward.
To keep: displacement changes where a rhythm sits, not what it is. Hold the beat still, locate the first note against it, and every shift becomes easy to hear and to play.
A chord is three notes stacked: root at the bottom, third in the middle, fifth on top. Singing each one trains your ear to hear inside harmony.
Hey {name}! A chord sounds like one thing, but it is really three notes together. Listen: first all together, then one by one.
The bottom note is the root — it names the chord. The middle one is the third. The top one is the fifth.
The third decides the mood. In a minor chord the middle note sits a little lower, and the whole chord turns darker.
Melodies love to end on home. When a tune stops one step early, you can feel which note it is missing. Sing it in your head now.
Your turn! Hear a chord and sing the note I ask for — bottom, middle or top. Then finish a tune by singing its last note.

A triad is two thirds stacked. In C major: C, E and G. From the root up to the third is a major third, four half steps; from the third up to the fifth is a minor third, three half steps. Together they span a perfect fifth, seven half steps.
Swap the order of the thirds and you get a minor triad: C, E-flat, G. The root and fifth stay; only the third drops a half step. That single note turns bright into dark.

The root is not always at the bottom. E, G, C is still a C major chord, only inverted. So musicians name chord tones by their job, not their height: the root names the chord, the third makes it major or minor, the fifth adds body.

To hear inside a chord, start at the edges. The bass is easiest: hum it first. The top note is the brightest: hum it next. The middle hides between them, so find it by singing up from the bass: one, three, five.

A daily drill: hold a chord and sing one, three, five, three, one slowly over it. Then sustain a single tone and listen for blend. When you are exactly in tune, your voice melts into the chord and the wobble stops.

The usual slip: asked for the third or the fifth, the voice drifts to the root, because the root pulls hardest. Check by singing up from the root and stopping on the note you want. Singing it an octave lower or higher is fine; it is the same note.

In real music, backing vocals mostly sing chord tones, often a third below the lead. Bass lines lean on root and fifth, like the oom-pah of a march or the boom-chick of country. Here a lead line with a harmony a third below.
To keep: a triad is root, third and fifth. The root names it, the third sets major or minor, the fifth gives stability. Listen for the bass first, then the top, then the middle.
Beats come in groups: twos (a march), threes (a waltz) or fours (most pop). The first beat of each group is the strongest — that is beat 1.
Hi {name}! Beats like to travel in groups, and the first beat of each group is a little stronger. That grouping is called the meter.
A march goes in two: left, right, left, right. Strong, weak, strong, weak.
A waltz goes in three: one, two, three — one, two, three. It sways and turns instead of marching.
To find beat one, listen for the low note and the strongest pulse. Music can start in the middle of a bar, so do not trust the first note.
Your turn! Is it a march or a waltz, in two, three or four? Then find where beat one is hiding.

Meter is the regular pattern of strong and weak beats. Each group is a bar, and the time signature names it: 2/4 has two beats, 3/4 three, 4/4 four. In these simple meters every beat divides into two.

4/4 has a second, lighter accent on beat three: strong, weak, medium, weak. That is why a slow four can sound like a two. The test is the bass and the chord changes: do they come every four beats, or every two?
6/8 is a compound meter: six eighth notes felt as two beats, each split into three — ONE two three, FOUR five six. It rocks gently. 3/4 fills the same bar with three beats, each split into two.
To find the meter, tap the beat that feels natural, then listen for the next low, heavy note and count the taps in between. Bass notes and chord changes usually fall on beat one.
Careful: many tunes begin before beat one, with a pickup, also called an anacrusis. Here a single note leads in, and beat one arrives with the bass.
A common mistake is to mix up meter and tempo. A waltz is in three whether it is fast or slow, and a march is in two at any speed. Count the group, not the speed.
In real music, marches are usually in 2/4 or 6/8, waltzes in 3/4, most pop and rock in 4/4, and Irish jigs in 6/8. Odd meters exist too: "Take Five", recorded by the Dave Brubeck Quartet, is in 5/4.
To keep: meter is how beats group. Find the heavy beat one, count to the next one, and check whether each beat splits in two, simple meter, or in three, compound meter.
The same notes can be played loud or soft (dynamics), short or smooth (articulation). Together they make the mood of the music.
Hi {name}! Music is not only which notes — it is how they are played. Here is the same tune, softly and then loudly.
Musicians call loud and soft dynamics. Growing louder is a crescendo; fading softer is a diminuendo.
Notes can also be short and bouncy — staccato — or smooth and joined — legato. Same notes, a different character.
Put it all together and you get a mood: fast, loud and major sounds joyful; slow, soft and minor sounds sad.
Your turn! Louder or softer, short or smooth, and how does it feel? There are no wrong feelings — but the clues are real.

Dynamics are marked with Italian letters, from very soft to very loud: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff. The m stands for mezzo, moderately. They are relative: forte in a lullaby is softer than forte in a brass band.
Gradual changes are drawn as hairpins: an opening one is a crescendo, a closing one a diminuendo, also called decrescendo. A single stressed note is an accent, marked with a small >.

Articulation is how each note starts and ends. Staccato, a dot, cuts the note short. Tenuto, a short line, holds it full length with a little weight. Legato, under a slur, joins notes with no gap. Staccato shortens the sound, never the beat: the next note still comes on time.
To hear dynamics, compare with what came just before, not with a fixed loudness. For articulation, listen to the ends of notes: is there silence between them, or does each one flow into the next?
When you play or sing, shape the phrase. Most phrases grow towards their highest or most important note and relax after it. Decide where the peak is before you begin.
The classic mistake: speeding up in a crescendo and slowing down in a diminuendo. Louder is not faster. Keep the pulse steady and change only the volume, as in this crescendo.

In real music, dynamics build form. Ravel's "Boléro" is one long crescendo from start to finish. Many rock songs set a quiet verse against a loud chorus. Mood comes from all the clues together: tempo, loudness, articulation, register and major or minor.
To keep: dynamics say how loud, articulation says how each note begins and ends. Both are relative, both carry the mood, and neither should change your tempo.
Phrases end in different ways (cadences), music can move to a new home (modulation), and every melody note suggests the chords that fit under it.
Hi {name}! A cadence is how a phrase ends — like punctuation. Five to one is a full stop. Four to one is a gentle "Amen".
Some phrases stop on five — a question mark. And a deceptive cadence sets up home, then surprises you with a sad chord instead.
Sometimes the music changes home altogether. That is a key change, or modulation — the ground shifts under your feet.
Under any melody note, some chords fit and some clash. A chord fits when the melody notes are inside it.
Your turn! Name the ending, hear whether the key changed, and choose the chord that fits the tune.

A cadence is the pair of chords that closes a phrase. The strongest is the authentic cadence, V to I: the bass falls from G to C, and the leading tone, B, rises a half step to C. It sounds final, like a full stop.
The plagal cadence, IV to I, has no leading tone, so it is softer: the "Amen" sung at the end of many hymns. The bass falls from F to C.
A half cadence stops on V. It sounds open, like a comma or a question, and the next phrase usually answers with a full cadence. Musicians call this pair antecedent and consequent.
I ii V , · I V I .

The deceptive cadence goes V to vi. The melody still resolves, B to C, but the bass steps up to A instead of falling to C. The vi chord shares two notes with I, C and E, so it can stand in for home with a darker color.
To tell them apart, follow the bass on the last two chords. G down to C: authentic. F to C: plagal. Stopping on G, unresolved: half. G up to A, with a minor color: deceptive.

A modulation makes a new note home. The smooth way uses a pivot chord that belongs to both keys. A minor is vi in C and ii in G; from it, D7, the V7 of G, leads to G, and F-sharp, the new leading tone, confirms the move.
Pop songs often skip the pivot: the last chorus simply jumps up a half step or a whole step. It is direct and dramatic, and you feel the floor lift.

Fitting a chord to a melody: a note fits when it is one of the chord's tones. G belongs to C major and to G major, so both work under it. Under F major, G is not a chord tone but an added color, the 9.
A common mistake is one chord per melody note. Chords usually change once or twice a bar. Choose the chord that holds the notes on the strong beats; the notes in between can simply pass through.
To keep: cadences are punctuation — V to I a full stop, IV to I an amen, ending on V a comma, V to vi a surprise. Modulation moves home, and a chord fits when it holds the melody's strong notes.
Musicians move music around: chord numbers into any key, a motif up a step (sequence), upside down (inversion) or backwards (retrograde), a rhythm twice as slow.
Hi {name}! Many musicians think of chords as numbers: one, four, five. In C that is C, F and G. In G it is G, C and D.
A sequence repeats a little motif one step higher, and then higher again. Your ear expects the next step before it comes.
Composers also flip a motif upside down — that is inversion — or play it backwards, called retrograde.
Rhythms can be stretched too: twice as slow is augmentation, twice as fast is diminution. The shape stays; the speed changes.
Your turn! Turn numbers into chords, continue a sequence, and say what was done to a motif or a rhythm.

Roman numerals name chords by scale degree. Build a triad on each note of the major scale and you get I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi and vii°. Upper case is major, lower case minor, and the small circle means diminished. In C: C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°.
Because the numbers describe the pattern, not the notes, they move to any key unchanged. ii–V–I is Dm, G, C in C major, and Gm, C, F in F major. Same progression, same feeling, new pitch.

A sequence repeats a motif at a new pitch. A diatonic sequence stays inside the scale, so step sizes shift: C D E, then D E F, with a half step at the top. A real sequence copies the intervals exactly: D E F-sharp.

Inversion turns every interval upside down: same size, opposite direction. The motif C, E, D, G goes up a major third, down a whole step, up a fourth. Inverted from C: down a major third to A-flat, up a whole step to B-flat, down a fourth to F.

Retrograde plays the notes in reverse order: G, D, E, C. Combine both and you get the retrograde inversion. Twelve-tone composers such as Schoenberg build whole pieces from these four forms: original, inversion, retrograde and retrograde inversion.
Augmentation doubles every note value; diminution halves them. The pitches and the rhythm's shape stay, only the time stretches or shrinks. Bach uses augmentation in some of his canons and fugues.

To recognize a transformation, trace the contour with your hand. Same shape, higher: transposition or sequence. Mirror image: inversion. Last note first: retrograde. Same shape, slower or faster: augmentation or diminution.

The usual confusion is inversion versus retrograde, since both sound "turned around". Check the first note: an inversion starts where the original started; a retrograde starts where the original ended.

To keep: numbers carry chords between keys, a sequence moves a motif in pitch, inversion mirrors it, retrograde reverses it, and augmentation and diminution change its speed. The idea stays recognizable every time.
Sheet music speaks Italian: tempo words (Adagio, Allegro), dynamics (p, f) and signs (staccato, fermata). The time signature tells how beats are grouped.
Hi {name}! Written music has its own words, mostly Italian. Adagio means slow, Allegro means fast and lively.
Small letters tell how loud: p is soft, f is loud, and two of them — pp or ff — mean very.
A dot above a note means short — staccato. A curved line over notes means smooth — legato. An eye-shaped sign, the fermata, means hold it.
The two numbers at the start are the time signature. In three-four, the top number says three beats in a bar; the four says each beat is a quarter note.
Your turn! Match the words to their meaning, read time signatures, and spot what breaks the rules of good voice leading.

Tempo words, from slow to fast: Largo, broad; Adagio, at ease; Andante, at a walking pace; Moderato, moderate; Allegro, lively; Presto, very fast. They describe character as much as speed, so composers often add a metronome mark. Andante, then Presto.
Changing the tempo: ritardando or rallentando, written rit. or rall., means gradually slower; accelerando means gradually faster; a tempo means back to the original speed. Listen to a ritardando.

Dynamics run pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff, from very soft to very loud; the m, mezzo, means moderately. Sfz, sforzando, is a sudden strong accent on one note. Cresc. and dim. spell out gradual changes in words. Here: p, mf, ff.

A curved line can mean two things. Over different notes it is a slur: play them smoothly. Between two notes of the same pitch it is a tie: play one long note and do not strike the second. Listen: two Gs, then the same two tied.

In a time signature the top number counts the beats in a bar, and the bottom number names the beat: 4 is a quarter note, 2 a half note, 8 an eighth. A large C means 4/4, common time; a C with a line through it is 2/2, cut time.
6/8 is not six slow beats. It is six eighths grouped in two threes, so a conductor beats two. 3/4 has the same six eighths, grouped as three twos.

The road map: repeat signs, two dots beside a double bar, send you back. First and second endings are played the first and second time through. D.C. means from the beginning, D.S. from the sign, al Fine up to the word Fine, al Coda on to the coda.

Classical part-writing adds rules: resolve the leading tone up, do not cross voices, and avoid parallel fifths and octaves, where two voices keep that interval while moving the same way. Listen: C–G to D–A, parallel fifths; then G falls to F instead.
A common mistake is to treat the words as exact speeds. Allegro literally means cheerful, and two Allegros can be quite different. Read the word for character and the metronome mark for speed.
To keep: Italian words set tempo and character, letters set loudness, small signs shape each note, and the time signature tells how many beats a bar has and which note gets one.
Every tune has a home note your ear finds by itself. Octaves are the same note higher or lower. Scales are families of notes with their own color.
Hi {name}! Even without chords, a tune has a home — the note where it feels finished. Listen, then hear the home note.
Two notes an octave apart sound like the same note, one high and one low — like a man and a child singing together.
A pentatonic scale has only five notes. It sounds open and folk-like, and almost nothing in it can sound wrong.
The blues scale adds one extra, crunchy note to the minor pentatonic — the blue note. You know it from countless songs.
Your turn! Find the home note of a tune, tell an octave from a near miss, and name the scale you hear.

The home note is the tonic. Your ear finds it from where phrases rest, from which notes are used, and from the leading tone, the note a half step below home that pulls up into it. Listen: a phrase that stops on B, then its resolution to C.

An octave is twelve half steps, and its top note vibrates exactly twice as fast. That 2:1 ratio makes the two blend so well that they share a name. One half step less, a major seventh, and the blend turns into a sharp rub.
A major scale has seven notes with this pattern: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. From C: C D E F G A B C. The two half steps, E–F and B–C, give it its shape.

The natural minor scale uses another pattern: whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole. From A: A B C D E F G A — the same notes as C major, with a different home. Its lowered 3, 6 and 7 make it darker.

The major pentatonic keeps only 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6. It has no half steps, so no two notes rub. Start the same notes on 6 and you get the minor pentatonic, A C D E G: the scale of countless rock and blues solos.
The blues scale adds ♭5 to the minor pentatonic. In C: C, E-flat, F, G-flat, G, B-flat. The blue note is usually a passing note squeezed between 4 and 5, not a place to rest.
To name a scale, find home first, then check the third: major or minor. Then listen for half steps. None means pentatonic; a chromatic squeeze between 4 and 5 means blues.

The common mistake is taking the first or lowest note as home. Many tunes start on 5 or 3 and only land on home at the end. This one starts on G, but home is C. Listen to where a tune rests, not where it begins.

In real music, pentatonic melodies appear in folk traditions around the world, from Scotland to China to West Africa. The minor pentatonic and the blues scale are the core vocabulary of blues and rock guitar.
To keep: home is where the music rests, an octave is the same note vibrating twice as fast, and every scale is a pattern of steps — major, minor, pentatonic or blues.
Texture is how many things sound at once: one line, a melody with chords, or several independent lines woven together.
Hi {name}! Sometimes you hear one note, sometimes several together. Counting them is a great ear workout. Here: one, then two, then three.
Spread-out notes are easier to count than notes squeezed close together. Listen for the bottom and the top first, then the middle.
When lines move on their own, each with its own rhythm, musicians call it polyphony. Try to follow just the low line.
Pieces are built from phrases too: a phrase comes back the same, comes back changed, or something new arrives.
Your turn! Count the notes in a chord, count the moving lines, and hear how the phrases are put together.
Texture describes how the lines in music relate. Monophony is a single line with no accompaniment, even when many voices sing it together in unison or in octaves, as in Gregorian chant.

Homophony is one melody supported by chords. In a hymn all the voices move together in the same rhythm; in a pop song a voice sings over strummed chords. Either way, one line leads and the rest support it.

Polyphony is two or more independent lines, each with its own rhythm and shape. The simplest kind is a round, or canon, like "Frère Jacques": the same tune enters again later and fits against itself. Here a short tune is answered an octave lower.
Counting notes in a chord is about density. Doubling a note in another octave thickens the sound without adding a new pitch name. Here C, G and E, then the same chord with an extra C on top.

To hear texture, follow the bass first, then the top line. Then ask: do the lines move together, with one leading? That is homophony. Do they move on their own, with different rhythms? That is polyphony.

Form is how phrases follow each other. Label each phrase with a letter: a repeat keeps its letter, a varied repeat gets a prime, new material gets a new letter. AABA is the 32-bar form of many jazz standards. Here: A, A prime, B, A.

A common mistake: more instruments does not mean polyphony. A full orchestra playing a tune with chords is homophonic; two flutes weaving independent lines are polyphonic. Count independent lines, not players.
In real music, Gregorian chant is monophonic, a Bach fugue is polyphonic, and most pop songs are homophonic. Many pieces move between textures to create contrast.
To keep: one line is monophony, a melody with chords is homophony, independent lines are polyphony. Count lines from the bass and the top, and label phrases with letters to see the form.
A quarter note is one beat; a half is two, a whole four, an eighth half a beat. A dot adds half the note again.
Music is counted in beats, like steady footsteps. Count four of them out loud: one, two, three, four. A quarter note lasts exactly one of those beats.
A half note is held for two beats, and a whole note for all four. Their shapes are hollow: the longer the note, the emptier it looks.
An eighth note has a flag and lasts half a beat, so two eighths fill one beat. Sixteenths are quicker still: four of them make a beat.
A dot after a note adds half of its value again. A dotted half note is two plus one: three beats. Rests are silences with the same lengths.
Your turn. Each question shows a note, a rest, or a short group. Say how many beats it lasts, counting the quarter note as one.
Why the quarter note is one beat: in 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4, the lower number 4 says the beat is a quarter. Other meters choose other notes as the beat.
Each value is half of the one before: whole, half, quarter, eighth, sixteenth. Doubling and halving is the whole system.
A dotted quarter is one and a half beats. It often pairs with an eighth note, and together they fill two beats, as in many folk tunes.
A common mistake is counting a rest as nothing. A rest still takes its beats: keep counting through the silence, then come in on time.
To add up a group, turn every sign into a number and add them: a quarter, two eighths and a half make one, plus one, plus two: four.
Where it lives: every written rhythm, every bar line and every theory paper of grade one starts here. Recap: halve and double, a dot adds half.
Count the letter names from the lower note to the upper, both included: C to E is a 3rd.
An interval is the distance between two notes. Its number comes from counting letter names, starting on the lower note and counting it as one.
C, D, E: three letters, so C up to E is a third. C up to G is C, D, E, F, G: a fifth.
From C to the next C is eight letters, so we call it an octave, not an eighth. The same letter twice on the same line is a unison.
A fast way on the staff: from a line to the next line is a third, from a line to a space a second or a fourth. Line to line is always odd.
Your turn. Two notes appear on the staff, one after the other or together. Count the letters and choose the number.
Sharps and flats never change the number. C to E flat is still a third, because the letters are still C, D, E. They change the quality, which comes later.
Melodic means one note after the other; harmonic means both together. The number is the same either way.
In the bass clef the counting is the same, only the lines have other names. Find the lower note first, then count up.
A common mistake is counting the steps between the notes instead of the notes themselves. C to E has two steps but three letters: it is a third.
A practice tip: say the letter names out loud as you count up, touching each line and space with a finger. After a few days you will see thirds and fifths at a glance.
Where it lives: every chord is built from thirds, and every melody moves by seconds and leaps. Recap: count the letters, both ends included.
Hear it, then sing it: one note, a rhythm on “da”, five notes, then four bars with the band.
Now the note is played first and then stops. Keep it in your ear, sing the same note, and hold it steady for two seconds.
Then a rhythm: two bars on one note. Listen once, and sing it back on “da”, starting on the next bar, with the click.
Five notes follow, moving by step. Listen to the shape: up, down, or up and back. Then sing the same five notes in the same rhythm.
Last, the first four bars of a well-known song, with the band. The pitch and the timing of every note are measured.
Your turn. Breathe low, stay relaxed, and sing at a comfortable volume. If a take misses, it waits for you: try again.
Why the note stops first: matching a note from memory trains the inner ear. The drone in the first steps helped; now the ear holds the note alone.
Singing a rhythm back is a standard part of graded singing exams. One clear syllable, “da”, makes every start easy to hear.
For the five notes, picture the steps as stairs. Most mistakes come from a step that was too big or too small, not from a wrong direction.
A common mistake is rushing to sing before the call has finished. Wait for your bar; the timing counts as much as the notes.
A practice tip: hum the note quietly before you sing it out. Humming lets you check the pitch without effort, and the louder note then starts in the right place.
Where it lives: every choir rehearsal and every lesson starts with hearing and singing back. Recap: listen fully, then sing: note, rhythm, melody, song.
Swing eighths are long-short, the click falls on 2 and 4; a scat call is one swung bar to copy; the blues is twelve bars in three lines: the tune, the tune again, an answer.
Swing eighths are uneven: long, short. Say doo-ba, doo-ba.
Straight first, then swung. The second note comes later and lighter.
In jazz the click falls on 2 and 4, like the drummer’s hi-hat.
A scat call: one short swung bar on “doo”. Listen, then copy it.
The blues is twelve bars long, and it repeats again and again.
Three lines of four bars: the tune, the tune again, an answer.
Your turn: copy the calls, then sing the head with the band.
Swing is not a fixed ratio. Near a triplet, the first eighth takes about two thirds of the beat; at fast tempos the eighths get straighter.
The twelve bars: four on the one chord, two on the four chord, two on the one, then the five, the four, and home for two.
I I I I · IV IV I I · V IV I I
Each line often leaves room: the singer takes two bars, the band answers in the other two.
A common mistake is swinging too hard, a stiff dotted rhythm. Keep it relaxed, like speech.
A practice tip: sing the head on “doo” first, then on “bah”, then with your own syllables. The syllable never counts, only the pitch and the time.
Listen for the form in recordings: count the bars on your fingers, one hand for each line of four. When the band goes back to the top, you should be at twelve.
Where it lives: every jazz singer’s first standards are blues tunes, and every scat solo grows from short calls. Recap: long-short, 2 and 4, twelve bars.
Answer the band, land on chord tones, stay inside the pentatonic, keep the beat.
Improvising means making up your own melody, right now, over the band. Pop improvising starts simple: a few notes, clearly in time.
First, call and response. The band plays two bars, you answer with two of your own. The answer does not copy; it replies.
Over the one, four and five chords, put a chord tone on the first beat of each chord, and end your phrase on one.
The pentatonic scale has five notes that rarely clash with these chords: one, two, three, five and six in major. In minor: one, flat three, four, five, flat seven.
Your turn. The scale’s degrees show while you sing. Stay in time, use only those notes, and finish on a chord tone.
Why chord tones on strong beats: the ear hears beats one and three as arrivals. A chord tone there sounds settled; anything else sounds like it wants to move.
A good answer often borrows one idea from the call: its rhythm, its first note, or its shape, and changes the rest.
Leave space. Rests let the band breathe and make your next phrase clearer. Two short phrases beat one long one.
A common mistake is losing the beat while thinking about notes. Keep the pulse in your body first; the notes can be simple.
A practice tip: start with only three notes of the scale, for example one, two and three. When those feel free, add five and six. Fewer notes make better ideas.
Where it lives: ad-libs at the end of pop choruses, gospel and soul call and response, and graded singing exams. Recap: answer, land, stay in the scale, keep time.
Through the break smoothly, strong but never pushed, short riffs clean before fast, phrases that tell the story.
Most voices have a break, a place where the sound wants to flip from low to high. Mix voice is singing through that place with an even sound.
Sirens on “oo” and a bright “nay” on five notes are common ways to practice it. Keep the sound light and let the pitch glide.
Belting is strong, speech-like singing. Here the phrases stay below your top notes. Never push the volume, and stop at once if it hurts or you feel hoarse.
A riff is a short run of notes on one vowel. Learn it slowly and cleanly first; the tempo rises only when every note is in tune.
Your turn. Then whole songs: make the melody yours but keep its long notes, lift the chorus, and hold the long notes steady to the end.
The app hears pitch, timing and loudness, not which register you use. So it measures a smooth glide through the break, not the name of the sound.
A loud phrase still needs a steady breath. Grow louder towards the peak note, then let the phrase come down softer.
Short riffs often use the pentatonic scale. Sing them at sixty percent first, then eighty, then full speed.
Pop phrasing moves the rhythm a little, ahead or behind the beat, like speech. Theatre phrasing tells the story: clear long notes and a chorus that builds.
A common mistake is getting louder by squeezing the throat. If the sound feels tight, sing softer and lower until it is easy again.
A practice tip: warm up before every style session with a lip trill and a few gentle sirens, and drink some water. Short, regular sessions build the voice more than one long push.
Where it lives: pop, rock and musical-theatre songs, and the style sections of graded exams. Recap: smooth break, never push, clean riffs, tell the story.
Play the head, then shells four to the bar, then the guide tones, then the Charleston, in every key.
Jazz guitar starts on the twelve-bar blues: three dominant seventh chords. First the head, the tune itself, played in the first positions.
A shell is three notes: the root, the third and the seventh. It is all the chord a band needs from the guitar.
Strum four even, short chords a bar, the root on string six or five, whichever keeps your hand closer to the last shell.
The guide tones alone, the third and seventh, make a line that shows the changes. Then the Charleston rhythm: beat one and the “and” of two.
Your turn. Each item starts in free time, then climbs the tempo ladder, and moves through all twelve keys.
Why shells: the bass plays the root and the piano may play too. Three notes stay out of their way and keep the sound clear.
Four to the bar is the oldest jazz guitar job: short, even chords that lock with the drummer’s ride cymbal.
Between C7 and F7 the third of one chord moves a half step to the seventh of the next. That is why guide-tone lines sound smooth.
A common mistake is letting the chords ring. Lift the fretting fingers a little after each strum, so the chords stay short.
A practice tip: learn the shells for one key slowly, saying each chord name aloud as you play it. Then move the same shapes to a new key: they never change, only their place on the neck.
Where it lives: big-band guitar, small-group comping and every jazz jam’s first tune. Recap: head, shells, guide tones, Charleston, every key.
Root, 3rd, 5th on beats 1–3, then a half step into the next chord on beat 4.
A walking bass plays one note on every beat. Roots and fifths came first; now the line walks up the chord itself.
On beats one to three play the root, the third and the fifth of the chord. They tell the band exactly which chord it is.
Beat four leads into the next chord from a half step away, below or above. The ear hears the new root coming.
Over the twelve bars of the blues the plan is the same in every bar. Keep the quarter notes even and the same length.
Your turn. Free time first, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys. Every note is measured against the chord.
Why a half step on beat four: it is the strongest pull in music. Any note a half step from the target sounds like it leads there.
From below or from above: when the note below would be lower than your lowest string, approach from above instead.
Dominant seventh chords have a major third. Over the blues, every chord is a dominant seventh, so the third is always four half steps above the root.
A common mistake is landing the approach late. Beat four is as long as the others; the new root arrives exactly on beat one.
A practice tip: sing the line while you play it, or say the names: root, three, five, step. When your voice knows the plan, your hands stop hesitating at each chord change.
Where it lives: every swing tune and jam session. Recap: root, third, fifth, a half step in, even quarters, every key.
Pitch means how high or low a note sounds. Comparing two notes — higher, lower, the same — is where every musical ear starts.
Hi {name}! Let's start at the very beginning. Every note has a pitch — how high or low it sounds. A bird is high, a big drum is low.
Now two notes. The second one goes up — it is higher. Listen once more and feel your ears "lift".
And this time it goes down — lower. Big jumps are easy; small steps take a little practice. That is what we train.
Two short tunes can be the same or different. Here, one note changed in the second tune. Did you catch it?
Your turn! Higher or lower, then same or different. No words to learn — just listen. Your ears already know more than you think.

Where does pitch come from? Every sound is something shaking — a string, a drum skin, your voice. Fast shaking makes a high note; slow shaking makes a low one. The speed of the shaking is called frequency.
On a piano, low notes are on the left and high notes on the right: every key is a little higher than the one before. Written music works the same way — higher on the page means higher in sound.
The most common mix-up: high and low are not loud and soft. A note can be low and loud, or high and quiet. Here is the very same low note, first soft, then loud — its pitch does not change.
How to compare two notes: hum them softly after you hear them. You will feel your throat work a little harder for the higher one. Many people also move a hand up or down with the sound — try it.
The closer two notes are, the harder they are to tell apart. The smallest step on a piano is from one key to the very next one — called a semitone, or half step. Here is a big jump, then a semitone.
For same or different, you do not need to remember every note. Keep the first tune in your head like a path, and listen for the moment the second one steps off it.
In real music, high and low have jobs. The bass plays low and holds everything up, like a floor. The melody — the tune you hum — usually sits higher, where the ear follows it easily.
Recap: pitch is how high or low a note is. Fast vibration sounds high, slow sounds low, and it has nothing to do with how loud it is.
A melody is a line of notes, one after another. Before any names, hear its shape: up, down, a hill or a valley.
Hey {name}! A melody is just notes one after another — like a line you could draw. This one climbs up, like stairs.
This one goes down the stairs.
And many tunes are a hill — up, then down — or a valley — down, then up. Try drawing it in the air as you listen.
Notice how the shape tells a story: going up builds energy, coming down relaxes. Composers use it on purpose, and you will hear it in almost every song you already love.
Your turn! Which way does each tune go? Draw it with a finger if it helps — musicians do it too.
The shape of a melody has a name: its contour. Picture it as a line drawn across the page, rising and falling like hills. Musicians feel this shape long before they know any note names.
A melody moves in two ways. A step goes to the very next note, smooth like walking. A leap skips over notes, bold like jumping. Here are steps, then leaps.
A tune can also stay put and repeat the same note. In your drawing that is flat ground — the line goes straight across before it moves again.
How to hear the shape: follow the direction note by note — up, down or same — and whisper it to yourself. Then step back and ask: did the tune end higher or lower than it began?
A common trap: a tune that rises overall can still dip a little on the way. Do not let one step down fool you — compare where it starts with where it ends.
Practice: sing a tune you like, slowly, and let your hand draw it in the air — up for higher, down for lower. Your hand becomes a picture of the contour.
In real songs, the melody often climbs toward its highest note at the most exciting moment, then comes back down to finish calmly. Next time you hear a chorus, listen for that peak.
Recap: contour is the shape of a tune — up, down or level, by steps or by leaps. Hear the shape first; the note names come later.
The beat is the steady pulse under the music — what you tap your foot to. Tempo is how fast that beat goes.
Hi {name}! Under almost every song there is a beat — a steady pulse, like a heartbeat. It is what your foot taps to.
A good beat is steady — every click the same distance apart. This one wobbles: some come early, some late. Feel the difference?
How fast the beat goes is called the tempo. Here is a slow one, then a fast one.
Musicians count the beat: one, two, three, four — and the first of each group feels a little stronger. Count along with this one.
Your turn! Is the beat steady or wobbly, faster or slower? Tap along on your knee — it makes it much easier.
The beat is the steady pulse you could clap along to. Its speed, the tempo, is measured in beats per minute — BPM. Sixty BPM is exactly one beat a second, like a clock ticking.
Double it and you get 120 BPM — two beats a second, about the speed of a brisk walk. Much dance music sits close to this tempo.
Beats come in groups called bars, or measures. The first beat of each bar is a little stronger. Most pop songs group beats in fours: ONE two three four.
A waltz groups them in threes: ONE two three, ONE two three. Listen for the strong click and count from it.
To find the beat in any song, tap your foot to whatever feels natural. Then count to four along with it, and listen for where the strongest hit falls — that is ONE.

The most common mistake is rushing. When music gets exciting, people speed up without noticing. Listen: these clicks start steady and slowly get faster. Steady means the same distance between every beat.
Practice: walk and count, one step per beat. Or play along with a metronome — a tool that clicks a perfectly steady beat. Start slow; steady is more important than fast.
In real music, tempo sets the mood. A slow ballad may sit around 70 BPM and feels calm; a fast dance track pushes past 120 and makes you move.
Recap: the beat is the steady pulse, tempo is its speed in BPM, and beats group into bars with a strong ONE.
Matching means singing the very same pitch you hear. Start from a hum, slide gently until it feels "locked in".
Hey {name}! Everyone can sing a little — even if you think you can’t. We start simple: hear a note, and hum it back.
When you match, the two sounds blend into one — it feels calm. When you are off, you hear a little wobble, a "wah-wah". Slide slowly until it disappears.
Your voice has its own comfortable zone. If a note feels too high or too low, sing it an octave up or down — it still counts.
Breathe low and relaxed, open your mouth a little, and start softly. Soft and in tune beats loud and pushed — always.
Your turn! Listen, then hum or sing on "ooo". Gently — no straining. The screen shows you where you are.

Matching pitch means singing the same note you hear. Your voice comes from two small folds in your throat, the vocal folds. Stretched tighter they vibrate faster and the note goes up; looser, it goes down. Your ear steers them for you.

Men’s voices usually sound about an octave lower than women’s and children’s. An octave is the same note at a different height — it sounds alike, just bigger or smaller. Singing a note an octave away still counts as a match.
How to hear whether you match: listen for the wobble. Two nearly equal notes make a slow "wah-wah". The closer they get, the slower it beats — until it disappears.
Practice: hum the note, then slide slowly up and down like a gentle siren, and stop when it locks in with the piano. Sliding finds the note more easily than jumping straight at it.
Start near the pitch of your speaking voice — that is your comfortable zone. If a note feels too high or too low, move it an octave and try again.
The common mistake is pushing. Singing louder or tensing your neck does not make the note more correct — it usually drags it off. Stay soft, keep breathing, and let your ear do the work.
In real music, this is the skill behind singing in tune. Choir singers match each other all the time, so their voices blend into one chord.
Recap: listen first, hum softly, slide until the wobble disappears. Any octave counts, and gentle always beats loud.
A key is the "home" a melody sits in. Transposing keeps every step of the tune and moves the home: same degrees, new note names.
Hi {name}! You can start "Happy Birthday" on any note and it is still the same song. That is transposing — same tune, new starting place.
The trick is degrees: count from home. C D E in C major is 1 2 3. In G major, 1 2 3 is G A B. Same numbers, new names.
Or move by an interval: up a fifth, every note goes up a fifth. C E G becomes G B D.
Why bother? Singers move songs to suit their voice, and horn players read in other keys every day. It is a real musician’s superpower.
Your turn! Pick the same tune in a new key, move it by an interval, say the new names — and finally sing it there.
To transpose is to move a piece to another key while keeping every distance between its notes. The tune keeps its shape and its degrees; only the letter names change.
Why it works: distances are counted in semitones, the smallest steps on the keyboard. Move every note up by the same number — here two semitones, a whole tone — and the tune keeps its exact shape.
Notice the F♯. In D major it is needed to keep the same pattern of steps that C major has. Play F instead and the tune bends out of shape — listen.
Method one — degrees: write the tune as numbers, then read the numbers in the new key. 3 2 1 in C is E D C; in F major it is A G F.
Method two — interval: choose the distance, such as up a fourth or down a tone, and move every note by it. Then check the new key’s sharps or flats.
The common mistake is moving the letters but forgetting the sharps and flats. C D E moved up to start on E becomes E F♯ G♯ — not E F G.
In real life, singers often ask for a song a tone lower to suit their voice. Some instruments read transposed parts: on a B♭ clarinet or trumpet, a written C sounds as B♭.
Recap: transposing keeps the shape and the degrees and changes the names. Count from the new home, and always check the sharps and flats.
Swing is measured: long quarters, a steady place against the ride, and the same tempo in the last chorus as in the first.
Hi {name}! Right notes are half of walking. The other half is time, and time can be measured.
First, long quarters. Each note rings until the next one starts. A short, dry note makes the band sound nervous.
Second, your place against the ride cymbal. On top is a few milliseconds ahead, laid back a few behind. A good bassist chooses, and stays there.
Third, no drift. The third chorus is as fast as the first, even when the drums drop out.
Your turn: walk with the band. I measure the length of every note, where it sits against the ride, and the tempo of every chorus.
Why long notes? The bass is the floor of the band. When the floor has holes, the soloist hears them first.
The ride plays one, two and a skip, three, four and a skip. Lock your quarters to its beats, not to its skips.
Playing on top pushes the band forward; it suits fast tunes. Laid back makes a ballad or a slow blues heavy and warm.
Up-tempo, from 220 to over 300, the hand stays loose and the notes stay long. Practice at the edge of clean, then step back.
The usual mistake is rushing when the drums stop. Count the bars in your head and keep the same length of beat.
Listen to the great walking bassists on records: the notes are simple, but every quarter is full and sits in the same place for chorus after chorus. That is the sound these levels measure.
To keep: long, placed, steady. The notes come from the walking rules; the swing comes from these three.
Chord tones on the downbeats: run down the dominant scale and add a half step where a chord tone would fall off the beat.
Hi {name}! Barry Harris taught one simple goal for lines: the chord tones land on the beats.
Run down the G7 scale from G in eighths and the chord tones fall on the off-beats by the second beat. Something has to give.
The fix is one extra half step, between the root and the flat seven. Now G, F, D and B sit on the beats.
The same idea works in a walk: chord tones on one and three, and passing notes, scale or chromatic, on two and four.
Your turn: play the lines with the band. I check that every downbeat is a chord tone.
Barry built his harmony on the 6th chord and the diminished chord a half step below it. Together they make an eight-note scale.
On the bass the diminished chord is a passing chord: C, C sharp diminished, D minor. It walks you up by half steps.
A pivot breaks a line that runs too low: the next note jumps up an octave and the line keeps falling from there.
Start from the 3rd, the 5th or the 7th and the half steps change place, but the goal stays: chord tones on the beat.
The usual mistake is adding half steps everywhere. Add one only where a chord tone would slip off the beat.
You will hear these lines in bebop solos on every instrument. On the bass they make a solo chorus sound like the horns, and they make a walking line sound inevitable.
To keep: downbeats are chord tones. Everything between them is a passing note that leads to the next one.
Know where you are in the form: two-feel and four-feel by section, stops and hits with the band, tags and endings.
Hi {name}! A tune is a road map: sections, repeats and an ending. The bassist is the one who must never get lost.
A common plan: the A sections in two, half notes on one and three, and the bridge in four, walking quarters.
Stop-time: the band hits only on one. You hit with them, short, and you keep counting through the silence.
A tag repeats the last turnaround, often three times, and the tune ends on one short hit together.
Your turn: the road map shows the sections. I check every bar is in its place and every section starts on time.
Pedal intros hold the dominant in the bass while the chords move above it. The tension breaks when the head comes in.
A Latin A section with a swing bridge changes the feel, not the tempo. The quarter note stays the same length.
Pushes put the next chord on the "and" of four, tied over the bar line. Skips are short notes that kick the two-feel along.
Lost a bar? Listen for the turnaround or the bridge and jump back in on its first beat. Never stop.
The usual mistake is counting bars but not sections. Feel the four-bar phrases; the form is built from them.
On a gig nobody hands you the form twice. Learn the road map of each tune before you play it: how many bars, where the bridge is, how it ends.
To keep: know the map before you play, feel each section change, and land every new section on one.
The Afro-Cuban bass plays the "and" of two and beat four, leaves the one empty, and anticipates the next chord.
Hi {name}! In salsa and son the bass does something strange: it does not play on one.
The tumbao: a note on the "and" of two, and a note on four that rings over the bar line, through the one.
The note on four is already the NEXT chord. The bass tells the band where the harmony is going.
Above it all sits the clave, a two-bar pattern: three hits, then two, or two, then three. Everything lines up with it.
Your turn: play the tumbao with the clave. A note on one counts as an extra note, and a late change counts as missed.
The tumbao, from Cuban music, anticipates: the bass plays on the “and” of two and on four, rarely on one. It pulls the band forward.
Where it lives: salsa, mambo and Afro-Cuban jazz are all built on the clave. Even when nobody plays it, everyone feels it.
Son clave comes from the Cuban son; rumba clave from the rumba, where the later third note gives a more restless feel.
Cha-cha keeps the one, then adds the "cha-cha" on four and its "and". Songo and Mozambique syncopate in sixteenths.
Afro-Cuban six-eight feels each beat in three. The bell pattern is long and asymmetric; count it slowly at first.
In Brazil the bass works differently: the samba and partido alto drive the sixteenths, the baião rocks on a dotted rhythm.
Latin jazz brings the tumbao to standards: the root of every new chord arrives an eighth early, on the "and".
The usual mistake is falling back onto one when it gets busy. Keep the one for the drums and the piano, and trust the silence.
Listen to salsa and Latin jazz records and follow only the bass: you will hear the empty one, the anticipations, and how the whole band leans on them.
To keep: the "and" of two, then four, and four is the next chord. Feel the clave over two bars.
Every odd meter is twos and threes: count the groups, accent their first note, and the bar stops feeling odd.
Hi {name}! Seven-eight sounds hard, but nobody counts to seven. Players count groups of two and three.
Two plus two plus three: one-two, one-two, one-two-three. The first note of each group gets the accent, so the listener hears the groups, not a long row of eighths.
Turn the groups around and the same seven feels new: three plus two plus two, or two plus three plus two.
Longer meters are just more groups: eleven is three, three, three, two; thirteen adds another two.
Your turn: play the riffs with the drums. I time every eighth on the bar, and I listen for the accents on the group starts.
Five-four is three plus two or two plus three quarters. Many prog riffs use it as a long, lopsided groove.
Odd groupings can sit inside four-four too: three, three, two eighths fill a bar and make it lean forward.
Mixed meters change from bar to bar, a seven-eight then a four-four. Read the meter before each bar like a chord.
Displacement moves a riff an eighth or a sixteenth later. The notes stay the same; the beat under them moves.
The usual mistake is rushing the last group of three. Give it its full length before the next one, or the bar shrinks to six.
Odd meters are everywhere in progressive rock, in Balkan and Middle-Eastern music and in modern jazz. The same twos and threes run through all of them, so the skill carries over.
To keep: count the groups, not the eighths, and accent each group start. Then speed up.
In a unison every note starts with the guitar or the keys: tight means within about a hundredth of a second, every time.
Hi {name}! Prog and fusion bands love unisons: bass and guitar playing the same riff together, as one instrument.
The guitar usually plays it an octave higher. Sometimes a fifth higher, so the bass sounds a fifth below and the riff gets a heavy, open sound.
Tight means your notes start with theirs, within about twelve milliseconds on average, and the spread stays small.
Fast runs, chromatic, whole-tone or diminished, test it most: every sixteenth lined up with the keys.
Your turn: play the riff with the band in your headphones. I measure how far each note is from theirs.
