A pedal riff keeps the low root between moving notes; the pick plays down and up so every note has the same attack.
A sequenced riff keeps its shape and moves it to each chord root. An ostinato keeps its notes while the chords change above it.
Odd-meter unisons combine both skills: the group accents and the lock to the band.
The usual mistake is listening to yourself. Listen to the guitar and put your note inside its note, so the two attacks become one.
Headphones matter here: the band plays only in them, so the microphone hears just your bass and can time it against the guitar.
Fusion and progressive bands rehearse their unison passages slowly for weeks. Do the same here: the tempo ladder raises the speed only after three clean takes.
To keep: one riff, two instruments, one attack. Slow it down until it is tight, then raise the tempo.
A riff can cycle against the band’s bar and meet it again later; a metric modulation turns one note value into the new beat.
Hi {name}! In polymeter the drums stay in four while your riff has its own length, five or seven eighths.
A five-eighth riff over four-four drifts against the bar line and meets the drums again after five bars.
Three against two: dotted quarters over the beat. Four against three: four notes in every bar of three. In both, the band's beat stays where it was.
Metric modulation: play triplet quarters, then make that triplet the new beat. One hundred twenty becomes one hundred eighty.
Your turn: I measure the new tempo against the written ratio, within two percent, and your first note in it.
Count the riff in its own groups and let the drums go round you. Do not try to count both at once, at first.
The dotted-eighth modulation is smaller: the dotted eighth becomes the new quarter, one hundred twenty to one hundred sixty.
Before the change, feel the new note value inside the old beat for a whole bar. Then simply keep it.
A seven-eight riff against four-four drums is the classic prog sound: the riff and the backbeat meet every eight bars.
The usual mistake is slowing back to the old tempo after a few bars. The new beat must stay new until the next change.
Progressive rock and modern jazz drummers use these devices all the time. When the bass keeps its own cycle steady, the band sounds deliberate rather than lost.
To keep: in polymeter count your own groups; in a modulation, the pivot note becomes the beat.
Five tiers of tunes, from blues forms to Coltrane changes: walk a whole chorus from the chart, at the tier’s tempo, without losing the form.
Hi {name}! A working jazz bassist knows tunes, not exercises. This ladder sorts the tunes into five tiers.
Tier one is the blues and modal tunes: few chords, long forms, time first.
Tier two is rhythm changes and the ii–V tunes. Tier three is minor tunes, bossas and ballads, where the feel changes.
Tier four is bebop up-tempo, two hundred and more. Tier five is Coltrane changes: in Giant Steps the key moves every two beats to a bar, then every two bars.
Your turn: only the chart is shown. Walk one chorus; I check the chord tones on every change, and on long forms that the second half keeps the tempo of the first.
Why tiers? A tune is hard for a reason: speed, harmony that moves, or a feel that is not swing. Each tier adds one of those.
In tier three the ballads are in two: a root on one, a fifth or a passing note on three, and the notes ring their full length.
In a bossa, the bass plays the root and the fifth with a push before beat three. The chord tones still land on the changes.
Up-tempo, think in half-bars: aim for the chord tone of the next change and let the passing notes take care of themselves.
Coltrane changes move by major thirds. Learn the three key centres as shapes on the neck before you add speed.
The usual mistake is losing the form in the bridge. Sing the melody in your head while you walk; it tells you where you are.
To keep: tier by tier, a whole chorus, from the chart. When every tier is done, the set list badge is yours.
Harmonics, tapping, double-stops and the fretless: each is measured by what it sounds like — the pitch, the chord, the timing, the cents.
Hi {name}! Fusion bassists made the bass sing above the band. These levels teach the sounds they used.
Natural harmonics: touch the string lightly over the twelfth, seventh, fifth, fourth or third fret, and pluck. Each one is a higher partial of the open string.
Tapping: the fretting hand sounds the root, the other hand taps the fifth, the octave and the tenth. Every note must be even in time.
Double-stops: a tenth or a root with its seventh, two strings at once. Both notes must ring, and the microphone hears whether they do.
Your turn. I measure the pitch of every harmonic, the evenness of the tapping, both notes of each double-stop, and on a fretless the cents.
The harmonic over the third fret is two octaves and a fifth above the open string. Touch a little above the fret, not on it.
Artificial harmonics: fret a note, then touch the same string twelve frets higher with the plucking hand. It sounds an octave above the fretted note.
Shells on the bass are the root and the seventh: the same shape for every chord, a fret apart between major seventh and dominant.
Comping on the bass uses the Charleston rhythm: one, and the "and" of two. Keep it short and let the drums fill the rest.
On a fretless, slide into the target from below and stop exactly on it. Vibrato comes after the pitch is right, never instead of it.
The usual mistake is pressing too hard on a harmonic, which kills it. Touch, pluck near the bridge, and lift.
To keep: every technique here is judged by its sound. If it sounds right, in time and in tune, it counts.
A chord tone on the beat, reached from a half step below or above, from two half steps away, or from the 5th above it (the dominant approach).
Hi {name}! A bebop line puts a chord tone on the beat. The note just before it can come from outside the chord.
From a half step below, or a half step above. Over C major 7, D sharp or F into E.
Two half steps make a longer lead-in: D, D sharp, E, or F sharp, F, E.
The dominant approach comes from the 5th above the target, like V going to I. B into E.
Your turn: every chord tone in turn on a held chord, then the 3rds and 7ths through ii–V–I. It starts in free time.
Why it works: the outside note is gone before the beat, and the chord tone lands where the ear checks the harmony.
Through ii–V–I, aim at the 3rd of each chord on beat 1: F, B, E in C. The approach note sits on the last 8th of the bar before.
A common mistake: the outside note lands on the beat and the chord tone after it. Then the wrong note is the one the ear hears.
Bass players walk with the same moves: a half step or the 5th before each new root. On a horn, guitar or piano they shape every bebop line.
How to practice: one approach type at a time, slowly, into every chord tone. Say the target before you play it, then let the lead-in find it.
To keep: target on the beat, approach just before it, from below, above, two half steps away or the 5th.
Surround the target from both sides before it lands: half step above and below, scale step above and half step below, the 4-note bebop enclosure, the delayed resolution.
Hi {name}! An enclosure surrounds the target. Into E: F above, D sharp below, then E on the beat.
The order can turn: below first, then above. D sharp, F, E.
The scale step above, then a half step below. Into G: A, F sharp, G. The upper note comes from the scale, the lower one from outside it.
The 4-note bebop enclosure: a whole step above, a half step above, a half step below, the target. F sharp, F, D sharp, E.
The delayed resolution circles once more: F, D sharp, D, D sharp, then E. Your turn, in free time first.
Where the notes fall: the target on the beat, the enclosure in the 8ths before it. Two notes take one beat, four take two.
Enclose every chord tone of ii–V–I: the roots, then the 3rds, the 5ths, the 7ths. Each one becomes a place you can land.
When the scale step above is only a half step, as F above E, the two enclosures sound the same. That is fine: the rule still holds.
A common mistake is to rush the enclosure and land early. Keep the 8ths even and let the target arrive exactly on the beat.
You hear enclosures all through the bebop era, on horns, piano and guitar, usually into the 3rd or the root of the next chord.
To keep: above and below, then the target on the beat. Learn one type at a time, in all twelve keys, first on a held chord and then through ii–V–I.
Swing with the click on 2 and 4, then the click on the "and", then a click that drops out for a bar. You keep the time, the click only checks it.
Hi {name}! In swing the drummer’s hi-hat closes on 2 and 4. Hear the click there and feel 1 and 3 yourself.
Swung 8ths: the first of each pair longer, the second shorter and lighter. Start with a scale and an arpeggio.
Later the click moves to the "and" of each beat. It feels off at first: count out loud and place the beat between the clicks.
Then the gap: three bars with the click, one bar silent. Keep playing through the silence and meet the click on the next 1.
Your turn: lines and comping with each click. The count-in and the moving cue on the staff stay with you.
Why: a band has no click. The bass and the drums give 2 and 4, and everyone else keeps the rest of the bar inside.
Comping in the Charleston rhythm: a chord on 1, another on the "and" of 2. With the click on 2 and 4, the second chord sits just before it.
Four to the bar is the oldest swing comp on the guitar: one short chord on every beat, all the same length, the 2 and 4 a little heavier.
A common mistake is to follow the click and drift with it. You lead; the click only confirms. Record a take and listen to the bar without the click: did the line slow down?
To keep: 2 and 4 first, then the "and", then the gap. Slow tempos are the hardest, because the space between clicks is longest. Stay there until it feels easy, then climb the tempo ladder.
Over V7 play the minor 6th a 5th above (Dm6 over G7); 3–5–7–♭9 on the V, the ♭9 falling to the 5th of I; a triplet down the scale keeps chord tones on the beats.
Over V7 play the minor 6th a 5th above (Dm6 over G7); a triplet down the scale keeps chord tones on the beats.
Hi {name}! Make it minor: over G7 think D minor. D minor 6 is D, F, A, B: the 5th, flat 7, 9 and 3 of G.
The same four notes from B are B minor 7 flat 5. Minor 6 and minor 7 flat 5 are one chord.
3 to flat 9: on G7 play B, D, F, A flat. The A flat falls to G, the 5th of C.
Now as a line: over G7, the D minor 6 arpeggio down, B, A, F, D, then land on E, the 3rd of C.
The triplet rule: going down the scale, a triplet from the root reaches the next chord tone on the beat. G, F, E, then D.
Your turn: each idea through ii–V–I in all twelve keys, in free time first.
Why minor works: the ii and the V share their notes, so the ii–V is one minor sound. You think less and hear the line.
Try it in the drill: the D minor scale over D minor 7, then the D minor 6 arpeggio over G7, landing on E, the 3rd of C.
The 3 to flat 9 cell is a diminished 7th chord built on the 3rd. Its four notes all lead somewhere in the I chord.
The same move works over every dominant: G7 takes D minor 6, C7 takes G minor 6, F7 takes C minor 6. Always the minor 6 a 5th above the root.
From the 3rd a triplet works too: B, A, G, then F. A triplet from the 5th or 7th would put a tension on the beat, so the rule avoids it.
A common mistake is to rush the triplet. Three even notes in the beat, then the chord tone on time.
To keep: over V think the minor a 5th above; 3–5–7–♭9 resolves to the 5th; triplets from the root and the 3rd.
Chord tones on the beats, scale or chromatic notes between, an approach into every change: over minor ii–V, altered dominants, the blues, rhythm changes and turnarounds.
Hi {name}! Every line here follows one rule: a chord tone on each beat, a passing note between.
Digital patterns come first: 1-2-3-5 and 1-3-5-7 on each chord, two chords a bar.

Then the forms: minor ii–V–i and the altered dominant, the jazz blues, rhythm changes with its bridge, and turnarounds. Over the altered dominant the targets are the 3rd, the flat 7 and the altered tensions.
Each line is new in every key, built from the rules, so there is nothing to memorise: read it, hear the chord under it, and let the beats land on chord tones.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder.
Turnarounds are where lines are made: I–vi–ii–V, I–VI7–II7–V7, and the tritone turnaround I–flat III7–flat VI7–flat II7.
The bridge of rhythm changes is four dominants, two bars each, down by 5ths. Aim at the 3rd of each one.
Digital patterns train the hand to find chord tones fast: 1-2-3-5 up from each root, then 7-5-3-1 down, two chords a bar, near the last note.
A common mistake is to run the scale from the root on every chord. Start each bar near where the last one ended, and let the line turn at the edges of your range.
On the bass, keep the line in one position as long as you can and shift on a chord tone, so the shift never lands on a passing note. On the guitar, the same: shift on the beat.
To keep: chord tones on the beats, approach the change, stay near the last note. Then take one form through all twelve keys.
A cadence chart is a short progression that lands on a key, written in Roman numerals: learn it once, play it in all 12 keys and in every voicing.
A cadence chart is a short progression that lands on a key: the ii–V–I, the turnaround, the backdoor, the tritone sub. Each is written in Roman numerals, so it fits every key.
In C the major ii–V–I is Dm7, G7, Cmaj7. Here it is in shells: root, 3rd and 7th.
In minor the ii is half-diminished, the V takes a flat 9 and the tonic is a minor 6th chord.
The backdoor reaches C from B flat 7, after F minor 7: a softer pull than G7.
Each level keeps the charts and changes the voicing: shells, guide tones, rootless, drop 2 and drop 3, four-way close, two hands, stride and a walking bass.
How your playing is measured: every chord as the level writes it, on time. On the bass, chord tones on the changes and approach notes into them.
To keep: think in numerals, not chord names. Then every key is the same job, and the ear hears where the chart lands.
A Roman numeral names a chord by its distance from the tonic. ii is the minor chord on the second degree, V7 the dominant on the fifth. Upper case means a major third, lower case a minor third.
The tritone substitution swaps V7 for the dominant a tritone away. G7 and D flat 7 share their 3rd and 7th, B and F, so D flat 7 resolves to C just as well, and the bass falls a half step.
A turnaround leads back to the top of a tune: I, vi, ii, V. With VI7 in place of vi the pull into ii grows stronger, because VI7 is the dominant of ii.
Some charts borrow from the parallel minor key: flat VI and flat VII. In a major key they colour the way home; in a minor key the same chords are part of the key.
Rootless voicings leave the root to the bass and add the 9th: Dm7 as F, A, C, E; G7 as F, A, B, E; Cmaj7 as E, G, B, D.
On the bass, a walking line plays each chord’s root on its first beat and leads into the next chord with a chord tone or a half step.
Practice one chart through all 12 keys, round the cycle of fourths, slowly at first. Say the numerals aloud as you play, then the chord names.
Find the lowest note first: that is the bass. Then read the distances: a big third on the bottom is major, a small one is minor. A different note in the bass makes a slash chord, like C/E.
Hi {name}! Here is C major: C, E and G, stacked in thirds. Look at the bottom note first. Here it is the root, and it gives the chord its name.
Now count up to the middle note. Four half steps is a major third: major. Three half steps is a minor third: minor. Listen to C, then C minor.
Two minor thirds make a diminished chord; two major thirds make an augmented one. Add one more third on top and it becomes a seventh chord, like G7.
If the bottom note is not the root, write it after a slash. These are the same three notes with E in the bass, so we call it C over E.
On the guitar it works the same way: find the lowest string that plays, name it, then read the shape. Your turn! Look, find the bass, and name it fast.

A triad is three notes stacked in thirds: root, third and fifth. Two thirds give four qualities: major is a major third then a minor third, minor the reverse, diminished two minor thirds, augmented two major thirds. Hear C, Cm, Cdim and Caug.

Inversions reorder the same notes. Root position has the root in the bass; first inversion puts the third in the bass, C/E; second inversion puts the fifth there, C/G. The name stays C; only the bass changes.
On the staff, a root-position triad sits on three lines or three spaces in a row. An inversion shows a gap of a fourth; the upper note of that fourth is the root.
Add a third above the fifth for a seventh chord. Cmaj7 is C E G B; C7, the dominant seventh, is C E G B flat; Cm7 is C E flat G B flat; Cm7♭5, half-diminished, is C E flat G flat B flat.
A slash chord names the chord, then the bass: G7/B is G7 with its third in the bass. The bass can also be a note outside the chord, as in C/D.
On guitar, find the lowest string that sounds; x marks a muted string. The open C chord, x32010, has C in the bass. The shape x20003 puts B in the bass under G, D and G: that is G/B.

Common mistakes: naming an inversion after its bass note, and mixing up minor and diminished. Check the fifth: perfect means minor, diminished means diminished. Spell in thirds, too: augmented C is C E G sharp, not A flat.
In real music, inversions make smooth bass lines, like C, G/B, Am stepping down. To keep: bass first, then rebuild in thirds to find the root, then read the third and the fifth.
A song is sections: keep each one’s groove, fill in the bar before the next, and land crash + kick on its 1.
Hi {name}! A song is made of sections — verse, chorus, bridge — and the drummer marks every change. Listen: a verse on the hi-hat, a fill, and the chorus on the ride.
Three jobs at every section change: the fill in the bar before, the landing — crash and kick together on the 1 — and the new groove right after.
A bridge often changes the feel. Half-time keeps the tempo but puts the snare on beat three only, so the music seems to slow down.
Count the bars. Sections are usually 4, 8, 12 or 16 bars long; the road map above the score shows where you are and cues the next section one bar ahead.
The band plays the chords from the chart, so you hear the form as you play. The app checks each section’s groove, the landings, that no bar was lost, and that the tempo holds into the chorus.
The most common slip is rushing into the chorus: the fill gets exciting and the new section comes early. Keep the fill inside the beat — the 1 comes when it comes.
Dynamics shape a song as much as grooves do: a softer verse, a louder chorus, a breakdown where almost everything drops out. Play the difference, not just the notes.
Band hits are written figures the whole band plays together. Catch them with crash and kick, and set them up with a short snare figure just before.
The ending is a section too: a short fill and one crash with the kick on the last 1, then let it ring while the band holds the chord.
In real music, session drummers often get only a chord chart with the form and a few hits written in. The rest — the grooves, the fills, the dynamics — is theirs to choose.

Your own songs work the same way: type the chords of each section and the tempo, and the band plays the form for you to drum. Chord progressions are free to use; recordings are not, so the app never needs one.
Count odd meters in groups of 2 and 3; in polymeter the cycles drift and meet again, in polyrhythm two limbs split the same beat; metric modulation turns one note value into the new beat.
Hi {name}! Odd meters are counted in groups of two and three eighths. Here is 7/8 as 2 + 2 + 3: the kick and snare sit on each group’s start.
Polymeter: a riff of seven eighths loops over cymbals in four. The riff starts in a new place every bar until both meet again.
Polyrhythm splits the same beat two ways at once. Three on the ride against two on the kick — both meet on every beat.
Metric modulation: a note value of the old tempo becomes the new beat. Here the triplet eighth becomes the new eighth, so the tempo moves up by half, smoothly.
Five-four is often three plus two quarter notes: a long half and a short half. Feel the bar as two uneven steps.
Linear drumming plays one limb at a time — never two together. The groove comes from the order of the limbs: right hand, left hand, kick.
Groupings over 4/4: accent every third sixteenth on the hi-hat and the accents slide across the beat — the bar stays in four, the ear hears threes.
A displaced groove keeps its shape but moves it — the backbeat a sixteenth or an eighth late. Count the original grid hard; the displacement only works against it.

In real music, odd meters and modulations are the language of progressive rock and fusion, and of much Balkan and Middle-Eastern music long before them. Groupings and displacement make a simple bar sound new.
Practice any of these slowly with the click on the group starts only. When the groups feel natural, raise the tempo a few beats at a time; the app moves the target up as your takes come out clean.
The common mistake in odd meters is to rush the long group. Feel the three as one longer step, not a hurry to the next bar.
Simple meters split the beat in two, compound in three. 6/8 and 3/4 have the same six eighths — the accents tell them apart.
Hi {name}! Six eighths can be two beats of three — that is 6/8 — or three beats of two — that is 3/4. Listen to the accents.
Odd meters group eighths in twos and threes. 7/8 can be 2 + 2 + 3 or 3 + 2 + 2: the signature over the bar says which, and your accents show it.
When the time signature changes, the bar line moves: count the new bar from its own 1. Here two bars of four, then a bar of three — the kick marks each 1.
In rests, keep counting the bars — enter exactly on the 1 they lead to. Here a figure, two silent bars, and the figure again.
In the exercises you play the counts on the kit or a pad: the accents must fall where the signature says. The app measures which strokes were louder, and when.
Say the counts out loud while you play: "1 2 3 4 5 6" with the accented numbers louder. Saying them keeps the grouping in your body, not just on the page.
Twelve eight is four beats of three — the slow blues and many ballads live there. It sounds like 4/4 with triplets everywhere.
Hear it in twelve eight: four big beats, each split in three.
A good drill: play the same six eighths for two bars as 6/8, then two bars as 3/4, without stopping. Only the accents move; the eighths stay exactly even.
In real music, 6/8 drives Irish jigs and much African and Afro-Cuban music; 3/4 is the waltz; 7/8 and 9/8 run through Balkan, Greek and Turkish dances, and through progressive rock.
The common mistake is to let the click decide the grouping. The click marks group starts; your hands must still feel which group is long.
The line or space tells the drum, the notehead tells drum (round) or cymbal (x), the marks tell how to hit it.
Hi {name}! On the drum staff each line or space is a drum: the kick in the lowest space, the floor tom above it, the snare in the middle, the toms higher, the cymbals on top with x noteheads.
A small circle over the hi-hat means open; an accent mark means louder; a note in brackets is a ghost note, very soft; a tiny note just before is a flam or a drag.
Slashes through a stem shorten the strokes: one slash plays eighths, two play sixteenths. A slash with two dots repeats the bar before; a thick bar with a number is that many bars of rest.
Read ahead: while one bar plays, your eyes are already on the next. Find the bar line, the time signature and any repeat sign before the count-in ends.
In the exercises you read the staff and play it on the kit: every note on its own drum, every mark as written. The app hears which drum you hit, when, and how hard.
Stems up are the hands, stems down the feet. Reading one direction at a time — hands first, then feet — makes a busy bar simple.
Tuplets carry their number in a bracket: 3 for triplets, 5 for quintuplets, 6 for sextuplets — that many notes evenly in the space of the beat.
Open and closed hi-hat: an x alone is closed and short; with a small circle above it the hat is open and rings until the next closed note or the foot.
Rolls are written as tremolo slashes too: three slashes on a long note ask for a closed, buzzed roll, as smooth as you can make it, from the start of the note to its end.
The common mistake is to read the floor tom as the kick: both are low round heads. The kick is in the lowest space, the floor tom one step higher.
To keep: position tells the drum, the notehead tells drum or cymbal, stems tell hands or feet, the marks tell how. Read one voice at a time, then stack them.
Know the shape before you play: 12-bar blues, AABA, verse–chorus; follow repeats, endings and D.S. al Coda without losing a bar.
Hi {name}! Forms have standard shapes. The blues is 12 bars; a jazz standard is often AABA, four sections of 8 bars. Mark each new section with a crash on its 1.
Charts save space with signs. Repeat bars send you back; a first ending is played the first time only, the second ending the second time.
D.S. al Coda means: go back to the sign, play until "To Coda", then jump to the coda. In these steps the road map shows only the signs — you follow them yourself.
The blues: twelve bars, the chord changing in bars 5, 7, 9, 10 and 11. A small fill in bar 12 sends the band back to the top.
In the exercises the chart shows the sections and their lengths. You keep time, count the bars, and land a crash with the kick on every section start.
Count in groups of four: "one-two-three-four, two-two-three-four…" — the second number tells you the bar. Most sections end on a multiple of four.
In a blues, the turnaround is the last two bars, leading back to the top. A small fill there tells the band the next chorus is coming.
In AABA the bridge, B, is the contrast: new chords, often a new key. Drummers mark it — a setup fill into it, a busier ride, then back to the A feel for the last A.
Songs in a verse and chorus form mark their sections with the band: fuller in the chorus, thinner in the verse. A crash on the 1 tells everyone the new section has begun.
The common mistake is to lose a bar in a long section and come in a bar early or late. If unsure, listen for the chord change that starts each section.
Quarter one beat, eighth half, sixteenth a quarter of a beat, half two; a dot adds half; rests are counted too.
A quarter note lasts one beat. Four of them fill a bar.
Eighth notes split the beat in two: one and two and.
Sixteenths split it in four: one e and a.
A half note lasts two beats: one stroke, then keep counting.
A dot adds half the value. A dotted quarter is one and a half beats.
A rest is silence of the same length. Count straight through it.
An eighth rest takes half a beat. Here every stroke lands on the "and": count the number silently, play the "and".
Flags and beams mean the same. An eighth alone has a flag; eighths or sixteenths inside one beat are joined by a beam, so you see where every beat starts.
On the drums a long note does not ring longer: the snare dies away at once. The written length is the space before the next stroke, so a half note means: wait.
The common mistake is rushing through rests and long notes: the next stroke comes early because nothing filled the gap. Count every beat out loud, played or not.
A reading tip: keep a quiet pulse with your left foot on the hi-hat while you read. The foot keeps the beats; the hands read the lengths.
Recap: a quarter is one beat, an eighth half, a sixteenth a quarter of a beat, a half two. A dot adds half, and rests count like notes.
Same height, same speed, same spot: same sound. One hand at a time; low sticks play p, middle mf, high f.
Even strokes sound alike: same height, same speed, same spot on the head.
One hand at a time first. The weaker hand needs the most work.
Height sets loudness. Low sticks play soft, p. High sticks play loud, f.
The middle height gives mf. Hold each level for a whole bar.
Your turn: even quarters, then eighths, then three heights on cue.
The app measures each stroke twice: when it lands against the click, and how hard it is. Even means both match the stroke before.
Throw the stick down and let it rebound to where it started. A stroke that ends at the height it began needs no extra effort for the next one.
The common mistake: the hand gets louder as it speeds up, or softer as it tires. Keep the height fixed and let the tempo change only the speed.
Watch your hands in a mirror or film them: two sticks at the same height look like a matched pair.
Dynamics are written under the staff: p for piano, soft; mf for mezzo-forte, medium; f for forte, loud.
A practice tip: one minute of quarters on each hand every day, with the click at a slow tempo. The weaker hand shows itself in softer, later strokes.
Recap: same height for the same sound, one hand at a time, low for soft and high for loud, and every level held steady.
Three heights: a full stroke for the accent (>), a low tap, a ghost note softer still (in brackets). The backbeat is loud on 2 and 4.
Three stick heights make three sounds: full, tap and ghost.
An accent is a full stroke from high up. It is written with >.
Taps are low, soft strokes between accents. Same hand, lower height.
A ghost note is softer still, almost silent. It is written in brackets.
The backbeat: accents on 2 and 4, ghosts in between. That is funk.
Your turn: accents and taps, then ghosts against the backbeat.
The down-stroke: an accent that starts high and stops low, ready for the taps after it. The up-stroke: a tap that lifts the stick for the next accent.
Keep the ghosts truly quiet. If they are as loud as the backbeat, the groove loses its shape. On an e-kit the app reads how hard each stroke is.
The common mistake: the taps creep louder after each accent. Keep the gap between the heights wide.
A moving accent puts the loud note on another sixteenth of the beat. The hands keep going; only the height changes.
In real music, ghost notes give funk, soul and R&B grooves their sixteenth-note motion: felt more than heard.
Practice the two heights slowly: one accent, three taps, over and over. Speed comes later; first make the difference between loud and soft clear and steady.
Recap: high and full for the accent, low for the tap, lower still for the ghost, and a loud backbeat on 2 and 4.
A grace note is a soft stroke just before the main one: one makes a flam, two (a quick double) make a drag. Grace stick low, main stick high.
A grace note is a small, soft stroke just before the main one.
A flam has one grace note, almost together with the main stroke.
Low hand, high hand: the grace stick starts low, the main stick high.
Swap hands every time: lR, then rL. The small letter is the grace.
A drag has two grace notes: a quick double bounce before the stroke.
On paper, grace notes are small notes just before the main note.
Your turn: flams hand to hand, then drags. Keep the grace soft.
Too open, and a flam sounds like two strokes; too closed, and both sticks land at once, a flat. Aim for one thick sound.
The flam accent: three notes a beat, the flam on the first. The sticking alternates, so each beat starts its flam on the other hand.
The flam tap: a flam, then a tap with the same hand, then the other side. A flammed double stroke.
The single drag tap: a drag, then one tap with the other hand.
The common mistake: the grace note gets loud. It should sit about as low as a ghost note, so the main stroke stays on top.
A practice tip: play flams slowly with the click on every beat, and listen to the space between the two sticks. It should stay the same on both hands, right flam and left flam.
Recap: one grace for a flam, two for a drag, grace low and soft, main high, hands swapping each time.
Three even strokes a beat (tri-o-la); leave out the middle one and you have the shuffle: long, short, snare on 2 and 4. Slow blues counts it in 12/8.
A triplet puts three even strokes in one beat: tri-o-la.
On the kit: triplets on the hi-hat, snare on 2 and 4.
Now leave out the middle triplet. Long, short: the shuffle.
The short note is the last triplet. It leads into the next beat.
Slow blues counts it in 12/8: four big beats of three.
Your turn: triplets, then the shuffle, then the slow blues.
The shuffle and swing eighths share the same long-short: the beat split in three, the first two thirds joined into one long note.
The common mistake: the short note slides toward a straight eighth, or a stiff dotted rhythm. Keep it on the last triplet. First the straight version, then the shuffle.
Count the triplets out loud before you drop one: tri-o-la, tri-o-la. Then whisper the middle syllable and play only the outer two.
The double shuffle puts the shuffle in both hands: the right on the hi-hat, the left on the snare, with accents on 2 and 4.
Where it lives: blues, early rock and roll, and many rock shuffles. A slow blues often sits at fifty to sixty beats a minute.
A practice tip: keep the click on every beat at first, then on 2 and 4 only. When the shuffle stays steady with fewer clicks, the feel is your own.
Recap: three even notes a beat, drop the middle one, keep the short note on the last triplet, snare on 2 and 4.
Ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a on the ride (the skip note on the last triplet of 2 and 4), the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4, a soft kick under every beat.
In jazz the time lives on the ride cymbal, not the hi-hat.
The ride pattern: ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a.
The skip note, the "a", is the last triplet of beats 2 and 4.
The left foot closes the hi-hat on 2 and 4: a crisp chick.
Feathering: the kick on every beat, so soft you feel it more than hear it.
Your turn: the ride first, then the foot, then the feathered kick.
The skip note is swung: at slow tempos it sits near the last triplet; at fast tempos it moves closer to a straight eighth.
Play the quarter notes a little stronger than the skip notes. The quarters carry the band; the skip is a light bounce.
Keep the hi-hat chick short and closed, never splashing. Together with the ride it marks 2 and 4, where the swing leans.
Feathering is a choice. Many drummers feather lightly or not at all, especially with a bass player who carries the low end.
The common mistake: the ride gets loud and the skip notes get lazy. Keep the ride light and the time steady; the whole band listens to it.
Practice the ride with the band in the app: lock the quarter notes to the walking bass, and let the skip notes float lightly between them.
Recap: ding, ding-a on the ride, a chick on 2 and 4, a soft kick under the quarters, and the ride always light.
Bossa: soft eighths, the bossa clave on the cross-stick, the kick on 1 and 3 with the "and" before. Samba: in two, the kick on each beat and the sixteenth before it, the hi-hat foot on the "and"s.
Bossa nova is soft and steady: eighths on the hi-hat.
The left hand plays the bossa clave as a cross-stick.
The kick: one, the "and" of two, three, the "and" of four.
Samba is faster and felt in two. The feet carry it.
Kick on each beat and the sixteenth before it; hi-hat foot on the "and"s.
Your turn: bossa first, then the samba feet, then the hands on top.
Bossa nova grew in Rio de Janeiro in the late 1950s out of samba: slower, quieter, close to the voice and the guitar.
The clave has two sides: a bar of three notes and a bar of two. 3-2 starts with the three side; 2-3 swaps the bars. Here is 3-2, then 2-3.
Keep it quiet. Bossa is played at a low volume; the cross-stick and the hi-hat should never cover the singer.
The samba kick plays the part of the surdo, the big Brazilian bass drum, which leans on the second beat of each bar of two.
The common mistake in samba: the sixteenth before each beat drifts late and the feet start to gallop. Keep it a true sixteenth, close to the beat.
Recap: bossa is soft eighths, the cross-stick clave and the kick on 1 and 3 with pickups; samba is the kick and the sixteenth before each beat, with the foot on the "and"s.
The clave is a two-bar key: the three side (1, "and" of 2, 4) and the two side (2, 3). 3-2 or 2-3 by the song; rumba moves the third note half a beat later.
The clave is a two-bar key the whole band locks to.
Son clave 3-2: three notes in the first bar, two in the second.
The three side: one, the "and" of two, four.
The two side: two and three.
Clave 2-3 starts on the two side: the same notes, bars swapped.
Rumba clave moves the third note half a beat later.
Your turn: the clave on the cross-stick, under ride quarters.
The three side is the tresillo: three plus three plus two eighths. Long, long, short. Feel it against all eight eighths of the bar.
The arrangement sets the direction, 3-2 or 2-3, and every part fits it. A drummer who flips it by mistake is heard at once.
The common mistake: evening out the three side. The second note sits on the "and" of two, not on beat two or three.
A practice tip: say the clave out loud while you play quarters on the ride, then swap: play the clave and say the quarters. Both ways train the same lock.
Recap: three side 1, "and" of 2, 4; two side 2 and 3; the song picks 3-2 or 2-3; rumba delays the third note.
Dum low, tak high, ka a soft tak from the other hand. Maqsum D T . T D . T ., baladi D D . T D . T ., malfuf 3 + 3 + 2; on the kit the dum is the kick, the tak the snare.
Middle-Eastern rhythms speak in strokes: dum is low, tak is high.
Maqsum: dum tak, tak dum, tak.
On the kit, the dum goes to the kick, the tak to the snare.
Baladi doubles the first dum: dum dum, tak dum, tak.
Malfuf is quick, grouped three, three, two: dum, tak, tak.
Ka is a soft tak from the other hand, filling the gaps.
Your turn: dum and tak on kick and snare; the ka comes later.
On the darbuka, the dum is the strong hand near the centre of the head, the tak the strong hand on the rim, and the ka the other hand on the rim.
Learn a rhythm by speaking it: say "dum tak, tak dum, tak" over a steady pulse, then play exactly what you said.
Maqsum and baladi differ in one stroke: the second stroke is a tak in maqsum and a dum in baladi. Maqsum, then baladi.
Some levels move the dum to the floor tom for a deeper, hand-drum sound. The rhythm stays the same; only the drum changes.
The common mistake: rushing the empty slots. The gaps belong to the rhythm; count all eight eighths, played or not.
The first levels leave the hi-hat out, so only the dum and the tak sound. A later level adds the hi-hat in sixteenths over the same rhythm.
Where it lives: maqsum and baladi sit under a large share of Egyptian and Arabic popular music. Recap: dum low, tak high, ka soft, and every slot counted.
A fill is a short break from the groove; start with one beat (4 e & a on the snare) and land crash and kick together on the next 1, in time.
A fill is a short break from the groove that leads into the next bar.
Start small: one beat. The groove plays beats 1, 2 and 3.
Beat 4 is the fill: four sixteenths on the snare.
Then land: crash and kick together on the next 1.
The fill never rushes. The 1 comes when it comes.
Your turn: groove, a one-beat fill, and land on 1.
Count while you fill: "four e and a, ONE". Saying the one out loud pulls you onto it.
Around the kit: the same four sixteenths can go snare, snare, high tom, floor tom. Moving down the toms is the classic sound.
Longer fills start earlier: two beats from beat 3, a whole bar from beat 1. The landing never moves.
The common mistake: the groove after the landing comes back late, or the hand stays on the toms. Go straight back to the groove on the 1.
In songs, fills mark the end of a phrase, often every four or eight bars, and the crash on the 1 tells the band a new section has begun.
A practice tip: play three bars of groove and one bar with the fill, again and again, with the click. Four-bar phrases are how most songs are built.
Recap: keep the groove, fill on beat 4, count it out loud, and land crash and kick together, right on 1.
Singles alternate R L R L; doubles play two per hand, R R L L, the second as strong as the first; rolls string doubles together and end on an accent.
Single strokes alternate hands: right, left, right, left.
Both hands must sound the same. Listen for a weak left.
Double strokes: two per hand. Right right, left left.
The second stroke comes from the bounce, but must match the first.
A five-stroke roll: two doubles and an accent. R R L L, R.
Your turn: singles, then doubles; slow first, then faster.
A seven-stroke roll is three doubles and an accent; a nine-stroke roll is four doubles and an accent.
Played open, as here, you hear every stroke. Played fast and close, the doubles blur into one smooth sound.
The common mistake: the second stroke of a double is weak, a bounce left to chance. Add a little finger push so the pair sounds even.
Start every pattern slowly with the click, and raise the tempo only when the two hands sound like one.
Singles drive fast fills; doubles give the smooth, even sound of a roll. Most drummers drill both every day.
A practice tip: play eight strokes with one hand, then eight with the other, then four and four, two and two, and finally singles. This ladder evens out the hands quickly.
Recap: singles R L, doubles R R L L with an equal second stroke, rolls built from doubles ending on an accent.
Build a groove limb by limb: the steady part first, then a limb in unison, then let one limb move while the others keep going. Read only the moving part.
Independence: each limb plays its own part while the others keep going.
Build it one limb at a time. First, the hi-hat alone.
Add the kick on every hand stroke: both together, in unison.
Now the kick moves, and the hi-hat stays exactly the same.
Read only the moving part. The steady part runs on its own.
Your turn: unison first, then read the kick under the hi-hat.
If a limb drifts, slow down until every limb lands exactly together on the beats they share.
Say the moving part out loud while you play: "one, and of two, three". Speaking it helps the foot find it.
The common mistake: the hi-hat hand copies the kick and stops on its notes. Keep the hand going like a clock.
An ostinato is a part that repeats unchanged; over it, one limb reads a new line every bar. Later levels change which limb reads.
Where it lives: every groove is independence. The hi-hat holds steady while the kick and the snare follow the song.
A practice tip: loop one bar for a minute before you change anything. Independence grows from repetition: the limbs learn the pattern, so the mind is free to read the next one.
Recap: the steady part first, then a limb in unison, then one limb moves; read only what moves, and slow down when a limb drifts.
The app plays a bar, you play it back in the next one: count while you listen, notice numbers and "and"s, come in right on 1, rhythm before dynamics.
Echo: the app plays a bar; you play it back in the next bar.
Count the beat while you listen: one, two, three, four.
Notice where each stroke falls: on a number, or on an "and".
Come in right on 1. Don’t wait to think.
Copy the rhythm first; loud and soft come later.
Your turn: listen, count, and echo it on the snare.
Count the rhythm in your head: a number for each beat, "and" for the second eighth. A rhythm you can count, you can play.
Keep the beat in your body while you listen, with a foot or a nod. Your bar starts from that beat, not from the last note you heard.
The common mistake: copying the speed of the last notes and rushing the start. The bar has four beats whatever the rhythm.
Later the echo grows: sixteenths, then a whole groove on kick, snare and hi-hat. Listen to one part at a time, the kick first, then the snare.
Where it lives: trading bars in a jam, learning grooves from records, and call and response with a band.
Start with short, simple bars: quarters and eighths only. When you echo them right every time, the levels move on to sixteenths and grooves.
Recap: count while you listen, place every stroke on a number or an "and", and come in right on 1.
Listen to the cymbal first, then the snare, then the kick: rock is straight eighths and a backbeat, swing the ride’s ding, ding-a, bossa the cross-stick clave, reggae the empty 1 and the drop on 3.
Every style has a fingerprint. Listen to the cymbal first.
Rock: straight eighths on the hi-hat, the snare on 2 and 4.
Swing: ding, ding-a on the ride, the hi-hat foot on 2 and 4.
Bossa nova: soft eighths and the clave on the cross-stick.
Reggae one-drop: beat 1 is empty; kick and snare land together on 3.
Straight or swung? That one question separates rock from swing at once. Then the cymbal: a hi-hat in rock, a ride in swing.
Then find the snare: a loud backbeat in rock, a light cross-stick pattern in bossa, a single drop on 3 in reggae.
The kick tells the rest: 1 and 3 in rock, 1 and 3 with pickups in bossa, and on 3 with the snare in the one-drop.
The common mistake: judging by the chords or the tempo. A slow rock and a soft bossa can share a tempo; the drum pattern decides.
Later levels add the shuffle, funk, samba and the jazz waltz, and then pairs that sound alike, like swing and the shuffle.
A listening tip: before naming the style, tap the beat and count one bar. Most styles give themselves away within a single bar, once you know where to listen.
Recap: cymbal first, straight or swung; then the snare; then the kick. Three questions name the style.
Choose where the beat sits — a little behind, on, or ahead; the snare alone laid back; the swing from almost straight to the full triplet — and keep it there on every note.

Hi {name}! Two drummers can play the same groove at the same tempo and feel completely different. The difference is where the notes sit around the beat. Listen: one bar right on the grid, then the same bar laid back.
Behind the beat sounds relaxed and heavy; ahead of it sounds urgent and driving. We are talking about ten milliseconds or so — you feel it more than you hear it.
Boom-bap and many soul grooves keep the hi-hat and the kick on the grid and lay only the snare back. Listen to the lazy snare.
Swing has a dial too. The second eighth of the beat can sit at 55 percent, almost straight, at 62 percent, light, or at 67 percent, the full triplet. Listen to the three.
In these levels the app measures where your notes sit, in milliseconds, against the target you were given. Calibrate the latency first: the pocket is smaller than most delays.
Pocket is also consistency. Ten milliseconds behind on every note is a feel; ten behind on some notes and on the grid on others is just uneven.
The common mistake is to drag the whole groove when you try to lay back. Keep the hi-hat steady and move only the snare. Listen: first everything late, then only the snare.
Practice the pocket with the click on 2 and 4, then on 1 only. The fewer clicks you hear, the more the feel has to come from you.
Swing changes with the tempo. Slow swing can sit near the triplet; fast swing gets straighter, because there is no time left for a long first note. Listen at a fast tempo.
In real music, a laid-back snare is a mark of soul, hip-hop and slow funk; pushing ahead is common in punk and fast rock; jazz drummers often keep the ride slightly on top to drive the band.
Recap: decide where the beat sits before you play, keep that place on every note, and let the measurement tell you how close you came.
In the one-drop nothing plays on 1: the kick and the cross-stick land together on 3 over a hi-hat in a triplet feel; steppers puts the kick on every beat, rockers on 1 and 3.
Hi {name}! The reggae one-drop leaves beat one empty. The kick and the cross-stick drop together on three, and the hi-hat floats above in a triplet feel. Listen.
Beat one is empty on purpose. The bass and the guitar’s off-beat chop carry it; the weight of the drums falls on three.
The cross-stick is the stick laid across the snare, its shoulder clicking on the rim. It is softer and drier than a snare stroke. Listen to it alone.
Steppers puts the kick on every beat, a driving march under the same cross-stick on three. Rockers puts it on one and three, with the hi-hat on the off-beats.
In the exercise the app checks the kick and the cross-stick on three, the hi-hat on its triplet places, and a steady tempo. Reggae is slow, so the space between the notes is the hard part.
The common mistake is a kick on one out of habit. Rock and pop train the foot to land on one; here it has to wait for three.
Keep the hi-hat light and even, the long note a little stronger than the short one. A small open hat at the very end of the bar leads back to the empty one.
Reggae grew in Jamaica in the late 1960s out of ska and rocksteady. As the tempo slowed down, the drums moved their weight from the off-beats to beat three.
Steppers came later and drives harder: four kicks to the bar, the same cross-stick on three. It sits well under dub, where the bass carries the song.
Practice slowly with the click on three only. When three feels like home, the empty one stops feeling like a mistake.
Recap: nothing on one, kick and cross-stick together on three, a light triplet hi-hat; steppers for drive, rockers in between.
Doubles with one foot (heel–toe or slide), then two pedals alternating: the app measures even spacing and even strength, since the kit cannot tell the feet apart.
Hi {name}! A kick double is two sixteenths with one foot. Listen to doubles inside a simple rock groove.
The heel–toe: the heel drops for the first stroke and the toe snaps the second. The second stroke must be as strong as the first — the app compares the two.
A double pedal adds a second beater for the other foot. Both strike the same drum, so the kit cannot tell your feet apart; the app listens for even spacing and even strength instead.
The gallop mixes an eighth and two sixteenths. With two feet the order of the feet keeps changing, which makes it a good test of evenness.
Start slow with short bursts on one and three, then whole bars. A weak foot shows up as every other stroke softer or late.
The slide technique: the foot slides up the pedal board, the first stroke from the middle and the second from the toe. It suits faster doubles than the heel–toe.
The common mistake is a weak second foot. Practice single-foot eighths with the weaker foot alone, then alternate slowly and listen for two equal strokes.
Endurance matters: a minute of sixteenths tells you more than ten seconds. The app compares the first and the last part of the take, so a tired foot shows.
In real music, double bass drives metal and some fusion, but drummers also use it lightly: a few fast doubles under a fill, or a rolling sixteenth line under a big chorus.
Keep the hands relaxed while the feet work. If the snare drifts when the feet get busy, slow down until both stay on the grid.
Recap: one foot first, the second stroke as strong as the first; then two feet, even in time and even in strength, held to the end of the take.
1, 3 and 5 build the home chord: 1 is rest, 5 is open and strong, 3 is the warm color in between.
Hey {name}! Every key has a home note — we call it 1. Listen: the chords lead you there, and you can feel it land.
Stack two more notes on top — 3 and 5 — and you get the home chord. Most melodies love to rest on one of these three.
Number 5 sounds open and strong, like a bright pillar. It feels stable, but a little "up in the air".
Number 3 is the warm one — it gives the chord its color. In a major key it sounds sweet and bright.
And 1 is total rest: nothing wants to move. Here are all three again — 1, then 3, then 5. Feel the difference?
A trick for the tricky pair: if you are not sure between 3 and 5, sing up from 1. Do-re-mi reaches 3; keep going to sol for 5.
Same shape in every key — only home moves. Ready? I play the chords, then one note: tell me 1, 3 or 5.
Scale degrees are numbers for the notes of a key, counted up from home. In C major, C is 1, D is 2, E is 3 and so on up to B, which is 7. The numbers stay the same in every key.
Why these three belong together: each is a third above the last. C to E is a major third, four semitones; E to G is a minor third, three. Stacked, they form the major triad on 1 — the tonic chord.
Against the home chord, 1, 3 and 5 all sound settled. The other degrees lean somewhere: 7 pulls hard up to 1. That contrast is your first clue — a note at rest is probably 1, 3 or 5.
A reliable strategy: hold the note in your head and sing down the scale to the nearest home note, counting as you go. From 5 it takes four steps — 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. From 3, two steps.
Degrees ignore the octave. A high C is still 1, and a G below home is still 5. Judge the feeling of the note, not how high it is.
In a minor key, 3 is a semitone lower — E♭ in C minor. 1 and 5 stay where they are; only the color turns darker. Listen to major, then minor.
The usual mistake is mixing up 3 and 5, especially high up. Ask: warm and sweet, or open and bare? Warm is 3, bare is 5. Still unsure — sing down to 1 and count.
In real music these notes are everywhere. Bugle calls and many fanfares use only 1, 3 and 5, because a valveless horn plays them easily. Countless melodies also end on 1, or pause on 3 or 5.
Recap: 1 is rest, 3 is the warm color, 5 is open and strong. Together they make the home chord, in every key.
A tour of the bass: the chromatic warm-up, scales, grooves, arpeggios, octaves and slap, and a first walk. Each one is measured in time.
Hi {name}! This family is a tour of the bass guitar: one level for each main tool, from the first warm-up to a walking line.
It opens with the chromatic warm-up: one finger per fret, one, two, three, four, and the plucking fingers alternating, index and middle.
Then scales and grooves: root, 5th and octave, rock eighths, a Motown line, a tumbao. The groove is where the bass lives.
The one thing to watch: every note in time and the right length. A bass note that ends early leaves a hole under the whole band.
Your turn: free time first where the notes are new, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys. Every note is measured.
Arpeggios spell the chord one note at a time: root, 3rd, 5th, then the 7th. They are the notes a bass line leans on.
Octaves are the disco and funk sound: the root on the E or A string, the octave two strings higher and two frets up.
The walking level closes the tour: one note per beat over a two-five-one and a blues, chord tones on the strong beats.
The common mistake is fast fingers and loose time. A simple line in perfect time is worth more to a band than a busy one that drifts.
Each tool here has its own family later, in more depth. This tour shows where each one fits, so the path never surprises you.

Where it lives: every band needs these tools: the warm-up before a gig, a scale in a fill, a groove under a chorus, octaves in a disco tune, a walk in a jazz club. To keep: notes in time and full length, alternating fingers, and the tempo ladder.
Index and middle in strict turns, rest strokes, both fingers equally loud: then string crossing, skipping, raking, the gallop and three fingers.
Hi {name}! This family trains the plucking hand: two fingers that sound like one, at any speed and on any string.
The rest stroke: pluck through the string and let the finger land on the next string down. Index, middle, index, middle, with no exceptions.
Then crossing strings, skipping strings, and long runs of sixteenths for stamina. The alternation never stops when the string changes.
The one thing to watch: the two fingers equally loud. If the middle finger is louder, it is usually because it is longer; curve it a little more.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder. The app measures the timing and the loudness of every note, so an uneven pair shows.
Raking: on a line that goes down across the strings, the finger that just played already rests on the next string, so it plays that one too.
The gallop uses three fingers for an eighth and two sixteenths, over and over: the driving sound of metal bass.
Where you pluck changes the tone. Near the neck the note is round and warm; near the bridge it is tight and bright. Later levels ask for both.
The common mistake is starting every phrase with the same finger. Let the alternation run on; the next note gets whichever finger comes next.
Anchor the thumb on the pickup or on the low string, and keep the fingers close. A relaxed hand plucks evenly for a whole set.

Where it lives: every fingerstyle bass line, from a slow ballad to a fast funk groove, depends on this hand. To keep: strict i and m, rest strokes, equal loudness, a light anchored thumb, raking on the way down, and the alternation running through every string change.
Play with the kick drum, the same length every time, ahead or behind on purpose. Groove is measured against the drummer, not a click.
Hi {name}! The pocket is the place where bass and drums lock into one groove. This family trains you to find it and stay in it.
Start with the kick drum. Play exactly when it plays, so the two sound like one low, thick note.
Then feels: the shuffle, sixteenth funk, swung sixteenths, half-time. Each feel asks for a new place inside the beat.
The one thing to watch: the same length on every note. When the lengths wander, the groove wobbles even if every onset is on time.
Your turn: these levels are about time, so the band plays from the first take, and the tempo ladder starts slow. Every note is measured against the drums.
Pocket on purpose: a few milliseconds ahead of the beat pushes the band forward; a few behind makes it heavy and relaxed. Choose, then stay there.
Half-time keeps the tempo but moves the snare to beat three. The bass follows the new feel with longer notes and more space.
Follow the drummer’s fills: when the drums fill into a new section, land the new root with the crash, exactly on one.
The common mistake is listening to yourself instead of the kick. Turn your attention to the drums, and let your own notes follow.
Practice with records: pick a song with a clear kick pattern and play only roots, matching every kick. Simple, and the fastest way into the pocket.

Where it lives: soul, funk, rock and pop records are built on a bass and a kick locked so tightly that they sound like one instrument. To keep: play with the kick, keep every length the same, choose ahead or behind on purpose, follow the fills, and listen to the drummer before yourself.
One finger per fret, or 1-2-4 low on the neck; the thumb behind the neck; light pressure just behind the fret. Then shifts, pivots, octaves and 10ths.
Hi {name}! This family trains the fretting hand: accurate, relaxed fingers that cover the whole neck.
One finger per fret: four fingers, four frets. Low on the neck, where the frets are wide, many players use 1, 2 and 4, the Simandl way.
Then shifts along one string, scales over two octaves, pivots on one finger, and wide shapes like octaves and 10ths.
The one thing to watch: light pressure. The thumb rests behind the neck, opposite the middle finger, and the fingertip presses just behind the fret.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys. The app hears every pitch, so a buzzing or late note shows.
A shift moves the whole hand along the neck. Slide lightly on the finger already on the string, arrive before the note, then press.
A pivot keeps one finger in place and swings the hand around it, to reach a fret just outside the position without a full shift.
Octaves and 10ths are wide shapes. The octave lies two strings up and two frets higher; the 10th adds a major third above the octave.
The common mistake is a squeezing thumb. Squeeze and the hand tires in minutes. Let the arm’s weight do the pressing.
Warm up with the chromatic pattern before long sessions, slowly, then stretch gently. The bass’s frets are wide; respect the hand.

Where it lives: every scale, walking line and fill depends on a fretting hand that moves without strain. To keep: one finger per fret or 1-2-4 low on the neck, the thumb behind the middle finger, the fingertip just behind the fret, the arm’s weight instead of a squeeze, and shifts that arrive before the note.
The end of a note is as exact as its start: real rests, staccato and legato, idle strings silent, a release on the “and”, palm and thumb mutes.
Hi {name}! On the bass, the end of a note matters as much as its start. This family trains you to stop notes exactly.
A rest is real silence. Lift the fretting finger until it barely touches the string, or touch an open string with the plucking hand.
Staccato is short, legato is joined. Same notes, two different grooves. Many bass lines release on the “and”, half a beat long.
The one thing to watch: the strings you are not playing. Open strings ring in sympathy; keep them still with free fingers of both hands.
Your turn: free time first where the notes are new, then the tempo ladder. The app measures how long every note lasts, not only when it starts.
Muted octaves: play the octave shape while the free fingers rest on the string between, so only the two notes sound.
Palm muting: rest the edge of the plucking hand on the strings near the bridge and pluck with the thumb. The note turns short and thick, a vintage sound.
In a groove, each note length is a choice. A short note on beat one leaves room for the snare; a long one fills the bar. Copy the lengths you hear.
The common mistake is letting every note ring until the next. That is legato by accident. Decide each length on purpose.
Practice one bar four ways: all short, all long, long-short, short-long. Record it, and listen to how the groove changes with the same notes.

Where it lives: the tight lines of funk, the short notes of reggae and Motown, the long ones of ballads. To keep: rests are real silence, every length is chosen, idle strings stay quiet, and the release is placed as carefully as the attack.
Rock, Motown, shuffle, disco, reggae, funk, bossa, samba, tumbao and more: each style has its own notes, lengths and place in the beat.
Hi {name}! Every style has its own bass language. This family plays them one by one, each with its band.
Rock drives straight eighths on the root. Motown moves: syncopated, melodic, with passing notes between the chord tones.
Disco bounces in octaves. Reggae leaves space, with the drums dropping on beat three. Bossa nova plays the root and the 5th in a gentle long-short pattern.
The one thing to watch: listen to the drums first. The kick and the hi-hat tell you where the bass notes belong in each style.
Your turn: style levels are timed with the band from the first take, and the tempo ladder starts slow. Every note and its length is measured.
The blues shuffle swings its eighths long-short, often walking root, 3rd, 5th, 6th and back. It is the base of countless songs.
Funk lives on sixteenths: a strong note on one, ghost notes and short stabs around it, and silence used as part of the groove.
The common mistake is playing every style like rock: straight and on the beat. Each style has a home inside the beat; learn where it is.
Listen to two records of each style before its level, and hum the bass line. When you can sing it, your hands learn it fast.

Where it lives: on any gig the bandleader may call a rock song, a bossa and a funk tune in one set. To keep: listen to the drums first, find the style’s place in the beat, copy its note lengths, hum the line before you play it, and keep the time steady.
A ghost is a dead, pitchless click: the fretting finger touches the string without pressing. Quieter than the notes, exactly on its sixteenth.
Hi {name}! Ghost notes are the secret of funk bass: short, pitchless clicks that fill the sixteenths between the real notes.
To make a dead note, lay a fretting finger across the string without pressing it to the fret, and pluck. You hear a thud, not a pitch.
Then ghosts in sixteenths, a ghost before the octave, and two-bar funk lines where real notes and ghosts take turns.
The one thing to watch: ghosts quieter than the notes. If they are as loud, the line turns into noise; the notes must stand out.
Your turn: free time first where the notes are new, then the tempo ladder. Every sixteenth is measured, ghosts included.
Why ghosts? They keep the plucking hand moving in even sixteenths, so the real notes fall exactly in place. They are a clock you can hear.
A ghost just before the octave makes the jump feel like one move: dead note, then the octave on the next sixteenth.
A ghost can also come from the plucking hand: pluck the string while the fretting hand damps it. Both ways give the same click.
The common mistake is a ghost that leaks pitch. Lift the finger a little more, or use two fingers flat on the string, until the note is gone.
Practice with a slow click: four sixteenths per beat, ghosts everywhere, then turn one ghost per beat into a real note. Move it around.

Where it lives: funk and soul bass lines, where the ghosts make the groove dance between the notes. To keep: touch, don’t press; no pitch at all; ghosts quieter than the notes; every one exactly on its sixteenth; and a slow click until the hand runs evenly by itself.
Down-strokes for drive, alternate picking for speed, palm muting for weight: every stroke the same loudness, in time.
Hi {name}! Many rock and punk bassists play with a pick. It gives a clear, punchy attack that cuts through loud guitars.
Down-strokes first: every eighth with a down-stroke. It drives hard, and keeps every note the same.
Then alternate picking for sixteenths, down on the beat and up between, string crossing, and the palm-muted chug.
The one thing to watch: up-strokes as loud as down-strokes. Listen for a limp up-stroke, and keep the motion small, from the wrist.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder. Every stroke, down and up alike, is measured for time and for evenness.
Palm muting: rest the side of the picking hand on the strings right by the bridge. The note gets short and thick, the chug of rock and metal.
Down-strokes for two minutes is a stamina level. Relax between strokes; the arm does little, the wrist does the work.
Inside and outside picking cross strings between or around them. Economy strokes keep the pick moving in one direction across two strings.
The common mistake is a stiff wrist that tires fast. Hold the pick loosely, let the wrist swing, and stop before it burns.
A thicker pick gives a firmer attack on bass strings. Try a few, then keep one, so the hand learns its feel.

Where it lives: rock, punk and metal records, where a picked bass punches through loud guitars and locks with the kick drum. To keep: down-strokes for drive, alternate strokes for speed, up-strokes as loud as down-strokes, palm muting for weight, a loose grip and a free wrist, and a short break whenever the arm tightens.
Leave the groove for a moment and land on a target, the root or the 3rd, exactly on beat one. Then solos built on chord tones.
Hi {name}! This family trains bass fills and solos. Every idea leaves the groove and comes back to land on a target note.
A fill is short: a beat or two at the end of a phrase. Then the next bar starts on its target, first the root, later the 3rd.
Later: two-bar answers over a vamp, pentatonic and blues solos, and two-five-one lines with guide tones and enclosures.
The one thing to watch: land on time. A fill that arrives late breaks the groove, however good its notes are.
Your turn: these levels play with the band and a form, so they are timed from the first take. Every landing is measured against the beat and the chord.
Why targets? A fill without a destination sounds like noodling. With a target, even three notes sound like a plan.
Landing on the 3rd is stronger than the root: it says major or minor. Over A7, land on C sharp; over D minor, land on F.
Trading fours with the drums: four bars of solo, four bars of drums, and you come back exactly where the form says.
The common mistake is too many fills. The groove is the job; a fill every four or eight bars is plenty.
Sing a fill first, then play it. If you can sing where it lands, your fingers will find it, and it will land on time.

Where it lives: a fill at the end of a chorus, a short answer to the singer, a solo chorus on a blues or a standard, trading fours at a jam. To keep: every fill has a target, the target is a chord tone, it lands exactly on beat one, and the groove comes back first. Fewer fills, better fills.
Slides that land on the beat, hammer-ons and pull-offs as loud as plucked notes, harmonics at frets 12, 7 and 5, vibrato on long notes.
Hi {name}! This family trains the fretting hand’s expression: slides, hammer-ons, pull-offs, harmonics and vibrato.
A slide: pluck once and glide the finger to the new fret, keeping the pressure on. The target note must arrive on the beat.
Hammer-on: pluck, then bring a finger down hard on a higher fret. Pull-off: pull the finger off sideways, so it plucks the string.
The one thing to watch: even volume and exact time. The slid, hammered or pulled note is as loud and as on time as a plucked one.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder. Every note is measured, whether it was plucked or not.
Natural harmonics: touch the string lightly right over the fret wire, without pressing, and pluck. Fret 12 gives the octave, fret 7 the octave and a 5th, fret 5 two octaves.
Vibrato on long notes: a small, even rocking of the finger along or across the string. It keeps a long note alive.
A pedal tone repeats one note, often an open string, while a line moves above it. The open string rings; the fretted notes change.
The common mistake is a slide that arrives late. Start the slide early enough that the target lands exactly on the beat.
Practice each technique on one string first, slowly, then inside short lines. Expression is a choice, so use it where the music asks.

Where it lives: singing ballad lines, funk slides into the root, harmonic chords in solo pieces and fusion. To keep: keep the pressure while sliding, land on the beat, hammer and pull as loudly as you pluck, touch harmonics right over the fret wire, and save vibrato for long notes.
The thumb strikes the low string and bounces off; a finger hooks a high string and snaps it. Octave slap and pop, ghost slaps, hammers, double thumbing.
Hi {name}! Slap bass turns the bass into a drum: the thumb is the kick, the popping finger is the snare.
The slap: the side of the thumb strikes the string over the end of the neck and bounces straight off, like a drumstick. The motion comes from turning the wrist.
The pop: the index finger hooks under a high string and pulls it away, so it snaps back against the frets. Slap the root, pop the octave.
The one thing to watch: let the thumb bounce. If it stays on the string, the note dies; if it digs in, the tone turns harsh.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder. Every slap and pop is measured for time and for its place in the groove.
Ghost slaps come from the fretting hand: slap the strings flat with the fingers to make a muted click between the real notes.
Hammer after the slap: slap a note, then hammer a higher fret on the same string. Two notes from one strike, the funk sound.
Double thumbing uses the thumb like a pick: a down-stroke through the string, then an up-stroke back with the thumbnail. It doubles the speed.
The common mistake is slapping too hard. A light, fast strike with a bounce is louder and cleaner than a heavy one.
Practice slap and pop slowly with the click, then add the ghosts. The groove comes from where the notes fall, not from how hard they hit.

Where it lives: funk, disco and gospel records since the 1970s, where the bass doubles as the drums. To keep: a light thumb that strikes and bounces, a finger that hooks and snaps, octaves slapped and popped, ghosts between them, and the groove placed by time, not by force, always with the click.
The same tune can be felt in two, in half-time, broken, as a ballad or in stop-time. The bass decides the feel and keeps the form.
Hi {name}! Walking in four is one feel. This family trains the others, the ones a jazz bassist switches between inside one tune.
The two-feel plays half notes on beats one and three, mostly roots and 5ths. It floats, and leaves room for the melody.
Broken feel mixes halves, quarters and space, conversing with the drums. Stop-time hits one note at the start of a bar, then silence.
The one thing to watch: the form. In stop-time and in broken feel the bar lines go quiet; count every bar so the band comes back together.
Your turn: these levels play with the band and a form, so they are timed from the first take. Every note and every feel change is measured.
Half-time feels the beat at half speed: the bass plays long notes, the drums put the backbeat on three. The tempo stays; the feel slows.
The ballad in two: slow, long notes that ring, with small pickups into the next chord. Space is part of the line.
A common arrangement: the head in two, the solos in four. The change into four is a lift the whole band feels.
The common mistake is losing the form after stop-time. Keep counting through the silence; the band returns exactly on the next section.
Listen to how the great bassists change feels on records. Mark where the two-feel turns into four, and play along with only those moments.

Where it lives: every jazz gig. A ballad may open in two, swing in four for the solos, stop for a break and return in two for the last head. To keep: roots and fifths in two, long notes in half-time and ballads, space in the broken feel, silence in stop-time, and the form counted through all of it.
A straight bow, parallel to the bridge, between the bridge and the fingerboard: long tones, separate bows, slurs, hooked bows and string crossings.
Hi {name}! This family trains the bow: a long, even, singing tone, the classical sound of the double bass.
Long tones first, on the open strings. Keep the bow straight, parallel to the bridge, about halfway between the bridge and the end of the fingerboard.
Then separate bows, one note per stroke; slurs, several notes in one bow; hooked bows, two notes in the same direction with a small stop.
The one thing to watch: an even sound from the frog to the tip. The weight of the arm goes into the string; the bow speed stays steady.
Your turn: slowly first, then the tempo ladder. The app hears every bowed note’s pitch, start and length.
Two bows exist: the German bow, held from below like a saw, and the French bow, held from above like a cello bow. Both are correct; keep the one your teacher uses.
Down-bow pulls toward the tip and is naturally heavier at the frog; up-bow pushes back. Strong beats usually take a down-bow.
String crossing under one bow: tilt the arm to the next string’s level just before you need it. The bow travels on, the angle changes.
The common mistake is a bow that drifts toward the fingerboard. Watch the contact point in a mirror and keep it in one lane.
Begin every session with a few long open-string tones, slowly. They are the scales of the bow, and they set the tone for everything after.

Where it lives: orchestras, chamber music, solo bass repertoire, and the bowed melodies some jazz bassists play. To keep: a straight bow parallel to the bridge, one contact lane, the arm’s weight in the string, an even speed from frog to tip, and long open tones every day.
Pluck with the side of the index finger, pulling across the string: long, even quarters that ring until the next one.
Hi {name}! Jazz pizzicato is the sound of the walking bass: a round, long note that rings under the whole band.
Pluck with the side of the index finger, not the tip, pulling across the string toward the next one. More skin gives a fuller sound.
Then pizzicato over a two-five-one, sustain at tempo, and a graded study. The notes stay long even when the tempo rises.
The one thing to watch: sustain. Each quarter rings until the next one starts; the fretting finger keeps its pressure through the whole beat.
Your turn: steady quarters with the click or the band, and the tempo ladder starts slow. Every note’s length is measured.
Pluck near the end of the fingerboard for a deep, round tone. Closer to the bridge gives more attack but less body.
At fast tempos use two fingers, index and middle, side by side as one, or in turns. The sound must not get thinner.
The arm helps: let its weight fall into the string, rather than plucking only from the finger. That is where the big jazz sound comes from.
The common mistake is lifting the fretting finger early. The note dies, the line gets choppy. Hold each note until the next finger lands.
Protect the fingers: build up playing time slowly, a little more each week. Blisters stop practice for days; patience keeps you playing.

Where it lives: every jazz club and swing record, every walking line on the upright since the 1930s, where the bass is the warm floor under the band. To keep: the side of the finger, pulling across, the arm’s weight in the string, each note ringing until the next one lands, and playing time built up slowly.
Fingers 1, 2 and 4 cover a whole step; each position moves the hand to a new place on the string; the octave harmonic, then thumb position.
Hi {name}! The upright has no frets, so the hand learns fixed places, called positions. This family trains them one by one.
In the low positions the hand covers a whole step with three fingers: 1, 2 and 4. The fourth finger plays with the third behind it for support.
Half position puts the first finger a half step above the open string; first position, a whole step. Each new position moves the hand up the string.
The one thing to watch: intonation. Without frets, every note is placed by ear. Check open strings and harmonics against the fingered notes.
Your turn: slowly first, then the tempo ladder. The app measures every note in cents, so you see how close each finger lands.
By the fourth position the hand reaches the middle of the string, where the octave harmonic sounds. It is a landmark you can always check.
Thumb position: above the octave, the thumb comes onto the string as a movable nut, and the third finger joins in. The hand covers more notes there.
Shifting: slide lightly on the finger that is on the string, and let the ear guide the landing. A slow shift you can hear is fine while learning.
The common mistake is a hand that creeps out of position. Return to a known note often, an open string or a harmonic, and reset.
Practice each position with a drone or the tuner, slowly. Intonation is built by listening, one position at a time.

Where it lives: classical studies, orchestra parts and jazz solos all rely on knowing where each position lies. To keep: 1, 2 and 4 for a whole step, the third finger behind the fourth, landmarks like the octave harmonic, light shifts guided by the ear, and frequent resets on a known note.
One octave, then two and three, in more and more keys; arpeggios, 7th chords and 3rds. In tune, with shifts that arrive on time.
Hi {name}! This family builds scales and arpeggios on the upright, from one octave in the easy keys to three octaves.
Start with one-octave scales and arpeggios in G, D and F, then B flat, E flat, E and the rest, and on to two octaves.
Then dominant and diminished 7th arpeggios, broken 3rds and running 3rds. Each pattern trains the ear and the shifts together.
The one thing to watch: shifts on time. Move early, slide lightly on the finger already on the string, and arrive in tune on the beat.
