Your turn: slowly first, free where the notes are new, then the tempo ladder, key by key. Every note is measured for pitch and time.
Why scales on the upright? They map the fingerboard. After a few weeks in a key, the hand knows where its notes are without looking.
Broken 3rds go up a 3rd and back a step: one, three, two, four, three, five. They train the ear to hear each interval clearly.
Three-octave scales climb into thumb position. The path starts them on E, the lowest string, then F, F sharp and G.
The common mistake is speeding up before the notes are in tune. Play slowly with a drone on the key’s root, and hear every note against it.
Mix bowed and plucked scales: the bow shows every flaw in intonation, the pizzicato keeps the walking hand ready. Both belong to the upright.

Where it lives: auditions, orchestra parts, walking lines and solos all draw on scales played in tune across the fingerboard. To keep: one octave before two and three, every key in turn, early light shifts, a drone to check the intonation, and both the bow and the fingers.
Every finger strong, even and free of the others: five-finger patterns, Hanon, held notes, trills. Even first, fast later.
Hi {name}! This family trains each finger to work on its own: the same strength, the same timing, whatever the others do.
It starts with five fingers on five keys, then Hanon’s patterns: C, E, F, G, A, G, F, E, one step higher each time.
Then held notes: one finger holds its key down while the others play. The held finger stays relaxed, not pressed hard.
The one thing to watch: evenness. Every note the same loudness and the same distance apart. A loose wrist and curved fingertips make it possible.
Your turn: free time first, until every note is clean, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys. Every note is measured.
Why bother? Melodies ask the weak fingers, four and five, to sing as clearly as the thumb. Independence is what lets a melody sound the same in any fingering.
Trills come next: two neighbouring fingers alternate fast, then measured, six or eight to the beat. The fingers stay close to the keys.
Repeated notes change fingers on one key, four, three, two, one. Each finger plays from the key surface, so the repeat stays light and fast.
The common mistake is pressing harder to go faster. Speed comes from less motion, not more force. If the forearm tires, slow down and shake it out.
A practice tip: a few minutes daily, before pieces, with the click low. Play each pattern once loud and once soft; both must stay even.

Where it lives: every scale run, every ornament and every fast melody rests on these patterns. To keep: even notes, a loose wrist, curved fingers, free time first, then the tempo ladder in all twelve keys.
How a note starts, how loud it is and how long it lasts: legato, staccato, portato, dynamics, accents and a top voice that sings.
Hi {name}! Right notes are half of music. This family trains the other half: how long, how loud, and how each note is joined to the next.
Legato joins the notes: one key comes up as the next goes down. Staccato separates them: short, light, bouncing off the key.
Dynamics come next: one even level, then a crescendo up the scale and a diminuendo down. Loudness comes from the speed of the key, not from pushing.
The one thing to watch: listen to the end of each note, not only its start. Where a note stops is part of the music.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder. A MIDI keyboard measures loudness and key release best; the microphone hears less of them.
Portato sits between the two: each note slightly separated but full, as if the notes were gently leaning. It is written as dots under a slur.
Accents every third or fourth note train the hand to choose. The accented note goes down faster; the others stay light and even.
Voicing: in a chord, the top note louder than the others. Weight goes toward the fifth finger while the rest of the hand stays light.
The common mistake is a crescendo that jumps at the end. Plan it: start soft enough that there is room to grow, and grow a little on every note.
A practice tip: record a scale and listen back with eyes closed. Uneven notes and early releases are easier to hear on the recording than while playing.
Where it lives: a singing melody over a soft accompaniment, a phrase that grows and fades, a chord whose top note sings. To keep: hear the length, the loudness and the join of every single note.
Real pieces, from Ode to Joy to Bach: hands separately, short sections, a slow steady tempo, then hands together.
Hi {name}! This family is real music: graded classical pieces, from the Ode to Joy theme up to Bach’s inventions and preludes.
Learn a piece in short sections, two or four bars. Each hand alone first, slowly, with the written fingering, until it plays without stops.
Then hands together, at a tempo where both stay clean. Join the sections one by one, and play across the joins, not only up to them.
The one thing to watch: one tempo from start to end. Choose the tempo of the hardest bar and keep it everywhere, even in the easy bars.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder up to the piece’s own tempo. Every note and every onset is measured against the score.
Why pieces and not only exercises? A piece asks for everything at once: notes, rhythm, touch and shape. It is where technique turns into music.
Fingering is part of the piece. The written fingering is chosen so the hand arrives ready; keep the same fingering every time, or the hand never learns.
Shape the phrase: most phrases grow toward a high point and relax at the end. Breathe between phrases, as a singer would.
The common mistake is starting from the beginning every time. Start where the mistakes are, play that bar three times clean, then add the bars around it.
Listen to a good recording before you start, so you know how it should sound. Then put the recording away and build your own playing, bar by bar.

Where it lives: these pieces have been played by piano students for centuries, and each teaches a skill: Bach the independent hands, Clementi clear scales, Burgmüller a singing line. To keep: small sections, one tempo, the written fingering.
Legato pedal: play the new chord, then lift and press the pedal at once. Change with the harmony; half-pedal for a clearer blur.
Hi {name}! The right pedal lifts the dampers, so notes keep ringing after the fingers let go. This family trains when to press it and when to change it.
Legato pedal: play the new chord first, then lift the pedal and press it again straight away. The new chord is caught, the old one cleared.
Change the pedal with the harmony. When the chord changes, the pedal changes; while the chord stays, the pedal stays down.
The one thing to watch: the change comes just after the new chord, never at the same moment. Pedal together with the keys and you get a gap or a smear.
Your turn. The pedal is measured from a MIDI keyboard with a sustain pedal; the microphone cannot hear it. Slowly first, then the tempo ladder.
Why legato pedal? It joins chords that the hand cannot join alone, like broken chords spread over two octaves, without blurring one harmony into the next.
Direct pedal goes down with the keys and up with them: short and rhythmic, for chords that should ring only as long as they are held.
Half-pedal lifts the dampers only part of the way up and back. Some of the sound is cleared, a held low bass keeps ringing, and the harmony above stays clear.
The common mistake is too much pedal. Listen: if a scale passage turns into a cloud, change more often, or use less depth.
Practice the foot alone first: play slow chords with the right hand only and change the pedal after each one, until the motion is automatic.

Where it lives: Chopin, Debussy, pop ballads and worship songs all lean on the pedal. To keep: keys first, the pedal right after; change with the harmony; and let the ear, not the foot, decide how much.
Octaves from a loose wrist, polyrhythms counted on their shared pulse, double 3rds and 6ths, leaps and hand crossings.
Hi {name}! This family is concert technique: scales in octaves, polyrhythms, double notes in one hand, big leaps and crossing hands.
Octaves come from the wrist, light and loose, with the thumb and fifth finger shaping the hand. The arm carries the hand along; it does not push.
Polyrhythm: three against two. Count the shared pulse of six: the right hand plays on one, three and five, the left hand on one and four.
The one thing to watch: tension. Hard technique tempts the hand to tighten. Stop at the first sign of strain, shake out, and start again slower.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys. Every note, every hand and every onset is measured.
Double 3rds and 6ths put two notes under one hand at once. Practice each pair of fingers slowly, listening that both notes sound together.
Four against three uses a shared pulse of twelve. Learn it slowly by saying the combined rhythm aloud, then let the hands take over.
Leaps: look ahead to the landing key, move early and fast, then play from close to the key. The jump is quick; the note itself is calm.
The common mistake is practicing only at full speed. Hard passages need slow, perfect repetitions; the speed you use most is the one the hand learns.
Keep sessions short: ten focused minutes on advanced technique, then music. A tired hand repeats its mistakes.

Where it lives: octaves in Liszt and Grieg, polyrhythms in Chopin and in jazz, double notes in Czerny’s studies and in Romantic concertos. To keep: a loose wrist, the shared pulse counted aloud, slow perfect repetitions, short sessions, and every level in all twelve keys before the tempo climbs.
The thumb (p) plays the bass on strings 6–4; i, m and a play strings 3, 2 and 1. A steady thumb, quiet fingers, then Travis, rest strokes and tremolo.
Hi {name}! Fingerstyle plays the bass and the chord with the fingers instead of a pick. Each finger has its own job.
The thumb, p, plays the bass on strings six, five and four. The index, middle and ring fingers, i, m and a, play strings three, two and one.
Arpeggio patterns break the chord string by string. Later the thumb alternates two bass notes while the fingers play between: Travis picking.
The one thing to watch: a steady thumb, like a bass player. The fingers move from their knuckles; the hand above them stays still.
Your turn: free time first, until every string sounds, then the tempo ladder. Every note is measured, the bass and the treble alike.
Free stroke: the finger plucks and moves up into the palm, over the next string. Rest stroke: the finger plucks and comes to rest on the next string, for a fuller tone.
The Giuliani patterns are classical right-hand studies: the same chord with a new finger order each time, until any order feels natural.
Tremolo, p a m i: the thumb plays a bass note, then the ring, middle and index fingers repeat one treble note. It sounds like one long, singing note.
The common mistake is a thumb that follows the fingers and loses the beat. Practice the thumb alone first, then add one finger at a time.
Keep the nails short and smooth, or slightly shaped, so every finger sounds the same. An uneven nail gives an uneven tone.

Where it lives: folk and classical guitar, Travis-style country, singer-songwriters with a capo. To keep: a steady thumb, each finger on its own string, a still hand, and every string sounding clearly.
Down on the beat, up between: strict alternate picking from a small wrist motion, then string crossing, economy, sweep and hybrid picking.
Hi {name}! This family trains the picking hand: clean, even notes at any speed, on one string and across all six.
Alternate picking: down, up, down, up, with no exceptions. The down-stroke falls on the beat, the up-stroke on the and.
Crossing strings is the hard part. Outside picking crosses from outside the two strings, inside picking from between them. Both must sound the same.
The one thing to watch: a small motion. The pick moves from the wrist and passes the string by only a little; big strokes cannot get fast.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder. Every note is measured for time and evenness, the up-strokes as much as the down-strokes.
Economy picking keeps alternating on one string, but crosses to the next string in the same direction as the last stroke, like a short sweep.
Sweep picking plays an arpeggio with one long motion across the strings. The fretting hand lets each note go as the next one sounds, so they never ring together.
Hybrid picking adds the middle and ring fingers to the pick: the pick on the low string, a finger on a higher one. It is the sound of country chicken picking.
The common mistake is speeding up before the strokes are even. Use the click and push the tempo only when every note at the current tempo is clean.
Hold the pick lightly between the thumb and the side of the index finger, with only its tip showing. A tight grip makes a stiff arm.
Where it lives: rock and metal riffs, bluegrass runs, fusion lines. To keep: down on the beat, up between, a small wrist motion, and speed only after every note is clean and even.
One finger per fret, fingertips just behind the frets, the least pressure that gives a clean note: chromatic runs, permutations, the spider, stretches.
Hi {name}! This family trains the left hand, or the right for left-handers: four fingers that are strong, independent and accurate.
One finger per fret: in position V, the first finger takes fret 5, the second fret 6, the third fret 7, the fourth fret 8.
Then the order changes: one, two, four, three; one, three, two, four. These permutations make every finger lead and follow.
The one thing to watch: the fingertip right behind the fret, with just enough pressure for a clean note. The thumb rests behind the neck, not squeezing.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder. The app hears each note’s pitch and onset, so a buzz or a late finger shows.
The spider crosses two strings: fingers one and three on one string, two and four on the next, then they swap. It breaks the habit of moving all fingers together.
Keep fingers close: a finger that is not playing hovers just above its fret, ready. Fingers that fly far away arrive late.
Stretches widen the hand: five or six frets under four fingers. Warm up first, start high on the neck where the frets are close, and move lower slowly.
The common mistake is squeezing. Press until the note is clean, then a little less. Any pain means stop.
A practice tip: five minutes daily is better than an hour once a week. Short, slow, accurate repetitions build the hand without strain.

Where it lives: every scale, chord change and solo depends on this hand. To keep: one finger per fret, fingertips just behind the frets, a light thumb, fingers hovering close, and the least pressure that still gives a clean note, from free time to the tempo ladder.
Pick once, then the fretting hand makes the notes: hammer-ons onto the fret, pull-offs that pluck the string. Even volume with the picked notes.
Hi {name}! Legato on the guitar means more notes than picks: the fretting hand sounds the notes by itself.
A hammer-on: pick a note, then bring another finger down hard on a higher fret. The string keeps ringing at the new pitch.
A pull-off: with both fingers down, pull the higher one off with a small sideways flick, so it plucks the string as it leaves.
The one thing to watch: even volume. The hammered and pulled notes should be as loud as the picked one; listen for the weak one.
Your turn: every finger pair, free time first, then the tempo ladder. Every note is measured, picked or not.
Trills are hammer-ons and pull-offs in a row, as fast as they stay even. Start with fingers one and two, then try the weaker pairs, three and four.
Legato pentatonic: two notes per string, one pick on each string, the second note hammered going up and pulled off going down.
Two-hand tapping lets the picking hand hammer a note high on the neck, then pull off to the fretting hand. It turns one string into wide arpeggios.
The common mistake is noise from the other strings. Rest the picking hand lightly on the low strings and let unused fingers touch the higher ones.
Practice slowly with a clean amp sound. Distortion hides weak pull-offs; a clean tone shows every one.

Where it lives: fluid rock solos, blues licks and fast fusion runs, where the notes flow without a pick on each one. To keep: firm hammers right behind the fret, pull-offs that pluck, every note as loud as a picked one, and the other strings muted throughout.
Slides, harmonics, bends that reach the pitch, vibrato, double stops and octaves: the voice of a guitar solo, each one measured in tune.
Hi {name}! This family trains the sounds that make a guitar sing: slides, harmonics, bends and vibrato.
A slide: pick once and glide the finger to a new fret, keeping the pressure on. A natural harmonic: touch the string lightly over fret 12 and pick.
A bend pushes the string across the fret to raise the pitch: a half step, then a whole step. Fingers behind the bending finger help push.
The one thing to watch: the bend must arrive at the target pitch. Play the target fretted first, then bend until the sound matches it.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder. The app measures every bend in cents, so you see how close it lands.
Vibrato is a small, regular bend and release, repeated. Narrow and slow for a ballad, wide and faster for rock. It comes from the wrist, like turning a key.
Bend and release: bend up, hold the pitch, then let the string down to where it started. A pre-bend is bent silently first, picked, then released.
Double stops play two strings at once, in 3rds or 6ths. Octaves in the Wes Montgomery style use the thumb, with the string between them muted.
The common mistake is a bend that stops short of the pitch. Check against the fretted target every time until the hand knows the distance.
Put the techniques into phrases: a slide in, a bend, a vibrato on the last note. A solo is these few sounds, placed with care.
Where it lives: blues, rock and soul solos, where one bent note can say more than a fast run. To keep: bends that reach the target, a steady vibrato, clean slides and harmonics, all measured in tune.
Rasgueado, picado and alzapúa inside the compás: the twelve-beat cycle of soleá and bulería, accented on 3, 6, 8, 10 and 12.
Hi {name}! Flamenco guitar has its own right-hand techniques and its own rhythm cycles. This family trains both.
Rasgueado: the fingers start curled and flick out across the strings one after another, so one strum becomes a quick roll of strokes.
Picado plays scales with rest strokes, index and middle alternating, crisp and loud. Alzapúa uses the thumb, down and up, mixing a melody and strums.
The one thing to watch: the compás. In soleá and bulería, count twelve beats and accent three, six, eight, ten and twelve.
Your turn: free time first for the notes, then the tempo ladder. Every stroke and every accent is measured in time.
The triplet rasgueado divides each beat into three even strokes. Keep the strokes equal in loudness, so the roll sounds like one smooth sound.
Seguiriya counts its cycle as two, two, three, three, two: long and short beats. Rumba is in four, close to pop, with a strong strummed groove.
Golpe, a tap on the guitar top with the ring finger, often marks the accents. It is part of the rhythm, not decoration.
The common mistake is strength from the arm. Rasgueado comes from the fingers opening fast; a relaxed wrist gives speed and volume.
Clap the compás before you play it: twelve claps, accents loud. When the cycle lives in the hands, the guitar techniques fall into place.

Where it lives: soleá, bulería, alegrías, tangos and rumba, played for dancers and singers who expect the guitar to hold the compás without a slip. To keep: relaxed fingers that flick, even strokes, accents on three, six, eight, ten and twelve, and the cycle counted aloud until it lives in the hands.
Listen to the melody notes on the strong beats: the chord that holds them fits. Home chord, the chord on 5, then the chord on 4.
Hi {name}! Here you hear a bar of a song and choose the chord under it, then play it: guitar strums, bass plays the root, keys play the chord.
Most songs lean on two chords: the home chord, and the chord built on the fifth note of the key, which wants to go home.
The clue is the melody on the strong beats. If it sings C, E or G, the home chord C fits. If it sings G, B or D, the G chord fits.
The one thing to watch: try each choice and listen. The wrong chord rubs against the melody; the right one sounds settled under it.
Your turn: choose, then play the chord. Later levels add the chord on four, then ask what comes next. Every played chord is heard and checked.
Why these chords? In a major key the home chord, the chord on four and the chord on five together contain every note of the scale, so almost any melody fits one of them.
The chord on four has F and A, the notes the other two lack. When the melody leans on F or A, think of it first.
Songs usually end a phrase on the home chord, and the bar just before it is often the chord on five. Use the shape of the phrase as a second clue.
The common mistake is following the lowest melody note. Weak-beat notes often pass between chord tones; trust the notes that fall on the beat.
Practice away from the app too: hum a song you know and strum along with only the home chord and the chord on five. Change when it starts to rub.
Where it lives: every campfire song, every jam and every first band rehearsal. To keep: the notes on the strong beats choose the chord.
Sit tall with the elbows level with the keys, number the fingers 1 (thumb) to 5, and rest them on C D E F G: the C position.
Hi {name}! Sit on the front half of the bench, feet flat, shoulders loose. Your elbows sit a little above the keys, and the bench far enough back that your arms can move.
Curve the fingers as if you held a small ball. Play on the fingertips, the thumb on its side.
Fingers have numbers: the thumb is 1, the little finger is 5 — on both hands. Music for beginners prints them over the notes.
The C position: right thumb on middle C, one finger per white key up to G. The left hand mirrors it: little finger on the C below, thumb on G.
Your turn: up and down the five notes, one hand at a time, slow and even with the click. The app listens for the right notes and the timing.
Height matters more than people think. Too low and the wrists sag; too high and the shoulders lift. Adjust the bench, or sit on a cushion, until the forearm is level with the keys.
Weight, not squeezing. Let the arm drop into each key and release it right after. A tight hand sounds hard and tires fast.
Even means equal: the same loudness and the same space between every note. Listen for the weak fingers, four and five, and give them a little more weight.
Hands together in the C position move in mirror image: when the right thumb plays, the left little finger plays too. Same note names, different finger numbers.
A common mistake is a collapsed first joint: the fingertip bends backwards. Keep it firm, like a small arch.
Recap: tall and loose, curved fingers, numbers 1 to 5, the C position in both hands, and slow even notes with the click before anything fast.
A scale has more notes than fingers: after finger 3 the thumb slides under to the next note, and the hand moves on without a bump.
Five fingers, but a scale has eight notes. The trick is the thumb: it passes under the hand to reach the next note.
In C, the right hand plays C D E with 1 2 3. Then the thumb slides under to F, and 1 2 3 4 5 finish the octave.
Move the thumb early. While finger 3 plays E, the thumb is already travelling under, so F comes on time and as loud as the others.
Coming down, finger 3 crosses over the thumb: F with the thumb, then 3 lands on E.
Your turn: the short pattern up and back, each hand alone, slow with the click. Keep the elbow quiet; only the thumb moves.
Listen for the bump. If the note after the thumb comes late or loud, the thumb moved too late. Practice just the pair E to F, slowly, until it sounds like any other step.
The left hand does it the other way round: going up, finger 3 crosses over the thumb; coming down, the thumb passes under.
Keep the wrist level and let the hand glide sideways. Twisting the wrist or lifting the elbow makes the crossing jerky.
Some scales cross after finger 4 too. In C major the right hand crosses once going up; longer scales repeat the same move every octave.
Practice it with the eyes away from the hands now and then. The thumb should find F by feel, because later the eyes will be on the music, not on the keys.
This one move is behind every scale and arpeggio you will play. Once it is smooth, the scale levels open on the path.
Tune with the tuner, hold the guitar close with the neck slightly up, press just behind the fret, and let every string of E minor ring.
Hi {name}! First, tune. The strings from thick to thin are E A D G B E. Open the tuner in Tools and turn each peg until the needle sits in the middle.
Hold it close: the body against you, the neck pointing a little up. The fretting thumb rests behind the neck, not wrapped over it.
Press with the fingertip just behind the fret wire, not on top of it. Close to the fret means a clean note with less force.
Your first chord is E minor: two fingers on the second fret of the A and D strings, and all six strings ring.
Your turn: play the chord one string at a time. Every string should sound; the app hears which ones are muted or buzzing.
Tune up to the note. If a string is sharp, go below it first and come back up: the string holds its pitch better that way.
A muted string usually means a finger is lying on it. Arch the fingers so only the tips touch, and check each string again.
A buzz means too far from the fret or too little pressure. Move closer to the fret before you press harder.
Next comes G major: three fingers, and again all six strings. Changing between E minor and G is the first real change you will practice.
Before every session, check the tuning again. New strings stretch and slip for the first days, and a guitar that is slightly out makes even a clean chord sound wrong.
Short, frequent practice builds calluses without pain. Ten minutes a day is better than an hour once a week, and a sore fingertip is a sign to stop for today.
One down-strum on every beat, the hand moving from the wrist, steady with the click — then down-up eighths.
Strumming is time first. Count one, two, three, four, and strum down on every number.
Move from the wrist, like shaking water off the hand. The arm stays relaxed; the pick or fingers brush across the strings.
Keep the hand moving even when it does not strike: down on the beat, up in the air between beats. That motion is your clock.
Then add the upstroke between the beats: down, up, down, up. Eighth notes, the same hand motion, now touching the strings both ways.
Your turn: quarters on E minor with the click, slowly. The app checks that each strum lands on the beat.
Slow is harder than fast for keeping time. Start at a tempo where every strum feels easy, and speed up only when four bars in a row are on the click.
Down-strokes on the beat are a little louder; up-strokes catch only the higher strings. That small difference gives the groove its shape.
The waltz is three beats a bar: a stronger first beat, then two lighter ones. One, two, three.
Changing chords comes from the same clock: keep strumming on the beat, and let the left hand arrive in time, even if the first strum of the new chord is not perfect.
With a pick, hold it between the thumb and the side of the first finger, only the tip showing. Without one, brush down with the nails and up with the thumb.
Recap: count, strum on the numbers, keep the hand moving between them, then add the ups. Time first, speed later.
Hold the stick a third of the way up between thumb and first finger, let it bounce back from the head, and count every beat as 1 e & a.
Hi {name}! Find the balance point, about a third of the way up the stick. Pinch it there between the thumb and the first finger; the other fingers wrap loosely.
Let the stick bounce. Throw it at the head and let it come back up by itself — you guide it, you do not push it into the drum.
Count out loud. Quarters are one, two, three, four. Eighths add "and" between them: one and two and.
Sixteenths split each beat in four: one e and a, two e and a. Four even strokes for every click.
Your turn: quarters with the click, one hand, then the other. The app measures how close every stroke lands to the beat.
Matched grip means both hands hold the sticks the same way, palms facing down. It is how almost every rock, pop and jazz drummer starts.
A tight grip kills the bounce and the sound. If your hand tires after a minute, loosen the back fingers and let the rebound do the work.
Height sets loudness. Strokes from the same height sound the same; that is the first step to even time.
Counting is not optional. Saying one e and a out loud keeps your place when the rhythms get busy, and every drum part is written in these counts.
Alternate the hands from the start: right, left, right, left. Even strokes from both hands are the base of every roll and fill that comes later on the path.
Recap: balance point, loose fingers, let it bounce, same height for the same sound, and count out loud, from quarters to sixteenths.
Hi-hat on every eighth, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4 — first the hands alone, then the kick joins.
This is the beat under a huge share of the songs you know. Three parts, one bar, played again and again with the band.
The right hand plays the hi-hat on every eighth: one and two and three and four and.
The left hand adds the snare on two and four — the backbeat. Hat and snare hit together on those beats.
The right foot plays the kick on one and three. Now all three: hat, kick, snare.
Your turn: start slowly with the click. The app checks each limb on its beat and that the bar repeats without drifting.
Build it in layers. Hat alone until it is even, then hat and snare, then add the kick. Each layer at the same slow tempo.
The usual slip: the right hand stops when the foot plays. Keep the hat going like a clock, whatever the other limbs do.
The backbeat is the loudest part. A strong snare on two and four over a lighter hat is what makes the beat feel good.
Once it is steady, move the kick: add one on the "and" of three. Small kick changes are the first variations the path asks for.
Sit at a height where the thighs slope slightly down, the hi-hat and snare close to you, and the kick pedal under the right foot without stretching. A comfortable setup makes steady time much easier.
Recap: hat on the eighths, kick on one and three, snare on two and four, built in layers, slow and steady before fast.
Stand tall and loose, warm up on a lip trill or through a straw, and slide onto the note until it blends with the drone.
Hi {name}! Stand with your feet under your shoulders, knees soft, head level. Breathe low, into the belly and the sides, without lifting the shoulders.
Hold one comfortable note while the drone plays with you. Listen for the moment the two sounds become one.
A lip trill or a straw makes singing easier: the air meets a small resistance, the voice balances itself, and the throat stays relaxed.
Can’t find the note? Start a little below and slide up slowly, like a siren, until it settles on the drone. The meter shows if you are above or below.
Your turn: hold the note with the drone, then the same on a lip trill, then slide onto it from above and below. Every take is measured.
Posture is not stiffness. Imagine a string lifting the top of your head while the jaw and shoulders hang loose.
For a lip trill, lips loose and together, blow until they flutter, and add a gentle hum. If the lips stop, press the cheeks lightly with two fingers.
With a straw, sing a held note or a slow glide through it. The sound is small but the pitch is clear, so the app measures it like any other note.
Matching pitch is a skill, not a gift. Most people who think they are "tone deaf" simply have not yet linked what they hear to what the voice does. Sliding builds that link.
Men and women often sing the same tune an octave apart: the same note names, a different height. Pick the octave that sits comfortably, low in your range, and match the drone there.
Recap: stand tall and loose, breathe low, warm up semi-closed, hold with the drone, and slide until the two sounds become one.
Strap the bass at the same height sitting or standing, rest the thumb, pluck with i and m in turn, and tune every string to within 15 cents.
Hi {name}! Set the strap so the bass sits at the same height whether you sit or stand. The neck points a little up, and the shoulders stay down.
Open the tuner in Tools. Play each open string, E, A, D and G, and turn its peg until the needle sits in the middle, within 15 cents.
Rest the thumb on the pickup. Pluck with the index finger and let it land on the next string: a rest stroke.
Then the middle finger, the same way. Index, middle, index, middle: the two fingers take turns, even in time and in loudness.
Your turn: steady quarters on an open string with the click. The app checks the timing, the evenness and, in the tuning step, the pitch of every string.
Practice the alternation slowly on one string before crossing strings. When the fingers cross to a new string, the finger that just played keeps resting on the string below, which also mutes it.
Sitting, rest the bass on the right leg and keep it upright against the body. Standing, the strap should hold it in exactly the same place, so the hands never need to relearn where the strings are.
Odd and even notes should sound the same. If the middle finger is louder, it is usually because it is longer: curve it a little more.
Tune up to the note, not down to it. If a string is sharp, go below the note and come back up; the string holds its pitch better that way.
The fretting hand: the thumb behind the neck, opposite the middle finger, and the fingertips just behind the frets. One finger for each fret.
Recap: same height sitting and standing, thumb anchored, i and m in turn with rest strokes, and every string in tune before you start.
TAB has a line for every string, the highest string on top; a number is the fret, 0 an open string, read left to right.
TAB draws the neck from the side: six lines for the six guitar strings, four lines for the bass. The top line is the highest, thinnest string.
A number on a line is the fret to press on that string. Zero means the open string, nothing pressed.
Read from left to right, like a sentence. Numbers stacked on top of each other are played together, as a chord.
TAB shows where to play; the stems and beams above it show when. A note with a beam is an eighth, a note alone on a stem a quarter.
Every line here is new, so there is nothing to memorise: read it in time with the click, and keep going even after a slip.
Many songbooks print TAB under the staff. Use the TAB for where and the staff for when, and after a while the two readings become one glance.
A common slip is reading TAB upside down: the top line looks like the low string because it is on top. It is the opposite. Picture looking down at the guitar on your lap.
Fret numbers also suggest the finger: in first position, fret one is the index finger, fret two the middle, fret three the ring finger.
Look ahead before you start: which strings the line uses, and where it goes highest. Then the hand is already in place.
Bass TAB works the same with four lines: G on top, then D, A and the low E at the bottom.
Recap: one line per string, the high string on top, numbers are frets, zero is open, read left to right, rhythm from the stems.
A riff is a short figure repeated under a song; play it in time, mute what should be short, and move the shape to play it in any key.
A riff is a short figure, one or two bars long, repeated through a song. It is built from a few notes around the root on the low strings.
Palm muting: rest the side of the picking hand on the strings, right by the bridge. The note gets short and punchy.
A power chord is the root and its fifth, often with the octave on top. It has no third, so it is neither major nor minor.
The shape moves: start the same riff on another fret of the low E string and it is in another key. That is how these riffs run in all twelve keys.
Every grade has its own riff: single notes, then power chords, sixteenths, slurs and a pedal point. Free time first, then up the tempo ladder.
Write your own riff: take three notes from the box around the root, choose a rhythm, and repeat it four times without changing anything. Then move it to another key.
A riff lives or dies by its time. Play it with the click until every repeat sits in exactly the same place; only then push the tempo.
Muted and open notes together make the groove: the muted chugs keep the pulse, the open accents answer them.
A hammer-on sounds a note without picking it: pick the first note, then press the next fret down hard. A pull-off is the reverse: flick the finger off the string.
A pedal point repeats the low root between the notes of a line. Keep the root short and soft so the line on top sings.
Recap: short figures, steady time, palm muting where the notes are short, and the same shape moved along the low string for every key.
Find C left of every two black keys and F left of every three; a five-finger position puts the thumb on the key note and one finger on each note above it.
The black keys come in groups of two and three, all the way up the keyboard. They are its map.
C is the white key just left of every group of two. F is just left of every group of three.
Play the black groups with fingers two and three, then two, three and four. Stay on the fingertips, close to the black keys.
A five-finger position: the thumb on the key note, one finger on each of the next four notes of the scale. In G every note is white; in F the fourth finger plays B flat.
Your turn: the black groups, then tunes in C, G and F, then every other key. Free time first, then with the click.
Find every C on the keyboard with your eyes closed, by touch: feel for the two black keys and slide left. Then do the same for F and the three black keys.
Every five-finger position follows the same steps: whole, whole, half, whole. Count them up from any key note and the black keys you need appear by themselves.
In D the third finger plays F sharp; in E the second and third play F sharp and G sharp. The hand moves a little forward, into the black keys.
The left hand mirrors the right: the little finger on the key note, the thumb on the fifth. Same notes, the finger numbers reversed.
When both hands play together, listen that they land at the same moment. Slow and together is worth more than fast and apart.
Recap: twos and threes are the map, C and F sit left of them, and a five-finger position starts with the thumb on the key note.
The treble clef circles the G line, the bass clef’s dots sit around the F line, and middle C sits on a short line between the two staves.
The right hand usually reads the treble clef. Its curl wraps around the second line from the bottom: that line is G.
The left hand reads the bass clef. Its two dots sit around the fourth line from the bottom: that line is F.
Middle C sits on a short extra line, just below the treble staff and just above the bass staff.
From a line to the next space is a step, one note up. From a line to the next line is a skip. Read the direction first, then the distance.
Your turn: short melodies in one clef at a time, steps only, first in C, G and F, then every key.
Read slowly at first and say each note name out loud as you play it; the names stick faster when the eyes, the voice and the hand work together.
Ledger lines extend the staff above or below. Count them like the staff lines: line, space, line, from the nearest landmark you know.
Landmarks beat counting lines: middle C, the treble G and the bass F. Read every other note as a step or a skip from the nearest landmark.
The two staves together are the grand staff. The same middle C can be written in either one; the hand that plays it decides.
Notes on lines skip one letter each: in treble, the lines from the bottom are E, G, B, D, F. The spaces between them spell F, A, C, E.
In bass clef the lines from the bottom are G, B, D, F, A, and the spaces A, C, E, G.
Recap: G clef, F clef, middle C between them, and every note read as a step or a skip from a landmark you already know.
The letter is the root and "m" makes it minor; play root, 3rd and 5th, move each chord to the nearest shape, and let the left hand take the root.
A chord symbol names the root: C, G, A, F. A small m makes it minor, as in A m. Play the root, the 3rd and the 5th together: a block chord.
Do not jump between chords: keep the notes they share and move the others the shortest way.
That way C, G, A minor and F all stay inside one hand position, and the music moves smoothly.
Pop accompaniment: the left hand plays the root low, the right hand the triad. One, five, six, four is the progression under countless songs.
Your turn, in every key: block chords first, then the left-hand root with the right-hand triad in halves and in quarters.
Try the same four chords in a new key each day. The shapes stay close, the names change, and soon you read the symbols without thinking.
A slash chord such as C over E asks for E in the bass under a C chord. In pop songs it often makes the bass walk smoothly between two chords.
A major triad is a major 3rd with a minor 3rd on top; a minor triad the other way round. The 3rd in the middle decides the colour.
An inversion puts another chord note at the bottom. The chord keeps its name; only the order of the notes changes.
Keep the right hand near middle C. If a chord climbs too high, take its inversion an octave lower.
The left-hand root should land exactly with the chord. Count the bar, and change on beat one without a gap.
Recap: the letter is the root, m means minor, the nearest shape keeps the hand still, and the left hand holds the root underneath.
Look before you play — key, time, hand position, the highest and lowest note — then keep the pulse and read ahead; never stop to fix a note.
Before you play, look: the key signature, the time signature, where the hand starts, and the highest and lowest note.
Then keep the pulse. A wrong note passes in a moment; a stop breaks the music. Keep going, slower if you need.
Read a little ahead of your fingers: the eyes on the next group of notes while the hand plays this one.
Read the shape, not every letter: up or down, step or skip. The ear checks the rest.
Every piece here is written for you on the spot, new in every key, so there is nothing to memorise. The levels grow from five fingers to both hands, sharps and flats, and chords.
After a take, look at what went wrong: the same kind of slip again and again, a leap or a key signature, shows what to read more of.
Read a little every day, at a level that feels slightly easy. Lots of easy reading builds the skill faster than a little hard reading.
Choose a tempo you can keep to the last bar. The first take sets the speed, and the tempo ladder raises it later.
With both hands, read the bass first: it moves less, and it tells you the harmony the melody sits on.
An accidental lasts to the end of its bar. A sharp on the fourth degree usually leads up to the fifth; a flat seventh usually falls to the sixth.
The top level gives thirty seconds to look before play opens, like the exam. Use them to find the hard bar and plan its fingering.
Recap: look first, then keep the pulse, read ahead, read shapes, and never stop to fix a note.
RLRR LRLL: two singles and a double, so the lead hand changes every group; accent the first note of each.
The paradiddle is right, left, right, right, then left, right, left, left. Para is the two singles, diddle the double.
Because of the double, the next group starts with the other hand. That is what makes the paradiddle so useful around the kit.
Accent the first note of each group and keep the other three low. Accent from a higher stick, taps from close to the head.
Start in eighths at a slow tempo, then climb to quarter note seventy: the tempo of the beginners’ grade.
Your turn: with accents, evenly without them, then leading with the left. The app checks the timing and where the accents fall.
Play it on a pillow or your knees away from the kit. The pattern lives in the hands, and quiet practice builds it just as well.
Move the right hand to the hi-hat and the left to the snare while you play paradiddles, and you hear the first grooves built from a rudiment.
The double must match the singles: the second stroke of the pair as loud as the first. Let the wrist and fingers share the work.
Say it out loud while you play: pa-ra-did-dle. The word has the rhythm and the sticking in it.
Later the paradiddle comes in sixteenths, inverted and around the toms. The 8th-note version is the foundation of all of them.
If the accents drift onto the wrong notes, slow down until each first note is clearly louder, then climb again.
Recap: RLRR LRLL, the lead changes every group, accent the first, doubles as strong as singles, slow before fast.
The top number counts the beats; 2/4 and 3/4 count quarters, 6/8 counts two big beats of three 8ths: 1-2-3, 4-5-6.
The time signature has two numbers. The top one counts the beats in a bar, the bottom one says which note gets the beat.
In 2/4 there are two quarter beats a bar, like a march. The first beat leans a little.
In 3/4 there are three quarter beats, like a waltz: one, two, three.
In 6/8 the eighth note is the unit, grouped in threes: two big beats a bar. Count one-two-three, four-five-six.
The lines here are new each time. Count a bar before you play, and keep the right hand on the beats. Count out loud the first time through.
Before each line, find the shortest note on the page. It sets how you count: in quarters, in eighths, or in groups of three.
Tap the beat with your foot while you read: two taps a bar in 2/4 and 6/8, three in 3/4. The foot keeps the bar while the hands read the notes.
3/4 and 6/8 both hold six eighths, but they group them differently: three pairs in 3/4, two threes in 6/8. Where the accents fall tells you which.
In 6/8 a dotted quarter fills a whole big beat; a quarter and an eighth split it long-short; three eighths fill it evenly.
A rest is counted like a note: say its number silently and let the stick wait.
Keep the hand-to-hand rule: the right hand on the beats, the left in between. The sticking then follows the rhythm by itself.
Recap: the top number counts beats, 2/4 and 3/4 count quarters, 6/8 two big beats of three, and rests are counted too.
Press the stick into the head so it bounces several times on each stroke, hand to hand, every buzz the same length.
A buzz is one stroke that bounces many times. Drop the stick and press it gently into the head as it lands.
It is written as a small z across the stem of the note.
Hand to hand, the buzzes join into one smooth sound: the closed roll, or buzz roll.
Each buzz should last the same time and sound the same in both hands. Listen for gaps between them.
Each stroke needs at least three bounces to count. Keep the grip loose; squeezing kills the bounce. This one needs an electronic kit or a MIDI pad. Short practice, often, works best.
Record yourself and listen back: a good buzz roll sounds like one long note, not like separate strokes. Any gap you hear is a place to slow down.
Practice each hand alone first: buzz, lift, buzz, lift, listening for the same number of bounces every time. Then join the hands.
The press comes from the fingers, not the arm. Too little and the stick bounces twice like a double stroke; too much and it chokes.
Play close to the centre of the head, where it bounces most evenly, and keep both sticks at the same height.
Start with quarter-note buzzes and rests between them, then eighths that join into a roll.
Orchestral and marching drummers use the buzz roll to hold a long note on the snare. In a band it swells into a crash.
Recap: drop and press, at least three bounces, even length in both hands, loose grip, and no gaps between the buzzes.
Listen to the whole rhythm with the beat in your body, then tap it back after the count-in; the notation appears only with the result.
First you hear a bar of clicks, so the beat is in your body before anything else.
Then the rhythm on the snare. There is nothing to read: just listen, and feel where the notes fall against the beat.
Then a count-in, and it is your turn: tap the same rhythm on the pad while the clicks keep going under you.
Say it inside while you listen: long, short, short. Words are easier to keep than sounds.
The rhythms grow from quarters and halves to eighths, dotted notes, 3/4 and 6/8, and syncopation. The notation appears with the result. Keep your answer steady.
Start each answer exactly on the first beat after the count-in. A late start shifts every note, even when the rhythm itself is right.
Clap along with the drums in songs you know, then stop and clap the rhythm back from memory. The same habit, away from the app.
Musicians learn rhythms by ear long before they read them. Echoing builds the memory that later makes reading fast.
Notice where each note starts, not how long it sounds: the tap only marks the start. A held note is just a longer wait before the next tap.
Two notes in one beat are eighths. A note that seems to come early, just before the beat, is a syncopation.
If you lose it, keep tapping the beat you remember and come back in on the next one. A steady answer with a small gap beats a rushed one.
Recap: feel the beat, listen to the whole rhythm, say it inside, then tap it back with the clicks.
A falling interval has the same size as the rising one; sing the lower note and slide back up to measure it.
Intervals fall as well as rise. A falling third, a falling fifth: the same sizes, in the other direction.
A minor third down sounds closer and darker than a major third down.
A fourth down feels like a step home; a fifth down sounds wide and open, like a bass line landing on its root.
Not sure? Sing the lower note, then slide up to the first one and feel the distance.
The ladder grows like the rising one: thirds, then fourths and fifths, the octave, seconds and sixths, and finally all twelve. Each level adds a few new intervals to the ones you know.
Mix the directions when you practice: a rising third, then a falling one from the top note. Hearing both ways makes each one clearer.
Sing a scale downwards from any note and stop on each degree: the falling second, third and fourth are all inside it, ready to compare.
Falling intervals are harder for most people because we practice rising ones far more. A few minutes a day evens it out quickly.
An octave down is the same note, lower. A half step down is the smallest move there is, a sigh.
Listen to the bottom note as the new home. Ask which degree of its scale the top note is: the fifth, the third, the octave.
Sixths down are wide but sweet; sevenths down sound tense and want to move on.
Recap: same sizes as going up, the lower note as the new home, and a slow slide up when you are not sure.
A triad stacks root, 3rd and 5th; the root sounds at rest, the 5th open and hollow, the 3rd decides major or minor.
A triad is three notes stacked in thirds: the root, the third and the fifth.
Played alone after the chord, the root feels like home.
The fifth sounds open and a little hollow, as if it could belong to more than one chord.
The third carries the colour: bright in a major chord, darker in a minor one.

Not sure? Hum up the chord from its lowest note, one, three, five, and stop where you meet the note. Later the chord is inverted, and then the note is on top. Take your time; listen to the chord again if you need.
Listen for the bass too: when the chord is inverted the bass is the third or the fifth, and the whole chord sounds lighter.
Play a chord on any instrument and sing its root, then its third, then its fifth. Then try singing them in a different order.
In an inversion the lowest note is no longer the root. Find the root by the sound of rest, not by its place.
The note on top of a chord is what we hear as its melody. Hearing whether it is the root, the third or the fifth is the first step to harmonising a tune.
A melody that ends on the root sounds finished; on the third, gentle; on the fifth, still open.
Sing the three notes after any chord you hear in a song. Soon the members jump out by themselves.
Recap: root, third, fifth; the root at rest, the fifth open, the third the colour, and hum up the chord when in doubt.
Count the notes as the second tune plays and mark the first one that sounds different.
You hear a short tune twice. The second time, one note is different.
Count the notes on your fingers while the second tune plays, and stop on the first one that sounds different.
Hold the first tune in your head as a shape: up, up, down. The changed note breaks the shape.
First you say near the start or near the end, then which note, then which note and whether it went higher or lower.
Each tune is new, in a new key, so listen fresh every time. Listen to the whole tune before you choose, and trust the first difference you hear.
Longer tunes are harder to hold, so the ladder adds notes slowly. If you lose the start, focus on the shape of the second half.
Try it with a friend: one plays a short tune twice and changes one note, the other finds it. Swap roles and make the change smaller each round.
Musicians use this skill to catch wrong notes in their own playing and in a band. It is the ear checking the eye.
Sing the first tune quietly to yourself while it plays. A tune you sang is easier to compare than one you only heard.
A note that goes higher than expected often feels brighter or surprising; one that goes lower feels heavier.
The first note never changes, so the comparison always starts from the same, familiar place.
Recap: hold the shape, count the notes, stop at the first difference, and only then decide up or down.
Intros: the iii–VI7–ii–V7 vamp or a blues’s last four bars. Endings: ♭VI–♭II–I in maj7 or 7, the tag ×3, the Dameron turnaround, the diminished walk-down.
Hi {name}! An intro can vamp on three, six, two, five: E minor 7, A7, D minor 7, G7, then the tune starts on C.
The Dameron turnaround moves by major 7th chords: C, E flat, A flat, D flat, then home.
To end, slide in from a half step above: A flat, D flat, C. As major 7ths it sounds soft; as dominants, bluesy.
The walk-down: E minor 7, E flat diminished, D minor 7, G7, C. The bass falls by half steps.
Each item starts in free time. Then the click, slowly, up the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys.
Why intros and endings? A tune needs a way in and a way out. The band agrees on them before the count-off, so everyone lands on the first bar together and stops together.
A blues often starts with its own last four bars: D minor 7, G7, then C7, A7, D minor 7, G7 back to the top.
The tag repeats the last turnaround three times before the final chord. Count the three: the band feels the end coming.
Hear the difference: A flat major 7 to D flat major 7 is gentle; A flat 7 to D flat 7 has a bluesy pull into C.
A common mistake: rushing the last chord. Hold the final chord its full length and let it ring.
On guitar these sit in drop 2 on the top four strings; on bass you walk them, a root on every new chord and a half step into the next.
Recap: vamp in, play the head, and end with a slide, a tag, or the walk-down. The ear topic asks you to name each one.
Left hand: the root and the 3rd an octave up (a 10th). Right hand: a four-note rootless voicing above it, each moving to the nearest next one.
Hi {name}! A ballad is slow and even: straight eighths, a chord or two a bar. “Evening Lamp” is our own sixteen bars of ballad changes.
The left hand plays a 10th: C low, and the E a 10th above it. If it is too wide, roll it from the bottom.
The right hand adds the 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th, no root. Then everything together.
The right hand keeps one place above the left hand, and each voice moves to the nearest note of the next chord.
First the left hand alone, then the right hand over the root, then both. Free time first, then a slow click.
Why 10ths? A 10th fills the low register warmly without the mud of a low 3rd right next to the root.
Two forms of the four-note voicing: A is 3, 5, 7, 9 from the bottom; B is 7, 9, 3, 5. Switch between them to keep the hand still.
On a minor 7 flat 5 or a diminished chord, the four notes include the root: that is fine, it is the chord itself.
A common mistake: playing loud. A ballad lives at piano to mezzo-piano; let the top note sing a little above the rest.
Practice each half of the chart on its own: bars one to eight, then nine to sixteen. Then play all sixteen bars without stopping, in free time first.
Recap: 10ths below, four notes above, small steps between chords, straight eighths, and patience.
On guitar the same chart sits in drop 2 on the middle strings; on bass you play it in two, a root and a 5th each bar.
Intro (the last four bars) → the head → one solo chorus → the head again → an ending. Each part is graded on its own.
Hi {name}! On a gig a tune has a road map: an intro, the head, the solos, the head out, an ending.
The intro is the tune’s last four bars. On a blues in F: G minor 7, C7, F7, D7, G minor 7, C7.
Then the head: the melody in the right hand, shells in the left. You play it again after the solo.
In the solo chorus the bars are yours: land a chord tone on each change, stay inside, or quote the head.
The Basie ending: the band hits the tonic, the piano answers with three notes, and one last hit.
First each part alone, then the whole tune in one take with the band. The result shows which part slipped.
Why a road map? On the bandstand nobody stops to ask where we are. Knowing the form by heart frees your ears for the music.
Back Porch Blues and Night Ferry are tunes written for this app, so their melodies are ours to play in any key.
In a minor tune the ending is a tag: D half-diminished, G7 flat 9, three times, then C minor.
Quoting the head means four notes of the melody inside your solo, in any key. Listeners love hearing the tune peek through.
The result screen names the part that slipped: the intro, the head, the solo chorus, the head out or the ending. Practice that part alone, then try the whole take again.
A common mistake: losing the form in the solo. Keep the chart in view and land on the first bar of the head out.
Recap: intro, head, one chorus, head, ending, all with the band. On guitar the head is chord-melody; on bass, two-feel for the head and walking for the solo.
Hear it, then find it on the neck: the answer is measured by what you play, in time.
Hi {name}! In these levels the band plays first, then it is your turn on the guitar.
Sing it inside first, then find the first note. Every line starts on a note I tell you: the root or the fifth.
For chords, listen for the root — the note the chord is named after, not always the lowest one. Play it on strings six and five.
Any octave and any position count. Play on the beat after the call; the call itself is never taken for your answer.
Your turn: the first call is short and slow. Listen once, breathe on the empty beat, then answer on the next bar line.
Why the guitar and not the screen? Because finding a sound on the neck is the skill a player needs on the bandstand: hear a line, find it, play it in time.
Start from the tonic. Most lines lean on it, and from home every other note is a distance you can learn to feel.
For rhythm, mute the strings with the fretting hand and strum: only the rhythm counts, not the pitch.
For the root finder, hum the note each chord rests on — its root, not its lowest voice. Chords come in inversions on purpose, so neither the top nor the bottom voice gives it away.
A common mistake is to answer late while still searching. Better to play a wrong note on time and fix it next round than to drop the bar.
Practice away from the app too: sing a line you know, then find it on one string first, then inside one position. The ear and the hand learn together.
Shells hold the 3rd and 7th; drop-2 puts the melody on top. The rhythm is the comp.
A jazz guitarist rarely plays full chords. Three notes are enough: the root, the 3rd and the 7th.
The 3rd and 7th move by step from chord to chord. That small motion is what makes the changes sound.
Comping is rhythm: the Charleston, four to the bar, or a push on the "and" of four into the next chord.
In chord melody the tune sits on the top string and a drop-2 voicing hangs under every melody note.
Your turn: shells first, four to the bar, then the Charleston. Keep the chords short so the bass and drums can breathe.
Freddie Green played short shells on every beat in the Basie band: barely heard alone, but the whole band leaned on them.
Drop-2: take a close four-note chord and drop its second voice from the top an octave. On the guitar it fits four neighbouring strings.
Voice leading: from one chord to the next, move each voice to the nearest note. The top voice then sings a line of its own.
Tritone substitution: a dominant can be replaced by the dominant a tritone away. They share the 3rd and 7th, and the bass slides down by half steps.
To keep: three notes are a chord, the rhythm is the comp, and the melody on top of drop-2 is chord melody. The drills measure each hit in time.
Listen to the great comping guitarists and notice how little they play: a short chord, a long silence, and every hit placed exactly with the drummer.
The 6th chord and the diminished make an 8-note scale; on the dominant scale, chord tones land on the beats.
Barry Harris adds one note to the major scale: the ♭6. C, D, E, F, G, A flat, A, B — the C6 chord and B°7 in turn.
Up or down, every chord tone of C6 falls on a beat and every other note sits between: the line swings by itself.
On a dominant, coming down from a chord tone, add a half step between the root and the flat 7th.
On the guitar we play it in position, swung, and harmonise each note with a drop-2 6th or diminished chord.
Your turn: the scale in two positions, swung, slowly. Feel the chord tones fall on the beats, then speed up.
Barry Harris taught in workshops for decades. His idea: the music lives in movement between rest and tension, and the diminished chord is the tension.
Lower one note of a diminished chord a half step and it becomes a dominant 7th. Four notes to lower give four dominants a minor third apart: the brothers.
The half-step rule: coming down a dominant scale from a chord tone, add one chromatic note between the root and the flat 7th, so the chord tones stay on the beats.
Pivot: when the line runs out of neck, jump the next note an octave and keep going in the same direction of the scale.
On the guitar, learn each idea in one position first, then in a second one. The drills check the notes and that chord tones land on the beats.
Sing the lines before you play them. Barry asked his students to sing everything, because a line you can sing is a line your fingers will find.
Count odd bars in groups of 2 and 3; in a modulation one note value becomes the new beat.
Seven eighths in a bar feel natural when you group them: two, two, three. Count it: one two, one two, one two three.
The click sounds only on each group, so lean on the first note of every group.
In a metric modulation the triplet of the old tempo becomes the new beat: the music speeds up by half without a jolt.
Keep the grid inside you and land on every new one. A lost bar is named in the result.
Your turn: say the groups aloud while you play the riff, slowly. When the count feels easy, let the band in.
Odd meters come from folk music long before rock: Balkan dances in 7 and 11, Indian rhythmic cycles, Greek and Turkish songs.
The same seven eighths can group 2 2 3, 3 2 2 or 2 3 2. The grouping is the feel, so the drills tell you which one they want.
Polyrhythm in a riff: groups of three sixteenths over four beats. The accents drift across the bar and meet the downbeat again after three beats.
Metric modulation: hear the new beat inside the old bar before it arrives. Here the dotted eighth of the old tempo becomes the new quarter.
A common mistake is to rush the long group. Keep every eighth equal; the result names a lost bar and the tempo of each section.
Practice with the click on group starts only, then on the first beat of each bar only, until the groups live in your body and not in the click.
Strum one chord with a clean tone and let it ring: the app names it, or says it is not sure. It never guesses.
Hi {name}! Strum a chord once and let every string ring. The app listens to the first half second and names the chord.
It hears every note and the lowest one. A minor with E in the bass is A minor over E.
When two names are close it says so and offers both. A string that did not ring is named, so you can fix the finger.
The other way round: pick a name and see every shape on the neck. Tap a shape to hear it.
The same ear works in the lessons and in Chord Rush: when a chord is asked, you can strum it instead of tapping the neck.
How it hears: a chord is a set of pitch classes. The app folds every note into twelve bins, one per note name, and compares that picture with the picture of each chord it knows.
A plucked string also sounds its overtones. The third overtone of E is a B, so a plain C chord can look a little like C major 7. The app only names the 7th when it really rings.
The lowest note decides the bass. Play C with E on the low string and you get C over E, a first inversion. Mute the low string and the root takes the bass again.
A common mistake is a buzzing or muted string. The answer still comes, but the app lists the note that did not ring, so you know which finger to move.
Distortion and a band from the phone speaker blur the picture. Use a clean tone and headphones for the backing, and strum once rather than a long pattern.
Use the shapes page to learn a new chord in every position: open, the E shape on string six, the A shape on string five and drop-2 for sevenths. Strum each one and check the name.
Build any chord and see it on the keys and the neck; voice a cadence with the smallest moves, then play it chord by chord.
Hi {name}! Pick a root and a quality, and the builder spells the chord, plays it, and shows it on the piano keys and as a guitar shape.
Or the other way round: tap notes on the keys or the neck, and it names the chord they make, in any inversion.
On the cadence page pick a key and a cadence: authentic, plagal, half, deceptive, two five one or the backdoor.
Each chord is voiced so the upper notes move as little as possible. Listen: the seventh of each chord slips down a half step.
Then press Play and play it yourself. With a keyboard on MIDI, hold each chord; with the microphone, strum or play it once. Each chord right at the first try counts.
A cadence is the end of a phrase. Authentic goes from the dominant to the tonic, a full stop. Plagal goes from the fourth chord home, the amen at the end of a hymn.
A half cadence stops on the dominant, like a comma. The deceptive one sets up the tonic and lands on the sixth chord instead.
The backdoor reaches home from the flat seventh: in C, F minor seven to B flat seven to C. It sounds softer than the dominant.
Smooth voice leading means a common tone stays and the others move by step. The builder tries every inversion and keeps the one with the smallest total move.
On the guitar it picks the shape nearest the last one on the neck, so the hand stays in one place.
How your playing is measured: on MIDI every chord tone must be held and nothing else; a seventh chord may leave out its fifth. On the microphone the chord recognizer listens to one strum.
Musicians keep the music going inside when it goes quiet. Sing along silently, keep your place with the click, and you will know exactly where the music is when it comes back.
Hi {name}! Here is a tune you know, with a click on every beat. Sing it along in your head, without a sound.
Now two notes go silent, but the click goes on. Keep singing inside — the tune should come back exactly where your inner voice is.
The same with a scale. It climbs, disappears for three notes and lands again. Which step did it land on? Count up silently with the clicks.
Chords too: a loop plays once, then two chords go silent. Keep the loop turning in your head and the right chord comes back.
That skill is called audiation. Practice it anywhere: hum a song, stop, keep it going silently, then come back in.
Audiation means hearing and understanding music in your mind when no sound is present. The term comes from the music educator Edwin Gordon. It is to music what thinking in words is to language.
It is more than memory: when you audiate, you predict. You know which note comes next and where the beat falls, so a wrong note jumps out at once. Listen — the second time, one note is off.
The pulse is the frame that holds the silent music. During a gap, count the beats in your head so the music returns exactly on time. Here four notes of the scale go silent.
Harmony can be audiated too. Start with the bass: it is the easiest part to carry silently, and the chords hang on it. Hum the lowest notes of this loop, then keep them going in your head.
A practice routine: sing a scale but voice only every other note; the silent ones still happen inside. Then try a song you know with whole bars left silent.
The common mistake is letting the tempo drift in the silence — most people rush. Keep the beat in your body: tap a finger, nod, or breathe with it.
Musicians audiate all the time: a singer hears the first note before the band starts, a sight-reader hears the page before playing it, a composer hears parts with no instrument at hand.
Recap: audiation is hearing music inside, with its pulse and its harmony. Keep counting, predict what comes next, and check yourself when the sound returns.
Major is bright, minor is darker, diminished is tight and tense, augmented floats, sus chords are open and want to resolve. The bass note tells you the inversion.
Hi {name}! A triad is three notes stacked in thirds. Major sounds bright and settled, minor sounds darker.
Diminished squeezes the top note down: small and tense. Augmented pushes it up: wide, floating, like a question.
Sus chords have no third at all. Sus four leans on the fourth and wants to fall to the third — listen to it resolve.
Inversions keep the same notes but change the bass. Root position, then the third in the bass, then the fifth. Listen to the lowest note.
Close position keeps the notes inside one octave; open position spreads them wide. Same chord, a fuller sound.
A triad stacks two thirds on a root. Major: a major third (4 semitones), then a minor third (3) — C E G. Minor: minor, then major — C E♭ G. Both span a perfect fifth, 7 semitones.
Diminished stacks two minor thirds: C E♭ G♭ — the fifth shrinks to 6 semitones, a tritone. Augmented stacks two major thirds: C E G♯ — the fifth grows to 8.
In a major key the triads fall in place: major on 1, 4 and 5; minor on 2, 3 and 6; diminished on 7. Augmented never appears in major; it lives on 3 of harmonic minor.
Sus chords replace the third. Sus2 uses the 2nd (C D G), sus4 the 4th (C F G). With no third they are neither major nor minor — open and undecided until the third arrives.
A listening order: first, stable or not? Major and minor are stable. Then sort the rest: bright or dark (major, minor), squeezed (diminished), stretched (augmented), or hollow (sus).
A common confusion is minor versus diminished: both start with a minor third. Listen to the top note — in diminished it is a semitone lower and pulls inward.
Inversions name the bass: root in the bass is root position; the third, first inversion (figured 6); the fifth, second inversion (6/4). The quality never changes — only the weight of the chord.
In real music, major and minor triads carry most pop, folk and classical harmony. Diminished chords often pass between two others, and a sus4 resolving to major is a favorite in rock and hymns alike.
Recap: two stacked thirds make a triad; their sizes give major, minor, diminished or augmented. Sus replaces the third, and the bass names the inversion.
Add a seventh to a triad and you get a four-note chord: maj7 is dreamy, 7 (dominant) wants to move, m7 is mellow, half-diminished is dark, dim7 is tense and symmetrical.
Hi {name}! A seventh chord is a triad with one more third on top. Major seven: soft, dreamy, a little jazzy.
The dominant seven has a tense core that wants to move on. Here it resolves home.
Minor seven is mellow and relaxed. Half-diminished darkens it by lowering the fifth. Diminished seven lowers the seventh too — pure tension.
Four notes means four possible basses: root position, then the third, the fifth and the seventh in the bass. The seventh in the bass sounds the most restless.
Tip: first decide if the chord is bright or dark, then whether it is calm or tense. That narrows it down fast.
A seventh chord is a triad plus the seventh above the root. Its name comes from two choices: the triad (major, minor or diminished) and the seventh (major, 11 semitones; minor, 10; diminished, 9).
The five types on C: maj7 is C E G B; 7 is C E G B♭; m7 is C E♭ G B♭; half-diminished, ø7, is C E♭ G♭ B♭; diminished, °7, is C E♭ G♭ B𝄫 — sounding like A.
In a major key: Imaj7 and IVmaj7; ii7, iii7 and vi7 are minor sevenths; V7 is the only dominant seventh; viiø7 is half-diminished. The full diminished seventh comes from harmonic minor.
Why V7 pulls home: G7 contains B and F, a tritone apart. B rises to C, F falls to E, and the tension dissolves into the tonic chord.
How to hear the seventh: find the triad first, then listen to the top. A major seventh sits a semitone under the octave and rubs sweetly; a minor seventh is a whole tone under and sounds bluesy.
A common mistake is in the names: plain “C7” always means the minor seventh, B♭ — the dominant sound. The major seventh must be written maj7 or Δ7.
The diminished seventh is built only from minor thirds, so it divides the octave into four equal parts. B D F A♭ resolves to C — and the same sound, respelled, can lead to three other keys.
In real music: jazz runs on sevenths, and ii7–V7–Imaj7 is its most common progression. Blues puts a dominant seventh on every chord. Classical music relies on V7 and vii°7 to drive its cadences.
Recap: triad plus seventh. Major triad with a major seventh is maj7, with a minor seventh it is the dominant 7. Minor gives m7; diminished gives ø7 or °7.
Color chords borrow notes from outside the key. The cadential 6/4, the Neapolitan, the augmented sixth and borrowed chords each add a typical color before the music goes home.
Hi {name}! First a plain cadence. Then the same with a cadential six four: the home chord over the fifth in the bass, delaying the V.
In minor, the Neapolitan lowers the second step. It sounds noble and dark, and leads to V.
The augmented sixth: two notes spread apart and move outward to the same note, in the bass and on top. It pours into V.
Borrowed chords come from the minor key while you stay in major. The minor four gives a sweet, sad touch on the way home.
Listen for the moment the color changes, then for where it goes next. Almost every color chord leads to V or straight home.
Chromatic chords use notes from outside the key without leaving it. They color the road to a goal — usually V or I — and each has a typical sound and a typical destination.
The most common is the secondary dominant: a dominant seventh aimed at a chord other than I. In C, D7 with its F♯ is “V of V” and drives to G.
The cadential 6/4 is the tonic triad over 5 in the bass — C E over G. It sounds like home, but works as V with two notes delayed: the 6 falls to 5 and the 4 to 3.
The Neapolitan is a major chord on the lowered 2nd: in C minor, D♭ F A♭. It usually has F in the bass — the Neapolitan sixth — and moves to V, D♭ dropping to the leading note B.
Augmented sixth chords put ♭6 in the bass and ♯4 above — A♭ and F♯ in C. Both slide a semitone outward to the octave G. Italian, French and German versions differ in their remaining notes.
Borrowed chords come from the parallel minor while you stay in major: iv (F A♭ C), ♭VI (A♭ C E♭), ♭VII (B♭ D F). The A♭ is the giveaway — a darker 6th inside a bright key.

How to hear them: catch the odd note, then follow it. A sharp rising by semitone points to a secondary dominant; a flat 6 or flat 2 sinking toward 5 or 1 points to a borrowed, Neapolitan or augmented-sixth chord.
A common mistake is hearing the cadential 6/4 as a real arrival home. Check the bass: if it sits on 5 and V follows, the “home” was only a delay.
In real music, Mozart and Beethoven place Neapolitan and augmented-sixth chords at big cadences. In pop and rock, ♭VI–♭VII–I and the minor iv are classic moves.
Recap: a color chord borrows a note from outside the key, and that note almost always moves by semitone toward V or I.
The verse tells the story and is calmer; the chorus is fuller, louder and repeats a hook; the bridge brings a new color before the last chorus. Follow the sections and you can map any song.
Hi {name}! This is a verse: light drums, a soft pad, and a melody that keeps moving to new notes.
And the chorus: the drums and bass get busier, everything is louder, and the same short hook comes back again and again.
The bridge changes the color: chords from outside the usual set, a new melody, and it ends wanting to go back to the chorus.
Put together, many songs go verse, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge, chorus. Older standards use AABA: a tune twice, a bridge, then the tune again.
A 12-bar blues has its own map: four bars on I, two on IV, two on I, then V, IV, and a turnaround back to the top.
Song form is the order of a song’s sections. Each section is a group of bars, very often 8 or 16, with its own job. Letters label them: the same letter means the same music.
The verse sets the scene. Its music returns each time with new words, so it tends to stay calmer and lower, leaving room for the story.
The chorus is the center. The title and the hook usually live there; words and music both repeat, the melody often sits higher, and the band plays fuller.
Many songs add a pre-chorus, a short build between verse and chorus, plus an intro and an outro to open and close.
The bridge usually comes once, after the second chorus. It brings new chords — often starting away from the tonic — and leads back into a final chorus, often the biggest.
AABA, the 32-bar song form, has four 8-bar sections: a tune, the tune again, a contrasting B — also called the bridge or middle eight — and the tune to finish. Many jazz standards use it.
The 12-bar blues: four bars of I, two of IV, two of I, then V, IV, I, and often V in the last bar as a turnaround back to the top.
I I I I | IV IV I I | V IV I V
How to map a song: count bars in groups of four and mark every change — a drum fill, the band thinning or swelling, the melody jumping up. Sections usually change every 8 or 16 bars.
A common mistake is calling the first loud part the chorus. Check what repeats: a chorus brings back the same words, a verse brings new words over the same music.
Recap: verse tells, chorus repeats the hook, bridge contrasts. Count in fours, listen for changes, and you can map almost any song.
