Baroque runs in busy, equal lines; Classical is a clear tune over a light accompaniment; Romantic is rich, wide and flexible in time; the 20th century stacks fourths and new scales; jazz swings; pop loops four chords over a beat.
Hi {name}! Baroque: two lines running in steady, even notes, both equally important, like a conversation.
Classical: one clear, singable tune on top, with a light broken-chord pattern underneath, and a tidy cadence at the end.
Romantic: rich chords, wide waves in the left hand, and a tempo that breathes — it pushes ahead and then holds back.
Twentieth century: chords built from fourths sliding in parallel, a whole-tone melody, and uneven groups of beats.
Jazz: swung eighth notes, a walking bass, a ride cymbal and short chord jabs.
Pop: four chords looping over a steady backbeat, with a catchy hook. Listen for the rhythm first, then the harmony.

Style periods are rough labels for how music was written at a time. The usual outline is Baroque (about 1600–1750), Classical (1750–1820), Romantic (1820–1900) and the 20th century. Jazz and pop grew up alongside in the 1900s.
Baroque: polyphony — several equal lines woven together — over a busy bass, a steady motor rhythm, and plenty of ornaments. Bach and Handel, harpsichord and organ.

Classical: one clear melody with accompaniment, balanced 4- and 8-bar phrases, tidy cadences. Haydn, Mozart, early Beethoven. A hallmark is the Alberti bass: a broken chord played low, high, middle, high.
Romantic: bigger emotions, richer and more chromatic harmony, wide piano textures, and rubato — a tempo that bends. Chopin, Schumann, Brahms, Tchaikovsky.
The 20th century went in many directions: Debussy’s whole-tone scales and parallel chords, Stravinsky’s shifting meters, chords built in fourths, and music with no home key at all.
Jazz: a swing feel with long-short eighths, seventh chords and extensions, improvisation, and a walking bass. Pop: a steady backbeat on 2 and 4, short chord loops, verse–chorus form and a hook.
A listening order: first the rhythm (motor, flexible, swung or backbeat), then the texture (equal lines, or a tune with accompaniment), then the harmony (plain or rich).
The classic mix-up is Baroque versus Classical. Both sound tidy, but in Baroque every line stays busy, while in Classical one tune leads and the rest support it.
Recap: rhythm, texture, harmony — in that order. Equal busy lines say Baroque, a clear tune says Classical, rich and flexible says Romantic, swing says jazz, a backbeat says pop.

Tonic is at rest (I; in minor i), pre-dominant moves away (IV, ii; iv, ii°), dominant pulls home (V, vii°; V and vii°7 with the raised 7th). vi (minor: VI) stands in for the tonic after V, and leads to the pre-dominant before IV or ii. iii sits between tonic and dominant.
Chords do three jobs. Tonic: home, at rest. Pre-dominant: moving away. Dominant: pulling back home.
In major, I is tonic. IV and ii are pre-dominant: both hold the 4th degree. V and vii° are dominant: both hold the leading note.
Minor works the same way: i tonic, iv and ii° pre-dominant, V and vii°7 dominant, with the raised 7th.
iii sits between: two notes with I, two with V. Before vi it sounds like a step away from home, after I like a softer tonic. So we don’t ask for it.
vi does two jobs. After V it stands in for the tonic: the deceptive cadence. Before IV or ii it moves on toward the pre-dominant. VI in minor does the same.
Your turn: hear the key, then one chord. At rest, leaning away, or pulling home?
Function explains why chords can replace each other. Play vi where I was expected and the music still rests, a little darker: that is the deceptive cadence, V to vi.
Pre-dominants share the 4th degree, the note that falls to the 3rd of I. ii often replaces IV before V: ii–V–I is the heart of jazz harmony.
Dominants hold the leading note and, with a 7th, a tritone that wants to close: in G7 the B rises to C and the F falls to E.
In minor the leading note must be raised: the natural minor v has no pull. That is why minor keys borrow V and vii°7 from harmonic minor.
Functions also come in longer chains. T, PD, D, T is the basic phrase; a pre-dominant can be stretched, IV then ii, and the tonic can step down through vi on the way to it.
Recap: listen for rest, for leaning away, for pull. The bass helps: 1 rests, 4 and 2 lean, 5 and 7 pull, and 6 depends on what comes next.

A mode’s colour note makes the cadence: ♭VII–I Mixolydian, IV–i Dorian, ♭II–i Phrygian — no leading note, unlike V–I. A vamp’s chords name the mode: I–II Lydian, I–♭VII Mixolydian, i–IV Dorian, i–♭II Phrygian, i–♭VI–♭VII Aeolian.
♭VII to I: the Mixolydian cadence of rock and folk. The ♭7 replaces the leading note.
In minor, a major IV gives the Dorian colour. ♭II to i is Phrygian: flamenco, metal.
Compare V to I: the leading note rises a half step into home. The modal cadences arrive more gently, by whole steps or from above.
A vamp repeats two or three chords. Their notes pick the mode: I–II Lydian, for the ♯4; i–♭VI–♭VII Aeolian, natural minor.
Ask first: is home major or minor? Then find the one chord that holds a note outside plain major or plain minor. That note names the mode. Your turn.
Each modal chord carries the mode’s one special note. ♭VII holds the ♭7, II holds the ♯4, IV in minor holds the natural 6, ♭II holds the ♭2.
Aeolian needs two chords to prove itself: ♭VI gives the ♭6, ♭VII the natural 2, so it cannot be Dorian or Phrygian.
Mixolydian rock often adds IV: I, ♭VII, IV, I. The three chords together use exactly the notes of the mode.
Modes over a drone and modes over chords are different skills. Over a drone you hear each note against home; over a vamp you hear the chords’ colours, as a band plays them.
Where you hear them: ♭VII–I ends countless rock songs; i–IV is the Dorian groove of soul and modal jazz; i–♭II is the sound of flamenco; I–II floats over film scores.
Recap: home first, then the colour chord. ♭VII Mixolydian, II Lydian, IV in minor Dorian, ♭II Phrygian, ♭VI with ♭VII Aeolian.
From the minor side jazz borrows ivm7, ivm6, ♭VImaj7, ♭VII7, ♭IIImaj7 and ♭IImaj7. On the way home: ♭VImaj7–♭VII7–I, the backdoor ivm7–♭VII7–I, and Tadd Dameron’s ♭IIImaj7–♭VImaj7–♭IImaj7–Imaj7.
From the parallel minor and its modes, jazz borrows major-7th colours: ♭VImaj7, ♭IIImaj7, ♭IImaj7 — and ivm7.
The classic move: IVmaj7 to ivm6. One note falls a half step, and the major key darkens for a moment.
On the way home: ♭VImaj7, ♭VII7, I. Or the backdoor: ivm7, ♭VII7, I.
Tadd Dameron’s ending, as in “Lady Bird”: ♭IIImaj7, ♭VImaj7, ♭IImaj7, Imaj7.

To name them, follow the bass: ♭II sits a half step above home, ♭III a minor 3rd above, ♭VI a major 3rd below, ♭VII a whole step below, and iv a 4th above. Then check the colour: major 7th or minor. Your turn.
Where they come from: ♭III, ♭VI, ♭VII and iv belong to the parallel natural minor; ♭II to Phrygian. In C: E♭, A♭, B♭, Fm and D♭.
In jazz these chords usually take a major 7th, except ♭VII, which is a dominant 7th: B♭7 in C, the chord of the backdoor.
♭IImaj7 to Imaj7 is not the tritone substitute. D♭7 has C♭ as its 7th and pulls hard; D♭maj7 has C and floats down.
The Tadd Dameron turnaround keeps the bass moving by 4ths and half steps: E♭, A♭, D♭, C. Each chord is a major 7th, so the colour stays bright while the roots wander.
IV to iv is the most common borrowing of all, in jazz and in pop alike: the 6th degree falls a half step, A to A♭ in C, and the line keeps falling to G.
Recap: borrowed chords colour a major key from the minor side; the bass tells you which one.

Bass first, then each chord’s quality. A secondary ii–V aims at another chord (Em7 A7 → Dm7); a tritone substitute keeps the 3rd and 7th and moves the root a tritone (D♭7 for G7); the V’s colour: 13 bright, 7♭9 and 7alt dark, 7♯11 lydian.
Writing down changes: first the roots, from the bass. Then each chord’s quality: minor 7, dominant, major 7.
Em7 A7 is a ii–V of its own, aimed at Dm7: a secondary ii–V. The A7 makes D sound like home for a moment.
A tritone substitute: D♭7 for G7. The 3rd and the 7th swap places, and the bass falls by half steps into the I.
The V’s colour: 13 bright, 7♭9 dark, 7alt darkest, 7♯11 lydian.
A walking bass line: the root on beat 1, chord or scale tones in the middle, then a half step into the next root, from below or from above. Your turn.
Roots first: hum the bass of each chord and find its distance from the last. 4ths up mean ii–V motion; half steps down mean tritone substitutes.
Then the quality, from the 3rd and 7th. Minor 3rd and ♭7: minor 7. Major 3rd and ♭7: dominant. Major 3rd and major 7: major 7.
The backdoor, ivm7 to ♭VII7 to I, arrives from a whole step below: Fm7, B♭7, C. It sounds softer than G7, with no leading note.
Tensions come last. The top of the voicing tells you: a 13th sits a whole step above the 5th, a ♭9 a half step above the root.
Secondary dominants are easy to miss when the ii is left out. A7 straight into Dm7 is still V of ii: write it as A7, and listen for the C♯ that leads into D.
For the walking bass, write beat 1 of every bar first — the roots — then fill in the approach notes, then the middle of each bar.

Planing moves one chord shape in parallel: diatonic planing stays in the key, so the qualities change; exact planing keeps one quality. Constant structure puts one quality on roots that move without a key. Voice leading is the opposite: notes stay, the rest moves by small steps.
Planing: one shape moved in parallel under a melody. Every voice moves the same way.
Diatonic planing stays in the key, so the qualities change: Cmaj7, Dm7, Em7. Exact planing keeps one quality.
Constant structure: one quality on roots that move without a key — Debussy, Bill Evans, modal jazz.
The So What voicing — three 4ths and a 3rd — is often planed: on E, then on D, inside D Dorian.
Voice leading is the opposite: common tones stay where they are, and the other voices move by the smallest steps they can. Listen for which of the two you hear. Your turn.
Planing came into harmony with Debussy, who moved whole chords in parallel to colour a melody instead of leading voices toward a goal.
In diatonic planing the melody note decides each chord: build the same kind of stack below it, using only notes of the key.
Exact planing ignores the key: every chord is the same, so the roots can land on any note. That freedom is what makes constant structure sound modern.
To hear the difference, follow an inner voice. In planing it moves exactly with the top; in voice leading it often stays still while the top moves.
Which shape is it? A maj7 sounds bright with a half step at the top, an m7 soft, a dominant 7 restless, and a stack of 4ths open and hollow, with no 3rd to say major or minor.
Recap: parallel or led, in the key or exact, and which shape. Those are the three questions of this unit.

The 12-bar blues is the standard; an 8-bar blues runs I V IV IV I V I V; a common 16-bar blues stretches the first four bars on I to eight. AABA puts the bridge third; ABAC starts its second half like the first and ends differently. Around the tune: an intro, a tag (the last phrase again) or a coda (a new ending).
Blues lengths. The 12-bar blues is the standard. An 8-bar blues runs I, V, IV, IV, I, V, I, V. A common 16-bar blues stretches the first four bars on I to eight.
Count bars from the first tonic until the form starts again. The move to IV is a landmark: bar 5 in the 12-bar, bar 3 in the 8-bar, bar 9 in the 16-bar.
Song forms: AABA puts a contrasting bridge third. ABAC starts its second half like the first and ends differently. ABAB alternates two phrases.
Around the tune: an intro before it, often a vamp like I–vi–ii–V.
At the end: a tag repeats the last phrase, a coda adds a new ending. Your turn.
The 8-bar blues “Key to the Highway” is the classic example of I, V, IV, IV, I, V, I, V. Other 8-bar blues exist; what they share is the length and the I–IV–V chords.
The 16-bar blues here holds I for eight bars before the usual last eight of the 12-bar. Count patiently: the IV comes late.
In AABA the bridge is the only new music; it usually moves to another key area and returns. In ABAC the third phrase returns to A, and C turns toward the final cadence.
A tag often repeats the last two bars three times over a turnaround before the final chord. A coda is new material: a vamp, a chromatic descent, a held chord.
An intro sets the key and the groove before the melody. Listen for the moment the tune starts: that is where you begin counting the form.
Recap: count bars, compare phrases with the first one, and notice what was added before or after the tune.

Mirror every note around the axis between the 3rds of the tonic chord (in C, between E♭ and E): C ↔ G, D ↔ F, E ↔ E♭, A ↔ B♭, B ↔ A♭. Major triads become minor: V → iv, IV → v, I → i, ii → ♭VII, vi → ♭III, iii → ♭VI; G7 → Fm6.
Negative harmony mirrors every note around an axis between the 3rds of the tonic chord: in C, between E♭ and E.
D and F swap, A and B♭, B and A♭. A major triad turns into a minor one.
So V, G B D, mirrors to F A♭ C: the minor iv. G7 becomes Fm6. IV becomes v, ii becomes ♭VII, vi ♭III, iii ♭VI.
Hear it in a cadence: G7 to C, then its mirror, Fm6 to C. The same pull home, from the minor side.
To tell them apart by ear: the dominant's B rises to C; the mirror's A♭ falls to G. A whole ii–V–I, Dm7 G7 C, mirrors to Gm7 Fm6 C.
It is a way to find minor-side colours for a major tune, not a rule of harmony. Your turn.
The idea goes back to the theorist Ernst Levy, and the musician Jacob Collier made it widely known. Its rule is simple arithmetic: in C, a note n mirrors to 7 minus n, counted in semitones.
The axis has two sides: between E♭ and E, and across the circle between A and B♭. No note mirrors onto itself.
Why it sounds right: the mirror keeps every interval, upside down. The leading note B rising to C becomes A♭ falling to G — a half step into the 5th of the tonic.
A ii–V–I in C mirrors to B♭, Fm6, Cm. Most players use only the dominant part: iv6 or ♭VII7 in place of V, landing on a major I.
Try it with a melody: a phrase that ends 2 to 1 in C, D to C, mirrors to F to G. Mirrored lines often land on the 5th where the original landed on the root.
Recap: mirror around the 3rds of I. V becomes iv, the colours come from the minor side, and the pull home stays.

There are only three diminished 7th chords. A 6th chord touches two of them; the third shares no note with it and is the scale’s own diminished: C6 or Cm6 + B°7 = the 6th-diminished scale, and B°7 = G7♭9 without its root.
There are only three diminished 7th chords. Every other one repeats the notes of one of these.
C6 touches two of them: C and A are in C°7, E and G in C♯°7. The third, B°7 — the same notes as D°7 — shares no note with it.
That one is the scale’s own diminished. C6 and B°7 together make the 6th-diminished scale, and B°7 is G7♭9 without its root: the dominant.
The other two make the 6th chord. Raise E♭ and G♭ of C°7, and it is C6. Raise only the G♭, and it is Cm6: the root sits a 4th above the raised note.
The minor 6th keeps the same partner: Cm6 and B°7 make the minor 6th-diminished scale. Your turn.
Why only three? A diminished 7th chord splits the octave into four minor 3rds. Move it up a minor 3rd and you get the same four notes again, so only three starting notes give new chords: C, C♯ and D.
The partner is always the diminished on the 7th degree, for any 6th chord: F6 takes E°7, B♭6 takes A°7, Gm6 takes F♯°7.

Because the two share no note, every note of the scale belongs to exactly one of them. That is what lets Barry harmonise any melody note: 1, 3, 5 and 6 take the 6th chord, the notes between take the diminished.

Two diminished chords together, C°7 and C♯°7, do not make the 6th-diminished scale. They make the half-whole diminished scale: eight notes with no tonic chord inside. That is where the two are easily confused.
Recap: the 6th chord touches two diminished chords and grows from them; the third is its partner, the dominant of the scale.

Passing: the bass moves by half steps into a new chord (I6–♯I°7–ii7, I6/3–♭III°7–ii7). Auxiliary: the bass holds and the chord comes back (C6–C°7–C6; over a C bass ♯IV°7 has the same notes). Dominant: vii°7 stands for V and goes home.
The bass climbs by half steps: C6, C♯°7, Dm7. The diminished passes between two chords a whole step apart.
On up: Dm7, D♯°7, C6 over E. And down: C6 over E, E♭°7, Dm7. The same notes, named by the direction of the bass.
Auxiliary: the bass holds C, the chord leaves and comes back. C6, C°7, C6: the root and the 6th stay, the 3rd and the 5th dip a half step. Over the C bass, F♯°7 — ♯IV°7 — has the same notes.
Dominant: B°7 is G7♭9 without its root. It stands for V and goes home.
Bass by half steps into a new chord: passing. Bass holds and the chord returns: auxiliary. Instead of V: dominant. Your turn.
A passing diminished also resolves up a half step, like a leading note: C♯°7 is the vii°7 of Dm7. What makes it passing is the chromatic bass between two chords.
The third passage of the scale: F6, F♯°7, C6 over G. Coming down, G, G♭, F: the same diminished from above.
The auxiliary works on IV too: F6, F°7, F6, with F and D held. Pianists use it to make a long chord breathe without leaving it.

How to tell them apart in a tune: follow the bass. A chromatic step into a new chord means passing; a held bass under a chord that leaves and returns means auxiliary; a diminished after a pre-dominant, going straight home, is the dominant.
A common mistake is to call every diminished a dominant. Play the bass alone first: if it walks by half steps, or sits still, the diminished is decorating, not resolving the key.
On the keys these passages are k-sixdim 5; the auxiliary with its two common tones held is k-sixdim 11.

Every 6th chord has a diminished neighbour on each side in the 6th-diminished scale: all four voices step to it and back (C6 → D F A♭ B → C6 → B D F A♭ → C6), from every inversion, with the bass moving too.
Barry Harris liked to say that chords move to chords. A 6th chord steps up to the diminished, and back.
And down to the diminished below, and back. Every voice moves by step inside the scale; no voice leaps.
Do it from each inversion of the 6th chord, and let the bass move too: the left hand plays the lowest voice an octave down.
In minor the same moves work: Cm6 steps to the same B°7, above and below, because the scale’s diminished does not change.
The voice-leading meter counts how far each voice moves: here never more than a whole step. Your turn on the keys.
Why it works: in the 6th-diminished scale the notes of the 6th chord and of the diminished alternate. So the scale step above or below every note of one chord is a note of the other.
This is what makes a static chord sound like it is moving. A bar of C6 becomes C6, B°7, C6, the line on top walking by step.
In a tune every chord can move this way: Dm7 as F6 with its E°7, G7 as Dm6 with its C♯°7, C as C6 with B°7. That is k-sixdim 9 and 10.
A common mistake is to move only the top voice and leave the others. Then two voices clash with the diminished. All four go together, every time.
Practice it slowly first, out of time, until your hand finds each neighbour without looking. Then add the click: one chord a beat, and the bass moving with the lowest voice.
Recap: 6th chord, diminished, 6th chord — up and down, from every position, bass included. Small steps, all voices.
Cm6 (C E♭ G A) over A is Am7♭5; over F it is F9 — the m6 is the 9 chord without its root (3, 5, ♭7, 9 of F). An m6 on its root, a m7♭5 a minor 3rd below, a 9 chord a 5th below.
Cm6: C, E♭, G, A. Put A under it, and the same notes are Am7♭5.
Put F under it: F, A, C, E♭, G — F9. The minor 6th is the 9 chord without its root: the 3rd, 5th, ♭7 and 9th of F.
One shape, three chords: an m6 on its root, a m7♭5 a minor 3rd below, a 9 chord a 5th below.
And the 9 chord wants to resolve: F9 goes to B♭, a 4th up. The minor 6th shape moves by step into B♭6.
In a ii–V–I in C: Dm7 is F6, and G7 is Dm6, the 9 chord without its root. Listen to the bass. Your turn.
Count it from F: F is the root, A the 3rd, C the 5th, E♭ the ♭7 and G the 9th. Leave out the F and the four notes left are Cm6.
In minor: Dm7♭5 is Fm6, so the minor ii–V–i the 6th-diminished way is Fm6 over D, G7, Cm6.
Bass players and pianists share this: the pianist keeps one m6 shape while the bass chooses the chord. One shape, three chords: that is why the minor 6th is so useful.
A common slip: calling Cm6 over F a D chord. Count from the bass, not from the top: F under C E♭ G A is F9.
The same holds in every key: Gm6 is Em7♭5 and C9 without its root; E♭m6 is Cm7♭5 and A♭9. Find the m6 first, then count down a minor 3rd and a 5th for the bass.
On the keys, k-sixdim 13 plays the minor 6th over its three basses in all twelve keys.

Drop-2 voicings sit on four adjacent strings — a six-string has three such sets (6–5–4–3, 5–4–3–2, 4–3–2–1). Play the 6th chord and its diminished up the scale on each; the shapes change where the G–B major 3rd falls inside the set.
A drop-2 voicing takes the second voice from the top of a close chord down an octave. It fits four adjacent strings.
Six strings give three sets: 6–5–4–3, 5–4–3–2 and 4–3–2–1. The same chord has a different shape on each, because of the major 3rd between the G and B strings.
The diminished in drop-2 is the easy one: four notes a minor 3rd apart keep the same shape when you move it three frets.
Up the scale: the 6th chord on 1, 3, 5 and 6, the diminished on 2, 4, ♭6 and 7. Find each top note on the set’s highest string and fit the chord under it.
Start slowly, one chord a beat, and say the string set out loud before you play. Your turn.
On 6–5–4–3 the voicings sit low and dark: good for a chord-melody bass register, less so for comping with a bass player.
On 5–4–3–2 the major 3rd between G and B falls between the two top strings, so every shape bends there by one fret.
On 4–3–2–1 the top string carries the melody: this is the set for playing a tune in Barry’s block chords.
Minor works the same way with the ♭3: Cm6 and B°7. Learn the minor scale of chords on the set you know best first.
Moving between sets: the same chord with the same top note can sit on two sets. Choose the one that keeps your hand in place, so the line on top stays smooth and the shapes change little.
A good routine: one key a day, the scale of chords up and down on each set, then a standard’s melody harmonised on 4–3–2–1.
Recap: three sets, two chords, eight shapes per octave on each. The guitar levels name the set in every item.
Scale degrees on the beats, a chromatic note between. At a half step, skip to the note above and come back: C C♯ D D♯ E G F F♯ G G♯ A A♯ B D C.
Barry’s chromatic scale keeps every scale degree on a beat. Between two degrees a whole step apart goes the chromatic note.
From E to F there is no note between. So skip up to G, and come back to F: the skip-back keeps F on the beat.
The whole octave up: the same skip from B to C, through D.
On a dominant the half step moves: from A to B flat, skip to C and come back.
Practice it in all twelve keys: free time first, then on the click, with every scale degree landing on the beat. Your turn.
Why it works: in eighths, every whole step takes two notes, so the degrees stay on the beats. A half step takes only one, so the skip adds the missing note.
How to hear it: tap the beat and listen for the scale on the taps. The skip sounds like a little turn just before the 4th and before the octave.
Coming down, the same rule: at a half step go to the scale note below and come back up. The scale’s own notes stay on the beats.
It works on the minor 6th-diminished scale too, with four skips. A common slip is to rush the skip: keep the eighths even.
Then two voices: the same chromatic scale with a second voice a 3rd, a 6th or a 10th below, both moving together. Later, every other interval.
To keep: degrees on the beats, chromatic notes between, and at a half step skip past and come back.
A scale outline gives each bar its scale, up from the root. On a dominant: the three important arpeggios, the 5-4-3-2 phrases, 3 to ♭9, and seven down to the 3rd.
A scale outline gives each bar its scale, up from the root. On a dominant: the three important arpeggios, then the scale down by the rule.
The scale outline of a tune: each bar its scale from the root up, chord tones on the beats. A chord that lasts two bars comes back down.
On C7, the three important arpeggios: on 1, the minor on 5, the major on flat 7. Each one 1, 3, 5, 8.
The 5-4-3-2 phrases, from Workbook 1. Here the 5 and the 3 on C7.
Then an arpeggio into the scale: C7’s arpeggio up, then the scale down by the rule from the next chord tone, so the chord tones stay on the beats.
Seven down to the 3rd: over D half-diminished to G7, play B flat 7 up, then down from its 7th, landing on B.
3 to 9 on C7: from the 3rd up to the 9th, E G B flat D. It is the minor 7 flat 5 inside the dominant, and it lands on the 9th.
Learn each device in all twelve keys, then put it into a scale outline. Your turn.
An arpeggio up, then the scale down by the rule from the next chord tone: C E G C, then E D C B B flat A G F E.
3 to flat 9 over the family: G7, B flat 7, D flat 7 and E7 all share the same four notes, the diminished on the 3rd.
The three important arpeggios can also start from their 3rd. The same three chords, on 1, the minor on 5 and the major on flat 7, but the line moves in smaller leaps.
The combined 5-4-3-2 lick. The exact notes come from a workshop attendee’s notes and wait for a check against the workbook.
The dominant rule in one breath: from 1, 3, 5 or flat 7 add one half step, or three; from 2, 4 or 6 add none, or two. Then the chord tones land on the beats.

The dominant rule from every degree: start on each degree in turn, on the beat, and come down the scale. From 1, 3, 5 or flat 7 add one half step; from 3, 5 or flat 7 you may add three; from 2, 4 or 6 add none, or two.
Practice each device round the cycle of fourths: C7, F7, B flat 7, and on through all twelve keys. Free time first, then the click, then a whole tune.
A common slip in an outline: playing Dm7’s own scale over ii. Barry says ii is V: over Dm7 to G7, play the G7 scale. A half-diminished chord becomes the dominant a major 3rd below it.
Feel the "and": comp on 2+ and 4+, push the bass onto the "and" of 4. Then write your own line over a move, a chord tone on every beat, and use it in a tune.
Feel the "and": comp on 2+ and 4+, push the bass onto the "and" of 4.
Barry taught feeling the "and". Comp a short chord on the "and" of 2 and of 4, and let the drums keep the beat.
Feel 6 in 4: a line in dotted quarters floats across the bar line while the band stays in 4.
Now hit only the ands: the 3rd of each chord on every and, nothing on the beats, while the drums keep the time.
Then compose: over I to VI7, or ii–V–I, write a line with a chord tone on every beat, scale or chromatic notes between. Play it twice, then in a tune.
Move the same short chord to the and of 1 and the and of 4. A new place in the bar, and the next beat stays clear.
The bass feels it too: push the next root onto the and of 4 and tie it over the bar line.
Every take is measured against the click, in all twelve keys. Your turn.
Barry said rhythm rules the world. Dance taught him to feel the and: the off-beat is where swing lives.
Try the game: hit only the ands, the 3rd of each chord, while the drums keep the beat. A common slip is to drift onto the beat when the line gets busy; count the ands out loud.
Feel 6 in 4 also comes in cells of three eighths. Each cell starts on a chord tone, and the cells keep crossing the bar line.
Count out loud, one and two and, and clap only on the and. When that is easy, play the chord there and let the metronome take the beats. Then move it around the bar.
Composing a line: pick a chord tone for every beat first, then fill the eighths between with scale notes or a half step.
The bass walks on the beats but leans into the next bar: the next root on the and of 4, tied over the bar line. The band still meets on the downbeat.

Then use it in a tune. Rhythm changes repeat I to VI7 and ii–V, so your line has many places to go. Harris and Rees had students write a line once and play it in every tune that has the same move, in every key.
A chord on the and sounds lighter than one on the beat. Keep the comp short and soft, so the soloist has room and the time feels wide.

A pivot is an arpeggio with some notes moved an octave: same order, new contour. The classic: the root on top, then drop to the 3rd below and climb 3-5-7. Cmaj7 = C, then E G B. The drop is a minor 6th over a major 3rd, a major 6th over a minor 3rd.
An arpeggio usually climbs straight up from the root: C, E, G, B.
A pivot moves some of its notes an octave. The order stays, the shape changes. The classic one: the root on top, then drop to the 3rd and climb.
Listen to the drop. Over a major 3rd it is a minor 6th; over a minor 3rd, a major 6th.
It works on any seventh chord: maj7, m7, 7, m7♭5.
And on the 6th chord and the diminished, Barry’s two home chords.
Practice it in all twelve keys: first in free time, then on the click. Your turn.
Any chord tone can sit on top. 3rd on top: drop to the 5th, climb 5, 7, 1. Then the 5th on top, then the 7th.
The mirror: the root at the bottom, leap up to the 7th, and fall: C, then B, G, E.
Through ii–V–I, a pivot on each chord’s downbeat keeps a chord tone on every beat: D, F A C; G, B D F; C, E G B.
Scale plus pivot: Barry’s scale comes down by the half-step rules, lands on a chord tone on the beat, pivots there, and the scale carries on down.

Pivot plus enclosure, a warm-up from Harry Likas and Barry: down the major bebop scale, a chord tone on every beat. Pivot: the next scale note jumps an octave. Enclosure: the chord tone above, the half step below, the target.
A common slip is to drop to the 5th instead of the 3rd. From the root on top, the next chord tone down is always the 3rd. Sing the drop before you play it.
Recap: a pivot moves notes of an arpeggio an octave. The next lesson puts one inside a falling scale line.
The melody stays on top; under each strong melody note goes a voicing of the bar’s chord that contains it: shells, then four-way close, drop 2, drop 3.
First the melody alone. Learn it until you can sing it, because every chord you add will sit under it.
Shells under it: the root in the left hand, and the 3rd and 7th of the chord just below the melody note.
Four-way close: the melody note is the top of a close four-note chord. A major chord under its root or its 6th becomes a 6 chord.
Drop 2: take the second voice from the top down an octave. The melody sings out above a wider, warmer chord.
Your turn: phrase by phrase, in all twelve keys. Free time first, then the click. Move each inner voice to the nearest note.
Only the notes on beats one and three, and the notes where a chord starts, get a chord. The notes between them pass by on their own.
A note that is not in the chord, like a 9th, stays single for now. The 6th-diminished blocks, coming later, give such a note the diminished chord.
Drop 3 takes the third voice from the top down instead. It spreads the hands further, a sound pianists and guitarists both love for ballads.
Common mistake: letting a lower voice climb above the melody. Check the top note first, then fill in the rest from the top down, one voice at a time.
Where it lives: big-band sax sections, Shearing’s locked hands, and every solo-piano ballad. The melody leads; the harmony follows it.
To keep: melody on top, a chord tone under it, the smallest move to the next chord. Sing the melody while you play the chords.
Melody on the top strings; under it, step by step: the bass note on the downbeats, a guide tone, a drop-2 voicing on the top four strings, a passing diminished.
Find the melody in one position on the top strings, so that a chord can fit under every note without a jump.
Add the root on string six or five on each downbeat. Two voices already sound like a small band.
Then a guide tone, the 3rd or the 7th, under the melody instead of the root. Now the harmony is clear without a bass.
Drop 2 on strings four, three, two and one, with the melody on string one. Notes outside the chord can take the diminished that contains them.
Your turn: each step on four bars, then a whole chorus, in all twelve keys. Free time first.
Pick the position from the highest melody note: it must sit on string one or two, with room for three strings below it. Then check the lowest note fits the same hand.
Chord on the strong beats, single notes between. The ear fills in the harmony, and the melody keeps moving.
The bass on the downbeats is the start of a solo-guitar texture. Later the bass can walk between the chords.
Common mistake: a voicing that leaves the melody on string two while the chord rings above it. Keep the melody the highest string sounding.
Where it lives: Joe Pass, Johnny Smith and Barney Kessel played whole tunes this way, with no band at all, from slow ballads to fast swing.
To keep: melody first, then the bass, then the guide tone, then the full voicing. Each step is a finished arrangement on its own, so play every step musically.
Learn the head’s changes step by step, then swap chords bar by bar: tritone sub, extra ii–V, backdoor, passing dim, line cliché, Coltrane. The melody must still fit each new chord.
Comp the head as written first: roots, guide tones, shells, rootless, drop 2, and then the melody over your own comp.
Now change bars. A dominant that resolves can become the dominant a tritone away: the melody’s 3rd turns into the new chord’s 7th.
Check every strong melody note against the new chord. A chord tone or a tension is fine; the 11th over a major chord clashes.
The backdoor, a passing diminished, a line cliché: each fits only where its chords are. The studio on the family page shows you where.
Then play your reharm: comp it, walk it on the bass, and play the melody over it, in all twelve keys.
A tritone sub keeps the 3rd and 7th of the dominant and slides the bass down a half step into the next chord. Under a melody root it gives a sharp 11.
An extra ii–V puts the related minor chord before a dominant, or the ii–V of the next chord in a bar that only holds a chord.
The Coltrane sub turns a ii–V into the Giant Steps cycle: three keys a major third apart, landing on the same tonic.
Common mistake: too many devices at once. Leave a bar as written between changes; the melody needs a place to breathe.
Where it lives: every jazz record of a standard. Players rarely play the changes exactly as written, but the melody always fits.
To keep: change a bar, check the melody, play it on your instrument, and hear the new colour. A good reharm makes the old melody sound new.
Hear it, sing it inside, then find it on your instrument. Start from home: the key comes first, and every note is a step or a leap from there.
Hi {name}! Here is a short tune. Before you touch your instrument, sing it quietly in your head.
The chords first tell you where home is. Find home on your instrument, then ask: does the tune go up or down, by a step or a leap?
Wrong notes are fine. Play one, listen, and slide up or down until it matches what you heard.
Later the tunes get longer, a note outside the key sneaks in, and you play the bass line under chords. Last of all, the rhythm counts too.
Your turn! Listen, sing it inside, and play it back. Mute the strings between notes so I hear each one clearly.
Playing by ear is translation: a sound in your head becomes a place on your instrument. It has three stages — hear it, sing it inside, find it. Skip the middle stage and you are only guessing.
Start with the key. The chords before each tune point to 1, home. Find 1 on your instrument first; then every note is a degree you already know, not a random pitch.
Next, the contour: up or down, and how far. A step is one or two half steps — the neighboring note of the scale. Anything bigger is a leap. Here: step, step, leap, step down.
A good listening strategy: lock in the first and the last note. Many short tunes end on 1, so the last note is often a free answer. Fill in the middle afterwards.
A note outside the key usually leans on a neighbor. Here E flat slides into E. If a note sounds "wrong but close", try a half step up or down from the scale note.
For a bass line, ignore the top of the chords and follow the lowest note. Most of the time it is the root: here C, F, G and back to C.

How the app hears you: with a microphone, play one clear note at a time, let it ring, and mute the others — chords and buzzing strings confuse pitch detection. With a MIDI keyboard every note arrives exactly.
The common mistake is hunting note by note before the tune is in your head. Sing it first, even twice. To keep: home first, then contour, then the notes.
Each fret is a half step. Learn the open strings and the natural notes on strings 6 and 5, and every other note is a step away — and it all repeats at fret 12.
Hi {name}! Every fret raises the note by a half step. Listen to the low E string climbing fret by fret.
Between most natural notes there are two frets. Only E to F and B to C sit side by side, one fret apart.
Learn string 6 and string 5 first: they name the root of most barre chords. G is on fret 3 of string 6, C on fret 3 of string 5.
At fret 12 everything starts again, an octave higher. And the same note lives in many places on the neck.
Your turn! I name a note, you tap it on the neck. Say the names out loud while you look — it sticks faster.
Standard tuning, from the thickest string (6) to the thinnest (1): E, A, D, G, B, E. Every pair is a fourth apart, except G to B, which is a major third.
There are seven note names and twelve half steps. Each fret is one half step. Here are the natural notes on string 6: frets 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10 and 12.
And on string 5: A at 0, B at 2, C at 3, D at 5, E at 7, F at 8, G at 10. These two strings are your map — barre-chord roots live here.
The fret between two naturals has two names. Fret 2 on string 6 is F sharp or G flat — same sound. Choose the name the key uses: F sharp in G major, G flat in D flat major.
Octave shapes carry names across the neck. From string 6 or 5: skip a string, two frets up. From string 4 or 3: skip a string, three frets up, because of the B string. G at fret 3 → fret 5 → fret 8.
Fret 5 of a string equals the next open string — fret 4 on the G string. That is also how guitarists tune by ear: the two notes should ring as one.
A good drill: one note, every place. Find all the Cs — string 5 fret 3, string 3 fret 5, string 2 fret 1, string 1 fret 8 — and say the name each time.
The common mistake is counting from the nut every time. Use landmarks instead: the dots at frets 3, 5, 7, 9 and 12. To keep: learn strings 6 and 5, then move by octave shapes.
No frets, so your ear places the finger. In first position each string covers the notes up to the next open string: one finger per step.
Hi {name}! A violin is tuned in fifths: G, D, A, E. Listen to the four open strings.
In first position, four fingers climb the string until the next open string takes over. On the G string: A, B, C, D.
Some fingers sit close together — B to C is only a half step. Viola and cello work the same way, just lower: C, G, D, A.
Sharps and flats sit between the fingers: F sharp is a little higher than F. Your ear decides exactly where.
Your turn! I name a note, you place it on the fingerboard. Then find every place a note lives in first position.
The bowed strings are tuned in fifths. Violin: G, D, A, E from the G below middle C. Viola: C, G, D, A, a fifth lower. Cello: C, G, D, A, an octave below the viola.
The double bass is the exception: it is tuned in fourths, E, A, D, G, like the low four strings of a guitar, and sounds an octave below where it is written.
On violin in first position, finger 1 is a whole step above the open string and finger 4 reaches the next open string's note. On the A string: B, C sharp, D, then E — the same as open E.
What changes from key to key is where the half step falls. With C sharp, finger 2 sits close to 3. With C natural, it slides back next to 1. Hear the difference.
On the cello the hand covers less: in first position each finger is a half step, so four fingers span a minor third. Reaching a whole step between fingers 1 and 2 is called an extension.
Check your intonation against the open strings. Finger 3 on the violin A string is D, an octave above the open D. In tune, the open string rings along in sympathy.
The common mistake is placing fingers by memory and not by ear, so the notes drift flat as the hand tires. To keep: tuned in fifths, finger patterns follow the key, and your ear has the last word.
On a guitar every interval is a shape you can move anywhere. The only catch: between the G and B strings, shapes shift up one fret.
Hi {name}! An octave on the guitar is a shape: two strings over and two frets up. Move it anywhere and it still sounds like an octave.
Same fret on the next string is a fourth. Two frets up on the next string is a fifth — the power chord.
A major third is one fret back on the next string, a minor third two frets back. Hear how the major one is brighter.
Crossing from G to B, the strings are only a third apart, so every shape moves one fret up. Remember the shift and the shapes never lie.
Your turn! Start from the dot and find the interval I ask for. Later, you will hear it and find it by ear.
An interval is a number of half steps, and on one string that is simply a number of frets. Open A to fret 7 on the same string is seven half steps: a perfect fifth, A to E.
Across to the next string you start from five half steps, a fourth. So: two frets back is a minor third, one back a major third, same fret a fourth, one up the tritone, two up a fifth.
Two strings over you start from ten half steps, a minor seventh. One fret up is a major seventh, two frets up the octave. Same fret, two strings over: A to G.
Any shape that crosses from the G string to the B string moves one fret up, because that pair is a major third apart. An octave from string 4 to string 2 is three frets up, not two.
The power chord is root, fifth and octave stacked as one shape. From G on string 6, fret 3: the fifth and the octave both sit at fret 5 on the next two strings.
In real music, sixths on the G and E strings, a string skipped between them, give the sweet double stops of soul and country. Slide the pair through the key: major sixth, major sixth, minor sixth.
The common mistake is forgetting the G–B shift, so a third or an octave comes out a half step flat. To keep: count half steps, start from a fourth on the next string, and add one fret past G.
Five open shapes — C, A, G, E, D — slide up the neck to play any chord (CAGED). Small triads on three strings and drop voicings for sevenths come from the same idea.
Hi {name}! A chord box is the neck standing up: strings left to right, frets top to bottom. A circle means open, a cross means do not play.
Major or minor: one finger changes. Listen to A major, then A minor — only the third moved down.
Slide an open shape up and put a barre where the nut was, and it plays another chord. The E shape at fret 3 is G major.
Three strings are enough for a triad. On the top strings, the same chord can be played in three inversions up the neck.
Your turn! Name the open chord, build triads, find the CAGED shape, then stack seventh chords. Bass players: root, fifth, octave, then arpeggios.
Read a chord name as six digits, string 6 to string 1. C is x32010: string 6 silent, then fret 3 (C), fret 2 (E), open G, fret 1 (C), open E. Only three note names: C, E, G.
A major triad is root, major third, fifth; minor lowers the third by one fret. Open E is 022100; lift one finger, 022000, and it becomes E minor.
CAGED names the five open shapes. Each one holds the root in a different place, so each can be barred and moved. The A shape at fret 3 is C major: x35553.
The shapes link up the neck in that order. For C major: the open C shape, the A shape at 3, the G shape around 5, the E shape at 8, the D shape at 10 — then C again at 12.
Same chord, different color: each shape puts a different note on top. Open C ends on E, the A shape on G, the E shape at fret 8 on a high C.
Small triads on strings 3, 2 and 1 cover the neck in three inversions: G-C-E at the nut, C-E-G at fret 5, E-G-C at fret 8. They cut through a band without clashing with the bass.
For seventh chords guitarists use Drop 2: take a close voicing, C-E-G-B, and drop the second note from the top down an octave. You get G-C-E-B, on the top four strings at frets 5-5-5-7.
The common mistake is learning shapes as finger pictures without knowing where the root is. Mark the root in every shape. To keep: five shapes, one chord, the whole neck.
A scale on the neck is a pattern under one hand. Learn it from a root on string 6, then the five pentatonic boxes that cover the whole neck.
Hi {name}! Here is G major, one octave up from G on string 6. Four frets, three strings, one hand that hardly moves.
The minor pentatonic has only five notes. Box 1 starts on the root on string 6: two notes on every string. This is A, at fret 5.
Each box joins the next one, five in all, until the pattern repeats at fret 12. The root dots tell you which box you are in.
Three notes on every string makes fast runs easy: the same picking on every string. Bass players learn approach notes that lead into the next root.
Your turn! Play the scales I ask for, from the lowest note up, and name the box you see.
A major scale is a pattern of whole and half steps: W W H W W W H. From G on string 6: G, A, then B, C, D on string 5, then E, F sharp, G on string 4.
The minor pentatonic is 1, flat 3, 4, 5, flat 7 — in A: A, C, D, E, G. No half steps at all, which is why almost nothing in it sounds wrong.
The same box is also C major pentatonic: C, D, E, G, A. Same frets, different home. Which one you play depends on the chord underneath and the note you land on.
Add one note, the flat 5 — E flat in A — and you have the blues scale. Use it as a passing note between 4 and 5, not as a place to stop.
Three notes per string turn a seven-note scale into a wider, even pattern. G major from fret 3: G A B, then C D E, then F sharp G A — each string fingered the same way.
Practice music, not just up and down. Play the scale in thirds: 1-3, 2-4, 3-5. It trains your fingers and your ear to skip, the way melodies really move.
The common mistake is running boxes without landing anywhere. End phrases on a chord tone and know which dot is the root. To keep: one pattern, one root, and the five boxes join into one neck.
The black keys come in twos and threes. C sits just left of the two, F just left of the three — and from there you can find any note, interval or chord.
Hi {name}! Look for the black keys in groups of two and three. C is the white key just left of the two black ones.
Each black key has two names. The one between C and D is C sharp, and also D flat — same key, same sound.
Octaves get numbers. The C in the middle of the piano is C4; the next C up is C5.
Count half steps, black keys included, to build an interval. Four half steps make a major third; stack a minor third on it and you have a major chord.
Your turn! Find the notes I name, then build intervals and chords right on the keys.
An octave on the keyboard has twelve keys: seven white and five black. The black keys alternate in groups of two and three, and that pattern is your map.
More landmarks: D sits between the two black keys, and the middle black key of the three is G sharp, or A flat. C and F sit just left of each group.
A full piano has 88 keys, from A0 to C8. Middle C is C4; the A above it, A4, is the tuning note at 440 hertz. Octave numbers change at every C.
White neighbors are usually a whole step apart, with a black key between. Only E–F and B–C are half steps. So C major is all white, and G major needs one black key: F sharp.
Build triads by counting half steps. Major is 4 + 3, minor 3 + 4, diminished 3 + 3, augmented 4 + 4. From C: C-E-G, C-E♭-G, C-E♭-G♭, C-E-G♯.
Names follow letters, not keys. The note a major third above C is E; a minor third above C is E flat, never D sharp, even though it is the same black key.
A practice tip: right hand plays a triad with fingers 1, 3, 5, left hand with 5, 3, 1. In scales the thumb passes under after 3 — in C major, after E in the right hand.
The common mistake is counting white keys from the far end. Jump to the nearest black group instead. To keep: groups of two and three, C and F to their left, and count half steps for everything else.
Each fret is a half step. Learn the E and A strings first; everything repeats at fret 12.
Hi {name}! A bass has four strings. From the lowest: E, A, D and G, each one a fourth above the last.
Every fret raises the note by a half step. Listen to the E string climbing fret by fret.
Most natural notes are two frets apart. Only E to F and B to C sit side by side, with no fret between them.
Learn the E and A strings first: the roots of most bass lines live there.
At fret 12 it all starts again, an octave up. Your turn: I name a note, you tap it on the neck.
The natural notes on the E string: frets 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10 and 12. Say them as you play them.
On the A string: A at 0, B at 2, C at 3, D at 5, E at 7, F at 8, G at 10.
The fret between two naturals has two names: fret 2 on the E string is F sharp or G flat. Use the name the key uses.
The same note lives on the next string, five frets lower: fret 5 on E equals the open A string.
Octaves carry names across the neck: two strings up, two frets up. G at fret 3 on E is also G at fret 5 on D.
The usual mistake is counting from the nut every time. Use landmarks instead: frets 3, 5, 7 and 12 carry dots.
To keep: E A D G, a half step per fret, the octave at 12. Five minutes a day of naming notes out loud is enough.
Root, fifth, octave: one shape, every key. Arpeggios and approach notes grow from it.
Hi {name}! On the bass one shape works in every key. Start on the root, on the E or the A string.
The fifth is one string up and two frets up. The octave is two strings up and two frets up.
Add the third and you have the chord. Major and minor are one fret apart.
Move the same shape two frets up and the key changes from G to A, while the fingers stay exactly the same.
An approach note leads into the next root: a half step below it, above it, or its fifth. Your turn: tap the shapes.
Root and fifth carry most bass lines in pop, rock and country. The octave adds lift without new notes.
The fifth also sits below the root: same fret, one string down. Handy when the root is on the A string.
Seventh chords add one more note: a major seventh is one fret below the octave, a minor seventh two frets below.
A half step below the next root pulls hardest. A half step above sounds bluesier. Try both into the same chord.
The usual mistake is looking for each note alone. Think in shapes from the root, and say the chord tone you land on.
Walking lines use all of it: a chord tone on the first beat, then steps, and an approach note on the last beat into the next chord.
To keep: root, fifth and octave first, then the third and the seventh, then the note that leads to the next root.
The bass is tuned in fourths, so each interval is one shape on every pair of strings.
Hi {name}! Every bass string is a fourth above the one below it. So a shape you learn once works on every pair of strings.
The octave: two strings up and two frets up. G on the E string at fret 3, and G on the D string at fret 5.
One string up: the same fret is a fourth, two frets up is a fifth.
Thirds sit one string up and back toward the nut: one fret back for a major third, two frets back for a minor third.
Your turn: I give you a dot on the neck and an interval, and you tap where it lands. Say the interval as you find it.
Small intervals stay on one string: a half step is the next fret, a whole step is two frets.
Sixths and sevenths sit one string up and further toward the body: a major sixth four frets up, a minor seventh five, a major seventh six.
The tenth is a bassist’s favourite: from the E string to the G string, the same fret gives a minor tenth and one fret up a major tenth.
On a guitar the G and B strings break the pattern and every shape shifts there. On the bass nothing breaks it: there is no shift to remember.
The usual mistake is counting frets one by one. Look at the shape instead: the hand learns the distance, and the ear checks it.
To keep: octave two over and two up, fifth one over and two up, fourth straight across. Practice them from every root on the E and A strings.
One finger per fret, four frets: the major scale and each pentatonic box fit under one hand.
Hi {name}! Put your second finger on the root, on the E or the A string. With one finger per fret, the whole major scale is under your hand.
The fingering is the same in every key: two notes on the root string, then three, then three. Move the hand and the key moves with it.
The minor pentatonic, box 1: the root under your first finger, two notes on each string. Most bass fills live in this box.
There are five boxes. Each one starts on the next note of the scale on the E string, and they link up the neck.
Your turn: play the scales from the root I show you, then look at a box and name it.
On a bass, a box keeps its shape on every pair of strings, because all the strings are a fourth apart.
A fill is three or four notes from the box that lead into the next chord. Fall from above into its root, or into its third.
The same box serves a major key too: A minor pentatonic and C major pentatonic have the same five notes. Over a C chord, aim for C, E and G inside it.
The usual mistake is playing the box only up and down. Play it in small groups, skip notes, and always say where the root is.
On a six-string bass, three notes per string run a scale across the neck without moving the hand. That has its own technique level.
To keep: one finger per fret, the root under finger two for the major scale and under finger one for the pentatonic box. Five slow minutes a day are enough.
Treble clef for the right hand, bass clef for the left. Middle C sits on a ledger line between them.
Hi {name}! Piano music has two staves: the treble clef on top, the bass clef below. Middle C, C4, sits on one short line between them.
Treble clef lines, bottom to top: E, G, B, D, F. The spaces spell F, A, C, E.
Bass clef lines, bottom to top: G, B, D, F, A. The clef’s two dots hug the F line.
A note on the staff is one exact key. G on the treble staff’s second line is G4, the G just above middle C.
Your turn: I show a note, you find that exact key — the right octave counts.
Landmarks beat counting: treble G (line 2), middle C, bass F (line 4). Read every other note from the nearest one.
Ledger lines continue the staff. A3 under the treble staff is the same key as A3 on the bass staff’s top line.
A sharp raises the note to the next key on the right, a flat lowers it to the left — often a black key, not always: E sharp is F.
The usual mistake is reading the bass clef as if it were treble — everything a third off. Say the clef before the note.
Two notes stacked on the staff sound together. Read the lower one, then count the lines and spaces up to the other: line to line is a third, line to space a second or a fourth.
To keep: landmark notes, the clef first, then the octave. Five minutes a day turns counting into seeing.
A triad is two thirds stacked. Major: 4 then 3 half steps; minor: 3 then 4. Inversions move the bottom note to the top.
Hi {name}! A major triad: root, four half steps up, three more. On C: C, E, G.
Minor swaps them: three, then four. C, E flat, G. Diminished is three and three; augmented four and four.
Move the root to the top and you get the 1st inversion: E, G, C — written C/E. Once more: the 2nd inversion, G, C, E.
A slash name tells you the bottom note: C/E is a C chord with E in the bass. Find the bass first, then the rest above it.
Your turn: I give the bottom note and the chord, you build it on the keys.
Seventh chords add one more third: maj7 C E G B, dominant 7 C E G B flat, m7 C E flat G B flat, half-diminished C E flat G flat B flat.
Jazz pianists play shells in the left hand: root, 3rd and 7th — the notes that name the chord. The 5th can go.
The usual mistake is counting white keys instead of half steps. Every key counts, black or white.
Inversions keep the hand still: from C to F to G, move only the notes that must move. C E G, C F A, B D G.
Black-key roots look strange but follow the same counts. D flat major: D flat, F, A flat. Feel the shape, then say the names.
To keep: count half steps, name the bass first, and let the hand keep its place. The technique drills then play the same shapes through every key.
A major scale is whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. Every key has its own pattern of black and white.
Hi {name}! C major uses only white keys. Notice the two half steps, where no black key sits between: E to F, and B to C. Everywhere else the scale moves by a whole step.
Start on G and keep the same pattern: one black key appears, F sharp.
Harmonic minor raises the 7th: A minor gets G sharp, a step and a half above F.
Each new sharp key adds one black key: D major has F sharp and C sharp. Keep the pattern and the keys follow.
Your turn: I give the first note, you play the whole octave up, in order.
Melodic minor going up raises the 6th and the 7th; it comes down as natural minor, with both lowered again. Exams ask for it in both directions.
Modes start the major pattern elsewhere: dorian is minor with a raised 6th, mixolydian major with a lowered 7th, lydian major with a raised 4th.
The usual mistake is guessing from the look of C major. Count the steps, then check the key signature.
Flat keys work the other way: F major has one black key, B flat; B flat major adds E flat, and each flat key after it adds one more flat.
Each scale also has its own thumb places. In most white-key scales the right-hand thumb plays the tonic and the 4th; in flat keys it waits for the first white key.
To keep: the step pattern decides every note. Play each new scale slowly, saying the names, before you add speed in the technique drills.
Chord tones on the strong beats, 1 and 3. On beat 4 an approach note leads into the next root: a half step, the next root’s 5th, or a scale step.
Hi {name}! A walking line plays one note on every beat. It starts simply: the root and the 5th, two notes a bar.
The rule of the walk: chord tones on the strong beats, one and three. Beats two and four may pass between them.
Beat four aims at the next root. The strongest pull is a half step. From C to F: G, then F sharp, then F.
Or play the next root’s 5th on beat four. C leads into F the way G leads into C: a small cadence in one note.
Or arrive by a step of the scale. Here C, D, E, then G steps down into F.
Your turn: walk with the band, in every key. On the piano the left hand plays the same line. Every note is measured: chord tones on one and three, an approach on four, even quarters.
Why chord tones on one and three? Those are the beats the ear checks. When they land on the chord, the band hears the harmony even with no piano playing.
From below or from above: choose the side that keeps the line inside your range. Near the low E string, approach from above.
The dominant approach is the target’s 5th: a fourth below it or a fifth above it. On the bass, a fourth below sits at the same fret, one string lower.
Real lines mix all three. A good habit: choose beat four first, then fill one to three. Here is a two-five-one with half steps into each root.
The common mistake is reaching the new root late, or a beat early. The approach is a full quarter, and the root arrives exactly on one.
Practice one chord change at a time, in all twelve keys. Sing the target before you play beat four: when the ear knows where the line is going, the hand follows.
Guitar music is written in the treble clef, an octave above the sound. In position I each finger takes one fret, 1 to 4.
Hi {name}! Guitar music is written on one staff, in the treble clef. Each line and each space is one note name.
The guitar sounds one octave lower than written. That keeps its low notes close to the staff instead of far below it.
The open strings, low to high: E, A, D, G, B, E. The low E hangs on three ledger lines; the high E sits in the top space.
Position I: the first finger at fret 1, one finger per fret up to fret 4. Strings 3 to 1 first: G and A, then B, C, D, then E, F, G.
Rhythm reads the same as on any instrument: a quarter is one beat, two eighths share a beat. Count aloud while you play.
Your turn: read in position I and play in time. The app hears every pitch and every onset, so read ahead, not note by note.
Why not just TAB? TAB tells you where to put a finger; the staff tells you what to play and when. The same E can be played in several places on the neck.
string 1 open · string 2 fret 5 · string 3 fret 9
A position is named after the fret of the first finger: position V puts the first finger at fret 5. Reading by position keeps the hand still while the eyes stay on the page.
Three landmarks below the staff: the low E on three ledger lines, middle C on one ledger line, and G on the second line. Read the rest as steps from them.
The key signature holds for the whole piece. With one sharp, every F is F sharp, on every string and in every octave.
The common mistake is looking down at the hand. Keep the eyes on the page and find the frets by feel, one finger for each fret.
Read a little every day: four bars, slowly, saying the note names. Speed comes later; keeping the beat through a wrong note comes first.
Bass music is written in the bass clef, an octave above the sound. Open strings: E below the staff, A in the bottom space, D on the middle line, G in the top space.
Hi {name}! Bass music is written in the bass clef. Its two dots sit around the line of F, which gives the clef its name.
Like the guitar, the bass sounds one octave lower than written. So its low notes stay close to the staff.
The open strings: E on a ledger line below the staff, A in the bottom space, D on the middle line, G in the top space.
First position: one finger per fret, frets 1 to 4. On the E string: F, F sharp, G, G sharp. On the A string: B flat, B, C, C sharp.
The lines of the bass clef, bottom to top: G, B, D, F, A. The spaces: A, C, E, G. Say them once a day until they are automatic.
Your turn: read in first position and play in time. Every note is measured, pitch and onset, so read ahead and keep the beat.
Why the staff and not only TAB? Charts, big-band parts and theatre books are written on the staff. Reading lets you play a new part right the first time.
Four landmarks: low E on its ledger line, D on the middle line, G in the top space, and middle C on one ledger line above the staff.
On the upright the low positions use three fingers, 1, 2 and 4, because the notes lie farther apart. Two frets’ worth, a whole step, fills the hand.
Some levels ask only for rhythm on one string. Count aloud, one and two and, and keep the click in your body, not only in your ears.
The common mistake is guessing from the shape of the line. Name the first note, then read each move as a step or a skip, up or down.
Read four bars a day, first in a key you know, then with a new key signature. Short and daily beats long and rare.
Five notes, five boxes: each box joins the next. The same boxes are a minor pentatonic from one root and a major pentatonic from the note three frets up.
Hi {name}! The minor pentatonic has five notes. In A: A, C, D, E, G. It has no half steps, so almost nothing in it sounds wrong.
A box is those notes under one hand, two on every string. Box 1: the first finger at fret 5, with the root under it on string 6.
Frets 5 and 8 take the first and fourth fingers; frets 5 and 7 take the first and third. The roots, on strings 6, 4 and 1, are your map.
The top notes of box 1 are the bottom notes of box 2. Box by box, five shapes climb the neck, and box 1 returns at fret 17.
The same notes from C are C major pentatonic: C, D, E, G, A. Same boxes, a new home three frets up.
Your turn: box 1 in A, slowly and in free time first, then the tempo ladder, then every key. The root on string 6 tells you where the box starts.
Why boxes? A solo needs notes that sit under the hand at speed. The five boxes cover the whole neck, and in each one the root lies in a new place.
Join two boxes with a slide. In box 1, slide on string 3 from fret 7 to fret 9, and the hand is in box 2.
Minor root, then three frets up, the major root: A minor and C major, E minor and G major. Over a C chord, land on C; over A minor, land on A.
Later levels add the blues note, the flat five, and the major pentatonic as a sound of its own. Box 1 stays the map they hang on.
The common mistake is running up and down without landing anywhere. End each phrase on a root or a chord tone, and always know which dot is home.
Learn one box a week: up, down, then short phrases inside it. Then join it to the box before. Say the root’s name each time you pass it.
A quarter is one beat, two eighths share a beat, a rest is a silence you count. Count aloud: 1 & 2 &.
Hi {name}! Rhythm starts with the beat, a steady pulse you can count. Count one, two, three, four, and play one note on each.
Eighth notes split each beat in two. Count one and, two and, and play on every number and on every and.
A rest is a silence you count. A quarter rest lasts one whole beat: keep counting, and keep the hand ready for the next note.
Now mix them: a quarter, two eighths, a quarter, then a rest. Say the counting aloud as you play; your voice keeps your hands honest.
On guitar, mute the strings and strum. On bass, use one open string. On keys, one key. Only the rhythm counts here.
Your turn: play with the click. The app measures every onset against the beat, so a clean rest counts as much as a clean note.
Why count aloud? The voice is a second clock. When you say “and”, the hand knows exactly where the half beat is.
On guitar and bass a rest means muting. Lift the fretting finger off the fret while it still touches the string, or touch the string with the plucking hand.
An eighth rest takes half a beat. Rest on the number and play on the and: that off-beat is the sound of reggae and ska.
Tempo is a choice, not a test. Start slow enough to play every rest cleanly, then let the tempo ladder raise it a little at a time.
The common mistake is rushing after a rest. Count the silence as carefully as the notes; the next note arrives exactly on its beat.
To keep: quarters on the beat, eighths on the number and the and, every rest counted, and the voice and the hand together.
Root and 5th, the Alberti bass, stride, shells: four ways for one hand to give both the bass and the harmony.
Hi {name}! Under a melody the left hand has two jobs: the bass and the harmony. The simplest way is the root and the 5th.
The Alberti bass breaks the chord: low, high, middle, high. In C: C, G, E, G. Classical sonatas are full of it.
Stride: a low bass note on beats one and three, a chord in the middle on two and four. The jump between them is the skill.
Shells, for jazz: the root plus the 3rd or the 7th. D minor 7 takes D and C, G7 takes G and B, C major 7 takes C and B.
Your turn: each new pattern starts slowly, in free time where the notes are new, then climbs the tempo ladder in all twelve keys. Keep the left hand softer than the melody.
Boogie-woogie walks the chord in eighths: C, E, G, A, B flat, A, G, E. Eight notes, one bar, over and over, under a bluesy right hand.
The left hand can also walk: one note per beat, chord tones on one and three, an approach note into the next root. The walking lesson shows how.
Keep left-hand chords above the C below middle C. Lower down, 3rds turn muddy; down there play single notes, 5ths and octaves.
Pop left hands are simple: the root in octaves, or root, 5th and octave, often in eighths under the chords of the right hand.
The common mistake is a left hand as loud as the melody. Play the left hand alone, then bring it one level down under the right.
Practice the left hand alone until it runs without thought, then add the melody one bar at a time. Every style here goes into all twelve keys.
Four seventh chords — maj7 dreamy, 7 restless, m7 mellow, m7♭5 dark — and ii–V–I chains them home.
Hey {name}! Jazz rarely stops at three notes. Add a 7th on top of a chord and it gets a whole new color.
Major 7: C, E, G, B. Dreamy and soft — the 7th sits just a half step under the octave.
Lower that 7th to B♭ and you get the dominant 7: bluesy and restless. It wants to move — here, to F.
Minor 7 lowers the 3rd too: C, E♭, G, B♭. Mellow and cool, more relaxed than sad.
Half-diminished, m7♭5, lowers the 5th as well: C, E♭, G♭, B♭. Dark and mysterious, like a question.
Now chain them: minor 7, dominant, major 7. That is ii–V–I, the most common move in jazz. Feel the middle chord pull home.
Two cousins: V–I is just the last two chords. I–vi–ii–V starts at home and wanders off — the classic turnaround.
Your turn! Hear one chord and name its color: major 7, dominant 7, minor 7 or half-diminished. Then name the progression — count the chords, and listen for where home is.
A seventh chord stacks one more third on a triad: 1, 3, 5 and 7. Its color comes from two choices — the kind of triad, and the size of the 7th: major (11 half steps above the root) or minor (10).
The four recipes. maj7: major triad, major 7th. 7: major triad, minor 7th. m7: minor triad, minor 7th. m7♭5: diminished triad, minor 7th. Here they are on C, one after another.
Why the dominant is restless: its 3rd and 7th — E and B♭ in C7 — form a tritone, the most unstable interval. In F the tritone resolves by half steps: E rises to F, B♭ falls to A.
In a major key each degree has its own seventh chord: Imaj7, iim7, iiim7, IVmaj7, V7, vim7 and viiø7. There is only one dominant — V7 — which is why it points home so clearly.
To hear the color, ask two questions. Does it want to move? Then it is the dominant. If it rests: bright is maj7, soft is m7. Dark, hollow and unstable is m7♭5.
The classic mix-up is maj7 against 7. Put the root on top and compare: the major 7th rubs a half step below it, the minor 7th sits a whole step below.
At the keyboard, walk through all four by lowering one note at a time: Cmaj7, lower the 7th — C7, lower the 3rd — Cm7, lower the 5th — Cm7♭5. Each step moves one note a half step.
In real music ii–V–I is everywhere; the standard “Autumn Leaves” is built from chains of it. In a minor key the ii is half-diminished: Dm7♭5, G7, Cm.
To keep: a seventh chord is a triad plus a 7th. maj7 rests, 7 pulls, m7 relaxes, m7♭5 darkens — and ii–V–I chains them home.
Natural minor, Dorian and melodic minor differ only at the top (6 and 7); swing plays eighth notes long–short.
Hey {name}! Two jazz secrets today: a minor scale with a bright top, and the swing feel.
Start with natural minor: C, D, E♭, F, G, A♭, B♭, C. Dark all the way up.
Raise just the 6th, A♭ to A, and you get Dorian — still minor, but cooler and brighter.
Raise the 7th too, and you have melodic minor: minor at the bottom, major at the top. In jazz it stays the same on the way down.
The trick: listen to the last four notes. Two dark ones, one, or none — natural, Dorian, melodic.
Now swing. Pairs of eighth notes go long–short, like a relaxed walk: doo-ba, doo-ba. Straight first, then swung.
In the exercise you write a lick as scale degrees. This one is 1, 3, 5, 7, 6, 5 — up the chord, then a step down.
Your turn! First name the scale — natural minor, Dorian or melodic minor. Then write two swung licks as numbers, and sing one back.
All three minor scales share the bottom five notes: C, D, E♭, F, G. Only the 6th and 7th change. Natural minor has ♭6 and ♭7, Dorian has 6 and ♭7, melodic minor has 6 and 7.
Why raise the 7th? B is a leading tone, a half step under C. It turns the V chord from Gm7 into G7, which pulls home far more strongly. Compare.
Classical melodic minor comes down as natural minor. Jazz keeps the raised notes both ways and treats it as a parent scale: its 7th mode is the altered scale, its 4th mode the Lydian dominant.
Each scale has its chord. Natural minor fits a tonic minor, Cm. Dorian fits Cm7 as a ii chord. Melodic minor fits Cm6 and Cm(maj7) — the bright minor home of jazz.

Swing splits each beat unevenly: the first eighth is longer, close to two thirds of the beat, the second shorter. At fast tempos the swing gets straighter, and players often accent the short off-beat note.
How to hear it: tap the beat and listen to the note between taps. Straight, it falls exactly halfway. Swung, it arrives late, on the last third of the beat.
The common mistake is over-swinging: dotted eighth plus sixteenth, a 3-to-1 split. It sounds stiff and jumpy, not relaxed. Compare it with real swing, about 2 to 1.
Practice: play or sing the melodic minor scale in swung eighths with a metronome on 2 and 4, saying the degree numbers. Then write short licks as numbers — it trains ear and hands together.
In real music: Miles Davis’s “So What” is built on D Dorian. Minor 6 chords, from melodic minor, close many minor-key jazz tunes. And swung eighths have been the basic pulse of jazz since the 1930s.
To keep: the three minors differ only in 6 and 7. Swing is long–short, about two to one, and relaxed.
C/E means a C chord with E in the bass: the bass can be the root, 3rd, 5th — or a note outside the chord.
Hey {name}! A slash chord is a chord over a bass note. C/E means a C chord with E at the bottom. Same chord, new floor.
Bass on the root first: plain C. Solid and grounded, nothing to add.
Bass on the 3rd: C/E. Lighter, as if the chord stands on tiptoe.
Bass on the 5th: C/G. It floats, waiting for something to happen.
The bass can also sit outside the chord. C/D sounds open and modern; C/B♭ hides a bluesy 7th underneath.
Bass notes tell a story too. In 1, 7, 6, 5 the bass walks down the scale — C, B, A, G — and the chords follow.
Your turn! You hear the bass note, then the chord — tell me which note is in the bass. Later, write a bass line as numbers, like 1, 7, 6, 5.
X/Y means chord X with note Y as the lowest note. When Y belongs to the chord, it is an inversion: C/E is the first inversion, C/G the second. When it does not, a new sound appears.
Sometimes a slash chord is just another name. C/A has A, C, E and G — exactly Am7. Writers choose the slash name when they want you to think of C on top of a moving bass.
C/G has a job of its own: in classical harmony it is the cadential six-four. It sits on the dominant bass and leans into G7, then home to C.
A favorite outside bass: F/G. Over G, the F triad gives the ♭7, 9 and 11 — a soft G9sus4 that still leads to C. You hear it all over pop, gospel and modern jazz.
Slash chords let the bass walk by step under steady chords. C, G/B, Am, Am/G, F: the bass falls C, B, A, G, F while the upper notes barely move.
The opposite is a pedal point: the bass stays put while the chords change above it. C, F/C, G/C, C — tension builds over the held C, then relaxes.
To hear the bass, ignore the chord and hum the lowest note. Then compare it with the chord: the root sounds solid, the 3rd light, the 5th floating, and a note outside the chord adds a new color.
Common mistake: playing the chord’s root in the bass anyway, or putting the slash note on top. The note after the slash must be the lowest — left hand on piano, lowest string on guitar.

In real music: Procol Harum’s “A Whiter Shade of Pale” rides a long descending bass under slash chords, and Bach loved walking bass lines. Pop ballads use C/E and G/B constantly to keep the bass smooth.
To keep: the letter after the slash is the bass. In the chord, it is an inversion; outside it, a new color or a new chord name.
C6 (C E G A) and B°7 (B D F A♭) take turns: C D E F G A♭ A B — eight notes, rest and tension alternating.
Hey {name}! Barry Harris — the bebop pianist and much-loved teacher — built his harmony from just two chords, moving together.
The first is a major 6 chord: C, E, G, A. Warm and settled — home.
The second is a diminished 7th: B, D, F, A♭ — stacked minor thirds. Tense, and it wants to go home.
Weave them together and you get the C 6th-diminished scale: C, D, E, F, G, A♭, A, B. Eight notes, not seven.
Here is the magic: give every scale note its chord, and they alternate — 6 chord, diminished, 6 chord. Rest, tension, rest.
Make the 6 chord minor — C, E♭, G, A — and you get the minor 6th-diminished scale. Same idea, darker home.
How to spot it: listen near the top. G, A♭, A — two half steps in a row. A plain major scale just goes G, A, B.
Your turn! Hear a scale up and down: is it the 6th-diminished scale or another? Count the notes — the others have seven. Sometimes you hear one note: does it live in the 6 chord or the diminished?

Precisely: the major 6th-diminished scale joins two four-note chords with no note in common. The tonic 6 chord gives 1, 3, 5, 6; the diminished 7th on the 7th degree gives 7, 2, 4, ♭6. Together: eight notes.
Why eight notes matter: in eighth notes, eight notes fill a bar of 4/4 exactly. Start on C on the beat, and every beat gets a C6 note — C, E, G, A — while the diminished notes fall between.
The harmonized scale in full: each scale note on top, its chord underneath. Notes from C6 get an inversion of C6; notes from the diminished get B°7. Up the whole octave:

What the diminished chord does here: B°7 is G7♭9 without its root, so it acts as the dominant. The scale goes home, dominant, home — that is why the harmonized scale sounds like constant motion and rest.
The minor 6th-diminished scale swaps C6 for Cm6 — C, E♭, G, A — and keeps the same B°7. Its notes: C, D, E♭, F, G, A♭, A, B. One note changes; the whole system stays.
The same eight notes are also known as the major bebop scale. Barry’s twist is how you think of them: not as a scale with an extra note, but as two chords taking turns.
Practice the scale from every note of C6 — C, E, G and A — so a C6 note always lands on the beat. From E: E, F, G, A♭, A, B, C, D, E.
The common mistake: starting on a diminished note on the beat. From D, the beats get D, F, A♭ and B — all tension, nothing lands. If a line feels lopsided, check what sits on the beat.
Barry Harris (1929–2021) came up in Detroit’s bebop scene and taught workshops in New York for decades. Many pianists’ block-chord voicings come straight from this harmonized scale.
To keep: a 6 chord plus the diminished chord a half step below its root — eight notes, rest on the beat, tension between.
Lower one note of a dim7 a half step → a dominant 7 on that note. Raise one → a minor 6 a fourth above it.
Hey {name}! Time for a Barry Harris magic trick. Start with a diminished chord: B, D, F, A♭.
Every note is a minor third from the next. It is perfectly symmetrical, so it belongs to no single key — it can turn into many chords.
Lower just one note a half step. A♭ drops to G, and the chord becomes G7, a dominant. The lowered note is its root.
Any of the four notes works. Lower F to E and you get E7. Four notes, four dominants.
Now go up: raise one note a half step. B rises to C, and you get F minor 6 — F, A♭, C, D. The root is a fourth above the note you raised.
So: down makes a dominant — bright, bluesy, pulling forward. Up makes a minor 6 — darker and softer. Back to back:
Your turn! You hear the diminished chord, then one note moves. Dominant 7 or minor 6? Later, find which note moved, and name the chord.
