Why lowering makes a dominant: G7♭9 is G plus B°7 — B, D, F, A♭. So the diminished chord is a dominant 7♭9 missing its root. Lower A♭ to G and the root is back: G7.
All four downs from B°7: B to B♭ gives B♭7, D to D♭ gives D♭7, F to E gives E7, A♭ to G gives G7. The lowered note is always the new root.
All four ups: B to C gives Fm6, D to E♭ gives A♭m6, F to F♯ gives Bm6, A♭ to A gives Dm6. The raised note is the 5th of the new chord, so the root is a fourth above it.
Symmetry in, symmetry out. The four dominants — G, B♭, D♭, E — are a minor third apart, and so are the four minor 6 chords — D, F, A♭, B.
How to hear the direction: after a downward move the chord still leans forward, bright and bluesy — a dominant. After an upward move it settles into a soft, shadowed minor. Listen:
At the piano, hold B°7 in the right hand and move each finger in turn, first down, then up, naming each chord aloud. Then do the same from C°7 and C♯°7 — that covers every key.
The common mistake is naming the wrong root. Down: the note that moved is the root. Up: the note that moved is the 5th — count a fourth up from it.
In playing, the move is a voice-leading tool: hold the diminished chord, then nudge one note at the last moment to land on the chord you need — B°7, G7, then home to C6.
To keep: one note down a half step — a dominant on that note. One note up — a minor 6 a fourth above it.
One note down → dominant 7; one up → minor 6; two neighbors up or down together → major 6.
Hey {name}! Quick recap. From B diminished, lower one note and you get a dominant, G7. Raise one and you get a minor 6, F minor 6.
Now move two neighbors together. Raise B and D to C and E♭: you get A♭6 — A♭, C, E♭, F. A major 6, sunny and settled.
Or lower two neighbors: B and D drop to B♭ and D♭. Now it is D♭6 — D♭, F, A♭, B♭. Another major 6.
This is the heart of Barry’s method: the diminished chord is the engine. Nudge it a half step and you land on the chord you need.
Three colors to tell apart. Dominant 7: restless. Minor 6: dark and soft. Major 6: bright and at rest.
A listening tip: still restless? Probably the dominant. Sounds finished? It is a 6 chord — then ask: sunny major or shadowy minor?
Your turn! The diminished chord sounds, then one or two notes move. What did it become: dominant, minor 6 or major 6? On the next level, name the exact chord.
The full map from one diminished chord: one note down gives a dominant 7, one note up a minor 6, and two neighboring notes moved together — up or down — a major 6.
Raise two neighbors and they become the 3rd and 5th of a major 6; the root is a major third below the lower one. B and D rise to C and E♭: C is the 3rd, so the chord is A♭6.
Lower two neighbors and they become the 6th and the root; the upper of the two is the root. B and D fall to B♭ and D♭: D♭ is the root, B♭ its 6th — D♭6.
Four pairs each way. Raising gives A♭6, B6, D6 and F6; lowering gives D♭6, E6, G6 and B♭6. Here are D6 and G6, both from moving F and A♭.

Count it up: one diminished chord reaches four dominants, four minor 6s and eight major 6s — sixteen chords, each one or two half-step moves away. That is why the diminished chord sits at the center of Barry’s system.
Telling 6 from m6: a minor 6 hides a tritone between its ♭3 and 6 — A♭ and D in Fm6 — so it sounds shadowed and a little restless. A major 6 has no tritone; it simply rests.
A listening order: first ask whether it still pulls — a dominant. If it rests, ask major or minor. For the exact name, find which notes moved and which way.
Common mistake: moving two notes that are not neighbors. Raise B and F — a tritone apart — and you get C, D, F♯, A♭: a D7♭5, not a 6 chord. Neighbors means a minor third apart.
Practice on all three diminished chords: B°7, C°7 and C♯°7. Move each pair up and down and name the major 6 — twenty-four in all, every major 6 twice.
To keep: two neighbors up — the raised notes are the 3rd and 5th. Two down — the upper lowered note is the root. Either way, a major 6.
B°7 makes G7, B♭7, D♭7 and E7 — doors to C, E♭, G♭ and A, four keys a minor third apart.
Hey {name}! You can turn a diminished chord into a dominant. Now follow it home. Lower A♭ to G: G7, which resolves to C.
Lower F to E instead: E7, which goes home to A — a minor third below C.
Lower B to B♭: B♭7, heading to E♭ — a minor third above C.
And lower D to D♭: D♭7, which lands on G♭ — a tritone away, the far side of the circle.
So one diminished chord is a doorway to four keys: C, E♭, G♭ and A, each a minor third apart. Barry used this to slip between keys.
A tip: hum the first home note and keep it. When the new home arrives, is it the same, three half steps up or down, or the strange tritone?
Your turn! First the reference: diminished, G7, C. Then the same diminished chord goes somewhere else. Same key, a minor third up, a minor third down, or a tritone away?
Why it works: each note of B°7 is the 3rd of one dominant, and that 3rd is the leading tone of a key. B leads to C, D to E♭, F to G♭, and A♭ — spelled G♯ — to A.
There are only three diminished 7th chords: C°7, C♯°7 and D°7. Every other is one of these renamed, because each repeats after a minor third. B°7 has the same notes as D°7, F°7 and A♭°7.
So three diminished chords, four keys each, cover all twelve keys. Learn the trick on B°7 and you hold the map to a third of all keys.
The diminished chord can also skip the dominant and resolve straight home, every note moving by step: B to C, F to E, A♭ to G. Hear it go to C, then to A.
A real modulation: start in C, slip through B°7 and E7, and arrive in A. The diminished chord is the hinge — it belongs to both keys.
How to hear where it went: keep the first home note in your ear and sing the new one after it. Three half steps is a minor third, up or down; six is the tritone, the farthest and strangest.
Common mistake: assuming a diminished chord belongs to one key. It never does — the bass and the next chord decide. And spell the tritone key as G♭ or F♯, whichever the music uses.
In real music the diminished 7th has been the classic pivot chord since the Baroque, and Romantic composers leaned on it for sudden key changes. Barry turned it into an everyday tool.
Practice: from B°7, resolve to each of the four keys and name it. Then repeat from C°7 (keys D♭, E, G, B♭) and C♯°7 (D, F, A♭, B).
Play it: the Key changes levels run this move in all twelve keys on piano, guitar and bass. I6, the diminished, the new V7, the new I6, then the other two diminished chords and the 7♭9.
To keep: each note of a diminished chord is a leading tone. Four notes, four doors — four keys a minor third apart.
maj7 → the 6 on its root; m7 → the major 6 a minor third up; 7 → the minor 6 on its 5th (and more for ø7, alt, sus).
Hey {name}! Barry Harris taught that almost any chord can be played as a 6 chord — major 6 or minor 6. Learn a few 6 chords, and you can play over everything.
Over Cmaj7, play C6: C, E, G, A. Same root — sweet and simple.
Over a minor 7, go up a minor third. Dm7 is D, F, A, C; F6 is F, A, C, D — the very same notes!
Over a dominant 7, play the minor 6 on its 5th. Over G7, D minor 6: D, F, A, B — the 5th, ♭7, 9th and 3rd of G7.
Put it together: Dm7, G7, Cmaj7 become F6, D minor 6, C6 — and the bass does the rest.
Three more for later. Over m7♭5, the minor 6 a minor third up. Over an altered dominant, the minor 6 a half step up. Over 7sus, the major 6 a whole step down.
Your turn! I name a chord, like G7 or Dm7, and you pick the 6 chord Barry plays over it. On the last level you only hear it: the chord, then four 6 chords over its bass.
The idea: Barry thought in two scales only — major 6-diminished and minor 6-diminished. So every chord gets a 6 chord, and with it a whole 6th-diminished scale to play on.
m7 → the major 6 a minor third up. Dm7 and F6 are the same four notes, so over Dm7 you play the F 6th-diminished scale: F, G, A, B♭, C, D♭, D, E.
7 → the minor 6 on the 5th. Over G7 play Dm6: D, F, A, B — the 5th, ♭7, 9th and 3rd. The tritone B–F is inside, so the dominant sound stays. Its scale: D, E, F, G, A, B♭, B, C♯.
maj7 → the 6 on its root: C6 over Cmaj7. For a brighter sound Barry also used the 6 on the 5th: G6 over C gives G, B, D, E — the 5th, 7th, 9th and 6th.
The other three. m7♭5 → minor 6 a minor third up: Dm7♭5 equals Fm6. Altered → minor 6 a half step up: A♭m6 over G gives ♭9, 3, ♭13, ♭7. Sus → major 6 a whole step down: F6 over G gives ♭7, 9, 11, 5.
ø → m6 ↑m3 · alt → m6 ↑½ · sus → 6 ↓1
A minor ii–V–i in 6 chords: Dm7♭5, G7alt, Cm6 become Fm6, A♭m6, Cm6 — three minor 6 shapes over a moving bass.
How to hear it: the bass names the chord, the 6 chord colors it. The same Dm6 shape over D is a Dm6; over G it becomes a G9. Listen to the bass change:
Common mistake: mixing up m7 and m7♭5 — both go a minor third up. Check the chord’s 5th: a perfect 5th (A in Dm7) gives a major 6, F6; a flat 5th (A♭ in Dm7♭5) gives a minor 6, Fm6.

One dominant, eight expressions: the four brothers G7, B♭7, D♭7, E7 share one diminished in their scales; the four minor 6ths on their 5ths, Dm6, Fm6, A♭m6, Bm6, share another. Dm6, the important minor, is natural; A♭m6, the tritone’s minor, is altered.
Resolving to C6: Dm6 moves by step; in A♭m6 the altered tones fall a half step. Dm6 also serves the whole ii–V.
To keep: maj7 → 6 on the root; m7 → major 6 up a minor third; 7 → minor 6 on the 5th; m7♭5 → minor 6 up a minor third; altered → minor 6 up a half step; sus → major 6 down a whole step.
Down the dominant scale, add half steps so chord tones land on the beat: one between 1 and ♭7; from 3, 5, 7 up to three; from 2, 4, 6 none, or two.
Hey {name}! Bebop lines sound smooth because the chord tones land on the beats. Barry Harris had clear rules for it, on the dominant scale.
Walk straight down C7’s scale in eighths, and A, F and D land on the beats — not chord tones. It sounds a bit lost.
Barry’s fix: add one half step, B, between 1 and ♭7. Now B♭, G, E and C all fall on the beat.
Why it works: each added note shifts the line by one eighth, sliding the chord tones back onto the beat.
Start on 3, 5 or ♭7 and you may add three: between 3 and 2, 2 and 1, 1 and ♭7. Each one only once. Parks allows three from the root as well.
Start on 2, 4 or 6 — notes outside the chord — and you add none, or two: between 2 and 1, and between 1 and ♭7.
Your turn! You hear a dominant chord, then a line falling down its scale. Was the half step between 1 and ♭7 added? Later, count the extra half steps, and check that chord tones hit the beats.
Why a straight scale goes wrong: coming down the dominant scale, chord tones and other notes alternate — except at the top, where 1 and ♭7, C and B♭, are two chord tones side by side.
One half step between them, B, restores the alternation, and it works from any chord tone. From 5: G, F, E, D, C, B, B♭, A, G — and G, E, C, B♭, G land on the beats.
Starting on the beat from a non-chord tone — 2, 4 or 6 — the basic rule is none. From D: D, C, B♭, A, G, F, E, D, C. After the first note, the chord tones already fall on the beats.

The counting logic: each added note shifts the rest of the line by one eighth, and two added notes cancel out. So from a chord tone you add an odd number — one or three — and from a non-chord tone an even number — none or two.
The added spots are fixed, each used once. From 3, 5 or ♭7: between 3 and 2, 2 and 1, 1 and ♭7. From 2, 4 or 6: between 2 and 1, and 1 and ♭7. Here is 5 with all three.
How to hear it: tap the beat while the line falls. A good line sounds anchored, with chord tones on the taps.
Common mistake: adding the half step in the wrong spot. Put A♭ between A and G instead, and A — not a chord tone — still lands on a beat. Add it between 1 and ♭7, where the problem starts.
Practice slowly, the click on 2 and 4, from every degree of C7.
In real music: the line from 1 with B added is what David Baker later called the dominant bebop scale. Charlie Parker’s and Bud Powell’s lines are full of these passing half steps.
Major works the same way with the 6 chord’s tones: the one half step goes between 6 and 5. Minor uses the flat 3rd; from the root it is the minor 6th-diminished scale.

The miscellaneous rule: go up from a note, then come down by its rule; an extra note that would fall on a beat goes to the bottom. Triplets: an eighth triplet follows its middle note, a sixteenth triplet its first.
To keep: chord tones on the beat. From a chord tone add one, or three; from a non-chord tone none, or two. The first fix is always between 1 and ♭7.
A scale exercise with a pivot inside: partway down, the rest of the line moves up an octave — same notes, same order, a new contour — so it keeps falling without running out of room.
Hey {name}! Scale lines love to run downhill — and sooner or later they hit the bottom of your instrument, or your voice.
Barry Harris’s answer is a pivot inside the line: at any moment, move the rest of it up an octave and keep falling. Same notes, more room.
Listen for the leap: the line walks down by step, then once — boing — it jumps up. Here it pivots later, before the 7th note.
Pivots keep a long line in a comfortable range, and the sudden leap gives it a fresh shape.
The trick: count the notes as they go by, and say the number where the line suddenly jumps up. Here: 1, 2, 3 — and up on 4.
Your turn! You hear one run that pivots once to stay in range. Before which note did it jump? Count along and catch the leap.
In a scale line the pivot is a change of octave in the middle. The notes and the rhythm stay the same; from the pivot on, the line simply continues an octave higher — or lower.
Why Barry used it: his material is mostly descending scale lines, and a long descent soon runs out of room. Pivots let a line keep falling for bars while it stays in one comfortable octave.
The pivot does not change the rhythm, so the beat placement survives: chord tones stay on the beats. A pivot on a beat, onto a chord tone, makes the leap sound most deliberate.
What you actually hear is a leap of a 7th, not an octave: a step down plus an octave up. From A to the high G, the jump is a minor 7th.
Pivots also go down. When a rising line climbs too high, drop the rest an octave: G, A, B♭, C, then D, E, F, G an octave lower.
Combine it with the half-step rules. From 5 with B added, pivoting before C: G, F, E, D, then C, B, B♭, A, G up an octave — chord tones still on the beats.
Common mistake: repeating the note at the pivot. The next note must be the next scale note, only in a new octave. If you hear a clean octave jump, a note was repeated. Wrong, then right:
Practice: sing or play a long descending line and pivot on a cue — every four notes, then every three. In the exercise, count the notes aloud and name the one where the leap lands.
In real music, octave displacement runs all through bebop: a line seems to break off and reappear an octave away, which keeps long phrases fresh and inside the instrument’s best range.
The same idea on an arpeggio is the lesson before this one: the root on top, a drop to the 3rd, the climb.
To keep: in a scale line, the pivot moves the rest of the line an octave — same notes, same rhythm. You hear it as a sudden leap of a 7th.
G7, B♭7, D♭7 and E7 share one diminished chord (their ♭9), so they can stand in for each other; G7 ↔ D♭7 is the tritone sub.
Hey {name}! Put G in the bass under B diminished, and you get G7♭9 — a dominant with a spicy flat nine.
Keep the same diminished chord and move the bass: B♭, D♭, E. Each makes another dominant 7♭9.
In Barry Harris’s thinking they are one family — we call them brothers: four dominants a minor third apart, sharing one diminished chord. So they can stand in for one another.
The brother a tritone away is the famous tritone sub. G7 and D♭7 share B and F, and both slide home to C.
In the exercise you hear plain dominant 7s. Brothers have roots three or six half steps apart. Anything else: not related.
Your turn! Two dominant chords: brothers from the same diminished family, or not? Later, name the brother: a minor third up, a minor third down, or the tritone sub.
Precisely: a 7♭9 chord is its root plus a diminished 7th built on its 3rd. G7♭9 is G under B, D, F, A♭. Any dominant whose 3rd, 5th, ♭7 and ♭9 are those four notes is a brother.
The four brother roots — G, B♭, D♭, E — form a diminished chord themselves. Each root is a note of B°7 lowered a half step: exactly the lowering rule you already know.
Tritone brothers share the tritone itself. In G7, B and F are the 3rd and ♭7; in D♭7 the same two notes are the ♭7 (C♭) and the 3rd. The roles swap, the tension stays.
Minor-third brothers share two notes too. G7 and B♭7 both contain D and F: in G7 they are the 5th and ♭7, in B♭7 the 3rd and 5th.
Using them in a ii–V–I: replace G7 with D♭7 and the bass slides down by half steps, D, D♭, C — the tritone substitution. Dm7, D♭7, Cmaj7:
Or use the brother a whole step below home: B♭7 to C, the Backdoor dominant, often after Fm7. It resolves softly, with A♭ falling to G.
How to hear brothers: sing the two roots. Three half steps apart, up or down, or six — brothers. A whole step, a fourth or a fifth — not from the same family.

Common mistake: treating every brother alike. The tritone brother keeps the tension and moves the bass smoothly; the minor-third brothers change the color more. E7 in place of G7 sounds most surprising — it leans toward A minor.
Practice: hold B°7 in the right hand and walk the left hand G, B♭, D♭, E, naming each 7♭9. Then resolve each one to its own home, and to C.
To keep: four dominants a minor third apart share one diminished chord — their 3, 5, ♭7 and ♭9. The tritone brother is the tritone sub.
Jazz lines squeeze a half step into a whole-step gap of the scale — like Barry Harris’s 6th-diminished scale (A♭ between G and A).
Hey {name}! Jazz players love to squeeze an extra half step into a scale. The line slides, and the strong notes stay on the beat.
Plain C major first: C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C. Wherever two notes are a whole step apart, there is room for one more.
Add A♭ between G and A — notes 5 and 6 — and you get Barry Harris’s 6th-diminished scale.
Another spot: between C and D, notes 1 and 2. Hear the little slide right at the start?
Now the dominant scale, coming down: C, B♭, A, G, F, E, D, C. The classic added note is B, between C and B♭ — notes 1 and 2, counted from the top.
The trick: count only the scale notes. The extra one is the tiny slide that gets no number — which two numbers does it squeeze between?
Your turn! You hear a scale with one extra half step. Where is it — between which two notes? First the major scale going up; later the dominant scale coming down.
Precisely: an added half step is a chromatic passing note. It fills a whole-step gap with the note in between. Half-step gaps — E–F and B–C in C major — have no room.
In major there are five whole-step gaps: 1–2, 2–3, 4–5, 5–6 and 6–7. Each gives a different eight-note scale, and each changes which notes land on the beats.
Why add a note at all: a seven-note scale in eighth notes drifts against the beat. Eight notes fill a 4/4 bar exactly. With A♭ added, going up or coming down, C, E, G and A land on the beats.
The two classic choices: A♭ between 5 and 6 over a major or 6 chord — Barry’s 6th-diminished scale — and B between ♭7 and 1 over a dominant. Both are known as bebop scales.
How to find it by ear: count the scale notes and listen for the spot where the line slides by half steps. Inside that slide, the note that is not in the key is the extra one.
Common mistake: counting E–F or B–C as an added note. Those half steps belong to the major scale. Compare E, F, G with E, F, F♯, G — only the second has an extra note.
Practice: sing the major scale and insert a half step in each of the five gaps in turn, saying the numbers aloud and the extra note as “and”. Then do the same down the dominant scale.
In real music these passing notes are the sound of bebop: Charlie Parker, Bud Powell and Barry Harris used them to keep long eighth-note lines flowing over the chords.
To keep: the extra note splits a whole step. Find the slide, then the note that is not in the key — that is the added half step.
Sing the 6th-diminished scale, sing the one note that turns a diminished chord into a dominant or minor 6, then sing half-step lines and the harmonized scale.
Hey {name}! Barry Harris taught by singing — in his workshops, whole rooms sang the scales and chords together. Now you sing his system.
First, sing the 6th-diminished scale: C, D, E, F, G, A♭, A, B, C. Watch for A♭ and A, side by side.
Next, the diminished chord holds and you sing the one note that moves. To make G7 from B diminished, sing G — a half step below A♭.
Then by degree: “raise the lowest note”. B goes up to C, and your voice has made F minor 6. Lower makes dominants; raise makes minor 6s.
Then it is your choice: sing any note a half step from the diminished, and I tell you what you made. Or hear a dominant and sing its home root — G7 goes to C.
Then Barry’s half-step lines: sing down the dominant scale in eighths, with the added half steps keeping chord tones on the beat.
Finally, the harmonized scale: you sing each note while the piano adds its chord underneath — 6, diminished, 6, diminished.
Your turn! Start at level one: listen to the scale, then sing it up from C — eight notes, A♭ and A both in there. A clear “la” works best.
Singing puts the system in your ear, not just your fingers. Use numbers or letter names so every note has a label: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, ♭6, 6, 7 for the 6th-diminished scale.
The hard spot is the top: G, A♭, A, then a whole step to B. Practice it slowly — G, A♭, A, then G, A, B — until the two half steps sound clearly smaller than the whole step.
Sing the two chords as arpeggios. C6 rises a major third, a minor third, then a whole step. B°7 is three minor thirds in a row — keep each one exactly three half steps.
To sing the moving note, first find its neighbor in the chord. For G7, hum A♭ inside B°7, then slide down a half step to G. The piano fills in the dominant.
From a dominant to its home root: home is a fifth below the dominant’s root, and the dominant’s 3rd rises a half step to it. In G7, find B and step up to C.
For half-step lines, sing at a slow tempo and tap the beat. Chord tones go on the taps; the added half steps pass quickly between them. Sing the line from 1:
Common mistake: half steps that drift. A♭ and A, or B and B♭, can blur into one note. Check against the piano, and slow down on the half steps until they are clean.
Choose a comfortable octave, or move the whole exercise to another key — the system works the same everywhere. If a line runs out of range, pivot: jump the rest up an octave.
To keep: label every note, find the moving note from its neighbor, and keep the half steps small and clean.
The band: a walking bass (one note a beat), Charleston comping (beat 1 and the "and" of 2) and a swung ride — over ii–V–I, minor ii–V–i or blues.
Hey {name}! Time to play with a band — a tiny one living in your phone. Bass, piano and ride cymbal loop a chord chart while you join in.
The bass walks: one note per beat, climbing through the chord, then stepping into the next chord by a half step.
The piano comps in the Charleston rhythm: on beat 1 and on the “and” of 2 — just the 3rd, the 7th and a color note.
And the ride cymbal: ding, ding-a-ding, ding-a-ding — the swing that pushes everything forward.
Three charts to choose from: the major ii–V–I, the darker minor ii–V–i, and the 12-bar blues. Here is the minor one.
A good start: pick a slow tempo, play just the roots with the bass, then try the 3rds. Feel how they lock in.
Your turn! Choose a chart, a key and a tempo, press play, and join the band — on your instrument or with your voice. No score here: just groove.
Each player has a job. The bass gives the roots and the time, the piano the harmony and rhythmic hits, the drums the groove. When you join, you are the fourth voice — leave them room.
A walking bass line, beat by beat: the root on beat 1, chord or scale notes on 2 and 3, and on 4 an approach note — often a half step from the next root. Here D, E, F, F♯ lead to G.
The Charleston rhythm: a hit on beat 1 and another on the “and” of 2, then space for the rest of the bar. Short, light chords, so the bass and the soloist can be heard.
The ride cymbal plays quarter notes with a swung skip into beats 2 and 4: ding, ding-a ding, ding-a. Drummers usually add the hi-hat on 2 and 4 — together, the heartbeat of swing.
The three forms. Major ii–V–I: four bars, Dm7, G7, then two bars of Cmaj7. Minor: Dø7, G7♭9, two bars of Cm6. Blues: twelve bars, three lines of four — one of the most played forms in jazz.
How to stay in place: find beat 1 by the bass root and the ride, then count bars — one-two-three-four, two-two-three-four. Knowing where the form starts again is half of playing with a band.
Common mistakes: rushing ahead of the bass, playing in the same low register as the bass, and losing count at the end of the form. Lock onto the ride, stay above the bass, keep counting.
A practice ladder: roots with the bass, then 3rds and 7ths with the piano, then a simple rhythm on the Charleston hits, then short phrases. Raise the tempo only when it all feels easy.

In real music: the Charleston rhythm comes from James P. Johnson’s 1923 song “Charleston”. Walking bass grew up in the swing era, and bebop drummers such as Kenny Clarke moved the time onto the ride cymbal.
To keep: the bass walks, the piano hits 1 and the “and” of 2, the ride swings — count the bars and fit into the space they leave.
Chord tones on beats 1 and 3, end on a chord tone, mix rhythms, use range, and approach chord tones by a half step.
Hey {name}! Improvising is not random notes — it is choices that fit the chords. I listen to your solo and give you five friendly pointers.
One: land on a chord tone — 1, 3, 5 or 7 — on beats 1 and 3. That is how a line “makes the changes”.
Two: end on a chord tone of the last chord, so your solo sounds finished — not like a question. Hear the difference?
Three: mix your rhythms — eighths, a quarter, a long note, even a rest. Silence is part of the solo.
Four: use some range. Reach at least a sixth between your lowest and highest notes — C up to A, say.
Five, the bebop spice: approach a chord tone from a half step away. D♯ slides into E, A♭ into G.
Your turn! Pick a chart, listen for one bar, then improvise — sing, or play into the microphone, one note at a time. Then read your five scores and a tip or two.
“Making the changes” means your line shows the chords even without the band. The way to do it: chord tones on the strong beats, 1 and 3; other notes on the weak beats, passing between them.
The strongest chord tones are the guide tones, the 3rd and 7th. Across a ii–V–I they move by tiny steps: C, the 7th of Dm7, falls to B, the 3rd of G7; F, the 7th of G7, falls to E in Cmaj7.

Endings: the root sounds most final, the 3rd and 5th almost as settled. On a major 7 chord, ending on the 7th or 9th sounds open and modern. Avoid the 4th over a major chord — it clashes with the 3rd.
Rhythm and space: think in phrases of one or two bars with a breath after each. Repeat a short motif and change it slightly — the ear follows a solo that remembers itself.
Range and shape: a phrase usually rises and falls like an arch. Use at least a sixth, and let the high point come once — a line stuck on three notes sounds as if it is circling.
Approach notes come in three kinds: from a half step below, from a half step above, or an enclosure — above, then below, then the target. Here F and D♯ close in on E.
Practice one pointer at a time: first only chord tones in quarter notes, then add approach notes, then rests and motifs. Record yourself and listen back once — it shows more than any score.
Common mistakes: running scales with no target, filling every beat, and ending on whatever note comes. Decide where a phrase will land before you start it.
In real music, jazz has always been learned by ear: players copy solos from records phrase by phrase and sing them before they play them. Even two bars of a favorite solo teach all five pointers.
To keep: chord tones on 1 and 3, a clear ending, rhythms that breathe, an arching range, and half-step approaches.
Voicings (any, shell 1-3-7, rootless 3-5-7-9), play it back, an even scale, and ii–V–I with guide tones in all keys.
Hey {name}! Plug in a MIDI keyboard, or use the keys on screen, and let’s get jazz harmony into your hands. Four short drills.
Voicings first. “Any voicing” means all four chord notes, in any order and octave. Cmaj7: C, E, G, B.
A shell is exactly three notes: the root at the bottom, plus the 3rd and the 7th. Cmaj7 shell: C, E, B. Lean, and very jazz.
Rootless: leave the root to the bass player and play 3, 5, 7 and 9. For Dm7: F, A, C, E.
“Play it back”: hear five notes from C major and play them. “Even scale”: C major up and down, and I measure how steady you are.
Last, ii–V–I in all twelve keys, around the circle: C, F, B♭ and on. Each chord needs at least its 3rd and 7th — the guide tones. Hear the 7th slide down to the next 3rd?
Your turn! Pick a drill. On a MIDI keyboard, play the chord and let go; on the screen keys, tap the notes, then send. I tell you what is missing or extra.
A voicing is the choice of which chord notes to play, in which octave and order. Close position keeps them inside an octave; open position spreads them out. The same Cmaj7, two sounds:
Shells come in two shapes: 1-3-7 and 1-7-3. Alternate them through a ii–V–I and the hand barely moves: Dm7 as D, C, F; G7 as G, B, F; Cmaj7 as C, B, E.
Rootless voicings also come in two shapes: 3-5-7-9 and 7-9-3-5. On G7 the second shape usually takes the 13th instead of the 5th: F, A, B, E.
Put them together: Dm7 as F, A, C, E; G7 as F, A, B, E; Cmaj7 as E, G, B, D. Few notes move, and each by a step or less.
The guide-tone rule behind it: the 7th of one chord falls a half step to the 3rd of the next, and the 3rd holds to become the next 7th. In ii–V–I: C to B, then F to E.
For the even scale, fingering keeps it smooth. Right hand in C: 1, 2, 3, then the thumb passes under to F: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Slow and even beats fast and bumpy — use a metronome.
For “play it back”, hear the phrase in your head before touching a key. Find the first note, then think in steps and leaps. Sing it once if you are unsure.
All twelve keys go around the circle of fourths: C, F, B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, G♭, B, E, A, D, G. Each key is a fourth above the last — the same move as V to I.
Common mistakes: close thirds too low sound muddy — keep them above roughly the C below middle C — and chords that blur into each other. Release one chord cleanly before the next. Low, then clear:
To keep: shells 1-3-7 and 1-7-3, rootless 3-5-7-9 and 7-9-3-5, and guide tones that move by a half step or stay put.
C6 = Am7, Cm6 = Am7♭5, and a diminished chord is a 7♭9 without its root — the bass decides the name.
Barry Harris taught that many chord names are the same four notes over a different bass. Listen: C6, then Am7. The upper notes stay; only the bass moves.
C6 is C, E, G, A. Start from the A and read up: A, C, E, G — that is Am7. Its root sits a minor third below the root of the 6 chord.
Minor works the same way. Cm6 — C, E♭, G, A — has exactly the notes of Am7♭5, the half-diminished chord on A.
A diminished chord is a 7♭9 chord without its root. B, D, F, A♭ with G underneath is G7♭9.
Put a bass a half step below any of its four notes and you get another dominant: G, B♭, D♭ or E. One diminished chord, four dominants.
Barry’s advice: think of the 6 chord. For Dm7 think F6, for Bm7♭5 think Dm6, and for G7 think Dm6, the important minor. The diminished belongs to G7♭9.
Your turn. First on paper: which chord has the same four notes? Then by ear: the same notes over a bass. Hum the bass — it names the chord.
Why it works: a 6 chord and the minor 7 chord a minor third below share all four notes. The 6th of one is the root of the other. Minor 6 and half-diminished pair up the same way: Fm6 equals Dm7♭5.
A diminished chord repeats every minor third, so there are only three of them: C°7, C♯°7 and D°7. Every other diminished chord is one of these, spelled from another note.
Each one serves four dominants a minor third apart. B°7 — the same notes as D°7 — belongs to G7, B♭7, D♭7 and E7. G and D♭ are a tritone apart, and so are B♭ and E: tritone substitutes, built in.
To find a dominant on paper: pick any note of the diminished chord and go down a half step — that is a root. A♭ gives G, B gives B♭, D gives D♭, F gives E.
By ear, the upper notes cannot tell you the name — the bass can. Over C, the notes C, E, G, A sound sweet and settled; over A they turn soft and minor. Hum the lowest note first.
The common mistake is going the wrong way. The minor 7 root is a minor third below the 6 chord: C6 is Am7, not E♭m7. And in a 7♭9 the root sits a half step below a diminished note, not above it.
How Barry used it: since Dm7 is F6 and G7 borrows B°7, a whole ii–V–I can be played with 6 chords and diminished chords. F6 over D, B°7 over G, then home to C6.
Practice: play a 6 chord with its root in the bass, then move only the bass down a minor third and name the new chord aloud. Do it in major and minor, then around the circle of fourths.
To keep: 6 = minor 7 a minor third below, minor 6 = half-diminished a minor third below, diminished = 7♭9 without the root. The bass decides the name.
Harmonize the 6th-diminished scale in Drop 2: 1, 3, 5, 6 get the 6 chord; 2, 4, ♭6, 7 get the diminished chord.
Barry Harris block chords put a full chord under every note of the 6th-diminished scale — four voices moving together. Listen to C, all the way up.
The rule: scale notes 1, 3, 5 and 6 — C, E, G, A — get the C6 chord. Notes 2, 4, ♭6 and 7 — D, F, A♭, B — get the diminished chord, B°7.
The voicing is Drop 2. Stack the chord close under the melody note, then drop the second voice from the top an octave. Close first, then Drop 2.
Played in order, the chords take turns: rest, tension, rest. Each diminished chord leans into the 6 chords on both sides.
Make the home chord minor, Cm6, and you get the minor version. The diminished chords stay the same; every E becomes E♭.
Pianists use it two ways: to comp, moving through the scale over one chord, and to harmonize a melody, one block chord per note. Here is E, D, C.
Your turn. Is a block chord a 6 chord or diminished? Where did a run stop? Major or minor? And in a short melody, how many diminished chords?
Why every note gets a chord: the scale is two chords woven together, so each of its eight notes belongs to exactly one of them. No note is left as a passing tone without harmony.
Drop 2 precisely: take the four chord notes in close position, melody on top. Count down from the top and lower voice 2 by an octave. C6 with C on top: E, G, A, C becomes A, E, G, C.
The result spans more than an octave, so it splits between the hands: left hand on the lowest note, right hand on the top three. It sounds open and warm, like a sax section.
Four Drop 2 shapes of C6 — C, E, G or A on top — and four of B°7 — D, F, A♭ or B on top — alternate up the octave. The diminished shapes all look alike: it is a symmetrical chord.
Minor: Cm6 with C on top is A, E♭, G, C. Here is the whole minor scale in block chords.
To hear major against minor, ignore the diminished chords — they are identical in both. Listen only to the 6 chords: is the 3rd E or E♭?
Comping with it: over one long C6, walk the top voice up and down the scale. The chords keep moving, yet the harmony never leaves C.
The common mistake: putting the 6 chord under a diminished note. D belongs to the diminished, B°7, not to C6 — so D gets B°7. Wrong, then right:

In real music, parallel block chords go back to Milt Buckner and George Shearing’s “locked hands”. Drop 2 is the more open cousin, standard in big-band sax writing. Barry’s system builds it from just two chords.
To keep: 1, 3, 5, 6 get the 6 chord; 2, 4, ♭6, 7 get the diminished — voiced in Drop 2, alternating rest and tension.
Comping = short chords in the gaps: Charleston (1, and of 2), reverse (and of 1, 3), Red Garland (and of 2, and of 4), anticipation, four to the bar.
Comping is how a pianist or guitarist accompanies in jazz: short chords placed in the gaps, while bass and drums keep the time. A few rhythms come up again and again.
The Charleston: a chord on beat 1 and on the “and” of 2. In swing that “and” arrives late, on the last third of the beat.
The reverse Charleston turns it around: the “and” of 1, then beat 3. The first chord comes just after the beat.
Red Garland, after the pianist in Miles Davis’s 1950s quintet: the “and” of 2 and the “and” of 4. Only off-beats — light, and pushing forward.
An anticipation plays the next chord early, on the “and” of 4, and holds it over the bar line. Here F arrives before its bar.
Four to the bar: a short, even chord on every beat — the sound of Freddie Green’s guitar in the Count Basie band.
Your turn. Bass and hi-hat keep the time — which rhythm is the piano playing? Ask first: does the first chord land on the beat, or just after it?

Why comping leaves space: the bass and drums already mark every beat, and the soloist owns the foreground. A few well-placed chords make the time feel stronger and give the soloist room to breathe — and something to answer.

Count “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and”. In swing each beat splits unevenly, about two thirds plus one third, so every “and” falls late. The Charleston is beat 1 plus the “and” of 2: a dotted quarter, then an eighth.
The reverse Charleston is the same pair shifted half a beat later: the “and” of 1, then 3. Compare them back to back.
Red Garland played with Miles Davis from 1955 to 1958. His stabs on the “and” of 2 and the “and” of 4 lean into beats 3 and 1, so the groove feels pulled forward.
An anticipation moves the harmony early: the next bar’s chord sounds on the “and” of 4 and is tied across the bar line. At chord changes, it pushes the tune ahead.
Four to the bar is swing-era rhythm guitar: Freddie Green played short, even chords on every beat with the Count Basie Orchestra for decades, locked in with the bass.
How to tell them apart: tap the beat. Does the first chord land on a tap — Charleston or four to the bar — or between taps — reverse, Red Garland or anticipation? Then count the chords in the bar.
The common mistake is playing the “and” straight, exactly halfway through the beat. Against a swing groove it sounds stiff. Straight first, then swung:
Practice with a metronome on 2 and 4: comp the Charleston through a ii–V–I, then mix patterns, and leave some bars empty on purpose. Silence is part of comping.
To keep: comp in the gaps. Charleston — 1 and the “and” of 2; reverse — the “and” of 1 and 3; Red Garland — the “and” of 2 and 4; anticipation — the “and” of 4; Freddie Green — every beat.
Four chords that lead home: I–vi–ii–V and its substitutes — iii for I, dominants for minors, tritone subs, and the Ladybird.
A turnaround is a short chord loop at the end of a section that leads back to the top. The basic one is I–vi–ii–V: Cmaj7, Am7, Dm7, G7, then home.
Start on iii instead: Em7, Am7, Dm7, G7. Em7 shares three notes with Cmaj7, so it sounds like home, only less settled.
Turn vi into a dominant and it pulls harder: I–VI7–ii–V, with A7 in place of Am7. Or make all four dominant: III7–VI7–II7–V7 — E7, A7, D7, G7.
Tritone substitutes swap a dominant for the one a tritone away: I–♭III7–ii–♭II7 — Cmaj7, E♭7, Dm7, D♭7. From E♭ the bass slides down by half steps to C.
The Ladybird, from Tadd Dameron’s tune “Lady Bird”: I–♭III7–♭VImaj7–♭II7 — Cmaj7, E♭7, A♭maj7, D♭7. A quick trip far away, then a half step home.
Your turn: four chords and back home — which turnaround? Follow the bass: thirds and fourths, or half steps? Then listen for bright dominants where minor chords should be.
Every turnaround is a dressed-up I–V–I. The vi and iii stand in for I — Am7 has the same notes as C6 — and ii prepares V. So the four chords say: home, still home, prepare, go.
A secondary dominant is the V of a chord other than I. A7 is V of Dm7: its C♯ is a leading tone to D. Compare Am7 to Dm7, then A7 to Dm7.
With all four dominant, every chord resolves a fourth up into the next: E7, A7, D7, G7, C. The bridge of Rhythm changes uses exactly this chain, two bars per chord.
Why the tritone substitute works: G7 and D♭7 share their 3rd and 7th — B and F in G7, F and C♭ in D♭7. Same tension, new bass. Likewise, E♭7 stands in for A7.
The bass gives each one away. C A D G: I–vi or I–VI7. E A D G: iii–vi or all dominants. C E♭ D D♭: tritone. C E♭ A♭ D♭: Ladybird, climbing in fourths after E♭.
The common mistake is trusting the bass alone. I–vi–ii–V and I–VI7–ii–V have the same bass; only the second chord differs — soft Am7 or bright A7. Listen to its color.
The Ladybird borrows a whole cadence: E♭7 to A♭maj7 is V–I in A♭. Then D♭7, the tritone sub of G7, slides a half step home to C.

In real music, I–vi–ii–V is the A section of Rhythm changes, from Gershwin’s “I Got Rhythm”, and turnarounds close countless standards and blues choruses. Players swap one for another freely in the same two bars.
Practice each one in C with the root in the left hand and the 3rd and 7th in the right, then in F and B♭. Say the bass notes aloud as you play.
To keep: I–vi–ii–V is the model. Swap I for iii, minors for dominants, dominants for tritone subs — and the bass tells you which.
The 3rd and 7th move by step through ii–V–I: 7 falls to 3, 3 holds as 7 — two lines, 7–3–7 and 3–7–3.
The 3rd and 7th of a chord are its guide tones. They decide its quality — major or minor, dominant or major 7. In Dm7 they are F and C.
Through ii–V–I they move by step. The 7th falls a half step to the next chord’s 3rd; the 3rd stays put and becomes the next 7th.
That gives two lines. From the 7th: C, B, B — 7, 3, 7. From the 3rd: F, F, E — 3, 7, 3. First one line on top, then the other.
In a minor ii–V–i — Dm7♭5, G7, Cm7 — the lines end a half step lower: C, B, B♭ and F, F, E♭.
Improvisers aim for these notes as each chord arrives; pianists use them to connect chords smoothly. This line lands on C, then B, then E.
Your turn. You hear a ii–V–I in shells — which line is on top? Follow the highest note: does it fall first and then hold, or hold first and then fall?
Why the 3rd and 7th: the bass usually plays the root, and the 5th adds little color. The 3rd says major or minor; the 7th says major 7 or dominant. Cmaj7 and C7 differ by one guide tone.
Why they move by step: in ii–V–I the roots rise by fourths. The 7th of Dm7, C, falls to B, the 3rd of G7. The 3rd of Dm7, F, is already the 7th of G7. Then F falls to E while B stays.
Inside G7, B and F form the tritone that drives the dominant. In classical harmony B rises to C; in jazz it often stays as the major 7th of Cmaj7, while F still falls to E.
In minor, Dm7♭5 has the same 3rd and 7th as Dm7 — F and C; only its 5th, A♭, differs. The tonic Cm7 brings E♭ and B♭, so both lines end a half step lower than in major.
The rule holds through longer chains. Over A7, D7, G7, Cmaj7 the top line falls G, F♯, F, E — a half step per chord — while the lower line goes C♯, C, B, B.
To improvise with them, put a guide tone on the first beat of each chord and fill in around it with scale notes. Here: C over Dm7, B over G7, and F resolving to E on Cmaj7.
The common mistake is keeping the old note when the chord changes. Hold C into G7 and it clashes as a suspended 4th; move it to B and the chord comes into focus.
Practice: play the root in the left hand and the two guide tones in the right through a ii–V–I in every key. Then sing one line while you play the other.
To keep: 3rds and 7ths are the chord’s identity. Through ii–V–I, 7 falls to 3 and 3 holds as 7 — the lines 7–3–7 and 3–7–3.
G7, B♭7, D♭7 and E7 share one diminished chord as their 7♭9 without the root (B D F A♭), so each can stand in for the V and resolve to C.
Hi {name}! Take G7 with a flat 9 and leave out its root. What is left is a diminished chord: B, D, F and A flat.
Now put another bass under the same four notes: B flat, D flat or E. Each bass turns the diminished into a dominant seven flat nine.
These four dominants are one family (Barry Harris: the related dominants). Their roots are a minor third apart, and every one of them resolves to C.
You know some of them already. D flat 7 is the tritone sub. B flat 7 is the backdoor. E7 is the flat-nine relative.
In a line, the half steps do the work: B goes up to C, F falls to E, A flat falls to G.
Your turn: each brother as an arpeggio into C, then inside a ii–V–I, comped, all four in turn, in a turnaround and in a blues. Lines start in free time.
Why it works: the diminished chord is the sound of the dominant. Its four notes pull by half steps into the tones of C.
The bass under the diminished chooses the colour. G is the plain dominant, D flat sounds altered, B flat and E add the flat and sharp nine.
In a ii–V–I, keep D minor 7 and C major 7 and swap the G7 for any brother. The ear still hears a cadence to C.
A common mistake is to treat the brothers as a chain of keys. They are four names for one job: the V of the same I.
Practice them in all twelve keys. In F the brothers are C7, E flat 7, G flat 7 and A7, and their shared diminished is E, G, B flat, D flat.
Bass players walk the brother roots: D, then D flat, then C is a chromatic line that every bassist knows.
Later you will hear a ii–V–I and name the brother that replaced the V. Listen to the bass first: it tells you which one.
iv7 – ♭VII7 – I: borrowed from the minor key, the ♭VII7 comes home from a whole step below.
Hi {name}! The front door to C is G7. The backdoor is B flat 7, and it often comes right after F minor 7.
Both chords are borrowed from C minor. That is why they sound darker than the plain ii–V, and warmer when C arrives.
Follow the guide tones: A flat falls to G, and the seventh of B flat 7 falls to the third of C.
Over B flat 7 a bebop line keeps chord tones on the beats and lands on a tone of C on beat one.
Your turn: comp the backdoor, play its guide tones, then a bebop line over B flat 7 into C, and the same colours inside a tune.
B flat 7 is also a brother of G7: it shares the same diminished chord. That is the Barry Harris reason the backdoor works.
Over B flat 7 the lydian dominant scale fits well: E natural sounds bright against the borrowed chord.
Other borrowed colours come from the same minor key: A flat major 7 after C, or F minor after F major.
In the tune you will play, bar six has F minor and B flat 7, bar twelve A flat major 7, and bars thirteen and fourteen the backdoor.
A common mistake is to resolve B flat 7 to E flat. Here it goes up a whole step, home to C.
Practice the backdoor in all twelve keys. In F it is B flat minor 7 to E flat 7 to F; in G it is C minor 7 to F7 to G. Say the chords before you play them.
Change the pair or the pentatonic with every chord: over Cmaj7 D and Em, over Dm7 F and G; over G7 the major pentatonic on A.
Hi {name}! Over a one-chord vamp, one triad pair is easy. Over a ii–V–I, every chord needs its own pair.
Over the dominant, try the triads on its root and on its second: G and A over G7, a bright lydian sound.
A pentatonic a fifth above the root gives a chord its colours: G pentatonic over C major 7, A minor pentatonic over D minor 7.
Change exactly when the chord changes. The new pair or pentatonic starts on beat one of the bar.
Your turn: pairs and pentatonics through ii–V–I, a minor ii–V–i, a blues and a modal form. Each line starts in free time.
Over an altered dominant, use the pair a tritone and a minor sixth above the root: D flat and E flat over G7 alt.
Over the minor seven flat five, the pair a half step and a minor third above: E flat and F minor over D half-diminished.
The minor pentatonic on the flat third also fits the altered dominant: B flat minor pentatonic over G7 alt.
Six notes of a pair or five of a pentatonic leave out the plain chord sound. That space is why the lines sound modern.
A common mistake is to keep one pentatonic through the whole form. The changes then disappear from your line.

Start slowly with one shape per chord, in free time, and name the pair or the pentatonic out loud. Then speed it up and let the shapes connect across the bar line, the last note near the next chord’s first.
Over a ii–V–I, reach the tonic through keys a major 3rd apart: Dm7 E♭7 A♭maj7 B7 Emaj7 G7 Cmaj7.
Hi {name}! Keep the first and last chords of a ii–V–I. In between, visit A flat and E, a major third apart, each with its own V.
C, A flat and E split the octave into three equal parts. That is the sound of Giant Steps, squeezed into one cadence.
A one-two-three-five cell on each chord makes the motion clear, two beats per chord.
In the comping, shells keep it simple: root, third and seventh on each chord.
Your turn: the line, then comp it in shells or drop 2. Bass players walk it. The line starts in free time.
John Coltrane put these changes over standard ii–V–Is. Countdown, for example, recasts the changes of a well-known standard this way.
Each V sits a fifth above its new key: E flat 7 to A flat, B7 to E, G7 to C. Hear the pull.
The three tonics form an augmented triad: C, E, A flat. Arpeggiate it to feel where the line is heading.
Keep the cells close: start each one on the root nearest the last note, so the whole line stays in one comfortable register.
A common mistake is to rush the last bar. C major 7 is home: hold it, and let the band arrive with you.
Practice it slowly first, two beats a chord, and say each new key as you reach it: A flat, E, C. Then try the same three keys from the other tonics, so the shape becomes yours in all twelve keys.
Intros: the I–vi–ii–V vamp or the tune’s last four bars. Endings: the Basie tag, ♭VI7–♭II7–I, or the iii–VI–ii–V tag three times.
Hi {name}! The simplest intro is a vamp on one, six, two, five, two beats each, until the band comes in.
Or play the last four bars of the tune. The listener hears where the form ends before it even starts.
To end, delay the tonic: A flat 7, D flat 7, then C. Both chords slide down by half steps into home.
The tag ending repeats three, six, two, five three times before the last chord, so the band can feel it coming.
Your turn: comp the intros and the endings, and play the Basie tag before the last hit.
The Basie ending: the band stops on the tonic, the piano answers with a short three-note tag, and the band plays one last hit.
A flat 7 and D flat 7 are borrowed sounds: A flat from the minor key, D flat 7 the tritone sub of G7, one of its brothers.
For the last-four-bars intro, use the real last bars of the tune you play: here F minor 7, B flat 7, then a turnaround to C.
Agree on the ending before you play. A nod on the last A section tells the band which tag is coming.
A common mistake is to slow down in the tag. Keep the time steady; only the last chord is held.
Practice each intro and ending in all twelve keys, with the band or a click. Count the bars out loud, so you always know where the form starts and where the last chord falls.
Slow tempo, full sound: the left hand plays a 10th or a shell, the right hand four notes (3, 5, 7, 9) above it.
Hi {name}! A ballad has room. The left hand plays the root and the tenth; the right hand a rootless chord above middle C.
Keep the right hand close from chord to chord; only the bass moves far.
With two chords a bar, a shell in the left hand is lighter: the root and the seventh, the right hand on top.
Play both hands exactly together, softly, and let each chord ring for its full length before the next one.
Your turn: a ballad progression in tenths, then in shells with two chords a bar. Guitarists play it in drop 2.
Start each chord in free time, then at a slow tempo: a ballad still has a pulse.
A tenth is a stretch. If your hand is small, roll it quickly from the bottom, or play the root and the seventh.
Over the A7 in bar six, the flat nine gives the ballad its ache: the right hand plays C sharp, G and B flat.
Leave the melody room. In a real ballad the right hand comps under the singer, softer than the tune.
A common mistake is to pedal through the changes. Lift the pedal with each new chord, so the harmony stays clear.

Listen to how great ballad pianists voice the top note of each chord: it moves by small steps and makes a quiet second melody. Try to keep your top voice moving by a step or holding still from chord to chord, all the way through the progression.
Over a drone, every mode has one colour note: Lydian’s ♯4, Mixolydian’s ♭7, Dorian’s 6, Phrygian’s ♭2. Listen for it against the home note.
A mode is a scale heard from its own home note. The drone holds home, so every step is heard against it.
Three bright modes. Lydian raises the 4th — it floats. Mixolydian lowers the 7th — bluesy, rock.
Three dark ones. Aeolian is natural minor. Dorian raises its 6th — minor but warm. Phrygian lowers the 2nd — Spanish, tense.
Compare Dorian with plain minor, Aeolian. Only the 6th differs: Dorian’s is a half step higher, and the whole scale brightens.
First ask bright or dark — the 3rd tells you. Then find the one note that differs from plain major or minor. Your turn.
All seven modes share the white keys; only the home note moves. C to C is Ionian, D to D Dorian, E Phrygian, F Lydian, G Mixolydian, A Aeolian, B Locrian.
Locrian is the darkest: ♭2 and a ♭5, so even its home chord is diminished. It is rare as a key, common over a half-diminished chord.
In a tune the colour note is the one the melody leans on. Dorian tunes keep touching the bright 6th; Mixolydian riffs land on the ♭7.
Jazz adds the modes of melodic minor: Lydian dominant (♯4 and ♭7) over a 7♯11 chord, and Altered (every tension lowered or raised) over 7alt.
Phrygian dominant, from harmonic minor, has a major 3rd with the ♭2 — the sound of flamenco and of much Middle-Eastern music.
The common mistake is naming the scale by its first note heard. Always name it from the drone — that is home.
Odd meters are groups of 2 and 3. Count the groups the snare marks, not every eighth. Polymeter loops a riff of another length over the beat.
Five beats can go long–short or short–long. 3 + 2 leans forward; 2 + 3 waits, then rolls.
Nine eighths: three even groups feel like a slow waltz; 2+2+2+3 limps at the end — the Balkan aksak.
The kick marks the bar, the snare marks each new group. Follow the snares and count their gaps.
The same eleven eighths can also go 4 + 4 + 3: two long groups and a short one. Same length, a different walk.
Your turn: hear the groups, then name them. Tap along with the snare if it helps, and say the group lengths out loud.
Odd meters live in rock and prog — five, seven and eleven are common — and in Balkan and Turkish dance music, where 9/8 and 11/8 are everyday meters.
Polymeter: the drums stay in 4 while a riff of 3, 5 or 7 beats loops over them. The riff’s first note drifts across the bar until both line up again.
To find the riff length, count from one loud riff note to the next — ignore the drums for a moment.
Metric modulation: a subdivision of the old beat becomes the new beat. If the triplets become the beat, the tempo grows by 3/2.
Dotted quarters becoming the beat slow it to 2/3; dotted eighths becoming the beat speed it up by 4/3. Listen for the hat: it plays the pivot before the change.
The common mistake is counting every eighth and losing the place. Feel the long group as one lazy step.
Most jazz changes are ii–Vs pointing at a home. The tritone sub slides into it from a half step above; the backdoor comes from ♭VII7; borrowed chords come from the minor key.
Major ii–V–I: minor 7, dominant, major 7. The bass climbs by fourths into home.
Minor ii–V–i: half-diminished, a dark ♭9 dominant, minor home.
Tritone sub: the V is replaced by the dominant a tritone away, so the bass falls by half steps: D, D♭, C.
Backdoor: iv minor to ♭VII7, then home — the bass steps up a whole tone into I.

Listen to the bass first: fourths up means a ii–V, a half step down means a tritone sub, a whole step up from below means the backdoor. Then check the colours: a minor home sounds darker and the dominant before it has a ♭9.
Standards chain ii–Vs into new keys. After a ii–V–I, the next ii–V can lead to IV, to the relative minor, a whole step down, or up a minor third.
To hear where it goes, keep the first home in your ear and compare the new one with it.
Modal interchange borrows from the parallel minor: iv m6, ♭VImaj7, ♭VII7, ♭IIImaj7, iiø7. Each darkens the major key for a moment.
Coltrane changes jump between three keys a major third apart, each reached by its own dominant.
Compare dominants around the cycle — roots falling by fifths — with dominants falling by half steps, the tritone-sub chain.
The common mistake is naming every dominant a V. Ask where it resolves: a dominant that falls a fifth is a V of the next chord, one that falls a half step is a tritone sub.
To keep: bass first, then the chord colours, then name what the changes do — ii–V, substitute, borrowed chord, or a jump to a new key.
Reharmonizing keeps the tune and changes chords under it. Find the bar that sounds different, then ask how: a new dominant, a borrowed chord, a passing diminished.
Reharmonizing means keeping the melody and putting new chords under it. Jazz players do it to refresh a standard. Here is the plain progression: I, vi, ii, V, I.
Secondary dominant: Am7 becomes A7, a dominant of its own that pulls hard into Dm7, the next chord.
Diminished passing chord: C♯°7 fills the gap between C and Dm7 — the bass rises by half steps.
Tritone sub: G7 becomes D♭7, and the bass slides down by half steps, D, D♭, C, into home.
Your turn: the original, then a new version. Follow the bass to find what changed, then name the trick.
Tritone sub: G7 becomes D♭7. The two share their 3rd and 7th, so the colour barely changes but the bass slides down by half steps.
Backdoor: Dm7 G7 becomes Fm7 B♭7 — the minor iv and ♭VII7 lead home from below.
Coltrane substitution: one ii–V–I becomes a tour of three keys: E♭7 to A♭, B7 to E, G7 home to C.
The melody stays the same in every version — that is what makes it a reharmonization, not a new tune. Each new chord must still fit the melody note above it.
Why they work: a secondary dominant aims at the next chord; a tritone sub shares the dominant’s tritone; a diminished chord connects two chords a whole step apart by a half step in the bass.
The common mistake is listening to the top of the piano. The bass tells the story; the voicings only colour it.
To keep: same tune, new chords. Find where the bass moves differently, then name the trick.
Hear a phrase as degrees of its chord: find the first note against the bass, then follow steps and leaps. Bebop lines add a half step so chord tones fall on the beat.
To transcribe, name each note as a degree of the chord under it. Over C7, an arpeggio from the root: 1, 3, 5, ♭7.
An enclosure circles its target: a note above, a half step below, then the target — here the 3rd.
A bebop line falls from the root with an extra half step between 1 and ♭7, so the chord tones land on the beats.
A line over a dominant mixes steps of the scale with chord tones. This one starts on the 5th, leaps to the ♭7 and walks down.
Your turn: sing the phrase back, then pick its degrees.
Transcribing is how jazz is learned: players copy phrases from records by ear, sing them, then play them in every key. Short phrases first — four to eight notes.
Start every transcription from the bass: hum it, then measure the first melody note against it. Is it the root, the 3rd, the 5th, the 7th — or a tension?
Then follow the shape: steps are scale notes, leaps are usually chord tones. A half step that does not belong to the scale is a chromatic approach to the next note.
Without the passing half step the same descent puts the ♭7 off the beat — compare the two.
The common mistake is writing what the hand would play instead of what the ear hears. Sing it first, slowly, and check every note against the bass.
To keep: bass, first note, shape, degrees — then check by singing along with the recording.
The jazz blues adds ii–Vs to the twelve bars; the Bird blues replaces most bars with ii–Vs. Rhythm changes has A sections of fast turnarounds and a bridge of dominants around the cycle.
A major blues: three dominant chords, I, IV and V, over twelve bars. Even the home chord is a dominant 7 — that is the blues sound.
A minor blues uses minor 7 chords on I and IV, and a ♭VI7 before the V in bar 9.
Rhythm changes: the A section turns around every two beats; the bridge holds each dominant for two bars — III7, VI7, II7, V7.
The Bird blues, after Charlie Parker, starts on a major 7 and walks down by ii–Vs.
Listen to how fast the chords move and whether they are minor or dominant. Your turn.
The blues is the most played form in jazz: twelve bars, three phrases of four. Musicians call each time through the form a chorus.
The jazz blues keeps the twelve bars but adds motion: bar 4 has a ii–V into IV, bar 6 a diminished passing chord, bars 8 to 10 a VI7–ii–V back home.
The Bird blues starts on Imaj7 and walks down by ii–Vs, a step at a time, until it reaches the IV chord in bar 5.
Rhythm changes is 32 bars, AABA, named after a famous Gershwin song. Its A sections are I–vi–ii–V again and again; its bridge is a cycle of dominants, each held for two bars.

A whole AABA chorus: eight bars of A, A again (it closes on I this time), the bridge goes somewhere new, then the last A brings you home. In the game a bell rings somewhere in the 32 bars — say which part starts there.

The common mistake is losing count of the bars. Feel each four-bar phrase as one breath, and listen for the IV chord in bar 5. To keep: count bars, follow the bass, and notice when the chord colours change.

A rootless voicing leaves the root to the bass: A has the 3rd at the bottom, B the 7th, and they alternate through a ii–V–I. An upper-structure triad is a major triad over the 3rd and ♭7 of a dominant: II gives the bright tensions (9, ♯11, 13); VI mixes 13 with ♭9; ♭III, ♭V and ♭VI give the dark ones (♯9, ♭9, ♭13).
Pianists in a band leave the root to the bass player. The hands play the colour: the 3rd, the 7th and a tension or two.
The same four notes can stand two ways. A puts the 3rd at the bottom; B puts the 7th at the bottom. B sounds a little darker and lower.
Through a ii–V–I the forms alternate — A, B, A or B, A, B — so each voice moves a step or stays. Listen for the lowest note of the first chord.
An upper structure: keep the 3rd and ♭7 of a dominant in the left hand, and put a major triad on top. A triad a whole step up, II, gives 9, ♯11 and 13 — bright.
A triad a minor 6th up, ♭VI, gives ♭13, the root and ♯9 — dark, altered. These two are the most played. Your turn.
Two more rootless sounds on a dominant: the 13 (3, 13, ♭7, 9) and the altered (3, ♭7, ♯9, ♭13). The altered one wants to fall into the next chord.
Five upper structures cover most of what you will hear over a dominant: II is bright; VI mixes the bright 13 with a dark flat 9; ♭III, ♭V and ♭VI hold the altered tensions.

Where do you hear these? Behind a soloist, a pianist moves the upper structure while the left hand keeps the 3rd and 7th: II for a bright, lydian dominant colour, ♭VI or ♭III when the line goes altered into the next chord.

Rootless voicings came from the pianists of the late 1950s, who wanted the bass player free and the chords light. With the root gone, the 9th and 13th fit under the hands, and A and B forms keep every chord in the middle of the keyboard.
The common mistake is naming the triad by its top note. Hear the whole triad as one colour against the bass: bright or dark first, then which.
A key change goes through a door: a pivot chord both keys share, a ii–V of the new key, a tritone sub, the common diminished, or no door at all (direct, or the pop lift).
A key change needs a door: a chord that leads out of the old key into the new one. Here are the doors jazz and pop use most.
A pivot chord belongs to both keys. Am7 is vi in C and ii in G, so D7 can take it straight to G.
A ii–V of the new key needs no shared chord. Fm7 and B♭7 aim at E♭, a minor third up.
The tritone sub swaps B♭7 for E7: the same 3rd and 7th, and the bass slides down a half step into E♭.
The common diminished: from C6, play B°7, lower F to E and it is E7, the V of A. Three notes stay, one moves a half step.
Direct: one phrase ends in C, the next simply starts in E♭. Pop does it up a half step for the last chorus.
Your turn: each door in all twelve keys, first in free time, then on the click. Lead every voice to the nearest note.
Raise one note of the diminished a whole step instead and you get a 7♭9 on that note. From B°7, B up to C♯ gives D♭7♭9, the door to G♭.
Key A’s own diminished opens the keys a minor third apart. The other two diminished chords open the other eight, so three cover all twelve.
Turnarounds travel too: I–VI7–ii–V, the tritone turnaround I–♭III7–♭VI7–♭II7, the Ladybird, and I–♯I°7–ii–♯ii°7 with the bass climbing by half steps.
The rhythm-changes bridge is a chain of dominants round the cycle: III7, VI7, II7, V7, each 7th falling to the next 3rd.
The melodic version: C’s 6th-diminished scale up, the diminished and E7, then A’s scale down to A.
To hear the door, find the chord where the old key stops. Shared by both keys: a pivot. A diminished sliding into a dominant: the common diminished. Nothing: direct.
Common mistake: spelling the new key from the old one. After C, E7 and A6 are spelled with sharps; B♭7 belongs to E♭.
To keep: every key change has a door, and every door works in all twelve keys.
Keep the first tonic in your ear. Each new I is a distance from it: a half step, a minor or major third, a tritone, a whole step.
Standards move through key centres, each with its own ii–V–I. To follow them, sing the first tonic and hold it in your ear.
When the next I arrives, sing from the old tonic to the new one and count the half steps. Three up is a minor third.
Four up is a major third, a bright jump. One down is a half step, a dark slide.
The tritone is the farthest key: six half steps, halfway round the circle. It sounds strange and new.
A tune with three centres, down a whole step each time, like Tune Up: D, C, B♭. Your turn.
Why it works: every new key brings its own ii–V. Hear the V7 resolve and you know where the new tonic is, even before it sounds.
Name the distance, then the key. From C, up a minor third is E♭, down a major third is A♭, down a whole step is B♭.
Common shapes in standards: down whole steps, as in Tune Up; a bridge a major third away; Coltrane’s centres a major third apart, round the circle in three.
Common mistake: hearing the ii chord as the new tonic. Wait for the V7 to land; the chord it resolves to is home.
Practice: play a standard’s changes slowly and say each key centre aloud as it arrives. Then sing each new tonic over its chord, and check it on the keys.
To keep: one tonic in the ear, count to the next, name it. Every centre is a distance from the one before.
Two layers: the bass is the surdo (root on 1, 5th on 3), the chords are the tamborim (1, 2, the "and" of 3). Straight 8ths, soft, the changes a little early.
Hi {name}! Brazilian comping has two layers. The low one is the surdo drum: the bass on beats 1 and 3, the root, then the 5th.
The high layer is the tamborim: the chord on 1, on 2, and on the "and" of 3. On guitar the thumb plays the bass and the fingers the chord; on piano, left hand and right hand.
The bossa-clave comp spreads over two bars: 1, the "and" of 2, 4, then 2 and the "and" of 3. Usually 3-2, sometimes 2-3: the same bars swapped.
The one thing to watch: the 8ths are straight, not swung, and the energy stays low. Samba is the same idea, twice as dense, with the accent on beat 2 of each 2/4 bar.
Your turn: free time first, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys. Thumb or left hand alone first, then both layers together.
The surdo has pickups too: a light note just before beat 3 and just before the next 1. Root on 1, 5th, 5th on 3, root. Keep the pickups short and soft so the bass does not gallop.
Anticipation: the new chord is often struck on the "and" before the bar line, not on the downbeat. In samba it comes a 16th early.
Voicings: on piano the left hand has the root, so the right hand plays without it — 3, 5, 7, 9 — or 6/9 and stacks of 4ths from the chord’s own scale.
The common mistake is looping one figure. Brazilian players vary it: the basic figure, the clave comp, the upbeats, a few bars each.
With a guitarist in the band, the pianist comps less: held pads and inner voices, and leaves the rhythm to the guitar.
Recap: bass on 1 and 3, chords on 1, 2 and the "and" of 3; straight, soft, varied; the changes a little early.
A two-bar figure in the clave: the bar on the clave’s three-side is played all on the offbeats, the bar on its two-side on the beats.
Hi {name}! The montuno, or guajeo, began on the Cuban tres guitar and moved to the piano. It repeats over two bars, and it lives inside the clave.
The rule: the bar that sits on the clave’s three-side is played all on the offbeats; the bar on the two-side, on the beats.
In 2-3 the figure starts on the beats; in 3-2 it starts on the offbeats. The direction comes from where the chords start against the clave.
The one thing to watch: never cross the clave. A 2-3 figure over a 3-2 clave sounds wrong, and moving it by a beat does not fix it.
Your turn: block chords on the grid first, then the figure, then the changes — free time first, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys.

Ponchando is the simple form: block chords on the attack points. The figure itself puts the line note in octaves, with the other chord tones between. Here over C, F, G and F: the octaves climb by step while the inner notes change with each chord.
The left hand doubles the line one or two octaves lower, and chord changes often come an 8th early.
Under it the bass plays the tumbao: nothing on 1, the "and" of 2 and beat 4, and the 4 already belongs to the next chord.
Jazz harmony entered the montuno in the 1940s: a ii–V in two bars, or a ii–V–I over four.
In songo the right hand plays on the four beats over a looping minor progression, while the drums and bass build the syncopation around it.
A practice tip: say the clave out loud while you play the figure. If your hands and your voice agree on which bar is the three-side, you are in clave.
Recap: two bars, in clave; the three-side on the offbeats, the two-side on the beats; 2-3 or 3-2 by where the chords start.
The montuno, played on the beats: Jorrín took the syncopation out for the dancers. A moderate tempo, the bell on every beat, the cha-cha-chá on 4, its "and" and 1.
Hi {name}! The cha-cha-chá was born in Havana in the early 1950s, in the charanga bands: flute, violins, piano, bass and percussion. Enrique Jorrín wrote it for dancers.
Jorrín took the syncopation out on purpose, so the dancers could follow. So the piano plays its montuno on the beats, in every bar: the octave line, then the inner notes.
The name comes from the dancers’ feet: three quick steps on 4, its "and", and the next 1. In the band the conga marks the 4 and its "and", and the bell plays every beat.
The one thing to watch: the tempo. The cha-cha sits around 120 beats a minute, relaxed and even. Push it much faster and it turns into a mambo.
Your turn: chords on the beats first, then the octave figure, then both hands, then with the band. Free time first, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys.
The figure is the montuno’s own: the line note in octaves, the other chord tones between. Over C, F, G and F the octaves walk G, A, B, A, and the loop comes back note for note.
The cha-cha grew out of the danzón: its last section, the montuno, was stretched into a whole dance. That is why the piano part is a montuno, only calmer.
Under the piano the bass plays a tumbao-like line: the "and" of 2 and beat 4, the 4 already the next chord. The güiro scrapes a long stroke and two short ones.
Jazz players love the cha-cha too: a ii–V–I fits the same figure, one chord a bar, the octave line moving by step from chord to chord.
The mambo goes the other way: the same montuno, syncopated in the clave, much faster, around 180, with big-band horns. In this unit you play both.
The common mistake is rushing. Count the dancers’ step while you play: two, three, cha-cha-chá. If the 4 and its "and" feel easy, the tempo is right.
Recap: the montuno on the beats, a moderate tempo, the bell on every beat, the cha-cha-chá on 4, its "and" and 1, in the drums and the dancers’ feet.
Cuba’s love song: slow, the bass on 1 and 3, the chord broken in even 8ths over it.
Hi {name}! The bolero is Cuba’s love song. It began with the trova singers of Santiago de Cuba, who sang to their own guitar; the first bolero, "Tristezas", dates from 1883.
It is slow, about 60 to 90 beats a minute. The left hand keeps the bass on 1 and 3: the root, then the 5th.
The right hand breaks the chord into 8ths, up and down, the way the guitar’s half-arpeggios did from the 1920s.
The one thing to watch: keep the 8ths even and soft. The singer floats freely over a steady pulse, so the pulse itself must not move.
Your turn: the left hand alone first, then both hands. Free time first, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys.
Many jazz ballads turn into boleros easily: keep the changes and put the bolero feel underneath. A ii–V–I is the place to start: D minor 7, G7, C major 7.
Some bass players add a note on 4: a half note, then two quarters. It leans each bar toward the next one.
In Cuba boleros are usually written in 2/4; elsewhere in 4/4. It is the same music, counted twice as fast on paper.
In the 1930s the bolero met the son: the bolero-son of Trío Matamoros, a little more syncopated. In the 1950s came the bolero-cha, with the cha-cha-chá underneath.
The common mistake is a heavy hand. The arpeggio is a carpet, not a melody: the top note of each turn should not stick out, and the bass speaks a little louder than the 8ths.
Recap: slow, the bass on 1 and 3, the chord broken in even 8ths, soft under a free melody.
A lick is a word of the language: learn it over its chords, in every key, up to tempo — then use it in a solo.
Hi {name}! Jazz players speak in phrases they own, the way you speak in words. Here is a short one over D minor 7, G 7 and C major 7.
Notice where it lands: the 7th of G falls a half step to the 3rd of C. The chord tones sit on the beats.
A word you can say only in one key is not yours yet. The same line a whole step down sounds like this.
So the grid has a column for every key and a row for every tempo. Only a clean, measured take fills a cell.
At three stars the lick joins your review, and Use it opens: the band plays, you improvise, and the app listens for your lick over the right chords.
Where do licks come from? From the chords. Take the chord tones, put them on the beats, and connect them with scale notes.
A chromatic note can lead into a chord tone by a half step. Players call it an approach note.
An enclosure surrounds the target: one note above it, one below, then the target itself on the beat.
The bebop scale adds a passing half step to the dominant scale, so going down in eighths keeps the chord tones on the beats.
Practice slowly enough to be clean, then climb. The ladder raises the tempo only after clean takes, and a level counts only on two different days.
Learn the lick in the keys the music lives in: around the circle of fourths, the way ii–V–Is move through standards. After C comes F, then B flat, then E flat.
To keep: chord tones on the beats, approach and enclose, every key, then use it in a solo. That is how vocabulary becomes yours.
Hear it, sing it inside, play it back, write it down, then move it to every key. Each step is measured.
Hi {name}! Transcribing is how jazz has always been learned: you take a phrase off the music by ear, with no paper. Listen to this one.
Loop it and slow it down until you can sing it in your head. Slowing it here keeps the pitch exactly the same.
Then play it or sing it back after the count-in. The app compares note by note, pitch and rhythm, and names the first note that went wrong.
Now write it down as degrees of the key. This one is five, six, seven, two, one.
Last, play it in all twelve keys, measured like a lick. Keep the phrases you love as your own licks, and use them.
Start with the shape before the notes: does it go up or down, by steps or by leaps? Sing the shape first.
Find the first note against the key. Is it the tonic, the third, the fifth? Everything else is measured from there.
Then the rhythm: where does each note start in the beat? Tap it slowly before you play it.
Short loops beat long ones. Two or three notes at a time, then join them. Slow is a tool, not a failure.
Showing the notes is allowed, but a phrase you saw counts less. The goal is to hear it, not to read it.
A band under the phrase helps: you hear each note against its chord, so a third sounds like a third. Turn the band on when the phrase has chords.
To keep: shape, first note, rhythm, play it back, write it, all keys. Do one phrase a day and your ear will grow fast.
Open a recording of your own; the app finds its beat and its line, and measures only what it found clearly.
Hi {name}! Here you practice over a recording of your own: a voice memo, your band at rehearsal, a take you made. It stays on this phone.
First the app listens to it once. It finds the beat, the melody and the bass line, and keeps what it found, so the next time opens at once.
The song is cut into short sections. Loop one, slow it down without changing the pitch, and when you are ready, play along on headphones.
Your notes are measured against the beat of the recording, and against its line when that line came out clearly. A steady small delay is forgiven.
When the app is not sure, it says so on the screen and measures less: timing only, or nothing. It never guesses a score.
How the beat is found: every sudden rise in the sound is an onset. The app looks for the spacing that repeats most and lays a grid of beats over it.
A ballad sung freely has no steady beat. Then timing is not measured at all, and the screen tells you so.
The melody comes out cleanly when one voice is the loudest pitched sound. A full band mix gives gaps, so notes may be checked only in part.
Bass players are checked against the bass line, drummers against the beat alone, keys and guitar against the melody.
Headphones matter: through a speaker the microphone hears the recording itself, and the take would measure the song, not you. A MIDI keyboard needs no headphones.
A slowed take counts a little less than one at full speed. Climb the speeds: seventy-five, ninety, then the real thing.
Your songs are kept on this device only. Rename them, see your last score, and delete the ones you no longer need to free space.
Loop one phrase of your recording, slow it down, then play or sing it back: it is compared note by note.
Hi {name}! The best transcriptions come from music you love. Open a recording of your own, and the app takes out its melody, phrase by phrase.
Pick a phrase and loop it. Slow it down until you can sing it in your head. The pitch stays the same.
Then play or sing it back after the count-in. The comparison is the one the transcription coach uses: pitch and rhythm, and the first note that went wrong.
Sing it an octave lower if that is your voice: the octave does not count as a mistake.
Each phrase you get right feeds your dictation rating and your daily goal. A slowed phrase counts a little less.
The melody is found where one voice is the loudest pitched sound: a cappella singing, a voice with one instrument, a solo line. A full band blurs it.
