Long phrases are cut into pieces of up to eight notes. Two or three short pieces are easier to hold than one long line.
Start with the shape: up or down, steps or leaps. Then find the first note against the key, and the rest follows from there.
When the recording has a steady beat, the phrase is timed at its tempo. When it does not, rhythm is judged on your own pulse, so a steady player who is a little slower is not wrong.
A common mistake is to loop a whole verse. Take three or four notes, get them right, then add the next few. Slow is a tool, not a failure.
Your recordings stay on this device. Keep the songs you are learning and delete the rest to free space.
A note has no meaning alone: the key gives it its job. B♭ is 1 in B♭ major and 5 in E♭ major.
Hey {name}! Here is a secret of ear training: a note on its own has no job. The key around it gives it one. Meet our note — B-flat.
Now chords in B-flat major, then the same B-flat. It sounds like home: settled, nothing wants to move. That is 1.
Now the chords move to E-flat major. Same B-flat, same piano — but now it floats, open and waiting. That is 5.
Why 5? Count up the E-flat major scale: E-flat, F, G, A-flat, B-flat. The fifth note from home.
And 5 loves to go home. Listen to it land on E-flat — ahh, relief.
Your turn! I play the chords, then this same B-flat. Tell me "one" or "five". Trust the feeling — resting is 1, floating is 5.
A degree describes a note’s job in a key, not its pitch. In B-flat major, B-flat is the tonic, 1. In E-flat major it is the dominant, 5. Same pitch; only the context changes.
Why does 1 feel like rest? It is the root of the home chord, the chord every cadence ends on. In B-flat major that chord is B-flat, D, F.
5 is also in the home chord, so it is stable — but it is the root of the V chord too, the chord that pulls home. In E-flat: E-flat chord, B-flat 7, E-flat chord.
A listening strategy: after the chords, sing home. If home is the very note you hear, it is 1. If you have to walk down 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 to reach home, it is 5.
The common mistake is judging by height: high means 5, low means 1. But the degree ignores the octave. This low B-flat is still 5 in E-flat major.

In real music this happens all the time. A note shared by two chords — a common tone — can stay put while the harmony moves, quietly changing its job. Hear B-flat on top, from B-flat major to E-flat major.
Recap: a note gets its degree from the key, not from itself. Hear the chords, find home, then measure the note from home.
Several notes sounding together make a chord. C–E–G: root, third, fifth. Lower the third a half step and major turns minor.
A chord is several notes sounding at once. First, a single note.
Now three notes: one by one, then together. That is a chord.
Their names: in C–E–G, C is the root, E the third, G the fifth.
Chords have a color. Major sounds bright; minor sounds darker.
Only one note changes: the third, a half step lower in minor. E becomes E-flat.
Chords are usually built from thirds: every other note of the scale. In C major take C, skip D, take E, skip F, take G. That is C–E–G.
A chord of three notes is called a triad. The root gives the chord its name: C–E–G is a C chord, G–B–D is a G chord.
Count half steps up from the root. Major: four to the third, then three more to the fifth. Minor: three, then four. Both reach the fifth at seven half steps.
Spread the notes out, or double one, and it is still the same chord. Here is C major low and wide, then high and close.
A common mistake: calling every quiet or sad-sounding chord minor. Register and mood do not decide; only the third does. Here is a low G major, then a high E minor.
In a song, the melody is one line on top, and the chords under it are the harmony. Here are four chords that bring a phrase home in C.
Major and minor chords differ by one note: the middle one. Major third = bright, minor third = dark.
Hi {name}! A basic chord has three notes: a root, a middle note, and a fifth on top. Here is C major — bright and sunny.
Now lower just the middle note by a half step: E becomes E-flat. That is C minor — darker, softer, a little sad.
Only one note moves! The root and the fifth stay put. Hear the light switch off and on: major, minor, major.
That middle note is a third above the root. Four half steps make a major third; three make a minor third. That is where the names come from.
The root will change every round, but the color does not. Here is G major, then G minor.
Your turn! I play a chord, you say "major" or "minor". Not sure? Hum the middle note: smiling means major, shaded means minor.
A triad is two thirds stacked. Major: a major third (4 half steps), then a minor third (3). Minor: the reverse, 3 then 4. Both span a perfect fifth, 7 half steps, from root to top.
Spell them with letters. D major is D, F-sharp, A; D minor is D, F, A. A major is A, C-sharp, E; A minor is A, C, E.
Inside a major key, chords I, IV and V are major; ii, iii and vi are minor. In C: C, F and G major; D minor, E minor and A minor.
The common mistake: calling quiet, slow or low chords minor and loud, high ones major. Register and mood do not decide; only the third does. Here is a low G major, then a high E minor.
A listening tip: sing the chord back from the bottom, 1, 3, 5, and focus on the step from 1 to 3. A wide, open step is major; a narrow one is minor.
In real songs the two colors alternate constantly. The pop progression I, V, vi, IV moves from major chords to the minor vi and back.
Two more triads exist. Diminished stacks two minor thirds and sounds tense; augmented stacks two major thirds and sounds unsettled. You will meet them later.
Recap: same root, same fifth — the third decides. Four half steps above the root is major, three is minor.
A phrase that ends V → I is resolved, like a full stop; one that stops on V is open, like a question.
Hey {name}! Music talks in sentences called phrases. The chords at the end are the punctuation — we call that a cadence.
This phrase ends with five going to one: V7, then I. It comes home, like a full stop. We call it resolved.
I – IV – V7 – I .
This one stops on V, the five chord. It hangs in the air, like a question mark. We call it open.
Only the ending matters. Skip the middle and judge the very last chord: does it rest, or lean forward? Here are just the two endings.
A test that never fails: when it stops, do you want to sing home? Listen — this open phrase is begging for it.
Your turn, detective! The key changes each round, so listen to the whole phrase and tell me "resolved" or "open". The last chord is your clue.
A cadence is the harmonic ending of a phrase. The authentic cadence, V to I, closes it. The half cadence stops on V and leaves it open.
Why does V pull to I? In C, the G7 chord holds B, the leading tone, a half step below C. Its F leans down to E. Both tensions resolve at once.
A gentler close is the plagal cadence, IV to I — the “Amen” at the end of many hymns. It resolves, but without the leading tone’s pull.
The deceptive cadence sets up V, then lands on vi instead of I. It sounds like a surprise turn: the phrase is not finished yet.
A listening strategy: when the music stops, sing home. If your note sits comfortably in the last chord, the phrase is closed. If it rubs, the ending is open.
The common mistake: hearing a half cadence as closed because V is a bright major chord. On its own it sounds stable; in the key it wants I. Judge the last chord against the key, not by itself.
In real music, phrases often come in pairs: the first ends with a half cadence, like a question, the second with an authentic cadence, like the answer. This pair is called a period.
Recap: V to I is a full stop; stopping on V is a question mark. IV to I closes gently, and V to vi is a surprise.
Hear the key, find home (1) with your voice, and reach 5 by climbing do-re-mi-fa-sol.
Hi {name}! Time for your own instrument — your voice. First I play the key, then its home note. Listen.
Singing home is simple: hum the very note you just heard. Match it, hold it, mmm.
Five is the fifth note of the scale: do, re, mi, fa, sol. Climb there and stop.
A shortcut: it is the jump in "Twinkle, Twinkle". Twin-kle, twin-kle — from 1 up to 5.
While you sing, the screen shows your pitch live. Too low? Slide up a little. Too high? Ease down. Any octave counts.
Your turn. Hear the key and home, wait for the chime, then sing what I ask: home, or five. Breathe low and keep your jaw relaxed.
1 is the tonic, the note the key is named after. 5 is the dominant, a perfect fifth above: seven half steps. Together they frame the key, and most melodies lean on them.
5 also lives below home: a perfect fourth down, five half steps. Same degree, another octave. Sing whichever sits comfortably in your voice.
To find home, let the chords finish and hum the note that feels like rest. Hold it until nothing in you wants to move.
To reach 5, climb the scale: do, re, mi, fa, sol — aloud at first, later silently. With practice you jump straight there, using the opening leap of “Twinkle, Twinkle” as your anchor.
Pitch starts in the body. Breathe low, keep the jaw loose, and sing on a soft “mm” or “oo”. Start the note gently on pitch instead of scooping up into it.
The common mistake is landing on 4 or 6 instead of 5. To check, sing down from your note: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. If you end on home, you were right.
In real music, 1 and 5 are the backbone of bass lines. In country, polka and many folk songs, the bass simply alternates root and fifth.
Recap: hear the key, settle on 1, then find 5 — seven half steps up, or five down.
Major third = 4 half steps, sweet; perfect fifth = 7, open and hollow; octave = 12, the same note higher.
Hey {name}! An interval is the distance between two notes. Today you meet three big ones: the third, the fifth and the octave.
A major third: four half steps, like C to E. Close and sweet — the bottom of a major chord.
A perfect fifth: seven half steps, C to G. Open and strong, like a horn call. It is the leap in "Twinkle, Twinkle".
An octave: twelve half steps, C to the next C. Same name, just higher — the two almost melt into one.
Together is trickier, so listen to the blend: the third is warm and full, the fifth hollow, the octave nearly one note.
Your turn. First the notes come one after the other, then together. Say "third", "fifth" or "octave".
An interval has a number and a quality. The number counts letter names, both ends included: C to E spans C, D, E — a third. C to G spans five letters — a fifth.
The quality refines the size. A third can be major, 4 half steps like C to E, or minor, 3 like C to E-flat. Fifths and octaves are called perfect: 7 and 12.
Played one after the other, an interval is melodic; together, it is harmonic. Melodic is easier at first; harmonic trains you to hear the blend.
Anchor each interval to a tune you know. The major third opens “When the Saints Go Marching In”. The fifth is “Twinkle, Twinkle”. The octave opens “Over the Rainbow”.
Intervals also go down. A falling fifth, G down to C, is the same size as C up to G — count the same way.
The common mistake is confusing the fifth and the octave, since both sound pure. In an octave you hear one note doubled; in a fifth, two clearly different notes.
In real music, the fifth is the rock power chord and the tuning of the violin’s strings. Thirds give harmony singing its sweetness: two voices a third apart.
Recap: count letters for the number, half steps for the quality. Major third 4, perfect fifth 7, octave 12.
The same chord can stand on its root (C), its third (C/E) or its fifth (C/G): the lowest note changes the feel.
Hi {name}! A chord can stand on different feet. Its lowest note — the bass — changes how the whole chord feels.
Bass on the root: C under a C chord. Solid and grounded, feet flat on the floor.
Bass on the third: E under a C chord, written C slash E. Lighter, a bit restless — it wants to keep walking.
Bass on the fifth: G under a C chord, C slash G. Strong but hovering, like it is waiting for something.
The trick: hum the lowest note, then find it in the chord. Here the bass is E — the middle note of C, E, G. So: third!
Your turn! I play the bass alone, then the full chord. Tell me "root", "third" or "fifth". The chord changes, the question does not.
An inversion is a chord with a note other than the root in the bass. Root in the bass: root position. Third in the bass: first inversion. Fifth in the bass: second inversion.
Pop and jazz charts write inversions as slash chords: the chord, a slash, then the bass note. G/B is a G chord over B, its third. F/C is F over C, its fifth.
Only the bass decides the name. The upper notes can come in any order and spacing: with E in the bass, both of these are C/E.
Why use inversions? They let the bass move by step. C, then G/B, then A minor: the bass walks C, B, A — smooth instead of jumping.

Each position has a typical role. Root position is stable and final. First inversion is lighter and moving. Second inversion is unstable: C/G before G7 at a cadence is the classic “cadential six-four”.
The common mistake is naming the top note instead of the bass. The melody grabs your attention, but the inversion lives at the bottom. Here C is on top, yet the bass is G: second inversion.
In real music, inversions build descending bass lines, common in pop ballads and Baroque music alike. C, G/B, Am, C/G, F walks the bass straight down the scale.
Recap: the lowest note names the inversion. Root is grounded, third is light, fifth is hovering; slash chords write it as chord over bass.
Letter names stay fixed; degrees count from the key’s home. To convert, count up the scale from 1.
Hey {name}! Every note has two names. Its letter — C, D, E — never changes. Its degree — 1, 2, 3 — is its place in the key.
Change the key and the numbers move with home. In G major, G is 1 — so D is 5, and F-sharp is 7.
To convert, count up from home. Which degree is B-flat in E-flat major? E-flat 1, F 2, G 3, A-flat 4, B-flat 5. Five!
The other way works too. Degree 4 in F major? F, G, A, B-flat. Careful: F major has B-flat, not B.
Some rounds play a note in the key: hear its degree first, then name it. In D major, this is 3 — F-sharp.
Your turn. I name a key, then ask for a note or a degree — or play one. Count from home; counting on your fingers is fine.
Letter names are absolute: C is always C. Degrees are relative: they number a scale’s notes from its tonic, 1 to 7. The same numbers work in every key, which is why musicians use them to transpose.
Every major scale follows one pattern of whole and half steps: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. The half steps fall between 3 and 4, and between 7 and 8.
That pattern decides the key signature. G major needs F-sharp, or the step from 7 to 8 would not be a half step. F major needs B-flat to keep 3 to 4 a half step.
Each degree takes its own letter, once. In D major, 3 is F-sharp, never G-flat: the letters must run D, E, F, G, A, B, C.
Degrees have names too. 1 is the tonic, 4 the subdominant, 5 the dominant, and 7 the leading tone, because it leads up to 1.
A shortcut for high degrees: count down from the octave. In A major, 7 is one step below the next A — G-sharp. That is faster than counting six steps up.
The common mistake: forgetting the key signature while counting. In E-flat major, 4 is A-flat, not A. Say the scale with its accidentals before you count.
Recap: letters are fixed, degrees move with home. Know the key’s accidentals, count from 1, and give every degree its own letter.
Echo a note exactly; to sing a named note, find home first, then climb to its degree.
Hi {name}! Two games today. First, echo: I play a note, and you sing that very same note back.
Tune like a guitar string: hum, listen, nudge until it locks in. Low or high octave both count. Try this G in your head.
Then the real trick: I play the key and its home note, and ask for a note by name — like "sing E".
Find it from home. In C major, E is 3: do, re, mi. And G is 5: keep climbing to sol.
Same idea in any key. In D major, F-sharp is 3 and A is 5.
Your turn. Echo the notes I play, then sing the notes I name, after the chime. Aim for the center of each note.
Two skills hide here. Echoing — matching a pitch you just heard — teaches your voice to follow your ear. Singing a named note teaches your inner map: name, then degree, then sound.
Echo in the octave that suits your voice. Lower voices usually sing an octave below the piano’s middle; that still counts as the same note. Here is E, then the E an octave lower.
To match a pitch, start the note softly, then nudge it up or down until it stops fighting the piano and locks in. Small, slow corrections beat big swoops.
For a named note, go through the degree. In F major, “sing A”: A is 3, so sing do, re, mi from F.
Some notes sit just below home. In G major, F-sharp is 7, a half step under G: sing home, then lean down one small step.
The common mistake: guessing from the letter alone. B is 7 in C major, a tense note under home — but in G major it is 3, calm and sweet. Always go through the degree.
This is how singers read new music without a piano: find the key, turn each note into a degree, then sing it from home.
Recap: echo by gentle tuning, any octave. For a named note, find home, turn the name into a degree, and climb there.
Lock in home first, then sing the numbers in order: steps walk the scale, 1–3–5 climbs the home chord.
Hey {name}! Now you sing little tunes from numbers. I say "one, three, five" — you sing those degrees, in order.
Steps are the friendly ones: 1, 2, 3 walks up the scale, and 3, 2, 1 walks back home.
Jumps skip notes: 1, 3, 5 climbs the home chord, and 5, 3, 1 slides down it like a banister.
And 5, 6, 5 is a little neighbor: step up from 5 and come right back.
Tip: for a jump, sing the notes in between silently. From 1 to 5? Think 2, 3, 4 on the way.
Your turn! Hear the key and home, then sing the numbers I give you after the chime. One clear note at a time.
Singing degrees is the core of solfège: each number names a step of the scale, sung relative to home. Numbers or syllables — do, re, mi — work the same way, as long as the name follows the function.
Degrees 1, 3 and 5 belong to the home chord and feel stable. The others are active and lean toward a neighbor: 7 rises to 1, 4 falls to 3, 2 falls to 1, 6 falls to 5.
Use those pulls to find active notes. To find 7, sing 1 and slip a half step down. To find 4, sing 3 and step a half step up.
For leaps, use the home chord as scaffolding. 1 to 6? Think 1 to 5, then one step up to 6.
Degrees also sit below 1. Many melodies start on 5 or 7 below home and rise into it.
A short daily routine: in one key, sing 1-2-3-2-1, then 1-3-5-3-1, then 1-5-1, checking against the piano. Then change key — the numbers stay the same.
The common mistake is drift: after a few notes, your sense of home slides sharp or flat, and every degree after it is off. Return to 1 often and compare it with the piano.
Recap: lock in home, use the home chord as scaffolding, and let active notes lean into their neighbors.
Remember a short sequence as degrees, then turn each degree into a name — or a name into a degree.
Hi {name}! You can name one note — now let us name a few in a row. Here are two notes in B-flat major.
The secret: remember numbers, not sounds. Those were 5 then 2. In B-flat major, 5 is F and 2 is C.
Hum it back once right away — a sung tune sticks much longer. Try three notes in G major: 1, 3, 5 is G, B, D.
Some rounds give you names to convert. In F major: A, G, F — which degrees? Count from home: 3, 2, 1.
And one round asks you to sing named notes. Find home first, then each name by its number.
Your turn! Listen and name, convert both ways, and sing. One note at a time — there is no rush.
Short-term memory holds only a few items at once. Turning sounds into degrees packs them tightly: three numbers are far easier to hold than three raw pitches. In D major: F-sharp, E, D is 3, 2, 1.
Look for patterns: steps, repeats, or a chord outline. 1, 3, 5, 8 is just the home chord climbing — four notes, one idea.
Get the first note right and the rest follow. Find its degree against home, then track each move: up or down, step or leap. In F major: A, B-flat, C, F is 3, 4, 5, 1.
To convert names, say the scale from home and count. In D major, A is 5, B is 6 and F-sharp is 3.
If one note slips away, keep the contour — the up-and-down shape. A sequence with the right shape and one wrong number is easy to fix on the next hearing.
The common mistake is naming each note the moment it sounds, and missing the next one. Listen to the whole sequence, sing it back, and only then name it.
This is how musicians learn riffs and melodies by ear: hear a short phrase, sing it, turn it into degrees, then find it on the instrument.
Recap: remember sequences as numbers and shapes, anchor the first note to home, and name only after the whole sequence has finished.
Every melody is a string of degrees: find home, then ask of each note how far it is from home.
Hey {name}! You already know dozens of melodies — and each one is just degrees. Listen: 1, 1, 5, 5, 6, 6, 5.
That is "Twinkle, Twinkle". Same numbers in any key, same tune. Here it is in G.
Frère Jacques walks: 1, 2, 3, 1 — step, step, and back home.
Not every song starts at home! "Ode to Joy" starts on 3: 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 4, 3, 2.
The trick: keep home in your ear, and for each note ask — above or below home, and how far?
Your turn. I play an opening, you say its degrees in order — then I reveal the song. Once, you will sing one from its numbers.
You recognize a melody by its pattern of intervals, not by its exact pitches. That is why you know a song in any key: the degrees stay, only the starting pitch moves. “Twinkle” in D:
Melodies can start on any degree. Many begin on 5 below home and rise into the key. “Happy Birthday” does: 5, 5, 6, 5, 1, 7.
Strategy: notice where the melody rests — usually the last note of a phrase. That is most often 1. Then measure the first note from there.
Then follow the motion. Most melodies move mostly by step, with an occasional leap for character. The second line of “Twinkle” is all steps down: 4, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 1.
Rhythm and meter are clues too. “Happy Birthday” sways in three beats per bar; “Twinkle” marches in four, even though both open with a repeated note.
The common mistake is assuming every song starts on 1. If your numbers come out strange, check the final note: if it is not 1, your home is in the wrong place.
Musicians use this to play by ear, to transpose on the spot, and to write charts. Once a melody is in numbers, you can play it in any key — here, F.
Recap: find where the tune rests, call it 1, and measure every note from there — up or down, step or leap.
Write a bar in two passes: first the notes as degrees, then the rhythm.
Hi {name}! Dictation means writing down what you hear: the notes and their rhythm. We go one short bar at a time.
Pass one: the notes. Sing the bar in your head and turn it into degrees. That one was 1, 2, 3, 1.
Pass two: the rhythm — how long is each note? Here: two quarters and a half note.
Eighth notes come in pairs, two to a beat. Listen: a quarter, two eighths, two quarters.
And the dotted quarter: long, then short.
Your turn! Hear a bar, say its degrees in order, then pick the rhythm you heard. Notes first, rhythm second — one thing at a time.
Melodic dictation means writing down a melody you hear: its pitches, its rhythm and its meter. Professionals work in stages, and so should you.
Before writing anything, gather three facts: the key, the first note’s degree, and the beat. Tap along and count how many beats make a bar — usually four or three.
Pass one, pitches. Sketch the contour first — up, down, same — then fill in exact degrees, checking each against home. This one: 1, 3, 2, 5.
Pass two, rhythm. Tap the beat and notice which notes take one beat, which share a beat, and which hold longer. Here: two eighths, then three quarters.
A dot adds half the note’s value. A dotted quarter lasts one and a half beats and is usually followed by an eighth; a dotted half lasts three beats.
Do not write during the first hearing. Listen, sing it back in your head, then write. On every replay, fill in only what is still missing.
The common mistake is straightening uneven rhythms. A dotted figure easily turns into even quarters on paper. Clap it back before choosing. Dotted, then even:
Dictation is the heart of ear-training exams and of transcribing solos. The same two passes work for one bar or a whole song.
Recap: key, first note and beat first; then degrees; then rhythm. Listen before you write.
Absolute pitch is rare and optional; relative pitch is the main goal. Here you train a feel for each note’s color.
Hey {name}! Welcome to a bonus corner. Absolute pitch means naming a note with no reference at all — no key, no chords. Like this A.
Honest truth: full absolute pitch is rare, and few adults ever gain it. Most great musicians rely on relative pitch — hearing how notes relate.
Still, many people find each note has a faint color of its own, and practice sharpens that feel. That is what we play with here.
Before each note you hear a messy cluster. It is no mistake: it wipes the last note from memory, so you cannot sneak in relative pitch.
The first level uses only the white keys: C, D, E, F, G, A, B.
Your turn! Hear a note, pick its name. Guess freely — this score is tracked apart from your other skills, so it cannot hurt them.

Absolute pitch, also called perfect pitch, is naming or singing a note with no reference. Relative pitch names notes by their relation to a known note or key. Most professional musicians rely on relative pitch.

Research links full absolute pitch to musical training in early childhood, and it is more common among speakers of tonal languages. Adults can improve with practice, but rarely reach effortless, instant naming.
Many people without it still have pitch memory: asked to sing a favorite recording, they often land close to its original key. The ear stores pitch even when naming it takes training.
How to practice: start with one or two anchor notes, say A and C. Listen for their character, then compare each new note to an anchor before you guess.
A note’s color shifts with register and instrument, so you are learning its name, not its height. Here is C in three octaves — the same note class each time.
The common mistake is quietly measuring from the previous note. That is relative pitch in disguise — a great skill, but here the cluster breaks the chain on purpose. Judge each note fresh.
Even partial pitch memory is useful: it helps you sense a song’s key quickly and start singing closer to the right pitch.
Recap: absolute pitch is a bonus, relative pitch is the foundation. Train with anchor notes, and judge each note fresh.
Find the third (bright or dark), then the one odd note: Dorian has a raised 6th, Mixolydian a flat 7th.
Hi {name}! A mode is a scale with its own mood. Same home note, a few notes shifted — and the color changes. Ionian is plain major.
Aeolian is natural minor: the 3rd, 6th and 7th are all a half step lower. Darker, more serious.
Dorian is minor with a bright 6th — dark, but with a hopeful lift.
Mixolydian is major with a flat 7th — bluesy, a bit rock and roll.
The trick: first the third — bright family or dark family? Then hunt for the odd note. Here: Aeolian top, then Dorian top. Hear the 6th lift?
Your turn! I play home, then a scale up and down. Name the mode. Higher levels add more modes — same trick, a different odd note.
The modes are seven scales made from the major scale’s notes, each starting on a different degree. Using only white keys: from C you get Ionian, from D Dorian, from G Mixolydian, from A Aeolian.
For the ear, it is easier to compare modes on the same home note, as this exercise does. Then each mode is simply major or minor with one or two notes changed.
Two more you will meet. Lydian is major with a raised 4: dreamy and floating, a favorite of film composers.
Phrygian is minor with a flat 2, a half step above home: dark and tense, heard in flamenco and metal. Locrian, with ♭2 and ♭5, is the rarest and darkest.
The method: settle home, decide major or minor third, then hunt the characteristic note — ♯4 Lydian, ♭7 Mixolydian, 6 Dorian, ♭2 Phrygian. If nothing stands out, it is plain major or natural minor.
Each mode’s color also lives in a chord. Dorian sounds like a minor chord with a major 6th; Mixolydian like a dominant 7th chord. Here are Cm6 and C7.
The common mistake is hearing Dorian as major because of its bright 6. Check the third first: Dorian’s is minor. The 6 only lifts a minor scale.
In real music, Mixolydian fills rock and folk riffs, Aeolian is the everyday sound of minor pop, and Dorian is central to modal jazz — Miles Davis’s “So What” is built on it.
Recap: same home, different colors. Third first, then the characteristic note names the mode.
Sing the right scale in your head along with the one you hear: the note where you disagree is the wrong one.
Hi {name}! Detective time. I play a scale with one note bent out of place — you find it. First, the real thing: C major.
Now number 4 is a half step too high: F became F-sharp. Hear it stick out?
Wrong notes can also slip down. Here number 6 drops: A became A-flat.
The trick: sing the right scale in your head along with mine, and count. That one was number 3 — E became E-flat.
Your turn. I play home, then the scale. Say the number of the wrong note — home and the top are always right.
Spotting a wrong note means comparing what you hear with what you expect. Once home is set, your ear predicts each next step of the scale; a wrong note breaks that prediction.
Every wrong note distorts the pattern of whole and half steps. Raise 4 to F-sharp, and the half step moves: 3 to 4 becomes a whole step, 4 to 5 a half step.
Raised notes tend to sound sharp and pushy, pulling upward. Lowered notes sound darker; a lowered 3, 6 or 7 hints at minor or blues. Here, 7 drops to B-flat.
The method: sing the correct scale silently, a hair ahead of the piano. The moment your inner voice and the piano disagree, note the number. On replay, check: higher or lower?
The common mistake is blaming the note after the wrong one. A wrong note makes the next step sound odd too, because the gap is wrong on both sides. The first surprise is usually the culprit.
To go further, practice descending scales too: sing down from 8 to 1 so your expectation works in both directions.
In real music, this is proofreading: catching a wrong note in a chart, in your own playing, or in a choir. It also helps you notice chromatic notes a composer added on purpose.
Recap: keep the right scale running in your head, mark the first disagreement, then decide whether it was raised or lowered.
A run is a fast scale passage on one vowel: know its scale (major, pentatonic, blues) and its shape, then sing it slow and clean before fast.
Hey {name}! A run is a quick string of notes sung on one vowel — the sparkle singers add to a melody. Runs are built from scales. This one is major: bright and clean.
The minor pentatonic has just five notes per octave, with bigger gaps. Soulful — an R&B favorite.
Blues adds one spicy extra: the flat 5, squeezed between 4 and 5. Hear the crunch?
Runs also have a shape: going up, going down, or a turn — up and back.
To sing one: start slow on "ah", keep every note separate and clean, then speed up. Clean beats fast!
Your turn! First say the scale — major, pentatonic or blues — and the shape. Then sing runs back after me. Breathe low, keep it light.
A run, or riff, is a quick ornament sung on one syllable — a melisma. It decorates a melody note, often at the end of a phrase, and always fits the scale and chord underneath.
The scale sets the color. Major runs sound sweet and bright; the minor pentatonic, 1 ♭3 4 5 ♭7, sounds soulful; the blues scale adds ♭5 for grit.
Pentatonic scales contain no half steps, so their notes rarely clash with the chord. That is why they are the standard material for runs in gospel, soul and R&B.
Every run has a target: the note it lands on, usually a chord tone like 1, 3 or 5. Know where you will end, then fill the path. Descending runs are the most common and the easiest to sing.
Practice slowly on “ah”, one note per beat with a metronome. Double the speed only when every note is in tune. Grouping notes in threes or fours helps you keep your place.
Keep runs light: less volume, less breath pressure, a relaxed throat. Move the pitch, not the jaw. Heavy, loud runs smear the notes together.
The common mistake is sliding instead of singing separate notes. A clean run has a distinct pitch on every note, like beads on a string, not a siren.
Runs are a hallmark of gospel, soul and R&B, and of Baroque arias, where long melismas show off the voice. Use them sparingly: one clean run says more than ten.
Recap: choose the scale, know the target, sing it slow and clean, then speed up.
Sing it before you play it, find the first note against the chord, then learn the line in short chunks, each landing on a chord tone.
Hi {name}! Here a phrase plays over its chords, and you play it back. First, sing it: if you can sing it, your hands can find it.
Then find the first note. Hear it against the chord: is it the root, the 3rd, the 5th or the 7th? Here it is G, the root of G7.
Now chunk it. Learn the first few notes, then the next few, each chunk ending on a chord tone on the beat.
Listen for the moves you know: an approach note, an enclosure, the bebop scale. Here F and D sharp enclose E.
Your turn: hear the phrase, replay it or slow it down if you need, then play it back in time. Every note counts on its own.
Why it works: singing ties the sound to your inner ear, so the hands follow a line you already hold, not a guess.
Find the first note by its place in the chord. Sing the root of the chord, then walk up to the note: one step is the 2nd, two steps the 3rd.
Chunks end where the line lands: a chord tone on a beat, often after an approach note or an enclosure. Those landings are your signposts.
A common mistake is starting from note one each time you slip. Repeat only the chunk that broke, then join it to the one before.
Slow it down rather than guess. At a slower speed the passing notes are clear, and the rhythm stays the same.
Every note counts on its own: a wrong note or a missed one costs only itself, and a steady answer a little slower than the call is still in time.
To keep: sing it, find the first note, chunk it, then play it in every key.
C6 and B°7 share no note and together make an 8-note scale: harmonise each scale note with whichever of the two holds it.
Hi {name}! Barry Harris built his harmony on two chords. The 6th chord: C, E, G, A.
And the diminished chord on the 7th: B, D, F, A flat. It shares no note with the 6th chord.
Put them together and you get an 8-note scale. Under each melody note goes the chord that holds it: 6th, diminished, 6th, diminished.
The diminished wants to go home: it is the sound of motion, the 6th chord the sound of rest. Play the scale of chords slowly and listen to it breathe in and out.
Your turn: build the shapes on the keys, from the note I give.
Borrowing: one voice of the 6th chord steps to its neighbour in the diminished while the others hold. G to A flat over C, E, A gives a new colour, then back.

Lower one note of a diminished chord a half step and you get a dominant 7th. Keep the diminished and put a bass a half step below any of its notes: a dominant with a flat 9. Barry’s moves are all half steps.
Any chord of a tune can move this way. A minor 7th is the 6th chord a minor third up: D minor 7 is F6. A dominant is the minor 6th on its fifth.
Spread the chords over both hands: drop the 2nd and 4th voices an octave into the left hand. The same four notes now sound wide and warm, the way big bands voice them.
To keep: two chords, eight notes, each note its own chord. The drills play this in every key, then over real forms.
Jazz pianists leave the root to the bass and play the 3rd, 7th and colours: rootless A and B, upper structures, 4ths.
Hi {name}! The bass plays the root, so the piano can drop it. D minor 9 without D: F, A, C, E. That is the A form, the 3rd at the bottom.
Move to G13 and only one note moves: F, A, B, E. Then C major 9: E, G, B, D. The hand barely travels.
The B form starts on the 7th: C, E, F, A for D minor 9. Use it to keep the hand in the middle of the keyboard.
Why drop the root? It frees a finger for the colours, the 9th and the 13th, and it keeps the left hand out of the bass player’s way.
Your turn: build each shape up from the note I give.
Upper structures: the left hand holds 3rd and 7th, the right hand plays a plain triad that adds colours. Over G7, an E flat triad gives flat 13, root and sharp 9.
The So What chord: three perfect 4ths and a major 3rd on top. D, G, C, F, A. Move it through the dorian scale for modal tunes, one step at a time, while the bass holds the root.
The altered dominant keeps 3rd and 7th and bends everything else: G7 with B, F, B flat, E flat pulls hard to C.
In a minor ii–V–i the colours change: D half-diminished, G7 with a flat 9 and flat 13, then C minor 6. The flat notes come from the minor key itself.
To keep: the 3rd and 7th name the chord, the rest is colour. Find the shape, then let it move as little as it can to the next chord.
Hold the given note in your ear, feel the distance, then land on the new note. Thirds, fifths and octaves are your anchors; every other interval sits near one of them.
Hi {name}! Listen: one note, then a note a fifth above it. Hum the first one, then let your voice open up to the second.
A third is a smaller step: the first two notes of a major chord. An octave is the same note, higher — it feels like coming home up there.
The trick: sing the notes in between quietly in your head. From the given note, count up the scale until you reach the interval, then sing only the last note out loud.
Going down is harder, because the voice likes to climb. Hear a note, then a third below it. Lean down gently, do not drop.
Inside a key you will hear the home chord first. Then you get a note that is not home, and you sing the interval from there. Keep the key in your ear while you sing.

An interval is the distance between two pitches. Its number counts letter names, both ends included: C to E is a third, C, D, E. Its quality comes from half steps: four make a major third, three a minor third.
The full set, in half steps: minor and major seconds 1 and 2, thirds 3 and 4, the perfect fourth 5, the tritone 6, the perfect fifth 7, sixths 8 and 9, sevenths 10 and 11, the octave 12.
Build the rest from your anchors: 1, 3, 5 and 8. A fourth is one step below the fifth; a sixth is one step above it; a seventh is one step below the octave. Hear C to F, then C to A.

Before you sing, audiate: hear the target clearly inside, then sing it. Some musicians tie intervals to famous openings: Twinkle, Twinkle leaps up a fifth, Wagner's Bridal Chorus starts with a fourth, and Over the Rainbow opens with an octave.
Descending intervals feel different, so practice them on their own. Hear the top note as a degree: a fifth down is often 5 falling to 1, the sound of a bass line coming home.

Inside a key, the quality depends on where you start. In C major, a third up from C is E, a major third; a third up from D is F, a minor third. Let the key choose, unless the exercise names the quality.
Common mistakes: wide leaps up land flat, minor and major get swapped, and the counting trick stays too slow. Use it to learn, then jump straight to the target.
To keep: the number from letters, the quality from half steps, anchors on 1, 3, 5 and 8, and hear it before you sing it.
Seven scales that land back on their own notes when moved: the repeating block in semitones = the number of transpositions (2, 3, 4, then 6).
Olivier Messiaen built his harmony on seven special scales, the modes of limited transposition. Move one up a little, and it lands back on its own notes.
Mode 1 is the whole-tone scale you know: six notes, a whole step apart. Move it up a whole step and you get the same six notes. So there are only two: on C and on C sharp.
Mode 2 is the diminished scale you know, started on its half step: half, whole, half, whole. Move it up three semitones and it lands on itself. So it has three transpositions.
The rule: find the block that repeats. Its size in semitones is the number of transpositions. Mode 1 repeats every 2 semitones, mode 2 every 3.
Mode 3 repeats the block 2, 1, 1 three times: nine notes. The block spans four semitones, so it has four transpositions.
Modes 4 to 7 repeat their block twice, every half octave, so each has six transpositions. Mode 5 has six notes, modes 4 and 6 have eight, mode 7 has ten.
Your turn! Count notes and transpositions, then tell modes 1, 2 and 3 apart by ear: whole steps only, half and whole, or whole, half, half.
Messiaen described the modes in his book The Technique of My Musical Language, from 1944. An ordinary scale has twelve transpositions; these have fewer, and that is the "limit".
By ear: mode 1 has no half steps at all. Mode 2 alternates half and whole. Mode 3 has groups of three notes in a row by half steps.
Chords live inside the modes too. The diminished seventh sits in mode 2, the augmented triad in mode 3. A chord with a seventh and a flat ninth, like C E G B flat D flat, is all mode 2.

Try it with the major scale: move C major up a semitone and almost every note changes, so all twelve keys are different. Move the whole-tone scale up a semitone and you reach its other version; one more semitone and you are back on the first.
To keep: find the repeating block, measure it in semitones, and you have the number of transpositions.

A row uses all twelve notes once. Its forms: prime (P), inversion (I, intervals mirrored), retrograde (R, backwards), retrograde inversion (RI); any form can be moved (Pn). The matrix lays them all out.
In twelve-tone music, Schoenberg's method from the 1920s, a piece grows from a row: all twelve notes, each used once, in a fixed order.
A row has four forms. Let us watch them on a short cell of four notes. The prime, P, is the cell itself.
Inversion, I, turns it upside down: every interval mirrored. Up a semitone becomes down a semitone. It starts on the same note.
Retrograde, R, plays the cell backwards. Retrograde inversion, RI, plays the inversion backwards.
Any form can start on another note. The prime moved up two semitones is P2: every interval stays the same.
The matrix lays out all the forms: the prime along the top row, the inversion down the first column. Every row is the prime started on that column's note.
Your turn! Name the form on paper and by ear, check whether a row uses every note once, and fill a gap in a matrix.
To tell the forms apart, look at the ends. Same first note with mirrored steps: inversion. The last note comes first: retrograde. Both: retrograde inversion. Same steps, new start: a moved prime.
By ear, follow the contour. The inversion draws the same shape upside down: where the cell climbs, it falls. The retrograde draws the shape backwards, so the last turn of the cell comes first.
A row of twelve notes has twelve primes, twelve inversions, twelve retrogrades and twelve retrograde inversions: up to forty-eight forms, all in one matrix.
The common slip in a row is a repeated note: then one of the twelve is missing. Count the pitch classes, not the octaves: a C up high and a C down low are the same pitch class.
Schoenberg's pupils Berg and Webern wrote with rows, and so did Stravinsky in his late works. To keep: P, I mirrored, R backwards, RI both.
E(k, n): k hits spread as evenly as possible over n pulses. E(3,8) is the tresillo, E(5,8) the cinquillo; other traditional rhythms are rotations, like the bossa nova of E(5,16).
Take eight pulses and three hits. Spread the hits as evenly as you can, and you get the tresillo you know.
Godfried Toussaint showed in 2005 that this one rule, k hits spread over n pulses, gives many traditional rhythms. He writes it E of k and n.
The rule comes from Euclid's algorithm, the ancient way to find a greatest common divisor. Bjorklund's version deals the rests out among the hits, again and again, until they are even.
Five hits over eight give the Cuban cinquillo. Seven over twelve give a West African bell pattern, and four over nine the Turkish aksak.
Draw it on a circle: the pulses go round like a clock, and the hits make a shape. Start on another hit and you get a rotation: the same circle, a new rhythm.
The bossa nova is such a rotation: Toussaint shows it is a rotation of five hits over sixteen.
Your turn! Count the hits, pick the circle you heard, build E of k and n, and find a rotation. Count the pulses "1 & 2 &" if it helps.

Even means the gaps between hits come in at most two sizes, one apart. E of 3 and 8 has gaps of 3, 3 and 2; E of 5 and 8 has gaps of 2, 1, 2, 1 and 2. Count the pulses from one hit to the next to find them.
Toussaint's list also has E of 3 and 4, E of 2 and 5, and E of 5 and 12.
The common slip is hearing a rotation as a new rhythm. Find the accented first pulse, then check whether the gaps are the same, only starting elsewhere.
Hear the difference between even and uneven. Three hits over eight with gaps of 3, 3 and 2 swing round the circle; squeeze two hits together and the shape goes lopsided.
To keep: k hits, n pulses, gaps as even as they get. Draw it on the circle, and turn the circle to start on another hit: that is a rotation, the same gaps in a new order.
Home (I) is the chord where the tension lets go — most often right after V.
Every key has a home chord, the I. Music leaves it, travels, and comes back. Finding home by ear is the first step of hearing harmony.
Home sounds like rest. The chord before it, V, sounds like a question that wants an answer.
Home does not have to come first. Here the progression starts away from home and arrives on the third chord.
Sometimes V leads you on and the music lands somewhere else, often on vi. That is a deceptive cadence: it sounds almost like home, but not quite.
A useful trick: hum the lowest note of each chord. On the home chord the hum feels settled, like the last note of a song.
Your turn: count the chords as they pass, and answer with the number of the one that is home.
Why does I feel like home? Its root is the key’s first note, and its notes are the most stable ones of the scale: 1, 3 and 5.
V pulls toward I because of two notes: the leading tone, 7, rises a half step to 1, and the bass falls a fifth to the root.
IV to I is the softer way home, the "amen" ending of hymns. It arrives without the leading tone, so it sounds gentle rather than final.
In minor keys home is the minor chord i, and V usually becomes major so it can still pull strongly.
A common mistake is to call the first chord home just because it is first. Wait for the rest: home is where the music would be happy to stop.
In real songs, choruses often begin away from home and land on I at the end of the line. Listen for it in the songs you know.
Progressions follow habits: V goes home, ii goes to V, and pop loops repeat four chords.
Chord progressions are not random. A few habits come back in thousands of songs, so the ear learns to expect the next chord.
The strongest habit: after V comes I. Hear the first chords, then guess before the last one sounds.
In jazz, ii goes to V and V goes to I. The bass falls by fifths: D, G, C.
Pop loops repeat: I, V, vi, then IV, and again. Once you know the loop, the fourth chord is no surprise.
To predict, sing the bass of where you think it goes, then compare with what you hear.
Your turn: three chords play. Choose the chord that comes next, and listen to each choice if you are not sure.
Why these habits? Chords whose roots fall a fifth share notes and resolve tension step by step. That is the backbone of tonal music.
Borrowed chords bring color from the parallel minor. ♭VI and ♭VII lead home with a heroic, film-music sound.
The minor four, iv, is the bittersweet one: IV turns minor just before home.
A secondary dominant points to another chord: a major chord on 3 pulls toward vi as if vi were home for a moment.
A common mistake is to guess by the melody alone. Follow the bass: it usually tells you the next root.

Practice prediction away from the app too: when a song you know is playing, pause it before a chord change and sing the next bass note. Then press play and check. A minute of this a day sharpens the ear fast.
Recap: V to I, ii to V, the four-chord loop, and a few colors: ♭VI, ♭VII, iv and secondary dominants.
A reharmonization swaps a chord for one that shares its job: ii for IV, iii for vi, ♭II7 for V7.
Arrangers often keep a melody and change one chord under it. The song stays the same, but the color changes.
Swaps that share notes are the gentlest: ii can replace IV, and iii can replace vi.
In jazz, the tritone sub replaces V7 with a dominant a half step above home, so the bass slides down to I.
The fastest way to find the change: follow the bass in both versions. The bar where it moves differently is the one.
Then ask what the new chord does: is it softer, darker, or does it lead home more smoothly?
Your turn: the progression plays, then plays again with one chord replaced. Answer with the number of the changed chord.
Chords have jobs. Tonic chords (I, vi, iii) rest, subdominant chords (IV, ii) move away, dominant chords (V, vii°) pull back home.
A swap inside the same job keeps the music flowing: vi for I gives a deceptive, darker arrival.
Borrowing from minor darkens one moment: IV becomes iv, or V becomes ♭VII.
The tritone sub works because V7 and ♭II7 share their 3rd and 7th, the two notes that make a dominant sound like a dominant.
A common mistake is to listen to the top notes only. Many reharmonizations keep the melody and change just the bass.

In real music, reharmonization is everywhere: a singer’s last chorus with a new chord under the final line, a jazz pianist’s second time through a standard, a film cue that darkens one familiar chord. Once you hear the trick, you hear it in many songs.
Recap: find the bar by the bass, then name the swap: same job, borrowed from minor, or a jazz substitution.
Work it out in order: home, bass, chords, melody — each step makes the next one easier.
Musicians learn songs by ear in a fixed order. Each step gives you a frame for the next one.
Step one, home: on which note does the tune want to end? That note is 1, and everything else is counted from it.
Step two, the bass: hum the lowest notes. Do they go up or down, by a step or a jump? The bass gives you the chord roots.
Step three, the chords: with the roots known, decide major or minor. A minor chord on 6 is vi, a major chord on 4 is IV.
Step four, the melody: sing it slowly and name each note as a degree. The chord under it usually holds the answer.
Your turn: each level is one of these steps on a new short tune. Listen as many times as you need.
Why this order? Home anchors the numbers, the bass anchors the harmony, and the harmony narrows down the melody notes.
Finding home: wait for the end of a phrase. The note where the tune comes to rest is usually 1, sometimes 3 or 5.
The bass moves slowly and repeats, so it is easier to follow than the chords on top. Sing it an octave higher if it is too low.
A common mistake is to start with the melody. Without home and harmony, every note is a guess.
In real practice, choose a short song you know, find home with your voice, then the bass, then the chords on your instrument.
Checking yourself matters as much as guessing: play your answer along with the recording. If it clashes, the bass or the chord quality is wrong; go one step back and listen again.
Recap: home, bass, chords, melody. Slow down and repeat as often as needed; the order matters more than the speed.

Write every root first, from the bass, as a degree of the key. Then each chord’s colour: minor or major 3rd, which 7th, then the top note (9, 13, ♭9, alt). A bass that is not the root is a slash chord.
A progression has two layers: where the roots move, and the colour of each chord. Hear them one at a time.
Roots first. Follow the bass and name each note against home: one, six, two, five.
Then the colour of each chord: a major or a minor 3rd, then which 7th. Here: major 7, minor 7, minor 7, dominant.
When the bass is not the root, the chord leans: C over E. The bass moves by step, the chord stays.
The top note last: a 13 is bright, a flat 9 is dark, altered is darker still.
Your turn: the roots of every bar first, then the colours. A right root already earns half.
Roots move in patterns. Down a fifth is the strongest pull: two to five to one. Learn to feel it before you name it.
A bass that falls by half steps into home is a tritone substitute: D flat seven instead of G seven. The 3rd and 7th stay, the root moves a tritone.
A bass that steps up a whole tone into home is the backdoor: F minor seven, B flat seven, C. It sounds softer, borrowed from the minor.
In minor, the two chord is half-diminished and the five has a flat nine: B half-diminished, E seven flat nine, A minor. Listen for the dark top note.
A common slip: hearing a slash chord as a new root. If the bass moves but the colour above does not change, it is an inversion.
Recap: bass first, then the 3rd and 7th, then the top. Long forms repeat: in an AABA, write the A once and listen for the bridge.
Hold the melody note and change what it means: the root, the 3rd, the 5th, the 7th, or a tension of a new chord.
Keep one note on top and put different chords under it. The note stays; its meaning changes.
F over six triads: F is the root of F and Fm, the 3rd of Dm and D flat, the 5th of B flat and B flat minor.
With 7th chords, F can also be a flat 7, as in G7, or a major 7, as in G flat major 7.
Then the tensions: F is the 9th of E flat 9, the 11th of C7sus4, and the sharp 11 of B7. Over B7 it is written E sharp.
Practice it in all twelve keys: free time first, the note always on top, each chord moving to the nearest voicing. Your turn.
Why it works: a melody note fits any chord in which it is a chord tone or an available tension. It must never be an avoid note, like F over C major 7.
How to build drop 2 with the note on top: write the close voicing under it, then drop the second voice from the top by an octave.
How to hear it: find the root in the bass, then count letters up to the held note. Three letters is the 3rd, seven the 7th.
A common slip is to let the top note move. Keep it exactly where it is and let the other voices do the work.
The common-tone diminished is the same idea: C6 to C diminished 7 and back, with C and A staying put.
At the top level you choose: harmonize the note eight ways, no chord twice, each one voice-led from the last.
To keep: the note stays, the meaning moves. Root, 3rd, 5th, 7th, then the tensions.
The melody holds; the bass walks down by step; each bass note makes a new chord: C, Cmaj7/B, C7/B♭, Am7, A♭maj7, G7sus4.
Hold C on top. Now walk the bass down a half step at a time.
Every bass note renames the chord under the same C: C, C major 7 over B, C7 over B flat.
Then A minor 7, where C is the flat 3; A flat major 7, where C is the 3rd; and G7sus4, where C is the 11th.
On the bass this is a real reharm role: you change the harmony by your note choice, while the band keeps the melody.
Count the result: one held note and six bass notes give six different chords, and the last one, G7sus4, leads straight back home to C.
Play it in all twelve keys: free time first, then on the click. Your turn.
Why it works: the held note stays a chord tone or a tension over every new bass note, so the line sounds planned, not wrong.
It is the line cliché turned upside down: there an inner voice moves inside a held chord; here the bass moves under a held melody.
How to hear it: keep the top note in your ear and follow only the bass. Name the new root, then the held note’s degree in it.
A common slip on the bass is to rush the half steps. Give each new chord its full length so the change is heard.
Arrangers use it under long melody notes in ballads. On the piano, the left hand walks while the right hand holds the note on top.
Try it from other held notes too: hold the 5th of the key and walk the bass down, then name every chord you make.
To keep: the melody holds, the bass walks, and every step is a new chord.
Two major (or two minor) chords a 3rd apart share one note: C to E keeps E, C to A♭ keeps C. The film sound.
A chromatic mediant is a chord of the same quality a 3rd away. C goes to E, A flat, A or E flat.
They share exactly one note. C and E share E; C and A flat share C; C and A share E; C and E flat share G.
Doubly chromatic pairs share nothing: C to A flat minor, or C to E flat minor. The most distant sound there is.
Coltrane’s cycle is built from them: C, A flat and E are major-third mediants, and their roots spell an augmented triad.
Play them voice-led in all twelve keys: the common tone stays in the same voice. Your turn.
Why it sounds like film music: the move is not functional. Nothing pulls home; the light changes while one note glows through.
Three moves explain them: P swaps major and minor on one root, R goes to the relative, and L moves one voice by a half step.
P and L in turn give the hexatonic cycle: C, C minor, A flat, A flat minor, E, E minor. One voice moves a half step each time.
P and R in turn give the octatonic cycle. Its major roots, C, A, F sharp and E flat, are the minor-third cycle of Barry Harris’s family of dominants.
C – Am – A – F♯m – F♯ – E♭m – E♭ – Cm
A common slip is to jump the whole hand. Find the shared note first, hold it, and move only the other two.
On the guitar the same moves sit on three strings: keep one finger on the common tone and move the other two.
To keep: same quality, a 3rd away, one note in common, or none at all for the doubly chromatic pair.
Borrow chords from the parallel minor: iv(m6), ♭VI, ♭VII7, iiø7, ♭III, ♭II. Minor plagal goes straight to I; in minor the borrowing reverses.
In C major, borrow F minor from C minor: I, IV, iv, I. The A flat darkens the IV for a moment.
The pop on-ramp: flat VI, flat VII, I. Both chords come from the minor key.
Minor plagal: iv minor 6, flat VI major 7, flat VII7 or flat II major 7 going straight to I.
The minor’s ii in major: D half-diminished, G7 flat 9, C major 7. The flat 13 of G7 is the 3rd of C minor.
The borrowed chord keeps the tonic but changes the mood for a moment: the music sounds darker, then comes home.
Comp each borrowing in all twelve keys, then use them inside a tune in the reharm studio. Your turn.
Why it works: the parallel minor shares the tonic, so its chords still point home, only darker.
Tadd Dameron’s turnaround uses three borrowed major 7ths: I, flat III, flat VI, flat II, then home.
From Mixolydian comes v minor 7: G minor 7, C7, F. It sounds like a ii–V into the IV.
In minor the borrowing reverses: the Picardy third ends on major I, Dorian gives IV7, and ii minor 7 replaces the half-diminished.
A common slip is a melody note the borrowed chord cannot carry: E over F minor clashes with A flat. The studio checks every bar.
Minor plagal endings close many ballads: ivm6 straight to I sounds warm and a little sad, with no dominant at all.
In the reharm studio you can put iv, flat VI, flat VII7, iiø7 or the minor plagal ending on a bar; the app checks the melody note against each new chord.
To keep: borrow from the parallel minor; minor plagal goes straight home; in minor, borrow from major and Dorian.
The bass holds one note, the tonic or the dominant, while the chords above it change: Dm7/G – F/G – A♭/G – G7.
A pedal is a bass note that stays while the harmony moves above it.
The dominant pedal holds G under the chords before C. It builds tension and sounds like an intro.
Over the G pedal, F over G is a G9sus4, and A flat over G is a G7 flat 9 sus.
On the bass the job is time and length: hold the pedal steadily while the band changes chords.
The tonic pedal is calm, like a drone; the dominant pedal leans forward, so the ear waits for the tonic to arrive.
Play both pedals in all twelve keys. Your turn.
Why it works: the held bass is a common tone of every chord, or a tension under it, so the ear hears one place while the colours change.
How to hear it: hum the lowest note. If it never moves while the chords do, it is a pedal. A 5th above home is the dominant pedal.
The push: anticipate the next bar on the and of 4 and tie it over. The pedal keeps moving forward while it stays on one note.
A common slip is to drift off the pedal when the chords get colourful. The bass stays; only the top moves.
Modal tunes live on pedals, and many intros and endings use the dominant pedal to set up the first chord.
Upper structures over a pedal give modern colours: a D triad over C is a lydian sound, an F triad over G a sus sound.
To keep: one bass note, many chords above it; tonic for calm, dominant for tension.
One chord shape under every melody note, moved in parallel: the melody picks the chord. Exact planing keeps the quality; diatonic keeps the key.
Take one shape, a major 7 in drop 2 with the root on top, and slide it under each note of a melody.
This is exact planing, or constant structure: every chord has the same quality, so the key disappears.
Diatonic planing keeps the shape but changes the quality to stay in the key.
Try three shapes: major 7, minor 7, and a stack of fourths. Then the guitar slides one drop 2 shape up the neck.
The melody decides: each new note brings its own chord, all with the same shape, so the harmony follows the tune.
Free time first, the melody always on top, in all twelve keys. Your turn.
Why it works: the ear follows the top line, and the parallel shape makes it thicker, like one bright voice.
How to hear it: if every chord sounds the same colour and the bass moves exactly with the melody, it is exact planing.
A common slip is to change the shape on a hard note. Keep the same intervals under every note, even the chromatic ones.
The So What voicing is planing too: three fourths and a major third, moved up a half step and back.
Planing is colour, not function: nothing pulls. Use it on a held tonic or a long melody note.
Choose the shape by the mood: major 7 is bright, minor 7 is soft, fourths sound open and modern.
On the guitar the drop 2 shape lies under the fingers: keep the hand shape and slide it along the neck with the melody on string one.
To keep: one shape, every note, the melody on top.
Approach a chord from its own voicing a half step above or below (D♭maj7 → Cmaj7); side-slip a half step out and back on purpose.
Play the target chord’s exact voicing a half step above, just before it. That is a planed approach.
From below works too: B major 7 into C major 7. Every voice slides by a half step.
Arrangers approach melody notes this way. It is not a dominant: it is a slide.
A side-slip goes a half step out and comes back: D minor 7, E flat minor 7, D minor 7, over a dorian vamp.
Use it on strong melody notes, the ones on beat one: a short slide just before the beat makes the arrival sound planned.
Play both in all twelve keys, free time first. Your turn.
Why it works: a half step is the strongest pull there is, and when every voice slides together the ear accepts any chord on the way.
How to hear it: a planed approach slides every voice; a dominant moves its 7th down to the next chord’s 3rd.
Side-slipping is an improviser’s device too: play a phrase a half step out, then resolve. On the piano it works in the comping.
A common slip is to stay out too long. One beat or one bar out, then back home.
The top level comps the side-slip on a dorian vamp at tempo, with the drums keeping the time.
You can approach every chord of a phrase this way. The rhythm stays the same; only the half-step slide is added before each target, in the same voicing.
To keep: same voicing, a half step away, just before the target; out and back, on purpose.
Replace ii–V with one sus chord (F/G = G9sus4); string sus or maj7 chords without function; colour the tonic with maj7♯5.
A ii–V can become one chord: F over G. It holds the ii’s notes over the V’s bass, a G9sus4.
A sus chord has no 3rd pulling to the next chord. It floats.
String sus chords on a moving bass and the music stops going anywhere: C7sus, A flat 7sus, B flat 7sus, G7sus.
Colour the tonic with major 7 sharp 5: E major over C. Brighter and less settled than major 7.
These sounds came from the modal jazz of the sixties, where tunes rest on sus chords and move by colour rather than by cadence.
Play them in all twelve keys. Your turn.
Why it works: without the 3rd and 7th tritone there is nothing to resolve, so the ear hears colour, not direction.
How to hear a sus: listen for the 4th where the 3rd would be. If it never falls, the chord stays sus.
The sequences here are the app’s own, in the spirit of Herbie Hancock’s writing: sus or maj7 chords on roots that move freely.
A common slip is to resolve the sus by habit. Let it float, then go to the next sus without a 3rd.
maj7 sharp 5 is the lydian augmented sound. Over a ii–V it lands on a brighter, more open tonic.
On the guitar, F over G is an F triad on the top strings over a G bass: an easy way to play the sus reharm.
To keep: sus floats, maj7 sharp 5 shines, and a moving bass under one shape is colour, not function.
The left hand walks the bass, the right hand holds a pad. Move one inner voice, thin the texture under a soloist, fill it out at the climax.
On the organ the left hand is the bass player. It walks: half notes first, then quarters.
The right hand holds a pad of three notes, the 3rd, the 7th and the 9th, and moves each voice to the nearest note.
Let one inner voice move while the others hold: a small counter-melody inside the pad.
Texture is the volume knob: two notes under a soloist, four at the climax.
Organists often play without a bass player, so the left hand must keep steady time; the right hand answers the soloist with short pad changes.
The levels play on the tonewheel organ, in all twelve keys. Your turn.
Why it works: the organ sustains, so a held pad fills the room and the walking line keeps the time moving.
Drawbars shape the tone: 888 is the classic jazz setting, with the third-harmonic percussion on the attack.
In a ballad, hold the pad and move the common-tone ladder on top: one note held while the chords under it change.
A common slip is to hold the pad too low. Keep it above the walking line so the bass stays clear.
The walking hand is measured like a bass player: steady quarters, chord tones on the strong beats, a half step into each new root.
Thin and full is a matter of voices: two notes leave room for the soloist, three or four add weight at the climax of a chorus.
To keep: the left hand walks, the right hand holds a pad, one voice moves, and the texture follows the music.
Functional reharms do the old chord’s job (pull or rest); colour reharms change the light, not the direction.
Every reharm belongs to one of two families. Functional chords pull toward the next chord, like a tritone sub.
Colour chords paint: a chromatic mediant changes the light while nothing pulls.
Functional: secondary dominants, tritone subs, an added ii–V, the backdoor, passing diminished chords.
Colour: common tones, mediants, modal interchange, pedal point, planing, side-slips.
A quick test: play the new chord and stop. If you want to hear the next chord at once, it pulls; if it could stay forever, it paints. Ask that question about every reharm you choose.
Sort each device, then hear it: does it pull, or paint? Your turn.
Why it matters: a reharm is valid when the melody note is a chord tone or tension of the new chord, and good when the voices move smoothly.
How to hear a functional chord: a 7th falling to the next 3rd, a bass moving by fifths or half steps into a goal.
How to hear colour: the chord could stay where it is. It is a new shade, not a step on the way.
A common slip is to mix them without a plan. Use function where the tune moves and colour where it rests.
Some devices do both: the backdoor is functional, and it is also borrowed from minor.
The ear items play a short demo of each device in a random key; answer by the feeling, then check the name in the Why line.
To keep: function pulls, colour paints; check the melody first, then the voice leading.
V7 can go anywhere but I: to ♭VImaj7, to iii, to IV, or through VI7 to ii. The surprise keeps the tune moving.
G7 wants C major 7. A deceptive resolution goes somewhere else.
G7 to A flat major 7: the bass steps up a half step to a borrowed chord.
G7 to E minor 7 keeps the melody on E and delays the tonic.
Or G7 to A7, which goes on to D minor 7: a new ii–V begins.

Another favourite is G7 to F major 7: the bass steps down, the melody can stay, and the cadence turns into a new phrase instead of an ending. Listen for the bass first, then name the chord it lands on.
Listen to where V7 goes, then name it. Your turn.
Why it works: the V7 sets up a strong expectation, and any chord that shares its leading note or bass motion can answer it.
The classical one is V to vi. In jazz the favourites are flat VI major 7 and IV major 7.
How to hear it: follow the bass after the V. Up a half step is flat VI, down a step is IV, up a step goes to VI7.
A common slip is to hear every surprise as a mistake. In a standard it often marks the end of a section.
On the piano, play G7 to each target with smooth voice leading: the 7th falls, the 3rd moves by step.
The bass player hears it first: plan the walking line to the new target so the band lands together.
To keep: V7 to anything but I is a deceptive resolution; follow the bass to name it.
A quarter lasts one beat, a half two, a whole four; a rest is a counted beat of silence.
Hey {name}! Rhythm lives on the beat — a steady pulse, like a heartbeat. Count along with the clicks: 1, 2, 3, 4.
A quarter note lasts exactly one beat. Count each one: 1, 2, 3, 4.
A half note lasts two beats. You play it once and let it ring through the next beat.
A whole note fills all four beats. One sound, a long ride.
A rest is a beat of silence. You still count it — you just don't play. Whisper its number instead.
When you tap, hold your finger down on long notes, for their full length. The app checks that too.
Your turn! After the count-in, tap the pad or press Space on every note you read. Then hear a bar and pick the notation that matches.

Note values are relative, not fixed times. A quarter note is one beat at whatever tempo is set, measured in beats per minute (BPM). The same bar at 72, then at 108 BPM: the rhythm stays the same, only the clock changes.
The time signature 4/4 says: four beats in each bar, and a quarter note gets one beat. Bar lines split the music into these four-beat boxes, and beat 1 of each bar is the strongest.

Every note value has a matching rest. A quarter rest is the squiggle. A half rest is a small block sitting on the middle line; a whole rest hangs below the fourth line, and it also means a whole silent bar in any meter.

To read a rhythm by ear, follow the beat and ask one question: on which beats does a new sound start? Here, on 1 and 4. Beat 2 is still ringing, beat 3 is silent. A note lasts until the next start or rest.

To perform it, count out loud, 1, 2, 3, 4, and clap only where a note starts. On a half note, keep your hand moving through the second beat, so the length is felt, not guessed. Start slowly, around 60 to 70 BPM.
The common mistakes: cutting long notes short, and hurrying through rests to reach the next note. A rest lasts exactly as long as the note it replaces. Hear two rests held honestly.

In real music, quarters often carry a walking bass line or a steady strum, while halves and wholes hold the long notes of hymns, chorales and sustained pads under a band. Rests give phrases room to breathe.
To keep: the beat is the ruler. Quarter = 1, half = 2, whole = 4, and each rest lasts exactly as long as its note.
Two eighth notes share one beat equally, counted "1 &".
Hi {name}! Split one beat into two equal halves and you get two eighth notes.
Count them with "and". The numbers sit on the beat; each "and" falls exactly halfway to the next one.
Two eighths take the same time as one quarter. Listen: one quarter, then two eighths — same beat, twice as busy.
Now mixed with a half note: two eighths, a quarter, a half. Feel the gears shift from fast to slow.
The usual slip is rushing the second eighth. Keep both halves even — the two eighths are twins.
Your turn! Tap every note you read after the count-in — two even taps for two eighths. Then hear a bar: pick it, or tap it back.
An eighth note is exactly half a quarter, so a 4/4 bar holds eight of them. Alone, an eighth has a flag. In groups, the flags join into a beam, and the beams usually show where each beat begins.
The numbers are the beats themselves; the "ands" are the off-beats. Hear a bar of steady eighths: the beat keeps the same speed, you simply hear its halfway points as well.
Listening strategy: keep a silent "1 & 2 &" grid running, then mark which slots have a sound. In this bar: 1, &, 2, 3, 4, & — two eighths, two quarters, two eighths.
To perform: tap the beat with your foot and the eighths with your hand, two hand taps for each foot tap. Say the counts aloud. When it feels easy, drop the counting and let the foot carry the beat.
The classic mistake is speeding up when the eighths arrive, as if busier meant faster. It does not: the beat must stay exactly where it was. Listen — a half note, then eighths, on the same pulse.

Steady eighths are everywhere: the hi-hat in most rock and pop drumming, driving bass lines, strummed guitar. In jazz the same written eighths are played long-short — that is swing, which comes later in the path.
To keep: two eighths equal one quarter. Count "1 & 2 &", keep both halves even, and never let the beat speed up.
A dot adds half the note's length: a dotted quarter is 1½ beats, usually followed by an eighth: long, short.
Hey {name}! A dot after a note adds half its length. A quarter is one beat, so a dotted quarter lasts one and a half.
It almost always brings an eighth along, so together they fill two beats: long, short.
Count it: the long note starts on 1 and holds right through 2. The eighth lands on the "and" of 2.
Compare: two quarters, then the dotted pair. Same two beats — but the second note moves later, onto the "and".
That long-short gives a tune a little skip forward. Hear it mixed with eighths.
Your turn! Tap what you read: hold the long note, then a quick tap on the "and". Then hear a bar and pick its notation.
The dot rule works on any note: it adds half of the note's own value. A dotted half is 2 + 1 = 3 beats. A dotted quarter is 1 + ½ = 1½. A dotted eighth is ½ + ¼ = ¾ of a beat.
A dotted quarter sounds exactly like a quarter tied to an eighth: the tie joins them into one held note. The dot is just a shorter way to write it. Hear the pair twice.

Compare a quarter and two eighths with the dotted pair. Both last two beats and both end on the "and" of the second beat. The only difference: in the dotted version, nothing new happens on that second beat.

The secret is subdividing. Count eighths: "1 & 2 &". Start the long note on 1, hold it through "& 2", and play the short one on the last "&". The pair can start on any beat — here it begins on beat 2.

The usual mistake is playing the eighth too early, right on the beat, which turns the dotted pair into two plain quarters. The opposite slip is confusing it with a dotted eighth and sixteenth, a much tighter skip inside a single beat.
Two dotted quarters and a quarter make 3 + 3 + 2 eighths: the tresillo. It is the backbone of Cuban music, of reggaeton and of countless pop grooves. Hear it on a low drum.
To keep: a dot adds half. A dotted quarter is 1½ beats, and the eighth after it lands on an "and".
Four sixteenths fill one beat; glue two into an eighth for eighth–two sixteenths or two sixteenths–eighth.
Hi {name}! Split one beat into four equal parts and you get sixteenth notes.
Glue the first two together into one eighth: long, short, short.
Glue the last two instead and it flips: short, short, long.
All three in a row. Listen for where the quick pair sits: at the start of the beat, or at the end?
Keep the beat slow and steady in your body. The sixteenths are tiny steps inside it — they never push it faster.
Your turn! Tap what you read, then hear a bar and choose it. In the last round you build the bar yourself from blocks: four sixteenths, eighth–two sixteenths, two sixteenths–eighth.
A sixteenth note is half an eighth: four per beat, sixteen in a 4/4 bar. It has two flags, or two beams in a group. Musicians count them "1 e & a, 2 e & a", with the "&" still exactly halfway.
Inside one beat, sixteenths can merge. An eighth then two sixteenths sounds on 1, &, a. Two sixteenths then an eighth sound on 1, e, &. Hear them alternate.
Listening strategy: find the "&" first. If the quick pair comes after it, the beat is long-short-short; if before it, short-short-long. If all four slots sound, it is four sixteenths.
pair after & → 1 & a · before → 1 e &

To perform, keep your hand moving in steady sixteenths the whole time — down, up, down, up — and only touch the drum or the strings where a note is written. Drummers and guitarists both work this way. Start slowly.

The common mistake is blurring long-short-short into a triplet, making all three notes even. Listen: long-short-short, then tri-o-la. In long-short-short, the first note is twice as long as each of the other two.
Sixteenths drive funk and disco: the hi-hat and the scratchy rhythm guitar often run in constant sixteenths. They are also the language of fast melodic runs and of many rap flows.
To keep: four sixteenths per beat, counted "1 e & a". Find the "&", and the shape of the beat becomes clear.
Syncopation puts the note on the "and" instead of the beat: syn-co-pa (eighth, quarter, eighth) and the lone "and" (eighth rest, eighth).
Hey {name}! Most notes like to land on the beat. Syncopation is when a note jumps in on the "and" between beats.
The classic shape is eighth, quarter, eighth: syn-co-pa. The long middle note starts on the "and" of 1 and rings across beat 2.
Compare with plain eighths. In syn-co-pa, beat 2 gets no new note — it's swallowed by the long one.
The eighth rest is the other off-beat trick: silence on the beat, a note on the "and" — a lone "and".
Feel the beat firmly in your foot, so the off-beats can pull against it. That tug is what makes music groove.
Your turn! Tap what you read — notes on the "and" get a tap, the beat under them doesn't. Then hear a bar and choose or build it.

Precisely, syncopation is an accent on a weak position, between the beats, while the stronger beat after it gets no new note. In 4/4, beats 1 and 3 are strongest, 2 and 4 weaker, and the "ands" weaker still.
Syn-co-pa is often written with a tie: eighth, eighth tied to eighth, eighth. The tie hides beat 2 inside a note that started on the "and" of 1. Same sound, two spellings.

A very common type is the anticipation, or push: a note arrives on the last "and" of a bar and is held over the next downbeat. Pop melodies and horn sections use it constantly to make the music lean forward.

Listening strategy: tap the beat with your foot and notice two things — notes that fall between the taps, and taps with no new sound above them. Here every note sits on an "and", and no beat sounds at all.
