To perform: count all the eighths aloud, "1 & 2 &", and say the "ands" louder than the numbers. Keep the foot on the beat whatever the hands do. Start slowly; syncopation is about precision, not speed.

The common mistake is letting the off-beat become the new beat. After a few syncopations the ear flips, and you end up half a beat out. Keep the pulse in your body and listen: quarter, a lone "and", syn-co-pa.
Syncopation is the engine of ragtime — Scott Joplin built a whole style on it — and of jazz, funk, Latin music and modern pop. In ska, the guitar plays short chords on the "ands", against the bass.
To keep: syncopation moves the note off the beat while the beat stays put. Feel the beat firmly, and that pull becomes groove.
A triplet splits one beat into three equal notes (tri-o-la) instead of two.
Hi {name}! So far you split beats into two and four. A triplet splits one beat into three equal notes: tri-o-la.
Hear the difference on the same beat: two eighths, then tri-o-la. Two marches; three rolls.
A word trick: "ap-ple" for two, "straw-ber-ry" for three. Say them over the beat.
The first note of every triplet sits right on the beat. The other two share the rest evenly — no hurrying to the next beat.
Mixed with quarters and halves, it's a little ripple in the flow.
Your turn! Tap what you read — three even taps inside one beat. Then hear a bar: two or three per beat? Choose it, or build it from blocks.

A triplet is a tuplet: three notes in the time normally taken by two. It is written with a bracket or beam and the number 3. An eighth-note triplet puts three notes in one beat, each lasting exactly a third of it.
Hear one beat divided three ways in a row: four sixteenths, a triplet, two eighths, a triplet. The beat never moves; only the number of slices changes.
Listening strategy: ignore the melody and ask how many notes fit between two beats. Two feels square, like marching. Three feels round and rolling. Four feels busy, but still square.
To perform, say "tri-o-la" on each beat and lean slightly on "tri", which sits on the beat. A classic drill: change between 2, 3 and 4 notes per beat while the metronome stays exactly the same.

The common mistake is rushing the first two notes, which turns a triplet into short-short-long — two sixteenths and an eighth. Compare: short-short-long, then a true triplet. In the triplet, all three gaps are equal.

Triplets are central to blues and shuffle, to the piano chords of 1950s ballads and doo-wop, and to drum fills everywhere. A 4/4 bar filled with eighth-note triplets is effectively 12/8: the two notations meet.
To keep: a triplet is three equal notes where two would normally go. Keep every gap the same, and the first note on the beat.
3/4 has three beats per bar; 6/8 and 12/8 have big dotted-quarter beats, each split into three eighths.
Hey {name}! Not every bar has four beats. In 3/4 there are three: ONE two three — the waltz.
The dotted half lasts three beats — two, plus half of two. One note fills a whole 3/4 bar.
6/8 rocks instead. Six eighths in two big beats of three: ONE-two-three FOUR-five-six. Each big beat is a dotted quarter, and the clicks mark only those.
Inside a big beat you'll meet a dotted quarter (one long note), quarter–eighth and eighth–quarter.
Both 3/4 and 6/8 hold six eighths — but 3/4 is three pairs and 6/8 is two triples. Count the clicks: three, then two.
12/8 is two bars of 6/8 glued together: four big beats, each split in three. It is the meter of the slow blues.
Your turn! Check the meter first. In 6/8 and 12/8, feel the big beats and the three inside each. Tap what you read, then hear a bar and choose or build it.

A time signature has two numbers. The top one says how many units fill a bar; the bottom one says which note is the unit: 4 is a quarter, 8 an eighth. So 3/4 is three quarters per bar, and 6/8 is six eighths.

A meter is simple when each beat splits into two, and compound when it splits into three. In compound meters, divide the top number by three to get the beats: 6/8 has two, 9/8 three, 12/8 four. Hear a bar of 12/8.

Listening strategy: first tap the pulse that feels natural. Then count the small notes inside each tap — two means simple, three means compound. Finally, count the taps from one strong downbeat to the next.

Six eighths can be heard as 3 + 3 or as 2 + 2 + 2. Switching between the two is called hemiola. Baroque composers used it at cadences, and Bernstein's "America" from West Side Story is built on alternating them.
To perform, conduct or tap the real beats: three per bar in 3/4, two per bar in 6/8 at a moderate tempo. Count 6/8 as "1 2 3 4 5 6" with the weight on 1 and 4, so the big beats stay in your body.
The common mistake is treating 6/8 as six equal beats, or as a fast 3/4. It has a lilt: long-short, long-short. Hear quarter, eighth, the typical 6/8 figure, swaying in two.
In real music, 3/4 is the waltz, from Johann Strauss to film scores. 6/8 drives Irish jigs and many lullabies. 12/8 is the home of the slow blues and of 1950s ballads with piano triplets.
To keep: the bottom number names the unit, and the split of the beat — into two or three — tells simple from compound.
Swing eighths are written even but played long-short (2:1); a quarter-note triplet puts three even notes across two beats.
Hi {name}, this is jazz rhythm. Swing eighths are written as plain eighths, but played long-short. First even, then swung.
How long is long? Think of a triplet. The first eighth takes two thirds of the beat, the second just the last third: doo-ba, doo-ba.
Syncopations swing too: a note on the "and" arrives late and lazy, on that last third.
New shape: the quarter-note triplet. Three even notes stretched across two beats. Only the first one lands on a beat.
It floats over the beat, as if the band slowed down for a moment — but the beat never moves.
Your turn! Everything here swings, at a brisk 116. Tap what you read — keep the off-beats late. Then hear a bar and choose or build it.

Swing is a reading convention. A chart marked "Swing", or headed with two eighths equal to a triplet quarter and eighth, means: play every written eighth pair long-short, two thirds plus one third. Nobody writes the triplets out; the style tells you.
In swing, the off-beat eighth often gets a light accent, and the drummer's hi-hat closes on beats 2 and 4. Hear swung eighths with quarters between them: each "and" lands late, with a small push.

A quarter-note triplet fits three quarters into the time of two beats, so each note lasts two thirds of a beat. It is exactly every other note of an eighth-note triplet. Hear two beats of eighth triplets, then the quarter triplet.

To place it, think of three triplet slots in every beat, and play the first slot of beat 1, the third slot of beat 1 and the second slot of beat 2. Only the first note touches a beat; the second comes just before beat 2, the third just after it.

Two common mistakes. Over-swinging: playing a choppy dotted eighth and sixteenth where a relaxed triplet feel is meant. And swinging everything: only the eighth pairs swing, while quarters and quarter triplets stay even.

Swing eighths are the default in most jazz, from big bands to bebop, and in the blues shuffle. Quarter-note triplets show up in melodies that seem to float over the bar line, in drum fills and in big-band ensemble hits.
To keep: swing is written even and played two thirds plus one third. A quarter triplet is three even notes across two beats.
Hey {name}! Odd meters count in quick eighths, and the eighths clump into groups of two and three. The low drum marks where each group starts.
That was 6/8: two even groups of three. Now 5/8: one group of three, one of two. It limps — charmingly.
7/8 adds another two: 2+2+3. Count it "1-2, 1-2, 1-2-3".
The same seven can be grouped other ways: 3+2+2, or 2+3+2. Listen for where the long group sits.
Longer ones: 9/8 here is 2+2+2+3, a Balkan favorite. 11/8 is 2+2+3+2+2.
Trick: don't count to eleven. Count the groups — short, short, long — and add them up.
Your turn! Listen to a few bars and tell me the meter — "seven eight" — or, at level 2, the grouping, like "two two three".

Odd meters are additive: instead of equal beats, the bar is built from short beats of two eighths and long beats of three. The beats are uneven, but the eighth note never changes speed. Turkish music calls such rhythms aksak, "limping".
Five can also be counted in quarters. Dave Brubeck's "Take Five" is in 5/4, felt as 3 + 2. It is the same long-short shape as 5/8, only slower. Listen at a relaxed pace.
7/8 lives in Balkan and Greek dance. The Bulgarian rachenitsa is 2 + 2 + 3; the Greek kalamatianos is 3 + 2 + 2. Same seven eighths, a completely different step. Hear the kalamatianos grouping.
Watch out: 9/8 can be additive, 2 + 2 + 2 + 3, as in the Turkish karsilama, or a plain compound meter, 3 + 3 + 3. Hear both: the first limps at the end, the second rolls evenly.
Listening strategy: follow the low accents and compare the gaps between them. A short gap is a 2, a long gap is a 3. Note the gaps — short, short, long — and you have both the grouping and the meter.
To perform, speak syllables: "ta-ka" for a 2 and "ta-ki-ta" for a 3, a trick borrowed from South Indian rhythm syllables. 7/8 as 2 + 2 + 3 becomes ta-ka ta-ka ta-ki-ta. Clap on every "ta".

The common mistake is squaring it off: evening out the groups, by clipping the 3 or stretching a 2, until the bar feels like plain 4/4 or 6/8. Keep the eighths perfectly even; the unevenness belongs to the groups, not to the notes.
Beyond the Balkans and Turkey, odd meters appear in progressive rock — Pink Floyd's "Money" is mostly in 7/4 — in modern jazz, and in film and game music that wants to feel restless.
To keep: odd meters are chains of 2s and 3s over a steady eighth. Find the long group, and you have found the meter.
A polyrhythm divides one span two ways at once: in "3 against 2" the high part plays 3 even notes while the low part plays 2.
Hi {name}! A polyrhythm is two even pulses at once, splitting the same stretch of time differently. Here the high click plays one number, the low drum the other.
That was 2 against 1: two high, one low. Easy — they meet on every low note.
3 against 2: three high over two low. They meet only on the first. In between you hear high, low, high.
4 against 3 is busier: four high over three low, like a gallop that keeps slipping.
5 against 4 and 5 against 3 are the tricky ones — the clicks almost blur together.
Trick: lock onto the low drum first and count its notes per cycle. Then count the high clicks from one meeting point to the next.
Your turn! Hear the pattern and name it high against low — "three against two" means three high, two low.

Precisely, a polyrhythm is two even pulses that divide the same span of time differently and meet at its start. It differs from polymeter, where two parts share one pulse but repeat in bars of different lengths.

The math behind 3 against 2: split the cycle into six slots. The three fall on slots 1, 3 and 5; the two on slots 1 and 4. Together: both, high, low, high. A handy English phrase for it: "nice cup of tea".
4 against 3 works the same way on a grid of twelve: the four land every three slots, the three every four slots. Hear how the two lines interlock into one uneven pattern.

Listening strategy: your ear picks one layer as "the beat". Here the roles swap — the low drum now plays three and the high click two. Practice hearing either layer as the beat; the pattern is the same.
To perform 3 against 2, tap on a table: right hand on slots 1, 3 and 5, left hand on 1 and 4, counting "1 2 3 4 5 6" aloud. Slowly the counting fades and the pattern becomes one motion.
The common mistake is letting one line give in to the other: the three turns lopsided, long-short-short, to fit around the two. Each layer must stay perfectly even on its own.

Cross-rhythms such as 3 against 2 are a foundation of much West African drumming and of Afro-Cuban music. In piano music, Chopin's Fantaisie-Impromptu sets four notes against three between the hands, page after page.
To keep: a polyrhythm is two even pulses over one cycle. Build it on the common grid — six for 3:2, twelve for 4:3.
Swing makes the first eighth of each beat longer: light 3:2, triplet 2:1, hard 3:1 — straight is 1:1.
Hey {name}! Straight eighths split each beat into two equal halves. Swing makes the first one longer and the second shorter. Straight, then swing.
Classic swing is 2:1, the triplet feel. The first eighth takes two thirds of the beat; the second gets the last third.
Light swing is 3:2 — just a lean, three fifths and two fifths. Players often swing lighter at fast tempos.
Hard swing is 3:1 — a dotted eighth and a sixteenth. Bouncy, almost jumpy.
All four in a row: straight, light, triplet, hard. The short note slides later each time.
Trick: listen only to the short note. Exactly halfway? Straight. A touch late? Light. On the last third? Triplet. Nearly touching the next beat? Hard.
Your turn! Listen to the eighths over the bass and tell me how they're played — straight or swing, and later, how much swing.
The swing ratio is the length of the long eighth divided by the short one. As percentages of the beat: straight 1:1 is 50/50, light 3:2 is 60/40, triplet 2:1 is about 67/33, and hard 3:1 is 75/25.

Drum machines and recording software set swing in the same percentages: 50% is straight, about 66% is triplet swing. Producers often dial in something between, around 55 to 60%, for a gentle lean. This is about 58%.

The ratio depends on tempo. In ballads players can swing deeply; at very fast tempos the eighths get straighter, because there is simply no room for a big long-short. Slow and deep, then fast and light.

Listening strategy: imagine an eighth-note triplet over each beat. Does the short note land on its last slot? That is 2:1. Before it? Lighter. After it, almost touching the next beat? Harder. Compare triplet swing with hard swing.
To play it, sing "doo-ba" over a metronome that clicks only on 2 and 4. Start from full triplets with the middle note silent, then relax the timing until it sounds like speech rather than arithmetic.

The common mistake is thinking swing is only a ratio. The feel also lives in accents, a light push on the off-beat, and in where the band sits against the beat. Still, the ratio is the part you can measure and train.

Triplet swing marks most jazz and the blues shuffle. Lighter swing is common in fast bebop and in hip-hop and neo-soul grooves. Hard, dotted 3:1 figures are more typical of marches and written dotted rhythms.
To keep: swing is a share of the beat — 50% straight, about 67% triplet. Listen to where the short note lands.
Iqa'at are cycles of dum (low) and tek (high): maqsum, baladi, saidi, malfuf — plus samai in 10/8 and karsilama in 9/8.
Ahlan, {name}! Arabic music rides on rhythm cycles called iqa'at. They're spoken in two sounds: dum, the deep center of the drum, and tek, the sharp rim.
Maqsum is the everyday one: dum tek, tek dum, tek.
Baladi opens with two dums: dum dum, tek dum, tek. Heavier, earthier.
Saidi moves the double dum to the middle: dum tek, dum dum, tek. It's the rhythm of Upper Egypt.
Malfuf is quick and spinning: one dum and two teks, grouped 3+3+2.
Two longer cycles: samai has ten beats, with a dum dum in the middle. Karsilama has nine, 2+2+2+3, ending tek tek tek.
Your turn! Listen for where the dums fall — low is dum, high is tek — and name the rhythm.

An iqa' (plural iqa'at) is a repeating rhythmic cycle, defined by where its dums and teks fall. Maqsum, baladi and saidi each fill a 4/4 bar of eight eighths; malfuf is usually written in 2/4 and played fast.
On the darbuka, the goblet drum, dum is a stroke of the strong hand near the center; tek is a sharp stroke on the rim. A tek played by the other hand is often called ka.
Listening strategy: ignore the teks and follow the dums. Maqsum starts dum-tek; baladi starts dum-dum. Hear them back to back — that second dum gives baladi away.
Drummers rarely play the bare skeleton. They fill the gaps with light teks and rolls, while the dums stay in place. Here is maqsum filled in: every slot sounds, yet the dums still mark the cycle.
Malfuf groups its eight eighths 3 + 3 + 2, the same grouping as the Latin tresillo. Played fast, it feels like a spinning pulse in two, a common choice for quick, light passages.

The long cycles belong to particular forms. Samai thaqil, in 10/8, carries the classical instrumental form called sama'i. Karsilama, in 9/8 grouped 2 + 2 + 2 + 3, is a lively dance rhythm of Turkey and Greece.

To learn a rhythm, speak it before you play it: "dum tek, tek dum, tek" over a steady foot. Then tap the dums with the right hand and the teks with the left on your knees. Keep the cycle going without stopping at its end.
The common mistake is mixing up maqsum and saidi. Both start dum-tek; the difference is in the middle, where saidi has two dums in a row and maqsum has tek-dum. Hear saidi again with that in mind.
Maqsum underlies a huge share of Egyptian song and of Mizrahi pop in Israel. Baladi is a staple of belly dance, and saidi accompanies the stick dance of Upper Egypt.
To keep: an iqa' is a cycle you recognize by its dums. Learn the skeleton, then hear it through the ornaments.
Keep the beat when the metronome goes silent; getting ahead is rushing, falling behind is dragging.
Hey {name}! Every musician carries an inner clock. This drill checks how steady yours is when nobody keeps time for you.
First, two bars with the metronome. Tap along on every beat and settle in.
Then the click goes silent for 2, 4 or 8 bars — your choice — and one bar comes back to check you. Keep tapping right through the silence.
Get ahead and you're rushing — the classic when you're excited. Hear a tapper speed up in the silence and land early.
Fall behind and you're dragging. Either way, the returning click tells the truth.
Trick: move with it. Nod, tap a foot, breathe in time. Your body keeps time better than counting alone.
Your turn! Pick a tempo and the silent bars, tap the pad or press Space on every beat, and I'll tell you: steady, rushing or dragging.

Your inner clock is your ability to keep a steady tempo without outside help. Its errors are measured in milliseconds: an early tap is rushing, a late one dragging. The goal is not perfection, but a small and consistent error.

Surprisingly, slow tempos are harder to hold than medium ones: the gap between beats is long, and the mind fills it badly. Here is 60 BPM — four clicks, then four silent beats. Try to feel where they fall.
The fix is subdivision. Count "1 & 2 &" in your head, so every gap has a landmark in the middle. Hear the same 60 BPM with the halves filled in: the silence suddenly has a shape.

Dragging sounds like this: on time with the click, then each tap a little late, so when the click returns the taps trail behind it. Rushing is the mirror image, and usually comes from excitement or tension.
A proven practice ladder: first the metronome on every beat, then only on beats 2 and 4, then once per bar, then with silent bars. Each step hands more of the job to you. Hear clicks on 2 and 4.

The common mistake is jumping when the click returns and you find you are off. Do not lurch to catch it; adjust gently over a beat or two, as a band would. And breathe — tension makes almost everyone rush.

In a band, the drummer and bassist hold the time for everyone, and studios often record to a click track. Steady time is also what makes deliberate freedom, like rubato in a ballad, sound intended rather than unsteady.
To keep: subdivide the silence, move with the beat, and correct gently. A steady inner clock is the base of every groove.
Hear a rhythm, wait for the four clicks, tap it back — each pass adds one beat.
Hi {name}! Beat Echo is a memory game for your hands. I play a rhythm, you tap it back.
Four clicks set the tempo. Then the rhythm plays on a woodblock, over a soft pulse.
Then four more clicks — your count-in. Start tapping right after them: same rhythm, same speed.
Each beat holds a quarter or two eighths. From four beats on, watch out for silent beats and lone off-beat eighths.
You start at two beats. Every rhythm you nail grows by one beat. Playing solo, one miss ends the game — so your longest echo is your score.
Trick: don't memorize taps — count it in your head, beat by beat, and tap what you count.
Your turn! Listen, wait for the four clicks, then tap the pad or press Space. How long can you go?
Beat Echo trains rhythmic memory: hearing a pattern once, holding it, and reproducing it in time. It is the old call and response of music teaching — the teacher plays, the student answers.
The key is chunking. Every beat in the game is one of four shapes: one note, two notes, a silent beat, or a lone ‘and’. Name each beat as it passes, and a long rhythm becomes a short list of words.
Listening strategy: anchor on the soft pulse under the woodblock. For each pulse, ask: did a note start with it, after it, both, or neither? Those four answers are the four shapes.
with = 1 · both = 1 & · after = (1) & · neither = (1)

To answer well, keep the beat in your foot or head through the count-in, and keep it going while you tap. Short, relaxed taps are more precise than heavy ones. Start on the beat right after the fourth click.

Two classic mistakes: a lone off-beat note gets pulled onto the beat, and a silent beat gets skipped, so the answer comes out shorter than the call. Hear both traps: a quarter, a lone ‘and’, a quarter, then a silent beat.
Once rhythms grow past four beats, group them in pairs of beats, the way you remember a phone number in chunks. Three short phrases are far easier to hold than six separate beats.

Call and response runs through African drumming, gospel and the blues. Jazz musicians "trade fours", answering each other in four-bar solos, and many drum traditions are taught entirely by ear, phrase by phrase.
To keep: hear in beat-sized words, keep the pulse running, and never skip the silent beats.
Keep the beat in one hand; spread the other hand evenly over the whole bar. They meet only on 1.
Hi {name}! Until now the two hands split each beat between them. Now one hand spreads its notes over the whole bar. Listen: five high notes over four low beats.
Five against three, in 3/4: the same idea in a shorter bar, so the notes sit closer together.
Seven against four: seven even notes in the time of one bar. Only the first note of each bar meets the beat.
Do not count the fast part note by note. Feel the bar as one long circle and spread the notes evenly around it.
In the exercise the click keeps the beat with your slow hand. Start slowly, and listen for the one place each bar where both hands meet.
Five against four lives on a grid of twenty. The five-part plays on every fourth step; the beat on every fifth. Only the first step is shared.
Seven against four lives on a grid of twenty-eight, which is too fine to count. Here the long circle is the only way: hear the seven as one smooth wave across the bar.
Practice it in layers: each hand alone against the click, then the two together very slowly, then let the beat hand run by itself while you listen to the other.
The common mistake: the fast hand bunches up near the beats and waits in between. Its notes must stay exactly evenly spaced, even where no beat helps them.
You hear these in jazz solos that float over the bar line, in Chopin and Scriabin, and in prog drumming, where a ride pattern in five sits over a groove in four.
To keep: one hand on the beat, the other evenly over the whole bar; they meet on 1. Feel the circle, not the count.
A note value you are already playing becomes the new beat: the hands keep going, the beat changes under them.
Hi {name}! Metric modulation changes the tempo without a jolt. Listen: quarter notes, then quarter triplets, and the triplet becomes the new beat.
Here the hands stay the same: even triplets all the way. Only the click moves, and two triplets now make one beat.
It also works the other way. Even eighths stay, and the click slows down: three of them now make one beat.
The secret is that nothing in your hands has to change. The new beat was already hiding inside the old rhythm.
In the exercise, keep your taps even through the change and let the new click settle in before you judge it.
Work out the new tempo by the ratio. Triplet quarter to quarter: times three halves, so 80 becomes 120. Dotted eighth to quarter: times four thirds, so 90 becomes 120.
The dotted eighth is the trickiest pivot. Group sixteenths in threes inside the old tempo, and each group of three becomes the new beat.
The trick is to hear the pivot value before the change. Feel it inside the old tempo for a bar, then let it become the beat.
The common mistake is to guess the new tempo instead of deriving it. Your taps rush or drag at the change. Keep them exactly even and the new tempo arrives by itself.
Drummers like Tony Williams and bands in prog and fusion use metric modulation to shift a whole band into a new tempo without stopping.
To keep: the old note value equals the new beat. Keep the hands even; the beat changes under them.
Two bars of 3 felt as three big 2s: the accents cross the bar line, the bar line itself stays.
Hi {name}! In 3/4 we feel one, two, three. Listen: two bars on the beat, then the same two bars in big twos. That is the hemiola.
Both at once: the beat below, three big notes above, over two bars. That is three against two, stretched across the bar line.
And over 4/4: eighths grouped three, three, two. It pulls across the bar and lands home on one.
There is also the bar that changes its mind: one bar in two big beats, like 6/8, then one in three, like 3/4.
In the exercise, keep the bar line in your body while your hands play across it, and land exactly on the next one.
The word comes from Greek for one and a half: three half notes take the place of two dotted halves. The total time stays the same; only the grouping changes.
Baroque and classical cadences use the hemiola to broaden the last bars before the final chord. Listen for it at the ends of minuets and courantes.
In jazz, Latin and pop, three, three, two is everywhere: the tresillo, the Charleston, countless riffs. It is the same idea inside one bar of four.
The common mistake is to let the bar line move with the accents, so the music suddenly sounds like it is in 2/4. Keep counting the bar quietly.
Practice by tapping the beat with your foot and the big twos with your hand. When that is easy, swap: hand on the beat, foot in twos.
To keep: the accents move, the bar line stays. Count the bar quietly while you play the big twos.
Count odd meters in groups of 2 and 3; a displaced figure keeps its shape and moves against the beat.
Hi {name}! 5/4 is not five equal counts: it is a three and a two. Listen to the hit at the start of each group.
7/8 is two, two, three: short, short, long. Say it with me: doo-ba, doo-ba, doo-ba-da.
The same seven can also be three, two, two. The long group comes first, and the whole bar leans differently.
Displacement moves a figure but keeps its shape. Here a riff starts on one, then the same riff an eighth later.
Keep the click as your anchor in the exercise: feel where each group starts, and the odd bar soon feels natural.
Every odd meter breaks into twos and threes. Nine eighths can be three threes or two, two, two, three; eleven is often three, three, three, two.
Balkan dances, Turkish aksak rhythms and prog rock live in these meters. Dave Brubeck brought 5/4 and 9/8 into jazz, and Mizrahi music knows 7/8 well.
Displacement is how jazz and funk players make a simple figure exciting: the same notes, shifted by an eighth or a quarter, land on new parts of the beat.
The common mistake in odd meters is stretching the long group or squeezing the short ones. Every eighth stays the same length; only the grouping changes.
Practice by speaking the syllables over a slow click, then clapping only the group starts, then playing the figure on your instrument. Speed always comes last.
To keep: odd meters are groups of two and three. Know the grouping before you play; a displaced figure keeps its shape.
Play it up and down in the same eight notes: C, E, G and A land on the beats both ways.
It is not a major scale with a passing note on the way down. The A♭ belongs to the scale in both directions, so the chord tones fall on the beats going up too.
One diminished chord, B°7, woven with four chords: C6 (major, and m7 through the relative), Cm6 (minor, m7♭5), C7 (the dominant), C7♭5 (altered, the tritone sub).
Barry built four eight-note scales on the same diminished chord, B°7. Each weaves it with a different chord, so that chord’s tones land on the beats.
The major 6th: C6 plus B°7. It serves major chords, and a minor 7th through its relative: Dm7 is F6.
The minor 6th: Cm6 plus B°7, with E♭. It serves minor chords and the half-diminished: Dm7♭5 is Fm6.
The dominant 7th: C7 plus B°7 — C, D, E, F, G, A♭, B♭, B. C, E, G and B♭ on the beats. It serves the dominant.
The 7♭5: C7♭5 plus B°7, with G♭. It serves the altered dominant and the tritone substitute: G♭7♭5 has the same four notes.
Each scale goes up and down in the same eight notes, two octaves, with its chord’s tones on the beats. Start on a chord tone, never on a diminished one.
Harmonize them the same way: every scale tone gets the chord or the diminished, in moving inversions. C7, then B°7 with D on top, then C7 with E on top.
Why one diminished serves all four: B°7 is G7♭9 without its root, the dominant of C. Whatever the home chord, the diminished pulls toward it.
A common mistake: mixing the two dominant scales. The 7th scale keeps G; the 7♭5 scale lowers it to G♭. Listen to the beat after F.
On a ii–V–I they line up: Dm7 takes the F 6th scale, G7 the G dominant scale or the D minor 6th, and C the C 6th. One diminished family links all three.
To keep: one diminished chord, four partners. Pick the scale by the chord you are on, and play it through all twelve keys.
Borrowing is oblique motion: in a chord of the 6th-diminished scale, one or two voices step to another chord’s note and come back while the others hold.
Take a C6 chord: A, C, E, G. Hold three notes and let the top one step down to F, from the diminished, and back to G.
That is oblique motion: one voice moves, the others stay. Barry called it borrowing — the voice borrows a note and returns it.
Any voice can borrow. Here the alto, E, dips to D and comes back.
Two voices can borrow together: soprano and alto step down at once, then return.
Then walk the scale of chords, C6 and B°7 in turn, and let one voice borrow on every degree. The held keys stay down.
Borrow from other places too. From the chord above: G rises to A♭ and returns. From another diminished, a half step outside the scale: C rises to C♯.
Or pass through the scale: the top voice runs up a third and back, G, A♭, A, A♭, G, over the held voices.
Over a ii–V–I: Dm7 played as F6 borrows one voice; G7, played as Dm6, borrows two voices from the diminished, which makes G7♭9; then C6.
The drills grade it voice by voice: the chord must sound, the borrowed note must move by the right step and return, and the held voices must really hold.
In drop 2 and drop 3 the same idea spreads over two hands, or over a string set on the guitar: the dropped voice can borrow too, low in the left hand.
A common mistake is lifting the whole hand when one finger moves. Practice slowly, rubato first, with the held keys pressed and only the borrowing finger free.
Each hand keeps its own job: a held note against moving fingers, two voices in one hand, an ostinato under a melody, different rhythms, touch and loudness per hand.
Hold one key down while the other fingers keep moving. The held finger stays still and relaxed, and the key stays down.
Two voices in one hand: the upper voice holds a long note while the lower fingers run underneath it.
Then let the hands disagree: the left hand repeats a short figure while the right hand sings a melody on top.
Different rhythms: three notes in the right hand against two in the left, the beats shared.
Touch and loudness per hand: one hand legato and singing, the other short and soft. A MIDI keyboard measures both, and the held notes too.
These exercises follow the idea of Isidor Philipp’s independence studies: some fingers hold, others move, so each finger learns to work alone. Ours are new patterns in all twelve keys.
Hold the weak fingers last. Holding a chord with 1, 2 and 3 while 4 and 5 trill is the hardest: keep the trill light and the chord quiet.
For 3 against 2, count the shared beat aloud and feel the right hand’s middle note fall just before the left hand’s second.
A common mistake: the staccato hand drags the legato hand short, or the soft hand gets loud with the other. Practice each hand alone first, then together slowly.
An ostinato frees the mind for the melody only when it runs by itself. Repeat the left-hand figure until you can talk over it, then add the right hand.
Every new item starts in free time, then quarter notes, then the tempo ladder. Speed comes last; independence comes first.
Stack the scale’s own 3rds on every degree: 3rds, triads, then 7th chords, arpeggiated and block, then drop 2 and drop 3 — up and down the scale.
Every scale holds its own chords. First play it note by note, up and down two octaves.
Take every other note and you get the scale in 3rds: C–E, D–F, E–G. Broken first, then both notes together.
Add one more 3rd for a triad on every degree, and another for a 7th chord. Play them broken, then all at once.
Drop 2: take the second voice from the top down an octave. Drop 3: the third voice. On the piano the left hand takes the dropped note.
On the guitar each drop lives on a string set: drop 2 on four neighbouring strings, drop 3 with a string skipped under the top three.
Every mode harmonizes itself. D dorian gives Dm7, Em7, Fmaj7, G7 — the notes of C major from a new home, so the chords move to new degrees.
Harmonic and melodic minor bring their own colours: an augmented triad on the 3rd, a diminished 7th on the 7th, a dominant on the 4th of melodic minor.
Barry Harris’s diminished scales alternate a chord and the diminished, so their 7th chords are moving inversions: C6, B°7, C6 over E, and so on up the scale.
Keep the top note as the melody. In block chords and drops the scale is on top, and the voices under it follow by step — that is why it sounds smooth.
On the piano, add the left-hand root under the block chords: the right hand keeps the voicing, the left hand names the chord.
A common mistake is rushing to the drops. If a triad on one degree hesitates, the drop on that degree will too: climb the ladder step by step, in every key.
BPM = beats per minute: 60 is one a second, 120 two a second. Feel the gap between clicks, not the sound.
Hey {name}! Tempo is how fast the beat goes, counted in beats per minute — BPM. Sixty BPM is exactly one beat every second.
Double it and you get 120: two beats a second, a brisk walk. Most pop songs live between 90 and 130.
Faster or slower? Listen to the gap between clicks, not the clicks themselves. Here is 100, then 115.
Tempo can also drift. This one speeds up — musicians call it accelerando. Its opposite, slowing down, is ritardando.
To guess a number, anchor on 60 and 120: is it slower than a second, about one, or about two a second? Then fine-tune.
Your turn! Faster or slower, steady or drifting, and finally: name the tempo. Tap along with a finger — it really helps.
Tempo is the rate of the pulse, the beat you would tap your foot to. One beat lasts 60 divided by the BPM, in seconds: at 120 BPM each beat is half a second; at 90, two thirds of a second.
Tempo is not how busy the music is. Here is 70 BPM, then the same 70 filled with four notes per beat. It feels faster, but the pulse has not moved.
Classical scores use Italian words, each a range rather than a number: Adagio slow, around 70; Andante a walking pace, around 90; Allegro fast, around 130; Presto very fast, 170 and more.
Styles have home tempos too. House music typically sits around 120 to 128, drum and bass around 170 to 175, and much hip-hop between 85 and 95.
To hear a number, compare with anchors. A clock's second hand is 60; a brisk march is 120. Then ask: closer to the lower anchor, the middle, or the upper one? 90 sits halfway.
The common mistake is an octave error: hearing 140 as 70, or the reverse, because you tapped every other beat. Both are valid feels; check which one the drums and the bass line really lock to.
Slowing down is ritardando. It often closes a piece; listen for the gaps stretching. Practice tip: keeping a slow tempo steady is harder than a fast one, so practice slow with a metronome.
To keep: tempo is the pulse, not the notes. Anchor on 60 and 120, feel the gap, and decide which level of the beat you are counting.
Twelve intervals, each a number of semitones with its own color: rub, step, sad, sweet, open, tense, hollow, warm, bluesy, longing, the same note.
Hi {name}! Between two notes there are twelve intervals, from one semitone up to the octave. Each has its own color. Let us meet them.
The small ones: a minor 2nd rubs, a major 2nd is just a step. A minor 3rd sounds sad, a major 3rd sweet.
The middle: the perfect 4th is open, like a hymn. The tritone, six semitones, is restless. The perfect 5th is wide and hollow.
The big ones: a minor 6th is bittersweet, a major 6th warm. A minor 7th is bluesy, a major 7th longing. And the octave — the same note, higher.
Together, intervals blend: listen for how much the two notes fight. Going down, sing the top note first, then the bottom.
Your turn! First up, then all twelve, then together, then down. Pick the interval — guess by color, then count if you need to.

An interval has a number and a quality. The number counts letter names, both ends included: C up to E is C, D, E — a third. The quality, major or minor, comes from the half steps: four make a major third, three a minor third.

Unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves are called perfect. The rest are major or minor. Stretch one half step further and you get augmented or diminished: C to F sharp is an augmented fourth, C to G flat a diminished fifth — the same tritone sound, spelled two ways.
Turn an interval upside down and it inverts: the numbers add up to 9, major becomes minor, perfect stays perfect. C up to E is a major third; E up to C is a minor sixth.
Played together, intervals range from smooth to rough. Octaves and fifths blend, thirds and sixths are sweet, seconds, sevenths and the tritone clash. Fifth, major third, minor second.

Many people use song openings as anchors: "Over the Rainbow" leaps an octave, Wagner's Bridal Chorus starts with a fourth, the big leap in the Star Wars main theme is a fifth, and Bernstein's "Maria" opens with a tritone. Pick tunes you truly know.
The most common mix-up is the fourth and the fifth. Sing up the scale from the low note: do-re-mi-fa stops at the fourth, do to sol reaches the fifth. The fifth also sounds more settled and hollow.
Beyond the octave, intervals are compound: a ninth is an octave plus a second, a tenth an octave plus a third. They keep the color of the small interval, opened out.
To keep: count letters for the number, half steps for the quality. Guess by color first, then check by singing the scale between the two notes.
Natural minor lowers 3, 6 and 7. A chromatic degree is a note outside the key — ♭3, ♯4, ♭6, ♭7 — that leans on a scale note next to it.
Hey {name}! In a minor key, home is still 1 — but the steps change. Hear the minor cadence, then home.
Natural minor lowers three degrees of major: 3, 6 and 7. That is what makes it darker.
Degrees still feel the same: 1 rests, 5 is strong. Here is 5, then 3 — in minor, 3 is the dark color.
Back in major, a chromatic degree is a note outside the key. Flat 3 is the blue note; sharp 4 is the Lydian lift; flat 7 is bluesy.
The trick: a chromatic note leans. Ask which scale note it wants to slide into — up or down — and name it from there.
Your turn! First every degree in a minor key, then chromatic ones in major. Feel home first, then the note.
Minor comes in three versions. Natural minor: 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7. Harmonic minor raises 7 back up, so it leans into home — in A minor, G sharp.
That raised 7 gives minor its strong dominant chord: E major, or E7, instead of E minor. It is the G sharp in the cadence you hear before every minor exercise.
Melodic minor raises both 6 and 7 on the way up, to smooth the gap between them; in classical practice it falls back to natural minor coming down. In jazz it keeps both raised.
Each minor degree has its pull. ♭6 sighs down into 5 — in A minor, F to E. 2 leans down to 1, and 4 tends to fall to ♭3.
A chromatic degree is spelled by where it goes. Rising, it takes a sharp: ♯4 to 5. Falling, a flat: ♭2 to 1, ♭6 to 5. Here, in C: D flat sinking into C.
Where they come from: ♭3, ♭6 and ♭7 are borrowed from the parallel minor. ♯4 often comes from a chord that leads to V — in C, D7 with its F sharp, then G, then home.
In blues and rock, the blue ♭3 often bends or slides up into 3 over a major chord. The clash is the point. Hear the slide.

The common mistake is naming a chromatic note by the nearest key instead of its direction. Ask where it wants to go. To keep: minor lowers 3, 6 and 7; chromatic notes lean, and their spelling shows the way.
Read ahead and hear it in your head first; then follow the notes one by one and catch the one that does not match.
Hi {name}! Sight-reading means hearing music from the page. Here are four notes — try to imagine them before I play.
The shape tells you a lot: a step moves to the next line or space; a skip jumps one over. Up on the staff means up in pitch.
Now follow along: same notes on the page, but one note is played differently. Did you catch it? It was the third.
The trick: point at each note as it plays, so your eyes and ears move together. A surprise is the note you are pointing at.
Your turn! Read, listen and say if it matches; then which note was different — in longer lines, in the bass clef, in minor; and at the top, three versions where only one is the written one.
Musicians call hearing music in your head "audiation". Sight-reading by ear is audiation from the page: you see the notes and hear them before any sound is made.
Before reading a single note, check the key signature and find home. One sharp means G major or E minor. Hum the home chord to set your ear.
Read the distance, not each letter. Line to the next space is a second; line to the next line, a third; line to the line after that, a fifth. C, E, G: two thirds, then a fourth up to C.
Then group notes into patterns you already know: a scale run, a broken chord, a repeated note. You read words, not single letters — music works the same way.
Rhythm is half of reading. Scan it first and tap it: here a quarter, two eighths, then quarters.
When you follow and something surprises you, decide two things: which note, and was it higher or lower than written? Here the third note goes up to A instead of G.
In the bass clef the lines, bottom to top, are G, B, D, F, A, and middle C sits on a ledger line just above. Same distances, new names.
The common mistake is reading letter by letter and losing the line. Look one note ahead, hear the shape, and let the eye run before the ear. To keep: home, distance, pattern, rhythm.
Chunk it: hear a rhythm in pieces of one or two beats, and count them to yourself. Short pieces are easy to keep.
Hey {name}! Remembering a rhythm is a real skill — drummers, dancers and singers use it all the time. Here is one bar.
The trick is chunking. Do not track every note — hear beat-sized pieces: a pair of eighths, a quarter, a half. Two or three pieces fill a bar.
Now the same or different? First the rhythm, then again — but one note moved by half a beat. Hear where it jumped?
Longer rhythms: count the pieces to yourself while you listen, then keep them going through what comes next. That is how you hold four bars.
Your turn! Same or different, then pick it out of three, then four bars with one tiny change. Chunk it — you have got this.
Short-term memory holds only a few chunks at a time. A bar of eight separate notes is too many; two or three beat-sized pieces is easy. Rhythm memory is the art of grouping.
Count it: "1 and 2 and". The numbers fall on the beats and each "and" halfway. The point is to place each note against the beat.
Keep the beat in your body as a frame. The pulse is the grid; each note is either on a beat or between beats. The ones between beats — syncopations — are what you most need to remember.
A famous chunk: three plus three plus two eighths, the tresillo. It runs through Latin music, reggaeton and a great deal of pop. Once you know it, you hear it as one word.
With short clicks, a long note and a short note followed by a rest sound alike. What you remember is where each sound starts — the attack points against the beat.
Music repeats itself. Many four-bar rhythms are a bar, the same bar, then a change. Listen for the repeat and spend your attention on the change.
The common mistake is losing the "1", the downbeat, so everything shifts. Tap or nod on every 1. To keep: feel the pulse, chunk into words, and watch where the pattern changes.
Follow the bass and the mood of each chord, chord by chord: bright, dark, tense. The one whose mood changed is the one that changed.
Hi {name}! Musicians remember whole chord progressions — that is how they learn songs by ear. Here are three chords.
Give each chord a word: major is bright, minor is dark. Follow the bass too — it walks under everything.
Now the same three — but the middle one changed. The bass moved and the color went dark. That is the one.
For long progressions, number them as you go — one, two, three, four — and keep the bass line humming in your head. When the color flips, note the number.
Your turn! The progression plays twice; say which chord changed. Three chords, then four, then six.
Musicians remember progressions as functions, not names. Roman numerals number the chords of the key: in C, C is I, F is IV, G is V, A minor is vi. The same numbers work in every key.
Each chord quality has its color: major bright, minor dark, a dominant seventh tense and wanting to move, diminished unstable. Hear C, A minor, G7 and B diminished.
The bass line is the spine. Hum it while the chords play: here C, F, G, C. Strong moves, like a fourth up or a fifth down, are the easiest to remember.
Many songs reuse a few patterns, so learn them as single units. I–V–vi–IV runs under a huge number of pop songs; ii–V–I is the core of jazz.
A change can hide in the color alone. Here the bass stays on F, but the second time F major becomes F minor — a chord borrowed from the minor key.
For long progressions, chunk in pairs: four chords are two gestures, six are three. Notice when the music returns home to I; it splits the line into phrases.
The common mistake is trying to hold every chord at once. Keep the bass and the colors, and listen for the moment something feels different. To keep: numbers, bass, color, pairs.
A good answer lands somewhere that makes sense: home to finish, a chord note to fit, or the call's own shape, moved, to echo it.
Hey {name}! Improvising starts with listening: a phrase asks a question, and your phrase answers. Here is a call — it sounds unfinished.
An answer that lands home sounds finished. One that stops on 2 or 7 sounds like another question. Hear both.
Over a chord, the safest notes are the chord's own. Over F major, F, A and C fit; B rubs against it.
And the classic trick: echo. Take the call's shape and play it again a step higher. The ear loves it.
Your turn! A call, two answers: which one finishes, which one fits the chord, which one echoes. Then try your own on the backing tracks.

Call and response is one of the oldest forms in music: one voice calls, others answer. It is central to West African traditions, work songs, gospel and blues, and lives on in jazz musicians trading phrases.
In theory terms, a question and answer form a period. The first phrase ends open, often on 2 or 5; the second starts the same way and ends on 1.
You have four tools to answer: repeat the call, move it (a sequence), vary it — same rhythm, new notes — or contrast it. Here the answer keeps the rhythm and changes the notes.
Put chord tones on the strong beats and let other notes pass between them. Going from G7 to C, a line on B rises to C and one on F falls to E: tension, then release.
The blues uses the form inside each verse: a line, the same line again, then a different line that answers it — AAB. Between the sung lines, the guitar answers the voice.
Practice tip: answer with three notes only, and sing before you play. A short answer that lands home beats a long one that wanders.

The common mistake is not listening: starting before the call ends, or playing something unrelated. Leave space, borrow from the call. To keep: end where it makes sense, and let the answer remember the question.
Bass as low as possible; the chord’s 3rd and 7th between C3 and G4; the melody in the two octaves above middle C.
Solo piano has three jobs: bass, chords and melody. Each has its own register.
The bass sits as low as you can: a root, or a root and a 5th.
The chord’s 3rd and 7th live between C3 and G4. Lower is muddy; higher is pretty but doesn’t say the chord.
The melody sings in the two octaves above middle C, like a voice or a horn.
The left hand has three positions: bass notes, bass shells, rootless voicings. Here is one chord in six places.
Check yourself by ear: if a chord sounds thick and grey, the 3rd and 7th sit too low; move them up into the middle.
Every take is measured in all twelve keys: free time first, then in time on the tempo ladder. Your turn — slowly, and listen to each register.
The lowest A, B♭ and B are rarely used: they blur. Octaves in the bass are an effect, not the default.
Thick right-hand chords over a low bass sound empty, because nothing sits between C3 and G4.
The top two octaves are for effects: bells, a doubled melody, crystal arpeggios.
A common mistake is a left hand that drifts up toward the melody until the hands crash. Keep the left hand below middle C and let the right hand rise.
Recap: the bass low, the 3rd and 7th between C3 and G4, the melody above middle C, effects at the top.
Where it lives: listen to any solo pianist play a ballad — the bass rings low, the chords sit warm in the middle, and the melody sings clearly above them, never buried.
Practice it with one chord: play it as a bass note, a shell, a bass shell and a rootless voicing, and say aloud which register each one lives in.
Three mangos — bass, chords, melody — and two hands: two in the LH, two in the RH, one shared, drop one, or juggle.
Three mangos, two hands. Siskind’s five answers are the whole map of solo piano.
One: two in the left hand. Stride, bass shells, shell stride.
Two: two in the right hand. A bassline below; the right hand shuttles, drapes or plays the chords in the line.
Three: one in each hand, the third shared — shared-hands voicings, mostly for ballads.
Four: drop a mango — most often the bass: closed position, drop 2. Five: juggle, and switch as you go.
Each solution has its own sound, and the textures ladder walks through them one at a time, on the same original tunes.
The great pianists mix freely. Dave McKenna called his version the third hand.

The textures ladder climbs the same way: melody and bass, shells, call and response, shell stride, notes under the melody, filled octaves — then the right hand over a bass, the blocks, shared hands and the ballads.
The last step is an arrangement: an intro, then each phrase in another texture.
Mango one in sound: the left hand alone carries bass and chord while the melody floats above.
Mango four in sound: no bass at all, the melody harmonised in a block under the right hand.
A common mistake is to stay in one texture for the whole tune. Change every eight bars and the arrangement breathes.

Where it lives: in solo recordings the textures change every few bars — stride for a chorus, a bassline under a right-hand shuttle, then a quiet shared-hands ballad. The changes keep the listener with you.
Root + one essential tone (3rd, 10th or 7th); Type A 1-3-7, Type B 1-7-10; the 9th under the thumb; the 5th or the tritone for the root.
Two-note bass shells — Bud Powell voicings: the root and one essential tone.
Alternate 3rd and 7th through a ii–V–I and the voices barely move.
Three notes: Type A is 1-3-7, a fairly high bass for any hand. Type B is 1-7-10, for a bigger hand.
Can’t reach a 10th? Add the 9th and take 9 and 10 with the thumb, when both keys share a colour.
The 5th can replace the root; on a dominant the tritone can — a built-in tritone sub.
Then shell stride: the bass on 1 and 3, the shell on 2 and 4.
Not at once: roll the bass an eighth early and land the shell on the beat; at medium and fast tempos leave the bass out.
Or reverse the roles: shells on the strong beats, the bass between. Bill Evans played the essentials first and the bass after.
Hear the difference: the two-note shell is light and open; Type A adds weight in the middle; Type B is wide and full.
A common mistake is a shell that jumps an octave on every chord. Choose the 3rd or the 7th so the top note moves by step.
Recap: root plus 3rd, 10th or 7th; Type A and Type B; the 9th under the thumb; the 5th or the tritone for the root.

Where it lives: Bud Powell comped with two-note shells under fast bebop lines; Kenny Barron and Monk play shell stride. Start slowly, keep the bass on the beat, and the shells will settle under any melody.
Walking 10ths; the Peace Piece pattern, reversed, skip beat, 3+3+2, anticipations, 3 against 4; LH breaks; stride-style comping; the shuttle.
Stride: bass on 1 and 3, a chord on 2 and 4, the melody on top.
Walking 10ths: every beat a 10th, moving by step into the next chord.
Vary it: low-high-high-low, the Peace Piece pattern — the bass on 4 walks into the next bar.
Anticipate the bass, group 3 + 3 + 2, play 3 against 4 — and take breaks while the right hand fills.
Stride-style comping: the left hand still covers bass and chord, but syncopated — Charleston, reverse, Red Garland.
Keep the bass low and the chord in the middle: the jump between them is the skill, so practice it slowly without looking.
His practice tip: play a whole tune in 10ths, on 1 and 3.
The shuttle, after Bill Evans: the left hand moves between a bass note and a mid-register voicing under a held right hand. The variation procedures here are our reading of his videos.
Listen to the 10ths walk: the bass and the 10th move together by step, like a second singer under the melody.
A common mistake is to rush the jump back to the bass. Land the bass on time and let the chord be short.
Recap: stride, walking 10ths, the variations, breaks, stride-style comping and the shuttle — each a new way for one hand to do two jobs.
Where it lives: the stride masters used walking 10ths and anticipations to keep the left hand from sounding like a machine. Change one thing every four bars and listen to how the groove opens.
Practice every variation in all twelve keys, free time first.
Melody on top, bass at the bottom, the thumbs and index fingers share the chord. Four rules: 3 and 7, no doubling, even spacing, no minor 9ths.
Shared hands: the right hand holds the melody, the left the bass, and both hands share the chord between.
Four rules: include the 3rd and 7th; don’t double; space the notes evenly; avoid minor 9ths.
Stop-start rubato: a chord, a stop, then the melody gesture — no pulse at all.
Repeated quarters: hold the voicing and repeat the left-hand thumb as a quiet timekeeper.
Stride ballad: swung stride at a ballad tempo. Then move an inner voice on long melody notes.
Let the melody sing out over the chord: the top fingers a little louder, the thumbs soft.
The corner thumb: one thumb takes two neighbouring keys, so four shared notes fit two hands.
Four-voice training: sing and play the ballad melody in the soprano, then the alto, tenor and bass.
Hear the repeated-quarter style: the voicing rings, and one soft inner note keeps the time.
A common mistake is to double the melody note inside the chord. Leave it out of the middle and the melody stands clear.
Recap: four rules, three ballad styles, then inner voices and four-voice training.

Where it lives: pianists like Mehldau, Hersch and Jarrett use the repeated-quarter style for intimate ballads, and many begin a ballad in stop-start rubato before the time comes in. Practice each chord slowly first: find the voicing, check the four rules, then play it in time.
The corner thumb and the hand split change with each chord: sometimes the left hand takes two shared notes, sometimes one. Choose the split that keeps both hands relaxed.
Beat-3 Charleston, lead-ins, Count Basie, push-offs, accent comping, two-bar patterns — then free comping by rule.
Lead-ins and two-bar patterns — then free comping by rule.
Comping is mostly off the beat — short jabs, like a boxer.
The Beat-3 Charleston starts the Charleston on 3: room for a melody in the first half of the bar.
The Charleston: a chord on 1 and on the and of 2. Short, like a jab, then wait for the next bar.
A lead-in: a chord on the and of 3, or on 4, leads into the next downbeat.
A push-off repeats a chord on a beat and the offbeat after it — a lift to the Count Basie rhythm.
A two-bar pattern: the Charleston in the first bar, a lead-in on 4 in the second, so the comp breathes across two bars.
Free comping by rule: one to four hits a bar, at least three rhythms, never three bars the same, anticipations that sound the next chord.
Keep every chord short and light, and let the click on 2 and 4 hold the time for you.
Accent comping is a coordination device: the left hand lands exactly with the right hand’s accents.
Two-bar patterns: a rhythm that takes two bars to come round, so the comp does not repeat every bar and the soloist hears a phrase, not a loop. Start with a lead-in in the second bar, then move it.
The Basie rhythm and the push-off placements here are our reading of his videos; the names are his.
Hear the Charleston and the Beat-3 Charleston side by side: the same two hits, half a bar apart.
A common mistake is comping on every downbeat. Leave space: a comp that answers the melody is worth more than a busy one.
Recap: name the rhythm, keep it light, vary it by rule, and anticipate into the next chord.

Where it lives: the great compers mix these rhythms freely, answering the soloist instead of repeating one pattern. Learn each by name first, then let them blend: a Charleston here, a lead-in there, space in between.
Free comping by rule is graded on what you choose: one to four hits a bar, at least three different bar rhythms, never three identical bars in a row, and every anticipation sounding the next chord.
Real phrases with rests between, varied starts and lengths, tied to the form: organized and varied, never monotonous or random.
Siskind’s rubric hears phrasing on a scale: monotonous, organized, varied, random. The two ends don’t work.
Start over a drone: an open 5th in the left hand, short melodies on the major scale, with rests.
Play one, rest one: a bar of melody, a bar of silence. Then play two, rest two.
Then trade with yourself: the right hand asks, the left hand answers.
The result now shows your phrasing: organized or varied is the goal; monotonous or random gets a tip.
Note choice has its own scale: bland, colourful, arbitrary. Arpeggios with chromatic neighbours move a bland line toward colour.
Every improvised take now shows its phrasing and note choice under the result.
Hear an organized line: two short phrases, a breath between them, the second answering the first.
A common mistake is the endless line with no rests: it sounds monotonous however good the notes are. Breathe, as a singer would.
Recap: real phrases, rests between them, varied starts and lengths, tied to the form; and notes that are colourful, not bland or arbitrary.

Where it lives: the clearest improvisers phrase like singers — a line, a breath, a reply. Siskind built his evaluation rubric for teachers around exactly this, and the app now checks it on every improvised take.
Over the drone, set a phrase timer in your head: two bars of melody, two bars of listening. Then let the lengths vary — one bar, three bars — while the rests stay real.
You improvise; each rule card checks one thing in what you play: a guide tone on each change, an approach, Barry Harris’s rules, an enclosure, a pivot.
Hi {name}! Here nothing is written. You improvise over the form, and the cards say what must be in your line.
Guide tone on each change: on beat 1 of every new chord, its 3rd or 7th. F over D minor, B over G7, E over C.
Approach each chord: the first chord tone of a new chord comes from a half step away.
Barry Harris’s rules: chord tones on the beats, scale tones between, or a half step into the next note.
Your turn. The band plays the form; the result shows each card with how many times you kept it. Start slow.
Enclosure cards ask for one type at least once every four bars: above then below, below then above, the scale step above, the bebop enclosure, the delayed resolution.
The pivot card: a chord tone on top, a drop of a 6th to the next chord tone, then the climb. C, E, G, B.
The lick card listens for one of the licks of the library, in any key, over the chord it belongs to. Learn it in the lick trainer first, then bring it here.
Triad pairs and superimposed pentatonics change the colour: over C major 7, D and E minor triads give the lydian sound; G major pentatonic sounds 5, 6, 7, 9 and 3.
A card is kept when enough of your notes obey it: most cards ask for four in five, the enclosures and the pivot for three of every four windows of four bars.
Keep the line inside the changes too: every note in the chord’s scale, or a half step into the next note. And play in every bar, at least two notes.
Piano: the left hand comps written shells or rootless voicings, the right hand improvises under the cards. Guitar: a bar of chords, a bar of line. Bass: a bar of walking, a bar of fill.
Hi {name}! Now you are the band and the soloist. The comping is written and graded note for note.
On the piano the split is middle C: everything above it is your line, checked by the cards.
Shells are the root with the 3rd or the 7th; rootless voicings leave the root to the bass and keep 3, 5, 7 and 9.
On guitar and bass the bars take turns: comp or walk one bar, play a line the next. The comping bars are written; the line bars are yours.
Your turn. Start slower than you think: the left hand must not wait for the right.
Why it matters: alone on the bandstand, a pianist or guitarist is the whole rhythm section. The comping keeps the form; the line tells the story.
Keep the comping short and low: a hit on each chord, under middle C, so it never covers the line.
Let the line breathe where the comping moves: a new chord in the left hand is a good moment for a guide tone in the right.
On guitar, change position as little as you can between the chord bar and the line bar: the line starts where the chord shape lies.
On bass, the fill ends on a chord tone of the next bar’s chord, so the walk that follows starts at home.

How it is graded: the written comping is checked note for note, like any voicing drill. Your line is checked by the level’s cards, and each card shows how many times you kept it, so you can see which part slipped when the tempo went up.
Build a chorus bar by bar from vocabulary cells and licks, check it against the rules, then play it note for note: free time first, then up the tempo ladder, in every key.
Hi {name}! Choose a cell for every bar: arpeggio, scale line, enclosure, guide tones, pivot, approach, a rest, or a lick.
The check under the grid counts the bars that start on a chord tone and the changes you reach by a step.
A scale line puts chord tones on the beats and scale tones between them, like this line down over G7.
An enclosure aims at the next chord: above, below, then its 3rd on beat 1. A pivot drops from the top note and climbs.
Save it, then play it: first in free time, the notes only, then in time up the tempo ladder. It moves to every key with the level.
Why write a solo: the vocabulary you drilled becomes a chorus you own. Once it sits, you can improvise the next chorus around it.
Vary the cells: two scale lines in a row sound like an exercise; an arpeggio, then an enclosure, then space, sounds like a phrase.
A rest is a cell too. One empty bar in four lets the band answer and gives the next phrase a start.
Licks borrowed into a bar move to the bar’s chord: a C7 lick becomes an F7 lick in bar 2 of the blues.
The check is a guide, not a wall: a bar that starts off the chord on purpose, an anticipation, is fine if you hear it.
When the chorus sits at tempo in every key, play it once more and then improvise a second chorus right after it, using the same cells. That is how written vocabulary turns into your own playing.
The church sound: IV to I again and again, triads rocking through their inversions, and bass walk-ups into the next chord.
Hi {name}! Gospel lives on the plagal move, four to one. Over a held C in the bass, the right hand rocks between C and F with the C on top.
Gospel players repeat that move through whole sections, not only at the end of a phrase.
Then rock it up the keyboard: root position, first inversion, second inversion, the top voice moving by step. Here C rocks to D minor in each position.
The walk-up: the bass climbs one, two, three, four, under C, B flat over D, C over E, and lands on F major seven.
The one thing to watch: keep the hands close and move each voice the shortest way. Free time first, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys.
The minor plagal: four, four minor, one. Listen to the inner voice: the sixth falls to the flat sixth, then to the fifth.
The gospel sus dominant is simply the four chord over the fifth: F over G. When the sus resolves, only the fourth falls to the third.
Passing chords colour the way: a chromatic dominant walk-up into four, one-six-two-five with an altered six, and a diminished chord between four and one over five.
Small slides make it sing: a grace note from a half step below into the third of each chord.
In melodies, gospel often avoids the seventh degree. Two gospel scales: one two three four five six, and one two flat three three five six. A tendency, not a rule: the seventh stays in the chords.
Slow gospel is often felt in twelve-eight: an octave in the bass on one and three, and the right hand repeating the triad on every triplet.
Recap: four to one again and again; rock through the inversions; walk the bass up; close hands, short moves.
Soul-jazz: the blues with added ii–Vs, comped with the Charleston in 3rds and 7ths. Funk: 16ths, the heavy "one", and one chord that lasts.
Hi {name}! Soul-jazz is jazz soaked in blues and gospel, the organ-trio sound of the sixties. Call and response sits at its heart.
The basic comp is the Charleston: beat one and the and of two, with just two notes, the third and the seventh.
The soul-jazz blues adds a two-five in bars four, eight, ten and twelve. Slow shuffles are central.
Funk turns the weight to the one: the first beat of the bar gets the heavy accent, with sixteenths moving underneath. Here a nine chord on every beat, muted strokes between.
The bass locks with it: the root on the one, an octave, dead notes between.
The one thing to watch: in funk the hand never stops moving, even through the rests. Free time first, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys.
Behind an organist, guitarists also comp in drop two, adding the flat nine, sharp nine or flat thirteen to the dominants.
Under the shuffle the bass walks, or plays the boogie figure: root, three, five, six, flat seven, six, five, three.
Funk often stays on one chord, or on a minor seventh and a related dominant. Players lean on dorian or mixolydian and the blues scale.
Funk chords are extended: minor elevenths, ninths, six-nines. Guitarists love the nine chord.
On the organ, loudness comes from the swell pedal, not the fingers, and the percussion speaks only on detached notes.
Soul-jazz solos grow from short repeated riffs moved through the chords, organ-style double stops, and the blues scale over the whole form. Play a phrase, leave space, then answer it.
Recap: the Charleston in guide tones over the blues with its two-fives; in funk, sixteenths, the one, and one chord that lasts.
Stride: bass on 1 and 3, a chord on 2 and 4. Boogie: one left-hand figure, eight to the bar. The bass and the parade drum: 1 and 3.
Hi {name}! Stride is the root of jazz piano. The left hand keeps four beats: a low bass note on one and three, a chord in the middle on two and four.
It took the oom-pah of ragtime and swung it, and the left hand strides further across the keys.
Boogie-woogie is eight to the bar: one repeating left-hand figure moved with the chords of the blues. Here the walking line.
The bass plays in two: the root on one and the fifth on three, like a tuba in a brass band.
In a second-line parade the bass drum holds the march pulse on one and three, and the tresillo, three, three, two, is a building block.
The one thing to watch: the left hand leaps but never rushes. Free time first, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys.
Stride grows in steps: a single bass note, then octaves, then tenths, rolled if your hand is small, then a bass that walks on three.
Two classic progressions: one, six seven, two seven, five seven, a chain of dominants; and four, sharp four diminished, one over five.
Boogie has three left-hand figures here: the five-six shuffle, the walking line, and broken octaves.
The second-line feel sits between straight and swung: measured long to short, about four to three.
In a parade the snare improvises off the march beat. Here you play the bass drum; the snare is for later, with a teacher.
Ragtime is the root: the same oom-pah left hand, played in straight eighths. Stride took it and swung it. Listen for the difference: straight is even, swung is long, then short.
Recap: stride, bass on one and three and chords between; boogie, one figure eight to the bar; the bass and the parade drum in two.
Count the 8ths in groups of two and three; comp on the group starts; change chords on a group boundary.
Hi {name}! Jazz borrows odd meters and feels them in straight eighths, grouped in twos and threes. Seven-eight here is two, two, three.
Nine-eight as two, two, two, three: the long group comes last and limps a little.
Comping marks the group starts. Here shells, the third and the seventh, on every group of seven-eight over D minor and G.
Then thin it out: only the first and the last group, then the next chord an eighth early. Change chords on a group boundary.
The one thing to watch: say the groups out loud while you play. Free time first, then the tempo ladder, in all twelve keys.
Count with numbers that restart on every group: one two, one two, one two three. Or the syllables ta-ka, ta-ka, ta-ki-ta.
A four-bar nine-eight cycle: three bars of two, two, two, three, then one bar of three, three, three.
The harmony follows the groups: two minor on the first groups, five on the rest, so the change falls where the long group begins.
Rotate the same seven eighths, two two three, three two two, two three two, so no grouping feels strange.
This stays a touch inside jazz. The hijaz colour lives in Improvise, as a scale option on a dominant that resolves to minor.
Practise in steps: clap only the group starts over an eighth-note click, then only the long group. Then the left hand on the group starts while the right hand plays every eighth.
Recap: straight eighths in groups; comp on the group starts; change chords on a group boundary.
An EQ boost makes one band of frequencies stick out: lows sound boomy, mids nasal or honky, highs hissy and bright.
Hi {name}! This hiss is pink noise: every frequency at once, evenly spread. It is the perfect test sound for your ears.
Now we boost the lows. Listen for a darker, rounder rumble, like the sound behind a wall.
A boost in the middle sounds nasal, a bit like talking through a phone or a tube.
A boost in the highs adds hiss and air, like steam or rain on a window.
Both versions always play at the same loudness, so only the color tells you. Ask yourself: boomy, nasal or hissy? That is low, middle or high. Take your time and play both again.

An equalizer raises or lowers chosen frequency bands. A parametric band has three controls: frequency (where), gain in decibels (how much), and Q (how wide). A high Q is a narrow spike; a low Q a broad hill.

A rough map of the spectrum: below 60 Hz sub, felt more than heard; 60 to 250 bass and weight; 250 to 500 the "mud" or boxiness; 500 to 2k the honk; 2k to 5k presence and bite; above 5k sizzle and air.
A shelf lifts everything above or below a point, like tilting a table. A high shelf adds air to the whole top end at once. Plain, then with a high shelf.
Cutting is often cleaner than boosting. Instead of adding highs to make a mix clear, take out some low mids around 300 Hz. Plain, then with that cut.
Engineers find problems with "boost and sweep": boost a narrow band hard, move it until the ugly ringing jumps out, then cut there. Here is a boost at 300 Hz, 1 kHz and 5 kHz on a voice.
The loudness trap: a louder version almost always sounds "better". That is why every comparison here is level-matched. When you EQ your own mix, match the levels before you judge.
The common mistake is boosting everything until nothing stands out. Small moves of 2 or 3 dB go a long way. To keep: name the band — mud, honk, bite, air — then cut first and boost second.
A high-pass filter removes the lows (thin, small sound); a low-pass removes the highs (dark, muffled sound). The cut-off is where it starts.
Hi {name}! A filter does not add anything. It removes everything on one side of a frequency, called the cut-off.
A high-pass lets only the highs pass. The lows are gone, so the band sounds thin, like a small radio.
A low-pass is the opposite. The highs are gone, so the band sounds dark and muffled, like music from the next room.
Where is the cut-off? Move a low-pass down and more of the sound disappears. Here it is high, then low.
So: thin means high-pass, muffled means low-pass. Then listen for how much is left: a little or a lot. Producers use both filters all the time, to make room for every instrument in a mix.

The names say what passes through. A high-pass lets the highs through and removes the lows — so it is also called a low-cut. A low-pass is a high-cut. The two names describe the same filter from opposite sides.
A filter does not cut like a wall; it slopes. The slope is measured in decibels per octave — 12 or 24 dB is common. Resonance, or Q, adds a peak right at the cut-off. Gentle, then resonant.
Both together make a band-pass. Keep roughly 300 Hz to 3.4 kHz and a voice sounds like an old telephone line — a favorite effect for intros and bridges.
In mixing, a gentle high-pass on nearly everything except kick and bass clears out rumble nobody needs — on a vocal, often somewhere around 80 to 100 Hz. A low-pass pushes a sound further back.
In dance music, a build-up often sweeps a high-pass upward until the track sounds thin, and the drop slams the lows back in. Filtered, then full.
To estimate a cut-off, ask what is still there. A low-pass: what is the brightest thing you hear? A high-pass: what is the lowest? Compare it with your frequency landmarks.
The common mistake is mixing up the names. Say what passes, not what is cut. To keep: thin means the lows are gone, muffled means the highs are gone, and the slope and resonance shape the edge.
Each octave doubles the frequency: 250 Hz is a low hum, 1 kHz a clear beep, 4 kHz a piercing whistle. Learn a few landmarks.
Hi {name}! A pure tone has just one frequency, counted in hertz: vibrations per second. This is 1000 hertz, one kilohertz, the classic test beep.
Halve it twice and you get 250 hertz, a low hum. It is two octaves lower. Phone speakers barely play it, so use headphones.
Double one kilohertz twice: four kilohertz, a piercing whistle.
Here are all three in a row: hum, beep, whistle. Remember them as landmarks.
Engineers use this to find a ringing or harsh frequency fast. Start from the landmarks, then go step by step: is it higher or lower than the beep, and by how many octaves?
Hertz counts vibrations per second. Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and the top end drops with age. Each doubling is an octave, so the whole range is about ten octaves.
Musical pitch is frequency too. The tuning A, A4, is 440 Hz; the A an octave up is 880. Listen to the doubling.
Some real-world numbers: the low E of a bass guitar is about 41 Hz, of a guitar about 82 Hz, and the top C of a piano about 4186 Hz. Cymbals and breath live far above that.
A real note is not one frequency but a stack: the fundamental plus harmonics at 2, 3, 4 times and more. Timbre lives in those harmonics, which is why EQ above a note's pitch still changes it.
More landmarks to learn: 125 Hz a deep thump, 500 Hz body, 2 kHz a nasal edge, 8 kHz a thin sizzle. Each is two octaves from the next.
Your ears are most sensitive around 2 to 5 kHz. At the same level, a tone there sounds louder than one at 125 Hz, so judge by height, not by loudness.

The common mistake is an octave error: pure tones are hard to place, and 1 kHz and 2 kHz can feel alike. Decide the octave first, then fine-tune. To keep: doubling is an octave, and four landmarks cover the map.
Reverb is the room ringing after the sound: short in a small room, long in a cathedral. Delay is a clear repeat, timed to the beat.
Hi {name}! These drums are dry: no room at all. Every hit stops dead.
Now in a small room. A short ring follows each hit.
And in a cathedral. The ring lasts for seconds, and hits blur together.
A delay is different: a clean copy of the sound, repeated in time. Here the echo comes an eighth note later.

Listen to the tail after the sound stops: its length tells you the size of the room. For a delay, tap the beat with your foot and notice where the echo lands: halfway to the next beat is an eighth note, on the next beat is a quarter note. A gap between the hit and the start of the reverb is called pre-delay.

Reverb is thousands of reflections. The first few, the early reflections, tell your ear the shape and size of the room; then they blur into a smooth tail. Decay time is how long that tail takes to fade by 60 dB.
Pre-delay is the gap before the reverb starts. In a big hall the walls are far away, so the first reflections arrive later. A little pre-delay also keeps a voice clear in front of its own reverb.
The wet/dry mix sets the distance. Little reverb puts a sound close to you; a lot pushes it to the back of the room. Close, then far.
Delay comes in flavors. Slapback is one quick repeat, about a tenth of a second, the sound of 1950s rockabilly vocals. Longer delays with feedback repeat and fade.
Delays are usually timed to the song. A quarter note lasts 60,000 divided by the BPM, in milliseconds: 500 ms at 120 BPM, so an eighth is 250 and a dotted eighth 375.
To tell them apart, listen after the sound stops. Separate, countable copies mean delay; a smooth wash with no distinct repeats means reverb.

The common mistake is too much reverb: every track gets a big room and the mix turns to mud. Use one or two shared spaces. To keep: decay is size, pre-delay is distance to the walls, mix is how far back.
