Pan places a sound between the left and right speakers; width is how far a stereo mix spreads. You need headphones to hear both.
Hi {name}! Put your headphones on. This sound is panned to the left.
Now to the right, and then back in the center, where it seems to sit inside your head.
A mix is a stage. This band is in mono: everything stands in one spot in the middle.
The same band, wide: the keys and the cymbals spread out to the sides and the space opens up.
To find a panned instrument, close your eyes and point to where it is. Your ears already know. For width, listen to the edges: does the sound reach all the way to your ears, or stay in the middle?
Pan works by level: send more of a sound to one speaker and it appears on that side. Equal in both and it seems to float in the middle — the "phantom center". Hard left, then just slightly left.
Your ears locate sounds by small differences between them, in level and in arrival time. Headphones exaggerate panning and put the center inside your head; speakers put it in front of you.
A common mix layout: kick, snare, bass and lead vocal in the center; guitars, keys and backing vocals out to the sides. Here the keys move to the left while drums and bass stay in the middle.
Width is the difference between left and right. When both are identical the sound is mono; the more they differ, the wider it gets. Mono, normal, wide.
Many listeners hear in mono: one phone speaker, a club system, a shop ceiling. Very wide tricks can thin out or vanish there, so engineers check every mix in mono too.
To hear width, compare the edges with the middle. If the sound reaches your ears from the sides, it is wide; if it stays in one spot between them, it is narrow.

The common mistake is making everything wide, which leaves no focus. Width comes from contrast: a solid center makes the sides feel wider. To keep: pan places, width spreads, and the center holds the song.
A compressor turns the loud hits down, so the quiet parts come up: punchy or flat. Drive adds grit; fuzz turns it into a buzz.
Hi {name}! These are raw drums. Notice how the hits jump out and the space between them is quiet.
Now heavily compressed, at the same loudness. The hits are squashed and the tails between them come up.
Attack is how fast the compressor grabs. Slow attack lets the start of each hit punch through.
Drive adds grit, and fuzz pushes it into a buzzing square sound. Clean first, then fuzz.
In these exercises loudness never gives the answer away, except when we ask which one is louder. Then listen closely: one or two decibels is a small but real step.

Dynamic range is the distance between the loudest and quietest moments. A compressor shrinks it: above the threshold, the ratio decides how much gets through. At 4:1, 8 dB over the threshold comes out as 2 dB over.
Gentle and heavy: a low ratio smooths, a high ratio flattens. Then make-up gain brings the level back up. Here is 2:1, then 10:1, at the same loudness.
Attack decides the punch. A fast attack grabs the very start of each hit and dulls it; a slower one lets the click through and squeezes only the body. Fast, then slow.
Release is how fast it lets go. Very fast release can make the background swell up between hits — "pumping". Some styles use it on purpose; elsewhere it is a fault.
A limiter is a compressor with a very high ratio and a ceiling no peak may pass. Mastering uses it to make a track loud — too much, and the music loses its life.
Distortion is a family, from subtle to wild: saturation adds warmth, overdrive grit, fuzz a buzzing square edge. All of them add harmonics, so listen for new fizz on top. Light, medium, full.
Level itself: about 1 dB is close to the smallest change most people notice. Here pink noise, then the same 2 dB louder. Louder almost always sounds better, so compare at equal level.

The common mistake is over-compressing until every hit is the same size. To keep: threshold says when, ratio how much, attack keeps or kills the punch, release sets the breathing; drive adds harmonics.
Speed is accuracy repeated, one small step at a time. Outside lines leave the key on purpose and always find the way back.
Each speed item starts in free time, then on a slow click, then climbs the tempo ladder towards concert tempo.
Keep the pick close to the strings and the fretting fingers low. Tension stops you long before the tempo does.
Outside by a half step: the minor pentatonic, the same shape a half step higher, then home again to the root.
Over G7 the major triads on D flat and E flat give the altered colours. Then the line resolves to C.
A take counts only when every note is in time, in every key. Outside sounds right only when the way back is clear. Your turn.
Why small steps: the hand learns a motion at the speed it practices. Ten clean takes a few clicks up beat one messy take far up.
Three notes a string gives an even group for 16ths and triplets alike. Sweeps let one stroke cross several strings, one note each.
Four notes a string stretches the hand across five or six frets. Hammer up, pull down, and pick only once on each string.
The altered triad pair comes from the melodic minor a half step above the dominant. Its two triads hold every altered tension between them.
A common mistake is staying outside too long. One bar out, one bar in: the ear needs the home key to hear the tension.
Where it lives: fusion players lean on side-slips and triad pairs, rock and metal players on sweeps and three notes a string, all of it built slowly on a click.
Recap: free time, then the ladder; clean before fast; out with a plan and back on a chord tone.
One guitar plays a trio: the thumb walks the bass, the fingers add shells and the melody on top. An arrangement is a plan for a whole tune.
First the walking line alone: the root on each chord, chord tones between, a half step into the next root.
Then the shell above it, short, on the "and" of 2 and 4, the comping a pianist would play.
In chord-melody the melody stays on top. Under it go drop 2 chords, a walking bass, or a passing diminished.
An arrangement plans the whole tune: an intro from the last four bars, the chorus, a reharmonised chorus, a tag.
A ballad chorus is played rubato: the time is yours and the notes are measured. Keep the bass even, the chords lighter. Your turn.
Why the shell sits on the "and": the bass owns the beat. A chord on the off-beat answers it, like a pianist answering a bass player.
The thumb plays the bass on strings six and five; the fingers take the guide tones on strings four to two. Keep the hand in one position.
Reharmonising a chorus: tritone substitutions, extra two-fives, a backdoor dominant. The melody stays the same while the colours change under it.
The tag repeats the last two bars before the final chord, so the ending is felt coming, not stumbled into.
A common mistake is a bass that rushes under a busy melody. Practice the bass and the melody alone first, then together, slowly.
Where it lives: solo jazz guitarists play whole sets this way, the bass walking under shells and the melody, with an intro and a tag around every tune.
Recap: bass on the beat, shells on the "and", the melody on top, and a plan from the intro to the tag.
Open rolls are doubles plus a release; ratamacues are drags leading into an accent. Every sticking is its own motion — make each one sound even.
A thirteen-stroke roll: six doubles, R R L L three times, then one accented single on the next eighth.
The buzz roll presses each stroke into the head. The app measures the pulse of your hands; the bounces between are yours.
A double ratamacue: two drags, then three strokes, the last one accented on the beat.
Stickings: four notes have fourteen orders of R and L. One sticking a bar, four bars a take, then faster.
Grace notes need the kit over MIDI: the flam or drag is soft and comes just before the main stroke. Start slowly. Your turn.
Count the strokes, not the time: five, seven, nine, ten, eleven, thirteen, fifteen, seventeen. The odd ones end on one accented single.
The ten-stroke roll ends with two singles, the last accented. That is why it feels different from the eleven.
The pataflafla puts flams on the first and fourth notes: flam R, L, R, flam L. Keep the flams the same width every time.
The triple paradiddle is three alternating pairs and a double: R L R L R L R R, then the same from the left.
A common mistake is a weak second stroke in the doubles. The app compares the two; aim for the second as strong as the first.
Where it lives: marching and concert snare drummers use every rudiment here, and kit players move them around the toms for fills and solos.
Recap: count the strokes, keep the release on the eighth, the graces soft and close, every sticking even.
One written line, many grooves. In jazz the ride and the foot never change while snare and kick move; in linear funk no two limbs play together.
Read one syncopated line, and play it on the kick under a rock beat, then as band hits with the crash.
In jazz the upbeat eighth falls on the last note of the triplet. Long notes go to the kick, short ones to the snare.
Spang, spang-a-lang on the ride with the foot on 2 and 4. The snare moves through the triplet, one figure a bar.
Linear funk: hat, snare and kick take turns on the 16ths. A group of three across the bar shifts against the beat.
The app checks that nothing in a linear groove sounds together, and that the ride keeps swinging. Your turn.
Why read one line many ways: a chart rarely tells a drummer what to play. It gives the rhythm, and the style decides the drums.
In funk the line goes on the kick under 16th hats, with ghost notes on the snare between the backbeats.
The independence ladder adds one limb at a time: snare figures, kick figures, both, then the foot on every beat.
Displaced grooves move the whole pattern a 16th later each bar. The backbeat lands on e, then and, then a.
A common mistake is the ride stiffening when the left hand gets busy. If it does, slow down: the time comes first.
Where it lives: big-band drummers read lines like these every night, and funk drummers build whole songs from linear patterns and ghost notes.
Recap: one line, five interpretations; the ride and the foot stay put; in linear grooves, one limb at a time.
Brushes: the left hand sweeps, the right hand taps the time. Soloing: count the form and land the next 1 with the crash and kick.
In a brushes ballad the left hand sweeps one slow circle a beat, and the right taps on 2 and 4.
The taps are measured: timing, swing and accents. The sweep is yours, shown but not scored.
Odd meters at tempo: 7/8 counted as 2 plus 2 plus 3. The hat accents mark each group.
Trading fours: four bars of time, four bars of solo while the band lays out. Play anything, but never lose the bar line.
Land each time section with a crash and the kick on its first beat, within a few milliseconds. Keep counting. Your turn.
Why the sweep is not scored: to a microphone it is noise, and many kits send no brush data at all.
Up-tempo brushes flatten into straight eighths: the right hand taps every eighth and the sweep becomes a short stroke.
In 11/8 and 13/8 the groups of three and two change the feel. Say the groups out loud before you play.
A chorus solo keeps the band playing. The form is your map: land each four-bar phrase, and catch the set-up hits at the end.
A common mistake is playing so much in the solo bars that the count slips. Leave space; rests are part of a solo.
Where it lives: in a jazz club the drummer trades fours with the soloists, plays brushes on the ballads and keeps the form for the whole band.
Recap: tap the time, sweep for the sound; count the groups; know the form and land it.
Hear the next note before you sing it. Diminished stacks minor 3rds, augmented major 3rds; a leap arrives, it never slides.
Diminished: C, E flat, G flat, two minor thirds. Augmented: C, E, G sharp, two major thirds.
A ninth is an octave and a step. Find the octave in your ear first, then the step above it.
A fast run is many small targets. Sing it slowly in tune first, then on the click, then faster.
Every session moves to a new key, so you learn the shapes, not the notes. All twelve keys come round.
The top of the range: just above your highest note, steady and unforced, then inside a phrase. Stop if it hurts. Breathe low. Your turn.
Why diminished feels unstable: it has no perfect fifth, and every note is a minor third from the next. It wants to resolve a half step.
Half-diminished keeps the minor third and the diminished fifth, but its seventh is a whole step below the octave.
Tritones and chromatic leaps need a reference. Think of a nearby simple interval, then bend your target from it.
In a chromatic run every step is a half step. Keep the vowel the same and let the pitch move, not the jaw.
A common mistake is pushing for the top note. Volume is not height: a light, steady note is the goal.
Where it lives: jazz singers outline diminished chords in bebop lines, soul and gospel singers run fast melismas, and every singer works the top of the range.
Recap: hear it first, shapes not notes, slow before fast, and the top floor light and steady.
Read four bars over the band, vary them, then improvise on their chords. Hold your written part while another plays, and sing each style its own way.
Quick study, first take: sing the four bars as written. The melody is never played to you; read it.
Second take: keep the long notes and move the rhythm. Third take: your own line over the same chords, landing on chord tones.
One part from the score: you sing the top line, the app plays the bottom one with you, in thirds and sixths.
Styles: pop and R&B sit off the beat, soul bends the third, musical theatre builds a phrase to its top note.
Scat over rhythm changes at tempo: land a chord tone on each new chord. Use headphones for the score parts if you can. Your turn.
Why read, vary, improvise: it is the RSL quick study. It shows you can read, interpret and create on the same music in a few minutes.
When you vary, keep the shape of the phrase. Move notes earlier or later, add a neighbour, but land where the original lands.
Holding a part: listen to the other voice as a partner, not a guide. If you drift to its notes, sing your line alone first.
The middle of three parts is the hardest: notes above and below pull at you. Find your first note against the bass.
A common mistake in style songs is singing every style the same. Listen to where the accents fall and where the voice bends.
Where it lives: session singers read a part at sight, backing singers hold harmonies against the lead, and good singers change their sound for each style.
Recap: read, vary, create; hold your part; give each style its own time and colour.
Hear the bass under two voices; keep a phrase in your ear after one hearing; and name several features of one excerpt at once.
Three voices, the top one written. Hum the lowest while it plays, then write it in the bass clef.
Root position moves the bass by fourths and fifths; an inversion lets it move by step.
One hearing: the phrase plays once, and Repeat waits until you answer. Fix the first note, the shape, the last note.
Describe the piece: smooth or detached? Loud, soft, or changing? Steady, faster, or slower? Major or minor?
Choose the description that gets every feature right. Each right feature earns credit even when one is wrong. Trust your ear, then write it calmly. Your turn.
Why the lowest voice matters: it decides the chord and its inversion. ABRSM asks for it at grade eight.
To hear past the top voice, listen first for the cadence at the end: the bass falling a fifth to the tonic is easy to catch.
One hearing is how music meets you in a band: no rewind. Sing the phrase back in your head before you write anything.
For several features, listen once for each one: the loudness, then the note lengths, the pulse, the key, the ending.
A common mistake is judging the tempo by how busy the notes are. Tap the beat; faster means the taps get closer.
Where it lives: arrangers write bass lines they hear under a melody, band players learn tunes after one hearing, and examiners ask you to describe what you heard.
Recap: the bass under the voices, one hearing held in the ear, one feature at a time.

Twelve semitones in equal parts: 2 × 6 = tritone, 3 × 4 = augmented triad, 4 × 3 = diminished 7th, 6 × 2 = whole-tone scale. The size of a part is also how many transpositions there are: 6, 4, 3, 2. G7 and D♭7 share a tritone; lowering any note of a dim7 gives one of four dominants.
An octave holds twelve semitones. Split it into equal parts and you get the symmetric chords and scales.
Two parts of six semitones: the tritone. C up to F sharp, and F sharp up to C, are the same size.
Three parts of four: major thirds, the augmented triad. Four parts of three: minor thirds, the diminished seventh.
Six parts of two: whole tones, the whole-tone scale you already know.
Symmetric means few transpositions. Move a diminished seventh up a minor third and the same notes come back, so there are only three. Augmented triads: four. Whole-tone scales: two. Tritones: six.
In harmony: G7 and D flat 7 share one tritone, B and F. That is the tritone substitution.
And lower any note of a diminished seventh a half step: you get a dominant seventh on the lowered note. B°7 gives G7, B flat 7, D flat 7 and E7.

Why the size of a part is the number of transpositions: move the chord by one part and it lands on its own notes. A diminished seventh on C, on C sharp and on D are all different; on E flat it is the one on C again.
Scales work the same way. There are two whole-tone scales, one on C and one on C sharp, and between them they hold all twelve notes.
The diminished scale alternates half and whole steps and repeats every minor third, so it has three versions too. Each holds two diminished sevenths.
The tritone substitution works because the 3rd and 7th stay: the B and F of G7 are the C flat and F of D flat 7. Both lead to C the same way, and their roots are a tritone apart too.
The four dominants of one diminished seventh have roots a minor third apart: G, B flat, D flat, E. The octave in four parts again, one level up.
Recap: twelve divided by the number of parts gives the interval, and the interval in semitones gives the number of versions. Six, four, three, two.

Three moves keep two notes of a triad and move the third by step. P: C ↔ Cm (the 3rd, a semitone). R: C ↔ Am (the 5th of major up a whole tone; the root of minor down one). L: C ↔ Em (the root of major down a semitone; the 5th of minor up one). P then L: C → Cm → A♭.
Two triads can share two notes. Move the third note by a step and you are on a new triad. There are three such moves: P, L and R.
P, parallel: C major to C minor. The root and fifth stay; the third moves down a semitone.
R, relative: C major to A minor. C and E stay; G moves up a whole tone to A.
L, leading tone: C major to E minor. E and G stay; C moves down a semitone to B.
Each move undoes itself. From A minor, R moves the root down a whole tone back to C major; from E minor, L moves the fifth up a semitone.
Moves chain. P then L: C, C minor, A flat. Two moves reach the chromatic mediants: C to E is L then P.

This is neo-Riemannian theory, named after the nineteenth-century theorist Hugo Riemann and developed by David Lewin and Richard Cohn. It describes chords moving by smooth voice leading, without asking which key you are in.
Alternate P and L from C: C, C minor, A flat, G sharp minor, E, E minor, and back to C. Six triads, all inside one augmented scale: the hexatonic cycle.
Alternate P and R: C, C minor, E flat, E flat minor, F sharp, F sharp minor, A, A minor. Eight triads inside one diminished scale: the octatonic cycle.
Alternate L and R and you pass through all twenty-four major and minor triads. On the Tonnetz, the grid of fifths and thirds, every triad is a triangle and every move flips it over one edge.
Chromatic mediants like C to A flat are a common sound in film scores: one note stays, the other two slide by step.
Recap: P keeps the root and fifth, R keeps the root and third of the major triad, L keeps its third and fifth. One note moves; two stay.

An interval and its inversion are one class (ic1 … ic6). Count the classes of every pair of notes: the interval vector. Major and minor triads <001110>, dim7 <004002>, augmented <000300>, whole-tone scale <060603>, major scale <254361>.
Any chord is a set of intervals. Count every pair of notes and you can read its colour on paper.
An interval and its inversion are one class: a fifth and a fourth are class 5, a major sixth and a minor third class 3. The tritone is class 6.
Six classes, so the count is six numbers: the interval vector. A major triad holds one minor third, one major third and one fifth: 0 0 1 1 1 0.
A minor triad has the same vector: the same intervals, upside down.
Symmetric chords show it at once. The diminished seventh: four minor thirds and two tritones, 0 0 4 0 0 2. The augmented triad: three major thirds, 0 0 0 3 0 0.
Class 1, a semitone or major 7th, rubs; class 6, the tritone, is restless. Hear a major 7th chord, then a dominant 7th: the first holds the rub, the second the tritone.
Your turn: list the pairs, fold, count.
The vector comes from post-tonal set theory, as Allen Forte laid it out in 1973: it compares chords that share no notes. Sets with the same vector hold the same intervals, in any order.
The whole-tone scale: six whole tones, six major thirds, three tritones, 0 6 0 6 0 3. No semitones and no fifths: that is why it floats.
The major scale: 2 5 4 3 6 1. Six fifths and a single tritone, between degrees 4 and 7: the sound of a key.
A dominant 7th and a half-diminished 7th share one vector, 0 1 2 1 1 1: turn C7 upside down and you get D half-diminished.
Next step: the trichords topic names sets by their prime form, like [0,1,6]. The vector tells you what each of those sets sounds like inside.
Recap: take every pair of notes, fold each interval to its class from 1 to 6, and count. Semitones rub, tritones are restless, fifths settle.
A triad plus a seventh above the root: maj7 (major triad, major 7th), 7 (major triad, minor 7th), m7, ø7 and °7.
Stack one more third on a triad and you get a seventh chord: four notes.
Major triad, major seventh: maj7. Soft and dreamy.
Major triad, minor seventh: plain 7, the dominant. It wants to move.
Minor triad, minor seventh: m7. Mellow and relaxed.
Diminished triad: with a minor seventh it is ø7, with a diminished seventh °7.
The name comes from two choices: the triad, and the seventh above the root. A major seventh is eleven half steps, a minor seventh ten, a diminished seventh nine.
Stack thirds on every step of C major and you get Cmaj7, Dm7, Em7, Fmaj7, G7, Am7 and Bø7. Only the fifth step, G7, is a dominant seventh.
Why the dominant pulls: in G7, the third B and the seventh F are a tritone apart. B rises to C, F falls to E.
The diminished seventh lives in harmonic minor, on the raised seventh step. In C minor it is B, D, F, A-flat, and it leads home to C minor.
On a chart: maj7 or a triangle for the major seventh; a plain 7 always means the dominant; m7; ø7, also written m7 flat 5; °7, also written dim7.
A common mistake: hearing m7 as a dominant because both have the minor seventh. Listen to the third first: bright means maj7 or 7, dark means m7, ø7 or °7. Then the top.
To keep: a triad plus a seventh. Five colours: maj7, 7, m7, ø7 and °7.
A chord on every step of the scale, named by its step: I ii iii IV V vi vii°. Capital = major, small = minor. V7 pulls home to I.
Build a chord on every note of the scale, using only the scale’s notes.
Name each chord by its step, in Roman numerals, from one to seven.
Capital letters are major chords: I, IV and V. In C: C, F and G.
Small letters are minor: ii, iii and vi. vii° is diminished.
ii = Dm · iii = Em · vi = Am · vii° = B°
Add a seventh to V and you get V7. It pulls hardest to I.
Numbers, not names: I, IV, V, I sounds the same in every key.
Why these colours? Stack thirds from each note with C major’s notes only. C, E, G is major; D, F, A is minor; B, D, F is diminished.
I, IV and V hold all seven notes of the scale between them. That is why three chords can harmonise so many simple songs.
The pop progression I, V, vi, IV — in C: C, G, A minor, F.
ii often comes before V. ii, V, I in C is D minor, G7, C — the move jazz is built on.
vi is the relative minor of I: A minor shares every note with C major. That is why vi can stand in for I.
Nashville numbers are the same idea in plain digits: 1, 4, 5, and 6m for the minor six.
To keep: the numeral is the step of the root, the case is the colour, and V7 pulls home to I.
Major: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. Natural minor lowers 3, 6 and 7. Its relative major shares its notes. Harmonic minor raises the 7th back, so V7 can pull home.
A major scale climbs in whole and half steps: W W H W W W H.
The half steps sit between 3 and 4, and 7 and 8. In C: E–F, B–C.
Natural minor lowers three steps: 3, 6 and 7. Here is C minor.
A minor uses C major’s notes, from A. It is C’s relative minor.
Harmonic minor raises the seventh again. Now V is major, and V7 pulls home.
A whole step is two half steps: C to D skips the black key between them. A half step is the very next key: E to F, with no key between.
Every major key has a relative minor on its sixth step, three half steps below: G major and E minor share one sharp, F major and D minor one flat.
The parallel minor is something else: the same tonic with other notes. C major and C minor share C, but three steps differ.
Why harmonic minor? In natural minor, chord v is minor and the seventh step is a whole step below home. Raise it and the leading tone pulls up to the tonic, and V becomes major.
The raised seventh leaves a gap of three half steps between the sixth and seventh steps: F to G-sharp in A minor. That gap gives harmonic minor its special sound.
A common mistake: thinking minor only changes the third. In natural minor the sixth and seventh are lower too. Sing up from the tonic and listen at the top.
To keep: major is W W H W W W H. Natural minor lowers 3, 6 and 7. Harmonic minor raises 7 again.
A mode is the major scale from another step. On one tonic, each is major or minor with one note changed: Lydian ♯4, Mixolydian ♭7, Dorian 6, Phrygian ♭2.
Play C major’s notes, but start and end on D. Same notes, a new home.
Compare on one tonic: each mode is major or minor with one note changed.
Mixolydian is major with a lowered seventh. Bluesy, rock.
Lydian is major with a raised fourth. Bright, floating.
Dorian is natural minor with a major sixth. Minor, but warm.
Phrygian is natural minor with a lowered second. Dark, with a Spanish edge.
Each mode starts on a different step of the major scale: Ionian on 1, Dorian on 2, Phrygian on 3, Lydian on 4, Mixolydian on 5, Aeolian on 6, Locrian on 7.
1 Ionian · 2 Dorian · 3 Phrygian · 4 Lydian · 5 Mixolydian · 6 Aeolian · 7 Locrian
Ionian is plain major and Aeolian is natural minor. Locrian, with a lowered second and fifth, is rarely used as a home.
From brightest to darkest: Lydian, Ionian, Mixolydian, Dorian, Aeolian, Phrygian, Locrian. Each one lowers one more note than the one before.
To find a mode’s notes, find its parent major scale. D Dorian comes from C major, because D is C’s second step. G Mixolydian comes from C too: G is its fifth step.
A listening tip: keep the tonic sounding, play the scale, and wait for the one note that differs from plain major or minor. That note is the colour.
In music: modal jazz often sits on Dorian, and many rock and folk tunes lean on Mixolydian’s flat seventh.
To keep: same notes, another home. Lydian sharp four, Mixolydian flat seven, Dorian natural six, Phrygian flat two.
Past the octave the numbers go on: a 9th is a 2nd plus an octave, a 10th a 3rd, an 11th a 4th, a 12th a 5th, a 13th a 6th. Take away seven to find the simple interval.
Past the octave, the numbers keep counting: eight, then nine, then ten.
A ninth is a second plus an octave: C to the D above the next C.
A tenth is a third plus an octave. Wide, but it still sounds sweet.
Take away seven for the simple interval: 9 is 2, 11 is 4, 13 is 6.
Chords use them on top: a ninth above a seventh chord adds colour.
Chords are stacked in thirds: 1, 3, 5, 7. Keep stacking and the next thirds are 9, 11 and 13. After 13 comes the root again, two octaves up.
Why call it a ninth and not a second? Above the seventh it sits on top of the chord as a colour, not crowded against the root.
The quality stays: a major second becomes a major ninth, a minor third a minor tenth, a perfect fifth a perfect twelfth.
A listening tip: sing the top note an octave lower, name the simple interval, then add seven.
A common mistake: adding eight. The octave note is counted only once, so a second plus an octave is a ninth, not a tenth.
On jazz charts: C9, F13, Cmaj7 sharp 11. The numbers are these wide intervals, counted up from the root.
To keep: past the octave, take away seven. Nine is two, eleven is four, thirteen is six, and the quality stays.
C6 = C E G A, calm, the jazz home. B°7 = B D F A♭, minor thirds only, tense. They share no note; together they make the 8-note C 6th-diminished scale.
A major triad plus the sixth: C6 is C, E, G, A. The jazz home.
A diminished seventh stacks only minor thirds: B, D, F, A-flat. Tense.
They share no note. Take turns: rest, tension, rest.
Their eight notes together make the C sixth-diminished scale.
Each scale note gets its chord: 6, diminished, 6, diminished.
There are only three diminished seventh chords, and each has four names a minor third apart. B°7 is also D°7, F°7 and A-flat°7: the same four notes.
The other two: C°7 is C, E-flat, G-flat, A; D-flat°7 is D-flat, E, G, B-flat.
Lower any one note of a diminished seventh a half step and you get a dominant seventh on that note. In B°7, lower A-flat to G: B, D, F, G is G7.
Make the 6 chord minor, C, E-flat, G, A, and keep B°7: that is the minor sixth-diminished scale. Same idea, a darker home.
At the piano: C6 in root position, then the next scale note up in the bass with B°7 above it, then C6 in first inversion. Climb the scale chord by chord, 6 and diminished taking turns.
Barry Harris taught these scales first as a chording tool: harmony for every note of a line, built from two chords.
To keep: C6 is home, B°7 is motion, and their eight notes make one scale.
Jazz eighths swing, long–short. The blues is 12 bars on I7, IV7 and V7. And ii–V–I is the move that brings a tune home.
Jazz eighths swing: long–short, long–short. First straight, then swung.
The blues is jazz’s home form: twelve bars, three chords.
Four bars of I7, two of IV7, two of I7, then V7, IV7, I7.
I7 I7 I7 I7 | IV7 IV7 I7 I7 | V7 IV7 I7 V7
The most common move in jazz: ii–V–I. In C: D minor 7, G7, C major 7.
ii and V lean forward; I is home. Tunes chain ii–Vs through many keys.
Swung eighths are played roughly like the first and last notes of a triplet, about two to one. At fast tempos they even out.
The basic 12-bar blues: I7 for four bars, often with IV7 in bar 2, IV7 for two, I7 for two, then V7, IV7, I7, and V7 to go round again.
In a blues every chord is a dominant seventh, even the I. That is a big part of the blues sound.
The jazz blues adds ii–Vs: bar 4 leads to IV with a ii–V, and bars 9 and 10 become ii and V of the key.
A lead sheet gives the melody and the chord symbols. The players make up the rest: the comping, the walking bass line, the solos over the form.
A listening tip: count the blues in groups of four bars, and follow the bass to hear when I, IV and V arrive.
Twelve bars in three groups of four: IV arrives at bar 5, V at bar 9, home at bar 11. The bass tells you which chord you are on. A jazz blues adds ii–Vs.
A blues chorus is twelve bars: three lines of four.
Bar 5 is the first big change: the IV chord arrives.
Bar 9 brings V, the strongest pull. Bar 11 is home.
Lost? Follow the bass: its note names the chord, I, IV or V.
A jazz blues keeps the form but adds ii–Vs and moves faster.
The blues uses dominant sevenths on I, IV and V. In F: F7, B-flat 7 and C7.
Many blues go to IV already in bar 2 and come back in bar 3. Players call it the quick change. The big IV in bar 5 is still the landmark.
Bar 12 often goes to V7: the turnaround that sends the band back to the top for the next chorus.
The minor blues has the same shape with minor chords: i for four bars, iv for two, i for two, then two dominants lead home.
In the jazz blues, bar 4 is a ii–V into IV, and bars 9 and 10 are ii and V. The form is the same; the chords move twice as often.
A common mistake: counting beats instead of bars. Count bar numbers on beat one only: one, two, three, four, then the IV.
To keep: bar 5 brings IV, bar 9 brings V, and bar 11 is home.
The same chord, spread out in different ways: close (inside an octave), drop 2 and drop 3 (a voice moved down an octave), shell (root, 3rd, 7th), rootless (3, 5, 7, 9), quartal (stacked 4ths).
Close: all four notes inside one octave. Compact.
Drop 2: the second note from the top drops an octave. Wider, smoother.
Drop 3: the third note from the top drops instead. Even wider.
Shell: just the root, the third and the seventh. A bare skeleton.
Rootless: 3, 5, 7 and 9. The bass player has the root.
Why drop 2? The close chord’s top voice stays the melody, and the dropped note opens space in the middle. It also lies well under the fingers on guitar.
A listening tip: hear the width first. Close sounds tight in the middle; drop 2 and drop 3 spread out, with a gap at the bottom.
The shell is the pianist’s left hand and the guitarist’s first jazz chord: the third and seventh say major or minor, dominant or not.
Quartal: notes stacked in fourths instead of thirds. Open and modern, as in modal jazz.
An upper structure puts a triad from the upper tensions over a dominant. A D major triad over C7 gives the 9, the sharp 11 and the 13.
To keep: close, drop 2, drop 3, shell, rootless, quartal. Same chord, different spacing. Listen for the width first, then for the root in the bass, and last for the top note.
close · drop 2 · drop 3 · shell · rootless · quartal
Find the key (where the tune rests), then the ii–Vs (a minor 7 and a dominant a 4th higher). Every ii–V points to its I, even in another key; every chord is home, on the way, or pulling home.
A lead sheet shows the melody and a chord symbol for every bar.
Find the key first: where does the tune rest? Usually the last chord.
Find the ii–Vs: a minor 7, then a dominant a fourth higher.
Each ii–V points to the chord after it, even in another key.
So every chord has a job: home, on the way, or pulling home.
I = home · ii = on the way · V = pull
A minor ii–V has a half-diminished ii and a dominant V that resolves to a minor I. In C minor: D half-diminished, G7, C minor.
Not every ii–V lands. Some move on to another ii–V instead: the tune keeps travelling before it comes home.
A dominant alone can point the same way. A7 in the key of C is not from the scale: it is the V of D minor, a secondary dominant.
The turnaround I, vi, ii, V fills the last bars and leads back to the top.
Analysts mark a ii–V with a bracket under the two chords, and an arrow from each dominant to where it resolves.
A common mistake: taking the first chord as the key. Many standards begin on ii or somewhere far away. Check the last bars and the key signature.
To keep: the key first, then the ii–Vs, then each chord’s job: home, on the way, or pulling home.
Other roads home: the backdoor iv–♭VII7–I, the tritone sub ii–♭II7–I, ii–Vs chained step by step, and Coltrane’s key centres a major third apart.
The plain road home: ii–V–I. D minor 7, G7, C major 7.
The backdoor: iv–flat VII7–I. F minor 7, B-flat 7, C. Home from below.
The tritone sub: D-flat 7 replaces G7. The bass slides down by half steps.
Chains: ii–Vs in a row, each one a step lower.
Coltrane cycles: key centres a major third apart, each reached by its own V7.
Why the tritone sub works: G7 and D-flat 7 share the same third and seventh, B and F, swapped. The tension is the same; only the bass changes.
The backdoor borrows from the minor key: iv is F minor and flat VII is B-flat, both from C minor. The B-flat 7 lands on C without the leading tone.
Chains can move down by whole steps, by half steps, or by minor thirds. Listen to the bass of each minor 7 chord to hear the step.
A dominant cycle drops the minor chords: III7, VI7, II7, V7, each dominant resolving to the next a fifth below.
John Coltrane built Giant Steps on centres a major third apart. Three keys divide the octave into equal parts, and each is reached by its own dominant.
A listening tip: follow the bass. Up a fourth is a ii–V; a half step down is the tritone sub; a whole step up into I is the backdoor.
Four voices, one chord at a time. Name each chord by its numeral: start from the bass (root position or ⁶), then ask what it does — rest, move away, or pull home.
A chorale: four voices, one chord at a time. Name each by its numeral.
Start from the bass. Bass on the root: root position.
Bass on the third: first inversion, written with a small 6.
Then ask its job: rest is I, away is IV or ii, pulling home is V.
The cadential six-four: I with its fifth in the bass, just before V. It decorates V.
Bass on the fifth is second inversion, written six-four. Outside the cadence it is rare in chorales: mostly passing or over a held bass.
V7 has four inversions: root position 7, then six-five with the third in the bass, four-three with the fifth, four-two with the seventh.
vi often follows V in place of I: the deceptive cadence. The bass climbs a step, from 5 to 6, instead of falling home.
In a minor key the numerals change case: i, ii°, III, iv, V, VI. V is major because of the raised seventh, the leading tone.
A listening tip: sing the bass line first. Its shape tells you the inversions, and a bass falling five to one tells you the cadence.
To keep: bass first for the inversion, then the chord’s job for its numeral: rest, move away, or pull home. The last two chords name the cadence, and the bass line names the inversions.
Keep stacking thirds past the 7th: 9, 11, 13. Alter them (♭9 ♯9 ♯11 ♭13) for spice, or swap the 3 for a 4 for sus.
Hey {name}! A seventh chord is a stack of thirds: 1, 3, 5, 7. Keep stacking thirds and you reach 9, 11 and 13 — the extensions.
A 9 is really the 2, an octave up; a 13 is the 6, up high. Same G7, three tops: plain 7, then 9, then 13.
Dominant chords love spice. Lower the 9 for ♭9, dark and tense; raise it for ♯9, the crunchy blues sound.
Raise the 11 for ♯11, a shimmering tritone above the root. Lower the 13 for ♭13, a dark pull downward.
Major chords wear softer colors: maj7, maj9, the sparkling Lydian maj7♯11, and 6/9, which has no seventh at all.
sus4 swaps the 3 for a 4, so the chord hangs in the air; 7sus4 adds the 7. add9 keeps the 3 and adds a 9, no seventh. And 7alt piles ♯9 and ♭13 onto a dominant.
Your turn! I play a chord together, then note by note upward. Listen to the top note and the color, and pick its name.
Stack thirds on G all the way up: G, B, D, F, then A, C, E. That is G13, and it holds all seven letters of the scale. Nobody plays all seven at once; players choose a few and leave the rest out.
The number tells you the context. A 9 means a seventh is in the chord too. Without the seventh it is add9: C, E, G, D. C9 is C, E, G, B♭, D.

The 11 is the tricky one. On a major or dominant chord, the natural 11 sits a semitone above the 3 and clashes. So players raise it to ♯11, or drop the 3 and call it sus. On a minor chord, the natural 11 sounds lovely: Dm11.

Each chord type has its own menu. Major 7 takes 9, ♯11 and 13. Minor 7 takes 9 and 11. The dominant 7 takes natural 9 and 13, or the altered ♭9, ♯9, ♯11 and ♭13. It is the only chord that welcomes them all.
To hear which one is on top, sing the root, then compare. The 9 is a whole step above the root. The ♭9 is only a semitone above it. The 13 sits a semitone below the 7 in a dominant chord.
A common mistake is putting colors too low. A 9 a step above a low root turns to mud. Keep the root alone in the bass and place the tensions above middle C, where they ring.
In real music, 9ths and 13ths are everyday jazz, soul and funk colors. The ♯9 is called the Hendrix chord after Purple Haze. Maj7♯11 is the dreamy Lydian sound of film scores and modern jazz.
To keep: extensions are 2, 4 and 6 an octave up, sitting above a seventh chord. Dominants take every alteration; the 11 needs care on major chords.
Same chord, different arrangement: close, drop 2 or spread; the bass note sets the inversion; jazz voicings leave notes out or add color on top.
Same chord, different outfit: a voicing is how you arrange its notes. Here is Cmaj7 in close position, all four notes packed as tight as they go.
Drop 2: take the second note from the top and drop it an octave. Wider and smoother — a big-band and guitar favorite.
Spread: the notes fly apart over more than two octaves, with lots of air inside.
Inversions are about the bass. Root position has 1 at the bottom; first inversion puts the 3 there, second the 5, third the 7.
Jazz pianists travel light. A shell is just 1, 3 and 7. A rootless voicing leaves the root to the bass player and adds 9 and 13.
Quartal voicings stack fourths: open and modern. An upper structure puts a bright triad over 3 and 7 — here D major on top of C7.
Your turn! You hear a chord together, then note by note. Ask yourself: tight or wide? What is in the bass? Then pick the name.

A voicing decides which notes you play, in which octave and in what order. An inversion only names the bass note. So two voicings can share an inversion: both of these are C major in root position, one close, one open.
Classical figures name inversions. A triad in root position, first inversion is 6, second inversion is 6/4. For seventh chords: 7, 6/5, 4/3 and 4/2. Here are C, C/E and C/G.

To hear the inversion, ignore the top and sing the lowest note, then ask which chord tone it is. Root position sounds grounded. Second inversion sounds restless: here C/G leans into G7, then resolves to C.
Good voicings move as little as possible. Keep the shared notes, and move the others by step. C, F, G7, C: each upper voice moves a step or stays put.
Jazz pianists use rootless voicings in two shapes: one built up from the 3, one from the 7. In a ii–V–I they barely move: Dm9, G13, Cmaj9.
The common mistake is a close chord too low. A third down in the bass sounds like mud. Spread the low notes, a fifth or an octave apart, and keep the thirds higher up.
In real music, Drop 2 is the sound of big-band sax sections and jazz guitar. Miles Davis's So What made a quartal voicing famous: three fourths with a major third on top.
To keep: the bass sets the inversion, the rest is the voicing. Spread low, keep thirds high, and move each voice as little as you can.
Roman numerals name a progression in any key. Pop loops I–V–vi–IV; jazz runs on ii–V–I; borrowed chords like ♭VI and ♭VII come from the parallel minor.
Hi {name}! Chords travel in familiar routes called progressions. Roman numerals name each chord by its scale step: uppercase major, lowercase minor.
That was I–V–vi–IV, the pop anthem. Start it on vi and it turns wistful: vi–IV–I–V.
I–vi–IV–V is the fifties doo-wop loop. I–IV–V–I is the plain, sturdy one.
Jazz runs on ii–V–I: a minor 7, a dominant 7, then home. The turnaround puts I and vi in front: I–vi–ii–V.
Tritone sub: swap the V7 for the dominant a tritone away. In C, D♭7 replaces G7, and the bass slides down by semitones.
Borrowed chords sneak in from the parallel minor. ♭VI–♭VII–I is the heroic ending. I–♭III–IV–I borrows too.
IV turning into minor iv sounds bittersweet. The backdoor, iv7–♭VII7–I, comes home from below instead of from V.
Your turn! I play a progression in some key. Follow the bass, notice where home lands, and pick the numerals.

Chords have jobs. Tonic chords (I, vi, iii) feel like home. Predominant chords (IV, ii) lead away. Dominant chords (V, vii°) create tension that wants home. Most progressions follow that path: tonic, predominant, dominant, tonic.
The strongest root move is down a fifth, as in V to I. Chain it and you get a circle progression: vi, ii, V, I. The roots fall A, D, G, C.
To hear a progression, follow the bass and sing it as scale degrees. Then listen for feel: I is rest, V leans forward, IV lifts away, vi is home in the shade.
A common mix-up is ii and IV. They share two notes and do the same job. Check the bass: in C, IV has F in the bass, ii has D.
In minor, ii–V–i darkens: iiø7, V7, i. In C minor that is Dø7, G7, Cm. The half-diminished ii sets up the minor ending.
Why does the tritone sub work? G7 and D♭7 share the same tritone, B and F (spelled C♭ in D♭7). Same tension, new bass.
In real music, I–V–vi–IV carries countless pop songs; melody and rhythm make them different. Rock loves ♭VII–IV–I, borrowed from Mixolydian. And jazz standards are chains of ii–V–I in changing keys.
To keep: chords have jobs, and the bass tells you which degree you are on. Fifths down pull hardest; borrowed chords add color from the parallel minor.
Give each phrase a letter: the same idea keeps its letter, a variation gets a prime (A′), a new idea gets the next letter.
Music is built from phrases, like sentences in a story. We label them with letters, and the first idea is always A.
If it comes back exactly, it is A again.
Same start, different ending? That is a variation, A prime.
A truly new idea, with a new shape, gets the next letter: B.
Four phrases make a form. AABA is the classic song form: say it twice, take a detour, come home.
ABAB swaps back and forth, like verse and chorus. AABB pairs them up. ABAC brings A back, then ends somewhere new.
Your turn! Listen phrase by phrase and give each one a letter in your head. Then pick: same, variation or new — or the four-letter form.
Form works in layers. A motif is a few notes; motifs make a phrase, often four bars; phrases make a section; sections make the whole piece. Letters usually label the sections.

Phrases end in cadences, musical punctuation. Listen: the first phrase ends on G, the 5, like a question. The answer starts the same way and ends on C, home. A question and an answer together form a period.

The classic forms: binary is AB; ternary is ABA; rondo keeps coming back to A, as in ABACA. The 32-bar song is AABA, four phrases of eight bars. Pop songs alternate verse and chorus, often with a bridge.
To hear form, remember the opening well; the rest is spotting its return. Changes of contour, register, key or texture mark a new section. A strong cadence marks an ending.
The common mistake is giving a new letter to a small change. Ask: does it start the same and keep its shape? Then it is still A, marked A′. Only a new contour from the start earns B.

In real music, many jazz standards use AABA, including Gershwin's I Got Rhythm, whose chords became a jazz staple. Beethoven's Für Elise is a rondo: its famous opening returns between contrasting episodes.
To keep: listen in phrases, label by contour, and track returns. Same idea keeps its letter, a variant gets a prime, a new idea gets the next letter.
A semitone is 100 cents. Hear the lean of tiny steps, and listen for the wobble (beating) of two notes out of tune.
Hi {name}! One piano key to the next is a semitone, and we split it into 100 tiny steps called cents. Today we hunt for much smaller gaps.
Here is 50 cents, half a key. The second note is higher.
Now 25 cents, lower. Do not analyze — just feel which way it leans.
Ten cents, higher. Tiny! Humming the first note softly helps you feel the second one pull away.
Two notes together tell on each other. In tune, they blend smoothly. Out of tune, you hear a wobble, called beating.
In a melody, one sour note sticks out like a crooked picture on the wall. Which one here?
Your turn! Two notes one after the other: say higher or lower. In the tuning drill, say in tune or out — or which melody note is off. First impressions are usually right.

An octave is 1200 cents, and an equal-tempered semitone is 100. Cents are a ratio, not hertz, so 10 cents sounds the same size in any register: about 2.5 Hz at A 440, but under 1 Hz two octaves lower.
How small can you hear? Trained musicians notice about 5 cents between two notes in a row; most people start near 10 to 25. Practice moves that line, so short daily sessions really help.

Beating is physics. Two close frequencies drift in and out of step, and the wobble rate equals their difference in hertz. 440 against 442.5 beats about two and a half times a second. As you tune closer, the beats slow down and vanish.
Beats tell you something is off, not which way. To find out, move one note a little. If the beats speed up, you went the wrong way; if they slow down, keep going.

In tune also depends on context. A pure major third is about 14 cents narrower than the piano's. Singers and string players often settle a major third a little low in chords. Compare the piano third with the pure one.
A common trap: loudness and brightness fool the ear. A louder or brighter note can seem higher when it is not. Compare pitch only, and hum the first note to hold it steady.

In real music, orchestras tune to an A, usually 440 or 442 hertz, and piano tuners count beats to set every interval. To keep: 100 cents per semitone, and beats that slow down mean you are getting closer.
Two voices move in parallel (same way, same distance), similar (same way), contrary (opposite ways) or oblique (one stays).
Hi {name}! Two voices can move together in four ways. Parallel: same direction, same distance, like dancers in step.
Similar: same direction, but different distances. Here the low voice steps up while the high one leaps up.
Contrary: one voice goes up while the other goes down. Composers adore this one.
Oblique: one voice stays put while the other moves.
Next, follow one line. Four two-note chords, then the lower voice alone: 1, 2, 3, 2.
The top voice is easiest to hear. For the lower one, hum quietly along with the bass and let it guide you.
Your turn! Name the motion — parallel, similar, contrary or oblique. Or, in the line levels, pick the scale degrees the lower or upper voice sang.

Combining independent lines is called counterpoint. What makes two lines independent is mostly their motion: contrary and oblique motion keep them apart, while parallel motion makes them blend into one.

Parallel means the same interval number each time: a third stays a third, even if a major third becomes a minor one in the key. Similar motion changes the distance. Watch the number, not just the direction.

A listening strategy: track the gap between the voices. Same gap means parallel. Gap changes but both move the same way means similar. Gap opens or closes fast means contrary. One note held means oblique.
Classical style forbids parallel fifths and octaves: the two voices fuse and lose their independence. Parallel thirds and sixths are welcome. Hear the hollow fifths, then the sweet thirds.
The classic two-voice cadence uses contrary motion: the lower voice falls from 2 to 1 while the upper rises from 7 to 8. Both land on C, an octave apart.
To practice, play one line and sing the other, then swap. The lower voice is the hard one, so sing it first.

In real music, Bach's two-part inventions are the classic school of two independent voices. Many folk duets, on the other hand, sing in parallel thirds. To keep: watch the gap, and contrary motion makes lines independent.
A set class groups a chord with all its transpositions and its mirror image; its prime form is the most compact spelling from 0, like [0,3,7].
Without a key, we name chords with numbers. Count semitones up from the lowest note: C, E, G is 0, 4, 7.
Flip it upside down and you get the minor triad. A set class counts a chord, its mirror and every transposition as one family, named by its most compact form: the prime form. Both triads are [0,3,7].
Some families have strong faces. [0,1,2] is a cluster of semitones. [0,2,7] stacks fifths: open and hollow.
[0,3,6] is the tense diminished triad. [0,4,8] is the augmented triad, dreamy and floating.
Harder ones hide a semitone. [0,1,6] adds a tritone: the Viennese sound of Schoenberg. [0,1,5] adds a fourth, [0,1,4] a minor and a major third.
The notes may be spread out or flipped, so listen for ingredients: a semitone crunch, a tritone itch, an open fifth.
Your turn! I play a three-note chord, together and then broken upward. Pick its family in prime form.

Set theory works with pitch classes: octaves and enharmonic spellings count as the same. C is 0, C♯ is 1, up to B, which is 11, and you count around a clock of twelve. G, C♯, C becomes the set 7, 1, 0.

Step one: normal form. Order the pitch classes inside one octave and try each one as the start. Keep the order with the smallest span. For {0, 1, 7} that is 7, 0, 1, spanning six semitones. Then subtract 7: 0, 5, 6.
Step two: try the mirror. Inverted, 0, 5, 6 becomes 0, 1, 6. The prime form is whichever packs the smaller intervals to the left, so [0,1,6]. That is why major and minor triads share [0,3,7].

To hear the family, listen for its three intervals. [0,1,6] has a semitone, a fourth and a tritone. [0,1,5] has a semitone, a major third and a fourth. [0,1,4] has a semitone, a minor third and a major third.
The common mistake is missing a disguised semitone. Spread out, it becomes a major seventh or a minor ninth. Both still count as a semitone: they are the same interval class.

In real music, [0,1,6] is so typical of Schoenberg and Webern that it is called the Viennese trichord. Webern built the row of his Concerto, Op. 24, from four [0,1,4] trichords. Stacked fourths, as in modern jazz, give [0,2,7].
To keep: reduce to pitch classes, find the most compact order, compare with its mirror, and start from 0. Then trust the interval ingredients.
A maqam is built from small note groups (ajnas); the first jins gives its flavor: Hijaz has the wide gap, Rast and Bayati the quarter tones.
Hi {name}! Arabic music organizes melody in maqamat. Each maqam is built from small groups of about four notes, each called a jins. The first jins gives the flavor.
That was Ajam, our familiar major scale. Hijaz is famous for its wide gap: a semitone, then a step and a half.
Kurd starts with a semitone and then whole steps, like Phrygian. Nahawand sounds like harmonic minor.
Now the magic ingredient: the quarter tone, a note between the piano keys. E half-flat sits right between E♭ and E.
Rast, on C, has a half-flat third and seventh: proud and warm. Bayati, on D, opens with a three-quarter step, soulful and earthy.
Saba is Bayati with a lowered fourth, and it sounds heartbroken. Sikah starts on E half-flat itself.
Your turn! I play a maqam up and down. Listen to its first four notes and their gaps: a wide Hijaz leap, a quarter tone, or plain steps. Then name the maqam, or just its jins.

A maqam is more than a scale. It has a tonic, two or more ajnas joined together, a pivot note where the next jins begins, and a typical path for the melody. Bayati on D is jins Bayati on D plus jins Nahawand on G.
Measure in semitones: a quarter tone is half a semitone, and the neutral step between a semitone and a tone is 1.5. Jins Rast goes 2, 1.5, 1.5. Jins Bayati turns it around: 1.5, 1.5, 2.
Four ajnas need no quarter tones. Ajam goes 2, 2, 1, like major. Nahawand goes 2, 1, 2, like minor. Kurd goes 1, 2, 2. Hijaz goes 1, 3, 1. Hijaz and Kurd differ only in the third note: F♯ or F.
Rast, Bayati and Sikah are one family. Bayati on D starts with D, E half-flat, F, G: the same notes as Rast on C from its 2nd degree. Sikah starts on Rast's 3rd degree, E half-flat itself.

A listening strategy: start with the 2nd degree. A semitone above the tonic means Kurd or Hijaz. Three quarters means Bayati or Saba. A whole tone means Rast, Nahawand or Ajam. Then the 3rd degree decides.
Saba is Bayati with its 4th lowered to G♭, so its first jins spans less than a fourth and never quite settles. Above it, F, G♭, A, B♭ form a Hijaz.
To sing the half-flat, sing E♭ and E, then aim right between them. Practice each jins slowly over a drone on the tonic, so you hear every step against home.

Two common mistakes. First, hearing the half-flat as out of tune and pulling it to E♭ or E. Second, mixing Hijaz with harmonic minor: Hijaz has its wide gap between degrees 2 and 3, harmonic minor between 6 and 7.

The app places every quarter tone exactly halfway. Real musicians are subtler: the half-flat E of Sikah, Bayati and Rast can differ slightly, and Turkish makam uses a different tuning system altogether.

In real music, maqamat shape Arabic, Turkish and many Jewish traditions. The Hijaz sound is the Ahava Rabbah mode of synagogue chant and the freygish of klezmer. The Aleppo Jewish tradition assigns a maqam to each Sabbath.
To keep: hear the first jins, starting from the 2nd degree. Semitone, neutral step or whole tone points you to the family; the 3rd and 4th degrees name it.
Sharp keys: the last sharp plus a semitone. Flat keys: the second-to-last flat (one flat = F). The relative minor is a minor third down.
Hi {name}! The sharps or flats right after the clef are the key signature. They hold for the whole piece. In D major, every F and C is sharp.
Sharps always arrive in the same order: F C G D A E B. Flats are the mirror image: B E A D G C F.
Sharp keys: take the last sharp and go up a semitone. Four sharps end on D♯, so this is E major.
Flat keys: the second-to-last flat names the key. B♭, E♭, A♭ — that is E♭ major. One flat is the one to memorize: F major.
Every signature also fits a minor key, the relative minor: on the sixth degree, a minor third down. Two sharps: D major or B minor.
Your turn! You will see a key signature on the staff. Count the sharps or flats and pick the major key — at the top level, sometimes its relative minor. This one is all eyes, no ears.

Why signatures exist: every major scale needs the same pattern of steps, tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. Starting on G, only F must rise to F♯ to keep that pattern. The signature prints it once instead of on every note.
Each new sharp is a fifth above the last: F♯, C♯, G♯, D♯, A♯, E♯, B♯. Each new flat is a fifth below: B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, G♭, C♭, F♭. So the order is the circle of fifths in disguise.
Signatures go up to seven: C♯ major has seven sharps, C♭ major seven flats. Three pairs sound the same: B and C♭, F♯ and G♭, C♯ and D♭. Musicians usually pick the one with fewer accidentals.

Minor keys borrow the signature of their relative major. The raised 7th of harmonic minor is never in the signature: it is written as an accidental each time. A minor has no signature, but its G♯ appears in the music.
So how do you tell a major key from its relative minor? Look at the first and last bass notes and chords, and hunt for that raised 7th. No signature plus G♯ everywhere points to A minor.
Accidentals in the music last until the bar line, on that line or space only. A natural sign cancels the signature for the rest of the bar.
Common mistakes: forgetting that one flat is F major, where the second-to-last rule cannot work. And naming sharp keys with flats: six sharps end on E♯, so the key is F♯ major, not G♭.

In real music, string players feel at home in sharp keys, near their open strings G, D, A and E. Wind bands and brass live in flat keys like B♭ and E♭. To keep: count, apply the rule, and check for a raised 7th.
Count letters first for the number, then semitones for the quality: a major 3rd above E is G♯, never A♭.
Hi {name}! Spelling an interval takes two steps. Step one: count letters, with the bottom note as 1. C, D, E — a third.
Step two: count semitones for the quality. C to E is four semitones, so it is a major third.
Now a trap. A major third above E? The letters say some kind of G. E to G is only three semitones, so raise it: G♯.
A♭ sounds identical, but A is four letters up, so E to A♭ is a diminished fourth. Letter first, accidental second. Always.
Handy numbers: minor third 3, major third 4, perfect fourth 5, perfect fifth 7. A fifth above B: B C D E F, six semitones — so F♯.
Augmented is a semitone wider than major or perfect; diminished, a semitone narrower than minor or perfect. C to F♯ and C to G♭ sound the same — an augmented fourth and a diminished fifth.
Your turn! I name an interval and a starting note. Count the letters, then the semitones, and pick the right spelling. Beware the twin with the wrong letter!
Intervals come in two families. Unisons, 4ths, 5ths and octaves are perfect. 2nds, 3rds, 6ths and 7ths are major or minor. There is no major fifth and no perfect third.
The full table in semitones: minor 2nd 1, major 2nd 2, minor 3rd 3, major 3rd 4, perfect 4th 5, tritone 6, perfect 5th 7, minor 6th 8, major 6th 9, minor 7th 10, major 7th 11, octave 12.
A shortcut: the major scale of the bottom note gives you every major and perfect interval above it. E major is E F♯ G♯ A B C♯ D♯, so a major 3rd above E is G♯ and a major 7th is D♯. Then adjust.
Flip an interval and the numbers add up to 9. Major becomes minor, augmented becomes diminished, perfect stays perfect. C up to A is a major 6th, so A up to C is a minor 3rd.
Twins sound alike but behave differently. In C major, the augmented 4th F–B opens out to E–C, while the diminished 5th B–F closes in to C–E. The spelling tells you where it goes.
Intervals beyond the octave are compound: subtract 7 from the number. A 9th is a 2nd plus an octave, a 10th a 3rd plus an octave. C up to D an octave higher is a major 9th.
Two common mistakes: counting the bottom note as 0, which turns a 3rd into a 2nd; and counting semitones first, which gives the sound but not the spelling. Letters first, from 1.
Practice downward too: count letters down. A major 3rd below F: F, E, D gives D, but F down to D is three semitones, so lower it to D♭. To keep: letters for the number, semitones for the quality.
Chords are spelled in every other letter (1 3 5 7 9); the accidentals set the quality. G°7 is G B♭ D♭ F♭ — F♭, not E.
Hi {name}! Chords are spelled in skips: every other letter. Root, third, fifth, like C, E, G.
The letters are fixed; accidentals set the quality. Major is a major third, then a minor third. E major: E, G, B, and the G must rise to G♯.
Minor puts the minor third first. Diminished is two minor thirds; augmented, two major thirds.
Sevenths add one more letter. G7 is G, B, D, F: a major triad with a minor seventh. Gmaj7 raises it to F♯.
Gm7 is G, B♭, D, F. Half-diminished Gø7 lowers the fifth to D♭. Fully diminished G°7 lowers the seventh too — to F♭, not E, because the seventh must be some F.
Ninths keep skipping: the 9 is the letter after the 7, so in G9 it is A. In G7♭9 it is A♭.
Your turn! I show a chord symbol and play it. Pick the spelling with every other letter and the right accidentals. Same-sound, wrong-letter answers are traps!
Chord formulas compare each chord to the major scale of its root. Major is 1 3 5, minor 1 ♭3 5, diminished 1 ♭3 ♭5, augmented 1 3 ♯5. Sevenths: maj7 1 3 5 7, dominant 7 1 3 5 ♭7, m7 1 ♭3 5 ♭7.
A three-step method. Write the letters in skips. Take the notes from the root's major scale. Apply the formula. B♭m7: letters B, D, F, A; B♭ major gives B♭, D, F, A; lower the 3 and 7: B♭, D♭, F, A♭.
Half-diminished is 1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭7; fully diminished lowers the 7 twice. C°7 is C, E♭, G♭, B♭♭. That double flat sounds like A, but the seventh must be some B.
To recognize the four triads by ear: major is bright, minor dark, diminished tight and tense, augmented hanging and unresolved. Here they are on D.
Sus and add chords keep the skip idea but change one member. Csus4 is C, F, G: the 4 replaces the 3. Cadd9 is C, E, G, D. C6 is C, E, G, A.
The common mistake is spelling from the keyboard. Cm is C, E♭, G, never C, D♯, G: the third must be some E. Also, an inversion never changes the spelling. C/E is still C, E, G, with E in the bass.

Why it matters: one diminished seventh sound has four spellings, C°7, E♭°7, G♭°7 and A°7. The spelling shows which note is the root and where the chord wants to go. To keep: letters in skips, then the formula.
The numeral is the scale step of the root; the case is the quality: in major I ii iii IV V vi vii°, in minor i ii° III iv V VI VII vii° (V and vii° take the raised 7th).
Hi {name}! A Roman numeral names a chord by the scale step its root sits on. In C major, a chord on D is chord two.
The case shows the quality: uppercase major, lowercase minor, a small circle for diminished. In major: I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi, vii°.
I, IV and V are the major pillars. ii, iii and vi are minor, and vii° is the tense diminished one, B, D, F.
In minor, steps six and seven vary. III, VI and VII come from natural minor; V and vii° take the raised seventh. In A minor: i, ii°, III, iv, V, VI, VII, vii°. That G♯ makes V major.
Two sevenths, two chords. VII is G, B, D, a step below home. vii° is G♯, B, D, and it leads home.
A secondary dominant borrows a V for another chord. V/V in C is D7, the dominant of G: a sudden push toward V.
Your turn! I name the key, play a cadence, then one chord. Find its step and its quality, then pick the numeral.
Numerals describe function, not pitch, so a progression keeps its name in every key. ii–V–I is Dm, G7, C in C major, and Gm, C7, F in F major.
Add a seventh to each degree of a major key and you get Imaj7, ii7, iii7, IVmaj7, V7, vi7 and viiø7. Only V has the dominant seventh: that is what makes it pull so hard.
Small numbers after the numeral show the inversion. V7 has the root in the bass; V6/5 the 3; V4/3 the 5; V4/2 the 7. Here is G7 in C, with B, then D, then F in the bass.
Real minor-key music mixes forms. Natural minor gives a minor v and a major VII; harmonic minor gives the major V. In A minor, both G to Am and E to Am are common.

A listening strategy: first sing the tonic, then sing the lowest note of the chord and name its degree. Then hear the quality: major, minor or diminished. Check the bass is really the root before you write the numeral.
Secondary dominants: V/ii is A7, V/iii B7, V/IV C7, V/V D7 and V/vi E7. The clue is a note foreign to the key, like C♯ in A7, that rises a semitone into the next root.
The common mistake is naming by the bass note. C/E, with E in the bass, is still I in first inversion, I6, not iii. Em is E, G, B; C/E is E, G, C.

Pop and jazz charts often write every numeral in capitals with a quality symbol, like IIm7–V7–Imaj7. To keep: the numeral is the root's degree, the case or symbol is the quality, the small numbers show the bass.
Clockwise by fifths adds a sharp (G D A E B F♯), counterclockwise adds a flat (F B♭ E♭ A♭ D♭ G♭); the relative minor is a minor third down.
Hi {name}! Go up a perfect fifth from C and you reach G. Keep going: D, A, E, B, F♯. Each step adds one sharp.
So G has 1 sharp, D 2, A 3, E 4, B 5, and F♯ 6. Here is A major, with three.
Go the other way, down by fifths, and you add flats: F, B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, G♭ — one to six flats.
Put them on a clock: C at the top, sharps clockwise, flats counterclockwise. At the bottom F♯ and G♭ meet: same sound, two names.
Neighbors on the circle are a fifth apart and differ by just one sharp or flat. Clockwise from D is A; counterclockwise is G.
Each major key shares its signature with a relative minor, a minor third down. C major and A minor; G major and E minor.
Your turn! I name a major key. Depending on the level, tell me how many sharps or flats it has, its relative minor, or its neighbor one step around the circle.

Why fifths? G major shares six of its seven notes with C major; only F becomes F♯. Each step clockwise raises the old 4th degree into a new leading tone. Each step counterclockwise lowers the old 7th.
Down a fifth is the same as up a fourth. So counterclockwise you can also count fourths: C, F, B♭, E♭. Jazz musicians call this the cycle of fourths and practice everything around it.
Twelve positions, fifteen major key names: at the bottom, B and C♭, F♯ and G♭, C♯ and D♭ overlap. An inner ring holds the relative minors: A minor under C, E minor under G, D minor under F.
Chord roots love to fall around the circle. iii, vi, ii, V, I falls by fifths all the way home: E, A, D, G, C.
Distance on the circle is distance in sound. A move to a neighboring key is smooth. A jump across the circle, a tritone away, is a jolt. Hear C go to G through D7, then C jump to F♯.
Common mistakes: turning the wrong way, so remember sharps go up by fifths, clockwise. And a wrong fifth: above B it is F♯, not F. B to F is only six semitones, a diminished fifth.

In real music, Baroque sequences and jazz standards such as Autumn Leaves march around the circle. To keep: clockwise adds a sharp, counterclockwise adds a flat, and neighbors are closely related keys.
Move every note by the same interval, spelling letters first. B♭ instruments read a major 2nd up, E♭ alto sax a major 6th up, F horn a perfect 5th up.
Hi {name}! Transposing means moving music by a fixed interval. Every note moves the same distance, so the tune stays the same tune.
Spell it like an interval, letters first. D up a major third: D, E, F, then four semitones, so F♯.
Some instruments sound a different note from the one they read. A B♭ trumpet or clarinet sounds a major second lower than written; the tenor sax, an octave lower again.
So to write for them, go up: concert C becomes written D. To find the sound, go back down.
The E♭ alto sax reads a major sixth higher: concert C is written A.
The F horn reads a perfect fifth higher: concert C is written G.
Your turn! Move a note by an interval, or switch between concert and written for an instrument. Count the letters first, then the semitones, and pick the spelling.

Transposition means two different jobs. One is moving a whole piece to a new key, for example to suit a singer's range. The other is writing for transposing instruments, whose written note differs from the sound.
A reliable method for a new key: think in scale degrees. C, E, G, E is 1, 3, 5, 3. In E♭ major, 1, 3, 5, 3 is E♭, G, B♭, G. Change the key signature first, then the notes follow.
Chromatic notes keep their relation to the key. F♯ in C major is a raised 4th; moved to D major, the raised 4th is G♯.
Why do instruments transpose? So one fingering gives one written note across a whole family. A saxophonist can switch from alto to tenor without relearning to read.

The name tells you what sounds when the player reads C. A B♭ trumpet reading C sounds B♭, a major 2nd lower. The tenor sax sounds a major 9th lower, the baritone sax an octave and a major 6th. Guitar sounds an octave below written.
Key signatures move too. A concert piece in E♭ major is written in F major for B♭ instruments, and in C major for the E♭ alto sax.

The common mistake is going the wrong way. The instrument sounds lower than written, so to write its part you go up. Check yourself: for B♭ trumpet and clarinet, alto sax and F horn, the written note should be higher than concert.

In real music, jazz fake books come in C, B♭ and E♭ editions, so every player reads in their own transposition. To keep: think in degrees, spell letters first, and write up for transposing instruments.
In a key, play the key's notes from the chord's root: ii is Dorian, iii Phrygian, V Mixolydian. Jazz tensions pick special scales: 7alt → altered.
Hi {name}! Every chord has a scale that fits it like a glove. Inside a key, play the key's notes starting from the chord's root.
In C major that gives seven modes: I Ionian, ii Dorian, iii Phrygian, IV Lydian, V Mixolydian, vi Aeolian, vii Locrian.
I Ion · ii Dor · iii Phr · IV Lyd · V Mix · vi Aeo · viiø Loc
Careful: m7 chords sit on ii, iii and vi, so the degree decides. Dm7 is Dorian, but Em7 in C is Phrygian.
G7, the V chord, takes Mixolydian: a major scale with a lowered seventh.
Jazz adds color. 7alt takes the altered scale, 13♭9 the half-whole diminished, and 7♯11 the Lydian dominant.
7♯5 takes whole tone, m(maj7) melodic minor, maj7♯11 Lydian, and a 7♭9 heading to a minor chord takes Phrygian dominant.
Your turn! I show and play a chord, at first with its key. Find its degree, or its tell-tale tension, and pick the scale.

A chord scale is a pool of notes: the chord tones plus the tensions between them. Some scale notes clash when held, usually one a semitone above a chord tone. Over Cmaj7, a held F rubs against E; D, the 9, rings.
The seven modes, from brightest to darkest: Lydian, Ionian, Mixolydian, Dorian, Aeolian, Phrygian, Locrian. Each step down lowers just one note.
Lyd · Ion · Mix · Dor · Aeo · Phr · Loc
Each mode has a signature note. Dorian has a natural 6, Aeolian a ♭6. Phrygian has a ♭2, Lydian a ♯4, Mixolydian a ♭7, Locrian a ♭2 and ♭5. Hear D Dorian, with B, then D Aeolian, with B♭.
The melodic minor scale has its own family of modes. Its 1st mode suits m(maj7), its 4th is Lydian dominant for 7♯11, its 6th is Locrian ♮2 for m7♭5, and its 7th is the altered scale for 7alt.

For dominants, ask three questions. Is the 9 natural or altered? Is the 11 natural or sharp? Is the 13 natural or flat? Natural 9 and 13 point to Mixolydian; ♭9 with natural 13 to half-whole diminished; ♭9 and ♭13 to altered or Phrygian dominant.
The common mistake is staying in the key's scale when the chord leaves it. In C minor, G7 resolving to Cm wants A♭ and E♭, its ♭9 and ♭13, not the A and E of G Mixolydian.

In real music, modal jazz made chord scales famous: Miles Davis's So What sits on D Dorian, then moves up to E♭ Dorian. To keep: chord tones first, then pick the tensions that fit, and the scale names itself.
Treble lines E G B D F, spaces F A C E; bass lines G B D F A, spaces A C E G; the alto clef points at middle C.
Hi {name}! A clef tells you which line is which note. The treble clef, or G clef, curls around the second line: G above middle C.
Treble lines from the bottom: E, G, B, D, F. The spaces spell F, A, C, E — FACE.
The bass clef, or F clef, has two dots hugging the fourth line: F below middle C. Lines: G, B, D, F, A. Spaces: A, C, E, G.
The alto clef, a C clef, points straight at its middle line: middle C. Violas read it all day. Lines: F, A, C, E, G.
Middle C is the bridge: one ledger line below the treble staff, one above the bass staff. Ledger lines just continue the pattern.
Learn a few landmarks, then count: line, space, line is always the next letter up.
Your turn! I show one note on the staff. Check the clef, find your nearest landmark, count, and pick its name.
Piano music uses the grand staff: a treble staff above a bass staff, joined by a brace. Middle C sits between them on its own short ledger line, belonging to both.

Learn six landmarks: bass G on the bottom line, bass F on the fourth line, middle C, treble G on the second line, C in the treble third space, and F on the top line. Every other note is a short count away.
Read shapes, not just single notes. Line to the next space is a 2nd; line to the next line is a 3rd. Three notes on consecutive lines, like E, G, B, form a stack of thirds: a triad.
Ledger lines continue the staff. Above the treble staff, the first ledger line is A and the second is C. Below the bass staff, the first is E and the second is C.
The tenor clef is another C clef, pointing at the fourth line. Cellos, bassoons and trombones use it for high passages. Its lines are D, F, A, C, E.
The common mistake is reading the bass clef with treble names. The same position reads two letters higher in bass clef: the bottom line is E in treble but G in bass. Always check the clef first.
Practice a few minutes every day, naming notes aloud, and time yourself. To keep: check the clef, find the nearest landmark, then count by lines and spaces.
Two triads with no common note give six notes: a chord scale minus one tone. G♭ + A♭ over C7alt, D + Em over Cmaj7♯11, E♭ + F over Cm7.
Hi {name}! Take two triads that share no note. Over C minor 7: E flat major and F major.
Together they are six notes of C dorian. Only the 9th, D, is left out.
Over C7alt: G flat and A flat. Root, flat 9, sharp 9, flat 5, flat 13, flat 7. The altered scale without its 3rd.
Over C major 7 sharp 11: D and E minor. 9, sharp 11, 13, then 3, 5, 7: lydian without the root.
Your turn: name the pair for each chord, then hear its colour over the chord and tell dorian, lydian and altered apart.
Where do you hear this? Saxophone and piano players of the 1970s and after, over modal vamps and altered dominants, use pairs to sound open and modern while staying exactly on the chord.
Why pairs? Two small shapes, each easy under the hand, give a wide modern sound with no scale running.
D and E major is a different pair: G sharp is the sharp 5. Over C major 7 sharp 5 that is lydian augmented.
Over a plain dominant: B flat and C give mixolydian without the 13th; C and D give lydian dominant without the 7th.
Play them in inversions: A, then B, then A from its 3rd, B from its 3rd, and so on. The line climbs without a leap.
A common mistake is to run the six notes as a scale. Keep them as two triads: three notes, then three, and let the line jump between the shapes. That jump is the sound.
To keep: find the one tone the six leave out. It tells you the scale.
A pentatonic built on another note colours the chord: G major pentatonic over Cmaj7 is inside, D major is lydian, E♭ minor over C7alt is altered.
Hi {name}! Over C major 7, G major pentatonic gives 5, 13, 7, 9, 3. Every note is safe.
Move it up to D: D, E, F sharp, A, B. Now the F sharp is a sharp 11. That is the lydian colour.
Over C7alt, E flat minor pentatonic: sharp 9, flat 5, flat 13, flat 7, flat 9. Five notes, all altered colour.
Over C minor 7, D minor pentatonic gives 9, 11, 5, 13 and the root: a dorian sound.
Your turn: pick the pentatonic for a colour, read its degrees over the chord, then hear which one is playing.
Name each note against the chord root, not the pentatonic’s. That is how you know what you are adding.
Listen to the same chord with two pentatonics: G major is calm and inside, D major lifts with the sharp 11. Same shape, a 5th apart.
A common slip: D minor pentatonic over C major 7. It holds F, the 11th, which clashes with the 3rd. Keep it for C minor 7.
Play it in groups of four: 1-2-3-4, 2-3-4-5, up the neck or the keyboard. The groups cross the beat and sound like a line, not a scale.
Over the altered dominant the same trick works a half step above the root: E flat minor pentatonic over C7 gives every altered tension and resolves well to F.
Practice it slowly over a vamp first, then over a ii–V–I: a different pentatonic on each chord, chosen for the colour you want to hear, not for the key of the tune.
To keep: same five-note shape, new root, new colour.
C/E is an inversion, D/C an upper structure (lydian), F/G a dominant sus. A triad over a 7th chord names its colour: D/C7 = 13♯11, A♭/C7 = 7♯9♭13.
Hi {name}! Three slash chords look alike. C over E: E is in the C triad, so it is just C with the 3rd in the bass.
D over C: the bass is not in the triad. D, F sharp, A over C are 9, sharp 11, 13. An upper structure, the lydian sound.
F over G: F, A, C over G are flat 7, 9, 11. A dominant with a 4th instead of a 3rd: G9 sus. It still wants to go to C.
Over a dominant, the triad names the colour. D over C7: 13 sharp 11, lydian dominant. A flat over C7: sharp 9, flat 13, altered.
Your turn: tell inversion, upper structure and sus apart, on paper and by ear.
The rule: bass inside the triad, an inversion. Triad a step above the bass, lydian. A step below, sus.
Careful in a progression: D over C before G is also D7 in third inversion, the V of V, leading to G over B.
