Natural tensions are 9 and 13, with sharp 11 for lydian dominant. Altered ones are flat 9, sharp 9, flat 13. G minor over C7 is natural: a plain C9.
Upper structures work over major 7 and minor 7 too. G over C major 7 is a major 9; F over C minor 7 is 11, 13 and the root, dorian.
Pianists voice these with the left hand on 3rd and 7th and the right hand on the triad, so the colour sits on top and the function stays clear underneath.
By ear, start from the bass: if it doubles a note of the triad you hear an inversion; if it sits under it, a new chord.
To keep: read the triad against the bass. Its notes are the chord’s colours.
A new chord works when it does the old one’s job (leads to the same place) and the melody note is its chord tone or tension.
Hi {name}! G7 goes to C. Three dominants can do that job: G7, its tritone sub D flat 7, and the backdoor B flat 7.
Now the melody. If it sings C, G7 has it as the 11th and D flat 7 as the major 7th. Both clash. B flat 7 has it as the 9th.
Between C and D minor, the passing C sharp diminished, A7 or E flat 7 all lead to D minor. Pick the one that holds the melody.
Over one long minor chord, a line cliché: C minor, minor-major 7, minor 7, minor 6. One voice falls by half steps.
Your turn: play the root, the 3rd, the 7th and the melody note. Any octave counts.
Over a dominant the melody may be any tension but the natural 11th and the major 7th. Over major 7, avoid the 11th; over minor 7, the flat 13.
Why the root? A tritone sub shares its 3rd and 7th with the V. Without the root nobody hears that you changed it.
An added ii–V splits a bar of V into ii and V: C, then D minor 7 G7, then C. The ii must hold the melody too.
The backdoor sounds softer than the tritone sub: F minor 7 to B flat 7 to C borrows from C minor and lands warmly. Hear it under the melody note G.
A good habit: write the melody note above each bar, list the chords that do the bar’s job, and cross out every one that clashes with the note. What is left is your palette.
To keep: first the job, then the melody. Both, or it is not a reharm.
The colours you learned by ear, under the hands: pentatonics and triad pairs over a vamp, upper structures, line clichés and your own reharm.
Hi {name}! Here the theory goes into the hands. First a pentatonic over a vamp, in groups of four.
Then upper structures: the left hand holds 3rd and 7th, the right hand moves a triad. D over C major 7 is the lydian sound.
Then triad pairs in inversions: A, B, A from its 3rd, B from its 3rd. Six notes, two easy shapes.
Then a line cliché over a held minor chord, and a melody you reharmonise with a passing diminished and a tritone sub.
Each level starts slow, without a click, until the notes sit. Then the click comes in and the tempo climbs to the target.
The lines are written out and checked note for note. Play them as written first; later, over the same vamp, make your own lines from the same notes.
Chords are checked by their notes in any octave and any order. A voicing that holds the right pitch classes passes, so you may spread it over both hands as you like.
The V changes colour halfway: A over G7 for a lydian dominant, then E flat over G7, altered, into C. Hear the pull grow.
Last, ii–V–I in lines: a minor pentatonic over the ii, the altered pair over the V, the lydian pentatonic over the I.
Keep the left hand relaxed and low in the upper structures; the right hand carries the colour and should sing a little louder than the shell.
To keep: hear it, name it, then play it. The ear lessons and these drills are the same colours from two sides.
Rootless 3-5-7-9 and 7-9-3-5 on strings 5–2 and 4–1, So What in 4ths, and Giant Steps with shells: the jazz pianist’s harmony on the neck.
Hi {name}! The bass plays the root, so the guitar can drop it. D minor 9 without D: F, A, C, E, on strings 5 to 2.
The same idea on strings 4 to 1, higher and brighter. A ii–V–I moves only one or two fingers.
So What: three perfect 4ths and a major 3rd. D, G, C, F, A for D minor, moved up and down the dorian scale.
Giant Steps: keys a major 3rd apart, B, G and E flat, each reached by its own V7. Shells keep the hand still.
Then upper structures on the top strings, triad pairs in inversions, pentatonic lines and line clichés. Each starts slow, without a click.
Rootless on guitar means drop-2 shapes of 3, 5, 7, 9: four strings, no root, the 9th on top or inside. The bass player gives the root.
In So What the same grip moves a whole step: on E and on D, both inside D dorian. Keep the hand shape and slide.
Giant Steps moves fast between three keys. Learn it slowly with shells, root, 3rd and 7th, then with drop-2 on the top four strings.
Upper structures on guitar: play the 3rd and 7th first, then the triad on strings 3 to 1. Two hits, one chord.
A line cliché sits well on guitar: the root rings on a low string while one finger walks the moving voice down a string by half steps, the other notes held.
To keep: fewer notes, chosen well. The root belongs to the bass; your notes are the 3rd, the 7th and the colours.
Inside every click live smaller, even pieces: two (eighths), three (triplets), four (sixteenths). Feel them and your taps stay steady.
Hi {name}! A click marks the beat, but inside each beat you can feel smaller, even pieces. Listen: the click, and two notes per click. Those are eighths.
Three even notes per click are triplets. Say trip-o-let, trip-o-let, with every syllable the same length.
Four per click are sixteenths: one-e-and-a. The click always lands on the first of the four.
Swing turns each pair into long-short. It is the triplet with the middle note left out.
In the exercise the click plays only the beats, and you tap the pieces. Feel the beat in your body and let your taps fall evenly between the clicks.

Subdivision means splitting each beat into equal parts. With a quarter-note beat, two parts are eighths, counted "1 and"; three are eighth-note triplets, "1 trip-let"; four are sixteenths, "1 e and a". Eighths, then sixteenths.

Why it helps: the longer the gap between clicks, the more room you have to drift. Subdividing gives your body checkpoints inside the gap, which is why slow tempos need it most. This is 50 beats per minute, felt in eighths.
Twos and threes feel different. Twos are square, like a march. Threes roll and lilt, like a 6/8 ballad. Listen to the same click with two, then three, notes per beat.
Swing eighths are written as even pairs but played long-short, close to a triplet with the middle note left out. The exact ratio varies: at fast tempos swing gets straighter. Straight, then swung.
A practice ladder: set a slow click and change the subdivision every bar — two, three, four — counting out loud. The beat must not move when the notes inside it change.
The common mistake with triplets is to play them as an eighth and two sixteenths: long, short, short. Real triplets are three equal notes. Listen: the wrong shape, then even triplets.
Another trap is rushing the last subdivision, squeezing the "a" of "1 e and a" towards the next click. Keep the last piece as long as the first.
In real music: blues shuffles live on triplets, funk hi-hats often run in sixteenths, and slow 12/8 ballads are four beats each split into three.
To keep: every beat holds two, three or four equal pieces. Feel them between the clicks, keep them even, and your time stays steady even when the clicks are far apart.
A click on 2 and 4, on beat 1 only or on the "and"s is still a steady clock. Keep your own beat and use the click to check where you are.
Hi {name}! Usually the click plays every beat: one, two, three, four. Here is the plain click with a tap on every beat.
Now the click plays only on two and four, the backbeat, like a snare in pop and jazz. Beats one and three fall in the silence between.
Harder: the click only on beat one. You fill in two, three and four yourself, evenly.
Hardest: the click moves onto the "and"s, halfway between the beats. Don't follow it; tap your beat against it.
Tip: count out loud, quietly. A click in an unusual place is still a steady clock; it only tells you where you are.
The backbeat is beats two and four in 4/4: the weak beats, played strong. In rock, pop and soul the snare drum carries it while the kick lands on one and three.
Jazz musicians practice with the click on two and four on purpose: it is where the drummer's hi-hat closes, and it makes the time feel like swing. Your taps fill one and three between the clicks.

The trap: hearing the two-and-four click as one and three. Then your whole bar flips and every tap lands on the wrong beat. Fix it by saying "one" out loud just before the first click: "one CLICK three CLICK".
With the click on beat one only, it marks bars, not beats. You carry three beats alone each time, so subdivide quietly and arrive exactly with the next click.
A click on the "and"s is like a ska guitar upstroke or a disco open hi-hat: it sits exactly halfway between your beats. Hear it as an answer to your tap, not as the beat itself.

Another common mistake is drifting into the click: little by little your taps slide until they land with it. Here the taps start on the beats and slip onto the offbeat clicks. If tap and click start to merge, you have moved.
A good ladder: click on every beat, then on two and four, then on one only, then on the "and"s, then one bar on and one bar off. Move up only when the step before feels easy.
To keep: the click is a reference, not a leader. Wherever it sits, your beat stays where it is, and the click only confirms it.
The click drops out and you keep the beat alone. When it comes back you hear at once whether you rushed or dragged.
Hi {name}! A metronome helps, but real time lives inside you. Here the click plays two bars, then stops for one, while the taps keep going.
When the click returns you hear at once whether you rushed. Listen: these taps run ahead in the gap and clash with the click when it comes back.
Now two bars on and two bars off. A longer silence means more time to drift, so stay calm and even.
The secret is to keep counting in your head and to move a little: a nod or a foot on every beat.
In the exercise, tap every beat right through the gaps. You win when your taps land together with the click as it comes back.
A gap click plays some bars and mutes others. It tests your internal clock: the sense of time that keeps running when nothing outside marks the beat. Here one bar on, one bar off, one bar on.
Why it matters: in a band nothing marks every beat. There are breaks, stops and quiet bars, and everyone has to come back in together. Your inner clock is what lets that happen.

When the click returns, compare. A tap before the click means you rushed; after it, you dragged. Many players rush in silence, especially at slow tempos. Here the taps drag through the gap and land late.
The strategy is to fill the gap. Feel the eighths inside each beat, count the bars as well — "one two three four, two two three four" — and move: a nod, a foot, a sway.
A practice ladder: one bar on and one off, then two and two, then one on and three off, then four and four. Slow tempos are harder than fast ones, because each silent beat lasts longer.
The common mistake is a sudden jump when the click comes back and you are off. In a band that sounds like a stumble. Adjust gently over two or three beats instead, and listen for what made you drift.

In real music: in stop-time, common in blues and jazz, the band plays only the first beat of each bar and the soloist carries the time alone in between. Listen: the hits, and the silence you must keep.
To keep: the beat lives in you, not in the click. Subdivide, count bars and move through every gap, and the click will find you exactly where you should be.
Anchor tempos to things you know: 60 is a clock's second, 120 a brisk march. From those you can find the others without a metronome.
Hi {name}! Musicians often count a song in without a metronome. That is tempo memory. This is 60 beats per minute: one per second, like a clock.
This is 120, twice as fast, like a brisk march.
And 90 sits between them: a relaxed walk.
Anchor tempos to things you know. A second hand is 60, a march is 120, and from those you can guess the others: a little faster, a little slower.
In the exercise there is no click. Start when you are ready and tap the asked tempo. Within three percent counts as perfect, so keep it even and don't rush.
Tempo is measured in beats per minute, BPM. At 60 there is one beat every second; at 120, two every second. Doubling the BPM halves the gap between beats. Here are 60 and 120.
Build a set of anchors. A clock's second hand is 60. Many marches sit near 120. Then pick a few songs you know by heart, look up their tempos once, and keep them as reference points.
Find the in-between tempos from the anchors. 90 is one and a half times 60: three beats in the time of two seconds. Listen: the click at 90 against hits at 60.
Rough feel ranges help too. Below about 70 is a slow ballad, 90 to 110 a relaxed mid-tempo, around 120 to 130 a typical dance groove, and above 160 starts to feel very fast or is felt in half time.
Watch out for half and double time. A song at 70 with busy eighths can feel like 140. Decide which pulse you are counting — the one your foot taps — before you name a number.
A daily drill: before you start the metronome, tap 60, 90 and 120 cold, then check. Guess the tempo of songs you hear and look them up. Your guesses will tighten within weeks.
The common mistake is a fast start: excitement pushes the first taps ahead, then you settle. Hear a few beats in your head before the first tap, and begin only when the pulse is already running.
To keep: anchor tempos to things you know — 60 a second, 120 a march, a few favorite songs — and work out the rest by ratios. Feel the pulse first, then tap.
Each hand keeps its own even rhythm; they meet on the beat. For 3 against 2 say "nice cup of tea".
Hi {name}! Drummers and pianists play a different rhythm with each hand. Listen: the low drum plays the beat, the high one plays twice as fast. That is two against one.
Three against two: one hand plays two even notes, the other plays three in the same time. They meet only on the beat.
A handy phrase for three against two is "nice cup of tea". Nice is both hands, cup the right, of the left, tea the right.
Four against three is the same idea, tighter: three on the left, four on the right.
In the exercise you tap two pads. Start slowly, keep each hand even on its own, and let them meet on the beat.

A polyrhythm is two even pulses with different counts sharing the same span of time. In 3 against 2, three evenly spaced notes and two evenly spaced notes fill one cycle. They coincide only on its first note.
The math: 3 against 2 lives on a grid of six. The three-part plays on 1, 3 and 5; the two-part on 1 and 4. Together: both, three, two, three — "nice cup of tea". Slowly now.
4 against 3 lives on a grid of twelve. The four-part plays on 1, 4, 7 and 10; the three-part on 1, 5 and 9. The combined rhythm is both, four, three, four, three, four.
A close cousin is the hemiola: three against two in sequence rather than at once. Six eighths are grouped as two threes, then as three twos, and the bar suddenly seems to change shape.

How to practice: each hand alone first, until it is even. Then speak the combined rhythm. Then put the hands together very slowly, and finally focus on one hand while the other runs by itself. Swap hands too.
The common mistake is letting the two parts melt into one lopsided rhythm, where the three-part bends towards the two. Check each hand on its own: its notes must stay exactly evenly spaced.
In real music, 3 against 2 is the foundation of much West African drumming and of Afro-Cuban grooves. Chopin's Fantaisie-Impromptu sets four notes in the right hand against three in the left.
To keep: a polyrhythm is two even pulses in one span. Find the shared grid, learn the combined pattern, and keep each hand even on its own.
Follow the written rhythm with your eyes as it plays, beat by beat, and notice where the sound stops matching the page.
Hi {name}! Reading rhythm also means catching mistakes. Here is a bar: quarter, two eighths, quarter, quarter.
Now the same bar with one slip: beat three has two eighths instead of a quarter. Did you hear the extra note?
Subtle slips are harder. Two even eighths played long-short, dotted. Listen: first even, then dotted.
Or a note comes a little early, a push. Here beat three arrives a sixteenth early.
In the exercise, follow the written rhythm with your eyes as it plays, beat by beat, and mark where the sound stops matching. You can play each answer again to compare it with what you heard.

Rhythm slips come in a few kinds: a missing or extra note, a wrong length, a note early or late, dotted instead of even, or triplets instead of eighths. Knowing the kinds tells you what to listen for. Here the written bar, then one with a note missing.
Prepare before you listen. Read the bar and count it in your head, and write or picture the beat numbers under the notes. While it plays, track beat numbers, not individual notes.
Three pairs that are easy to confuse: straight eighths split the beat 1 to 1; swing is about 2 to 1; a dotted eighth and a sixteenth is 3 to 1. Listen to all three.
A tie removes an attack, so a tied note sounds like a missing one. Here four quarters, then the same bar with beats two and three tied: you hear only three notes.

An anticipation, or push, brings a note in before its beat, often by an eighth. It is common in pop and only an error if the page does not show it. Here beat three of the second bar comes an eighth early.
The common mistake is listening to the whole bar as one blur. Narrow it down: was beat one right? Beat two? The slip is almost always in one beat, and once you find which, naming it is easy.

In real music, this is how teachers, conductors and band leaders work: they follow the page in time and stop exactly where the sound and the score part ways. The same skill helps you check your own playing.
To keep: count the bar before it plays, follow beat numbers while it plays, and ask which kind of slip it was — missing, extra, long, short, early, late, dotted or triplet.
Drum notation puts the kick low, the snare in the middle and the hi-hat on top. Read one voice at a time, then put them together.
Hi {name}! A drum part is written on one staff: the kick low, the snare in the middle, the hi-hat on top with little crosses. Listen to a basic rock beat.
The hi-hat keeps eighths, the snare hits two and four, and the kick plays one and three. First the hi-hat and snare alone.
Move the kick and the groove changes. Here it adds a kick on the "and" of three.
A fill breaks the groove for a moment, usually on the snare at the end of a bar, and leads back to beat one.
In the exercise you play three pads: kick, snare and hi-hat. Read one line at a time first, then put them together slowly.

Drum notation uses a five-line staff with a neutral percussion clef, and each line or space means a drum, not a pitch. In the most common layout the kick sits in the bottom space, the snare in the third space, and the hi-hat just above the staff with an x notehead.
Usually the hands are written with stems up and the feet with stems down. Cymbals take x noteheads, drums take round ones, and the toms sit on the lines and spaces between snare and kick.
Read the feet on their own first: here the kick on one, three and the "and" of three. Count eighths aloud, "one and two and", and place each kick on its syllable.
Know the basic grooves by sight. Four-on-the-floor puts the kick on every beat, the sound of disco and house. Half-time moves the snare to beat three only, so the same tempo feels twice as slow.
Charts save space with signs. A slash with two dots repeats the previous bar, and "fill" or slashes over a bar ask you to improvise one. Many drum parts are mostly a written groove plus these signs.

The common mistake is mixing up kick and snare, since both are round notes in spaces. A quick check: in rock and pop the snare almost always falls on two and four. If your "snare" lands on one, swap them.
A good drill is to say the groove before you play it: "boom" for kick, "tak" for snare, "ts" for hi-hat. Then tap the hands on a table and the kick with your foot, slowly, adding one voice at a time.
To keep: position tells the drum, the notehead tells drum or cymbal, the stems tell hands or feet. Read one voice at a time, then stack them.
Keep the first bar's speed and length in your head; when something changes, the music stops matching that picture.
Hi {name}! Bands sometimes change tempo or meter in the middle of a song, and you have to notice at once. Listen to this groove: the kick marks every beat one.
Here it suddenly gets faster in bar three. Count the bars on each kick.
And here the meter changes: four beats per bar, then three.
Small changes are harder. Keep a clear picture of the first bar's speed in your head, and compare every bar with it.
In the exercise you hear a groove and answer what changed, or in which bar. React to the feel first, then check by counting.

Three things can change under you: the tempo, the meter, or the feel. A tempo change makes every beat faster or slower. A meter change adds or removes beats in the bar. A feel change, like half time, keeps the beat but moves the groove.
Tempo can change suddenly or gradually. Here it slows suddenly in bar three, from 100 to 84.
A gradual change is harder to catch: an accelerando creeps up bar by bar. Compare each bar with the first one, not with the bar just before it.

The best tell between tempo and meter is the hi-hat. If the space between hat notes changes, the tempo changed. If the hats stay even but the kick comes early or late, the meter changed. Here 4/4 turns into 5/4.
A feel change keeps the beat but moves the backbeat. In half time the snare moves from two and four to three alone, and the groove suddenly feels twice as slow, though the tempo has not changed.
The common mistake is to call a meter change a tempo change, because in both the kick arrives at a surprising moment. Check the hat before you answer.

In real music, many progressive rock pieces switch meters, and Balkan folk music lives in meters like 7/8 and 9/8. Even in simple songs, live bands drift in tempo — noticing it early is how you stay together.
To keep: hold the first bar as your reference. Hats closer or wider means tempo; kick early or late with even hats means meter; snare moved with the same hats means feel.
Your hand is the conductor: it keeps the beat steady while your voice reads the notes. If the voice hesitates, the hand keeps going.
Hi {name}! Singers in a choir read a line and keep the beat at the same time. Here we practice both: sing the notes and tap the beat.
Look at the line: it moves by step and ends at home. One note on every tap.
A half note lasts two taps, and two eighths fit inside one tap. Keep the hand even whatever the voice does.
Your hand is the conductor. If the voice slows down on a hard note, the hand keeps going and the voice catches up.
In the exercise we grade both: the notes you sing, and how steady your taps are. Hear the key first, then start on the count.
Tapping while you sing puts the beat outside your voice. The voice is busy with pitch; the hand holds time. Conductors do the same with a baton, and choirs follow it.
Before you sing, scan the line. Find the key and sing its home note. Look for the highest and lowest notes, the leaps, and the long notes. Ten seconds of looking saves most mistakes.
Match note values to taps: a whole note lasts four taps, a half two, a quarter one, and two eighths share one tap. A dotted quarter lasts a tap and a half, so the next note starts on the "and".
For pitch: a step is the next note of the scale. For a leap, think of the home chord, C, E, G, and hear the target in your head before you sing it.

The common mistake: the hand starts tapping the rhythm of the notes instead of the beat, or it waits for the voice. On a half note the hand taps twice while the voice sings once. The hand never stops, not even in a rest.
A practice order: first tap the rhythm while counting the beats. Then sing the pitches slowly without rhythm. Then put both together at a slow tempo, and only then speed up.

In real music, choir singers, session singers and music students do this daily. Solfège systems and the Kodály method pair singing with movement for the same reason: the body keeps time so the voice can read.
To keep: scan first, find home, and let the hand lead. Tap the beat, not the notes, and let the voice fit its notes onto the taps.
Two triads with no shared note make six notes of a chord scale. Play them as lines (1-3-5, inversions, cells) and as chords (over the root, spread, block).
Hi {name}! A triad pair is two triads that share no note. Over C minor 7: E flat and F.
Six notes, one left out. Every chord has its pair: G and A minor over C major 7 leave out the 11th; G flat and A flat over C7 altered leave out the 3rd.
As a line: one triad, then the other, each a little higher. Root position first, then 3-5-1 and 5-1-3, then alternating inversions.
As harmony: the root and 7th in the left hand, the two triads taking turns on top.
Your turn: pairs in every key, as lines and as chords, measured on your instrument.
Find the pair by the tone it leaves out. Over a dominant, B flat and C leave out the 13th; G minor and A minor leave out the 11th, the avoid note, so they sound inside.
Melodic minor gives strong pairs: F and G over C minor-major, C and D over C7 sharp 11. Harmonic minor gives G and A flat over G7 flat 9.
Intervallic cells: two notes of one triad, two of the other, or each triad open, root, 5th and 10th. The wide leaps are the modern sound.
Spread voicing: one triad’s root and 5th in the left hand, its 3rd as the 10th, the other triad on top. Block chords: every melody note sits on top of its own triad.
Advanced: slide the pair a half step up for a bar, then back. Outside, then inside: the return makes the tension sound planned.
A common mistake is to run the six notes as a scale all the time. Keep the two shapes audible: three notes, then three.
To keep: two triads, six notes, one tone left out. That tone names the colour.
On three strings each triad is one small shape; the pair is two shapes a step apart. On bass, play the pair as arpeggios through the changes.
Hi {name}! On strings 3 to 1, a triad is one grip. Over D minor 7, F and G are two grips side by side.
Climb the neck: the next inversion of F, then of G, then back down. The same on strings 4 to 2.
On bass the pair is an arpeggio: F A C, G B D, over the D minor vamp. It outlines the colour without a chord.
As a line on three strings, play one triad, then the other, each group starting a little higher. On guitar the hand moves up the neck as the line climbs.
Your turn: shapes, lines and the changes in every key, measured on your instrument.
The same two shapes work on strings 4 to 2. Learn each pair on both string sets so you can stay in one area of the neck.
Comping with a pair: the first triad on beat 1, the second on the "and" of 2, over each chord of a ii–V–I. The bass player has the root, so the shapes can stay small.
The six notes as a scale in one position give a hexatonic run. Play it slowly first, then keep the triads audible inside it.
On bass, change the pair with each chord: over D minor 7 F and G, over G7 the pair of its colour, over C major 7 its own. The line outlines the harmony by itself.
Advanced: slide the pair a half step up for one bar, then back. It sounds outside, then resolves inside.
To keep: two small shapes a step apart, six notes, one tone left out.
Each note of a chord moves to a note of the next. Shared notes stay, the rest move by step. Chords a 3rd apart keep two notes, a 5th apart one, a step apart none.
Voice leading is how each note of one chord moves to the next. Good voice leading keeps shared notes and moves the rest by step.
Four voices: soprano on top, then alto, tenor, and the bass at the bottom. Here only the alto moves.
Count what stays. Chords a 3rd apart share two notes, a 5th apart one, a step apart none.
In a ii–V–I, smooth voice leading moves each voice a step or holds it. Jumpy voice leading plays every chord in root position, so the hand leaps.
Drop 2 takes the second note from the top an octave down: the same chords, wider and more open. Your turn.
Why it matters: smooth lines are easier to sing and to play, and the harmony sounds connected instead of stacked. Arrangers check it chord by chord.
In a ii–V–I the 7th of each chord falls a half step to the 3rd of the next. Listen for that slide inside the chords.
To hear which voice moved, sing the top note of both chords, then the bass. If neither changed, the move is inside: alto or tenor.
The common mistake: hearing a new chord and assuming everything moved. Often two notes stay put and only the colour changes. Listen for the notes that ring on.
You hear it in Bach chorales, in choir writing, and in jazz piano and guitar, where drop 2 is the standard voicing under a melody.
To keep: hold the shared notes, move the rest by step, count what stays. Drop 2 is close position opened up: the same notes, the same top.
Land on the note right away, stay in tune, and keep it still to the very end — on easy, flowing breath.
Hi {name}! This unit is all about one note. You hear it, you match it, and you hold it — like parking exactly between the lines.
Breathe in low and easy, then let the sound ride on the air. No pushing: a relaxed, steady flow keeps the pitch steady too.
First I check how fast you land. Hear the difference: a slide up into the note, then a clean start right on it.
Then intonation: how close you are, in cents. A hundred cents make one half step. Here is the note, then the same note a bit flat.
And drift: as the air runs low, notes like to sag. Keep the last second as true as the first.
Level two asks for straight tone: no vibrato at all, a pure, still line, like a choir or an organ pipe. I measure that stillness.
Short notes count too: start each one right on the pitch, with no scoop from below.
Your turn: listen, then sing on "ah" and hold until the bar fills. With headphones the note keeps sounding; without them it stops when you start.

Pitch matching is two skills working together: the ear hears the target, and the voice finds it. Holding adds a third: keeping pitch, tone and loudness steady for the whole note. All three improve with short, regular practice.

Support starts with the inhale. Let the belly, lower ribs and back expand while the shoulders and chest stay quiet. As you sing, keep the ribs gently open so the air leaves slowly and evenly. Singers call this support; it is balance, not force.

The onset is how a note begins. A breathy onset lets air leak before the sound; a hard onset presses the vocal folds shut and pops them open. Aim for a balanced onset: air and sound start together. Think of a silent "h", or start from a hum.

To check yourself, record a few notes and listen back, or cup a hand behind one ear. Not sure if you are flat or sharp? Start slightly below and slide up slowly until the sound locks in. Here is a note a little flat, then in tune.

The two classic faults are the scoop, sliding up into every note, and the sag at the end, when the air runs low. Think of the note from above before you start, and finish while you still have air. A shorter clean note beats a longer sinking one.

Straight tone, with no vibrato, is a style choice: early music, many choirs, a lot of pop. It should come from steady air, not a locked throat. If your neck tightens to keep the note still, let a little vibrato back in.

Look after the instrument. Warm up for a few minutes with hums or lip trills, sip water through the day, and practice in your comfortable middle range. Stop if you feel pain or get hoarse, and rest. Hoarseness that lasts more than two weeks is a reason to see a doctor.
To keep: low, easy breath, a balanced onset, land right on the note, and make the last second as true as the first.
Vibrato is a regular wave around the note, about 5–7 times a second, that a free voice lets happen — then you learn to switch, speed and size it.
Hey {name}! Vibrato is a gentle, regular wave in the pitch. You don't shake it in: it appears when the voice is free and the breath keeps flowing.
The piano can't sing a vibrato, so listen to its speed in clicks: about five to seven waves every second.
Width is how far each wave swings, in cents. Pop voices keep it narrow, classical voices swing wider, but the center always stays on the note.
A good vibrato is regular: every wave the same speed and size. Hear steady pulses, then uneven ones. I score that evenness.
Level three starts straight, lets the vibrato bloom on a cue, then turns it off again. Hold still, then simply relax and let it come.
Later you choose the speed: about five waves a second, or a quicker six. Here is five, then six.
In phrases, vibrato goes only where you want it, usually on long notes. Sing the short ones straight and let the last one shimmer.
Your turn: listen to the note, then sing on "ah" and follow the cues on screen. Keep it easy — never force a wobble.

Vibrato is a regular wave in pitch, with a small wave in loudness riding along. It has two measures: rate, usually about five to seven waves a second, and extent, how far it swings. We hear the center of the wave as the note.
Extent changes with style. Pop and musical-theater singers often keep it narrow; classical singers may swing up to about a half step each way. Either way, the center must sit on the pitch.

A healthy vibrato is not made by the jaw, the tongue or the belly. It appears on its own when the breath flows steadily and the throat is free: a natural pulse of a balanced voice. That is why you allow it rather than build it.

Two things go wrong. A wobble is too slow and too wide, often from fatigue or heavy pressure. A bleat, or tremolo, is too fast and tight, usually from throat tension. Hear about four pulses a second, then eight; good vibrato lives between them.

To find it, hold a comfortable middle note in straight tone, then release: soften the jaw, keep the air moving, think of the sound floating. Another classic drill: alternate slowly between two notes a half step apart, then speed up until it becomes a wave.

The common mistake is forcing it: a shaking jaw or a pumping belly makes a fake, uneven wave. Watch your jaw in a mirror; it should stay still. The other mistake is vibrato on every short note, which blurs the melody.

In opera and art song, vibrato is nearly continuous. Early music and many choirs use it sparingly, to blend. Pop, jazz and musical theater often use a delayed vibrato: the long note starts straight and blooms at the end.
To keep: vibrato is a regular wave of five to seven per second, centered on the note. Let it come from free breath, and choose where it goes.
Hold notes low to high with the same easy breath; in messa di voce, swell soft – loud – soft while the pitch stays put.
Hi {name}! Your range is every note you sing comfortably, from the easy bottom to the easy top. The app measured yours when you glided on "ah".
Now you hold five notes spread across it: low, low-middle, middle, high-middle and high. Three seconds each, steady and in tune.
Low notes like a relaxed, speech-like sound. Don't press down into them; they may be a little quieter, and that's fine.
High notes need steady air, not more squeeze. Keep the jaw and neck loose and let the sound get lighter as you climb.
Level five is messa di voce: one note that grows from soft to loud and back to soft, on a single breath.
The trick: the pitch must not move. Many voices go sharp as they get louder and flat as they fade — hear it go wrong.
I measure how much the loudness changes and how still the pitch stays. Your turn: hear the note, sing on "ah" — and stop if anything strains.

Your full range is every note you can make; your comfortable range, or tessitura, is where the voice sits easily for a whole song. Voice types such as soprano, alto, tenor and bass depend on that comfort zone and on color, not only on the extreme notes.

The voice has registers. Chest voice uses thicker vibrating folds and feels speech-like; head voice and falsetto use thinner folds and feel lighter. Between them is the passaggio, the shift. For many voices a first shift lies roughly between the E and G above middle C.

To smooth the shift, don't carry the heavy low sound upward. Let it thin out gradually as you climb, and narrow the vowel slightly. Sirens on a lip trill, on "ng" or through a straw are classic, gentle tools for this.

Messa di voce, Italian for "placing the voice", is a classic bel canto exercise: one note swells and fades on one breath. It trains the breath and the vocal folds to change loudness without changing pitch.

Why does pitch drift? More breath pressure tends to raise pitch, and as you fade, the voice tends to sag. So as you grow, think slightly down; as you fade, keep the energy up. Start with a small swell, soft to medium and back, over four to six seconds.

The common mistake is reaching: lifting the chin, raising the larynx and pushing volume for high notes, or pressing the chin down for low ones. Keep the head level and the neck long, and let high notes be lighter and low notes quieter.

Range grows slowly, over months. Warm up before you visit the edges, spend only short moments there, and come back to the middle. If a note hurts, scratches or leaves you hoarse, stop: tomorrow's voice matters more than today's top note.
To keep: one easy breath across the whole range, lighter as you rise, and a swell that changes loudness, never pitch.
Glides are smooth and land exactly; melodies are right, in tune and connected; leaps land without overshooting; fast passages stay with the beat.
Hey {name}! Now your voice starts to move. First, glides: one smooth slide between two notes, like a siren, with no steps on the way.
The piano can only give you the two ends. I check that your slide is even, always moving one way, and lands right on the target.
Then melodies: you hear a short tune and sing it back. Every note counts: the right pitch, in tune, and connected.
Connected means legato: one line of sound, the air never stops. Move quickly from note to note instead of sliding slowly between them.
Wider intervals come next: thirds, fifths, even an octave. Picture the target before you jump, and don't overshoot it.
Finally, faster transitions: the same moves with more notes per beat. Now rhythm counts too, so stay with the pulse.
Your turn: listen, then sing it back on "ah" or "la". Extra listens are allowed; they cost a little melodic-memory rating, never your pitch rating.

A glide, or portamento, is a continuous slide in pitch. As an exercise, the siren warms up the whole voice and smooths the register shifts. As expression, a slide is a spice: lovely now and then, tiring on every note.
Legato means the air keeps flowing and the vowel stays the same while the pitch changes quickly and cleanly. Compare connected notes with detached ones, staccato, where each note stops short.

Before a leap, hear the target inside before you sing it. Anchor on the home chord: 1, 3, 5 and the octave. Going up, prepare lightness instead of reaching with the neck; going down, keep the brightness so the low note doesn't land flat.

Know the usual traps. Big leaps up tend to fall short; descending scales tend to sink; repeated notes tend to sag. On the way down, think up a little. Hear a falling line that sinks, then the same line in tune.

Fast passages need a light, flexible voice. Keep the air moving and avoid putting an "h" before each note. Practice slowly with a metronome, in small groups, then raise the tempo step by step. Accuracy first, speed second.
To sing a melody back, remember its contour, up or down, step or leap, and where it sits in the key. Chunk longer tunes into short phrases. Notice the last note: it often lands on 1, 3 or 5.
Many notes on one syllable is called melisma. You hear it in Handel's Messiah, in gospel and R&B runs, and in Middle Eastern singing, where fast, exact ornaments are part of the style.
To keep: connect the notes with steady air, hear each target before you go, watch the way down, and build speed only on accuracy.
Every mode is the same ladder with a few rungs moved — hear which ones, and sing each step clean and connected.
Hi {name}! A scale is a ladder of notes from home to home. Major is the bright one: sing it with even steps, each one clean.
Natural minor lowers the 3rd, 6th and 7th: the same climb, but darker.
Modes move just one or two rungs. Mixolydian is major with a lowered 7th — hear it near the top.
Pentatonic skips the half steps: five notes, no clashes. It's the sound of folk songs and blues.
At first you hear the whole scale and echo it. Later you hear only the starting note, and the scale has to come from inside you.
The top levels go up in one mode and down in another. Here: up in major, down in minor. Feel which notes change on the way down.
Your turn: listen, then sing it up — and back down if asked — on "la" or note names. I grade the right notes, intonation and clean, connected steps.
A scale is a set of notes in step order, from the tonic to its octave. Major follows the pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. The half steps, 3 to 4 and 7 to 8, give it its shape.

Minor has three forms. Natural minor lowers 3, 6 and 7. Harmonic minor raises 7 again, for a leading tone, leaving a wide step between 6 and 7. Melodic minor raises 6 and 7 going up and traditionally comes down natural.

The modes start the major pattern from different notes. Each has a color note: Dorian is minor with a raised 6, Phrygian minor with a lowered 2, Lydian major with a raised 4, Mixolydian major with a lowered 7. Here is G Dorian: listen for E natural.
To hear a mode, sing it over a held tonic, a drone. The color note rubs or glows against it. Here is G Lydian over a G drone: the raised 4, C sharp, floats.

Sing scales on one vowel or in solfège, slowly at first. Most intonation trouble lives in the half steps: singers make them too wide. Keep 3 to 4 and 7 to 8 small, with the leading tone close to home.
Major pentatonic uses 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6. Minor pentatonic uses 1, ♭3, 4, 5 and ♭7, the backbone of blues and rock solos. Add a ♭5 and you have the blues scale.
The common mistake is slipping back into major halfway through a mode, because the ear knows major best. Anchor on 1, 3 and 5, and aim deliberately at the color note.

Modes are everywhere: Scarborough Fair is usually sung in Dorian, The Simpsons theme is Lydian, and much rock and folk is Mixolydian. To keep: the same ladder with different rungs moved; know which ones.
Keep your own note in your head while another one sounds: intervals over a held note, the missing chord note, then a line in thirds or sixths.
Hey {name}! Harmony means singing a different note that fits with the one you hear. The piano holds one note; you sing the other.
Start with intervals over a held note. A fifth above sounds open and hollow; a third above sounds sweet.
Keep your note in your head, not your ear on the piano. If you drift toward the held note, you end up singing along with it.
Next, a chord with a hole in it: root and fifth sound, and you sing the missing third. Later, any note can be the missing one.
Then a whole line against a melody: a third above it, later a sixth or a third below. Two lines moving together, like a duet.
Use headphones here: the app keeps playing while you sing, and the mic must hear only you. I check that your note is in tune and steady.
Your turn: listen to the held note or the melody, then sing your part on "ah" — in tune, steady, and your own.

Harmony is two or more pitches at once. The most stable intervals are the unison, the octave and the fifth. Thirds and sixths are the sweet ones, which is why most harmony parts live there. Seconds and sevenths clash and want to move.
A part a third above follows the key, so its thirds are sometimes major, sometimes minor. Over C, D, E, F, G in C major, the second voice sings E, F, G, A, B.
Move that part down an octave and it becomes a sixth below. Sixths sound warm and open, a favorite for a lower voice under the tune.
When two voices are in tune, they blend and almost fuse into one sound. Slightly out, you hear a slow beating, a wobble in the sound. Hear a third in tune, then one that is a little sharp.

Practice in layers: sing the melody, then your part alone, then your part against the melody. Know your degree in the chord, for example the 3. Covering one ear lightly helps you hear yourself inside the blend.
The usual mistakes: drifting into the melody, and leaving the key by singing a major third where the key wants a minor one. Think in scale degrees, not in fixed distances.

Close harmony in thirds is the sound of the Everly Brothers, barbershop quartets and countless pop backing vocals. Unaccompanied groups often tune major thirds slightly lower than the piano, so the chord rings.
To keep: thirds and sixths, shaped by the key; your note held in your head; blend until the beating stops.
Find home from the tonic, read steps and skips from the staff, and keep the written rhythm — no melody to copy.
Hi {name}! Sight-singing means reading a melody and singing it without hearing it first. You get only the home note and a count-in.
Find home first. Every note on the staff is a step or a skip away from it. Steps move to the very next line or space.
Thirds skip one: line to line, or space to space.
Rhythm matters as much as pitch. A quarter note gets one beat, a half note two, and eighths go two to a beat.
In minor, watch for the raised seventh: the leading tone that pulls up to home.
Sing on "la", note names or do-re-mi, whatever helps you. If one note slips, keep going: the next beat is a fresh chance.
Your turn: read the melody, hear the tonic and count-in, then sing it in rhythm. I grade the right notes, intonation and timing.

Sight-singing is reading pitch and rhythm and singing them with no instrument. It rests on relative pitch: knowing how each note relates to the tonic. Some read with movable do, where do is always home; in Israel most musicians use fixed note names; numbers work too.
Before you sing, scan for half a minute: key and time signature, the first note's degree, the highest and lowest notes, the leaps and any tricky rhythms. Then set the key by singing 1, 3, 5 and back.

Steps are easy; leaps need an anchor. Leaps inside the home chord, 1, 3 and 5, are the easiest. For any other leap, find the nearest chord note and step from it. Here, 1 leaps to 5, then steps down home.

Keep the pulse going inside you, tapping or conducting lightly. Count the subdivisions in long and dotted notes: a dotted quarter lasts one and a half beats. Never stop to fix a note; the beat moves on.
In minor, sing the tonic triad first: 1, ♭3, 5. Watch for the raised 7, and in harmonic minor for the wide step from 6 to 7: in A minor, F to G sharp, three half steps.
The common mistake is singing the right shape in the wrong key: the intervals drift and home moves. When you feel lost, hear 1 in your head and find your degree from it.
Practice a little every day with simple tunes, folk songs and hymns, slightly below your level, so you can keep going. Read a new melody each time; the skill is reading, not memory.
To keep: scan, set the key with 1, 3, 5, anchor every leap, and keep the beat whatever happens.
Ornaments are quick, light decorations that return to a steady main note; dynamics change the loudness while the pitch stays put.
Hey {name}! Ornaments are tiny decorations around one main note. Quick and light: the main note is still the star. First, a grace note — a flick from above.
An upper mordent goes main, up, main — fast — then holds. The lower mordent dips below instead.
A turn circles the note: above, the note, below, the note — quick and even.
A trill alternates fast between the main note and the one above, then settles on the main note.
I check the shape — the right notes in order — the speed, and that the main note lands in tune and stays steady. Think light and loose, not loud.
The other half is dynamics: a crescendo grows from soft to loud, a decrescendo fades, and the swell does both. The pitch stays exactly where it is.
Your turn: listen, then sing on "ah" — the ornament quick and clean, then hold the main note. For dynamics, shape it with your breath, never by pushing.
Ornaments decorate a main note. Some are written as small notes or symbols; in Baroque music singers were also expected to add their own, especially on repeats.

Two small notes look alike. The acciaccatura, with a slash, is crushed in as fast as possible. The appoggiatura, a leaning note, takes real time from the main note, falls on the beat and resolves by step. Hear the acciaccatura, then the appoggiatura.

Names vary. In Baroque terms the mordent dips to the note below and back; the version that flicks to the note above is the upper, or inverted, mordent. A turn uses both neighbors: above, main, below, main.

A trill alternates the main note with the scale note above, a whole or half step depending on the key. In Baroque and Classical music it usually starts on the upper note; later music often starts on the main note. Many trills close with a small turn.

Sing ornaments light and on flowing air, with a relaxed throat and no "h" before each note. Learn them slowly and evenly, then speed up. For a trill, alternate two notes in a steady rhythm and speed up only while it stays even.

Dynamics run from pianissimo, very soft, to fortissimo, very loud: pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff. Change loudness with breath energy, not by squeezing the throat, and keep the pitch level: louder tends to go sharp, softer tends to go flat.

The common mistake is a heavy, slow ornament that hides the main note. Style matters too: trills and appoggiaturas belong to Baroque and Classical arias, while pop, gospel and R&B decorate with riffs and runs.
To keep: ornaments are quick and light and return to a steady main note; dynamics change loudness, never pitch.
Tab shows string and fret; hear the tonic and count-in, then play each note clean and in time.
Hi {name}! Grab your guitar. You read a short melody in tab and play it, and the mic listens to the notes and the rhythm.
Tab has six lines, one per string; the top line is the thin high E string. The number is the fret to press, and 0 means the open string.
Read left to right, like words. Here every note comes one at a time, so a melody can cross strings.
You hear the tonic, then four clicks. Start right after the fourth click, at that tempo, and give each note its written length.
Let each note ring clearly and mute the strings you aren't playing, so the mic hears one clean note at a time.
Your turn: read the tab, hear the tonic and count-in, then play. I grade the right notes, their tuning and your timing — so tune up first!

Tab shows where to play, not what the note is called. The six lines are the six strings: the top line is the high E string, the bottom line the low E. A number is a fret, and numbers stacked vertically are played together.

Standard tuning, from low to high, is E, A, D, G, B, E. Each fret raises a string by a half step, so the 5th fret of one string matches the next open string, except on the G string, where the 4th fret matches B.
The same pitch lives in several places. The G above middle C is the 3rd fret on the high E string, or the 8th fret on the B string. Tab chooses the place for you; the staff tells you only the pitch.
Plain tab often leaves out rhythm, so read it beside the staff or listen first. Count the beat aloud, start right after the count-in, and give each note its full length.
For a clean note, press just behind the fret with the fingertip, not on top of it, and use only as much pressure as the note needs. Keep the other fingers off the strings that should ring.
Tab also has symbols: h for a hammer-on, p for a pull-off, a slash for a slide, b for a bend, and x for a muted string.

Common mistakes: reading the tab upside down, as if the top line were the low string; rushing the long notes; and playing out of tune because the guitar was never tuned. Tune first, then play slowly and in time.
To keep: lines are strings, numbers are frets, the top line is the high E. Tune, count in, and let each note ring for its full length.
Remember the shape, not the letters: chunk the growing chain into small groups and sing or tap it back.
Hey {name}! Echo Chain is a memory game. I play a short melody and you repeat it. Every round the chain grows by one note.
The notes come from a few pads: 1, 2, 3 and 5 of the key. Learn their sound, and the chain gets easier to follow.
Don't memorize letters. Remember the shape: up, a little down, a jump, back home.
Group the chain in small chunks, like a phone number: three notes, a breath, three more.
Sing it back or tap the pads. When you sing, each note counts within 80 cents by default — almost a half step either way. You can tighten that in settings.
Your turn: listen to the chain, then sing or tap it back. How long can you make it?

Echo Chain trains short-term musical memory: holding a sequence of pitches in mind and reproducing it. Most people hold only about four to seven items at once, so a long chain needs a strategy, not just effort.
Hear each pad as a scale degree. 1 is home and restful, 3 is bright, 5 is open and stable, 2 is a passing step that wants to move. Knowing their roles turns sounds into meaning.
Contour is the melody's shape: which way each move goes, and whether it steps or leaps. Hear 1, 3, 2, 5: up a skip, down a step, up a leap.

Chunking packs several notes into one unit. Group the chain in threes or fours, and notice patterns you already know, like 1 2 3 or the chord 1 3 5. Each familiar pattern takes the memory space of a single item.
While the chain plays, sing along silently in your head. Then, before you answer, replay it inside once, calmly.

The common mistake is rushing: answering at once while the last notes are still fuzzy, or trying to remember the newest note on its own. Each round repeats the old chain, so rebuild it from the start every time.

This is how musicians learn by ear: call and response in gospel and blues, a teacher singing a phrase for a student to copy, a band picking up a riff. To keep: degrees, contour, chunks and a silent replay.
Read the whole statement, then hunt for the one detail that could be a bluff — bluffs are always a near miss.
Hi {name}! Truth or Bluff is music theory as a race. A statement appears — is it true, or a bluff? No sound needed, so you can play it anywhere.
True! G major has one sharp, F sharp. Now this one: A C E is an A major triad. Bluff — C is a minor third above A, so it is A minor.
Bluffs are sneaky: always a near miss. One sharp too many, a minor third called major, the wrong relative minor. Check the one detail that matters.
Pick your topics — keys, intervals, chords, scales, rhythm, harmony, jazz, or the interval trios, also by ear — and a level: easy, medium or hard.
Solo you have sixty seconds; streaks earn bonus points and a wrong answer costs two seconds — and shows you why. Or play a friend on this device, or online.
Your turn: read, think, and call it — truth or bluff. Fast, but not careless.

Truth or Bluff tests theory facts you can check in your head: key signatures, intervals, chords, scales and note values. Each statement has one detail that decides it; your job is to find that detail fast.
Keys: the order of sharps is F, C, G, D, A, E, B, and each new sharp key is a fifth higher: G has one, D two, A three. Flats run the other way, B, E, A, D, G, C, F: F has one, B flat two.

Intervals: count the letters for the number, then the half steps for the quality. C to E is a third with four half steps, so major; C to E flat has three, so minor. A bluff often keeps the number and swaps the quality.

Chords: check the third, then the fifth. Major has a major third and a perfect fifth, minor a minor third and a perfect fifth, diminished a minor third and a diminished fifth, augmented a major third and an augmented fifth. A C E is minor; A C E flat is diminished.

Relatives: every major key shares its signature with the minor key a minor third below. C major and A minor have no sharps or flats; G major and E minor share one sharp. A favorite bluff names the minor a major third below.
Strategy: read the whole statement before you answer, since the bluff can hide in the last word as easily as the first. If unsure, check the one deciding detail with a rule, then commit.
To keep: find the deciding detail, whether the number of sharps, the size of the third or the relative key, and check it with a rule, not a feeling.
A blues chord has four notes: root, third, fifth, flat seventh. Sing its third or seventh — the guide tones; they move by half steps from chord to chord.
A blues chord has four notes: root, third, fifth and a flat seventh.
The third and the seventh are the guide tones. They name the chord.
The root belongs to the bass. Your notes are the third and seventh.
From C7 to F7, both move by a half step.
So a guide-tone line barely moves: E, E-flat, E.
Your turn: one guide tone per chord, a half note each, in slow swing.
Over G7, the five chord, the guide tones are B and F. Back to C7, B falls to B-flat and F falls to E: half steps again.
Why these two: the third says major or minor, and the seventh says the chord wants to move. Together they spell the harmony even with no piano.
Find them fast: from the root, the third is two whole steps up, and the flat seventh is a whole step below the next root.
A common mistake is singing the root because it feels safe. Leave the root to the bass; the guide tones are what make your line sound like the changes.
A practice tip: hum the line slowly over the chords before you swing it. When the half steps feel automatic, sing it in time with the band.
Where it lives: every jazz line leans on guide tones, and scat solos aim for them on strong beats. Recap: third and seventh, half steps, the root to the bass.
Hear it once, keep it, sing it back in time; sing an interval from a given note; find the rule of a sequence and sing the bar that was not played.
A singer’s ear: hear it once, keep it, sing it back.
Sing it back: hear the whole phrase before you breathe in.
Copy the rhythm as well as the notes. Timing counts first.
Intervals from a note: hear one note, then sing a third above it.
Measure from the given note, not from what you sang before.
The bar not played: a pattern climbs two bars; you sing the third.
Your turn: echo, then intervals, then the missing bar.
Hear it inside before you sing it. If you can hum the phrase silently in your head, your voice can find it.
An interval has a size you can feel: a third is a small, sweet step up; a fifth is open and wide. Measure the gap itself.
In a sequence every bar is the first one moved by one step. Find the rule, then use it once more. Here the answer: E, F, G, E.
The common mistake: starting to sing while the phrase is still playing. Wait for the end, then come in on the beat.
Where it lives: learning songs by ear, finding a harmony part, and the aural tests of graded singing exams.
A practice tip: sing back short phrases from songs you know, then from songs you don't. Record yourself and compare: the timing first, then the notes.
Recap: listen to the end, keep the rhythm, measure from the given note, and find the rule of the pattern.
Plan where you breathe, keep the note steady to the end of the breath, and cross your break without a crack.
Hi {name}! A singer is judged at the end of the breath: does the note still stand still, or does it sink?
So the last quarter of a long note counts double. Spend less air at the start, and the end stays easy.
A breath is heard as a silence of a quarter second or more. In a breath plan you breathe at the marks, and only there.
Most voices have a spot where the sound wants to flip — the break. A slow siren on "oo" shows where yours is.
The microphone hears a break as a sudden jump, a gap, or a sudden change in loudness. Chest, mix and head voice are real, but a phone cannot tell them apart — so only the smoothness counts.
Breath support is not pushing. It is a slow, even release of air, so the note has fuel all the way to its end.
Breathe low and quiet, through the nose or the mouth. A noisy gasp steals time from the music and dries the throat.
Plan breaths where the words or the music pause — at the end of a phrase — never in the middle of a long note.
The levels grow from ten seconds on one note to twenty seconds on a fading phrase. Rest between takes.
For the break, sing softer and on narrower vowels as you go up. Let the sound get lighter instead of louder.
Never push to reach a high note. If it hurts or your voice is hoarse for days, rest — and see a voice doctor if it stays.
A common mistake is to take a huge breath and lock it in. Take a normal breath instead, and let it out slowly and evenly, like a long, quiet sigh.
To recap: steady to the end of the breath, breathe only where you planned, and cross the break lighter instead of louder.
Keep the key in your ear when nothing plays, and find any chord tone by its name when a chord does.
Sing a song alone and the key slowly moves — usually down. That slow slide is called drift.
The app compares each phrase with the first one. Your notes inside a phrase are checked apart from that slide.
The trick: before a phrase ends, hear the home note in your head, then land on it.
With a chord, the chord keeps sounding, one tone is missing, and you are asked for it by name: the 3rd, the 5th, the 7th.
Tensions are the jazz colours above the chord: the 9th, the 11th, the 13th. Here is a 9th on top of a major seventh chord.
Research on singing alone finds a median error of about twenty cents, and a clear drift in about one take in five. It is normal — and trainable.
Fine tuning into a drone trains the same ear: the beating between your voice and the drone slows down and stops when you are exact.
Sing the tonic again after a phrase, with nothing played between. If you come back flat, you were sinking on the way.
In a chord, the 3rd tells major from minor and the 7th gives the jazz colour. Those two are the guide tones you will use in scat.
Leaps past the sixth are found through the octave: a seventh is an octave less a step, a ninth an octave plus a step. Each note counts only in its own octave.
Headphones help in every chord level: the chord stays out of the microphone, so only your voice is measured.
A common mistake is to listen to yourself only. Keep listening to the key in your head, and compare every phrase ending with the very first note.
To recap: drift is the slow slide of the key, note error is the tuning inside a phrase, and chord tones are found by name and settled fast.
Loudness steps, accents and arcs, a late narrow vibrato, scoops, falls and bends — each with a shape the microphone can see.
Steps of loudness — soft, medium, loud — need a clear difference: about four decibels each.
An accent is one note clearly above its neighbours. A phrase has an arc: up to its peak note, then softer.
There is no absolute volume on a phone: only the change inside one take counts. Keep it still, about a forearm away.
Jazz singers start a long note straight and let a narrow vibrato bloom near its end — about 15 to 40 cents each way.
A scoop starts a little below and arrives fast. A fall drops away at the end. The blue-note bend slides from the minor third up toward the major third.
Dynamics live in the breath, not the throat. A crescendo is more air with the same shape of the mouth.
Keep the pitch still while the loudness moves. Most singers go sharp when louder and flat when softer.
In a song, the chorus usually lifts: the app checks that it is at least three decibels louder than the verse.
Vibrato on purpose: on the last note of a phrase, never on every note. In close harmony, none at all, so the chord rings clean.
A ghost note is there but much softer — eight decibels or more below its neighbours. It makes a line swing.
Tone colour — breathy, bright, twang, belt — is real, but a phone microphone cannot measure it fairly, so it is never scored.
To recap: loudness is relative to you in one take, accents and arcs give a phrase its shape, and jazz vibrato comes late, narrow and on purpose.
On top, laid back or rushing — judged from the average of eight notes or more, after your phone delay is removed.
Sing "dah" right with the click. Your phone hears you a little late, so first we measure that delay once.
Rests and pickups: come in on the "and", exactly. Anticipations push the next downbeat an eighth early.
Swing eighths are long-short: "doo-bah". The clicks move to 2 and 4, like a jazz drummer's hi-hat.
Laid back means a little behind every click, evenly. One note is never judged — a sung onset is only good to a few hundredths of a second.
The inner clock: the click stops for four bars. Keep singing on the beat; it comes back on a downbeat and tells you where you are.
Why calibrate? A phone adds tens of milliseconds between your voice and the app. Bluetooth headphones add two hundred or more — use wired ones, or calibrate with them.
Articulate for timing work: "dah", "doo-bah". A clear consonant gives a clear start; a legato vowel blurs it.
A swing ratio of two to one is a triplet feel. At fast tempos players flatten it — the app expects that.
Back-phrasing, the way Billie Holiday did it: start a phrase late, then catch up so the last note lands on its beat.
Bebop lines put chord tones on the beats and chromatic notes between them, swung. Each note is checked for pitch and for its start.
A common mistake is to rush the notes after a rest. Feel the rest as part of the music, count it, and come in on its far edge.
To recap: calibrate once, articulate clearly, aim for an even average, and trust the inner clock when the click goes quiet.
Hear the run, sing it back on one vowel: slow and clean first, then 80, 100 and 120% of full tempo. Each note is checked for pitch and for its start.
A run is a fast line on one vowel. Start with five notes, up and down, at sixty percent of full tempo.
Speed comes from accuracy. Pass it clean, then the same run returns at eighty, a hundred and a hundred and twenty percent.
Then the shapes singers use: pentatonic and blues runs, and turns: the note above, the note, the note below, the note.
Last, a melisma: many notes on one syllable, as in Handel. Keep the vowel open and the air moving; no breaks between notes.
Your turn: listen to the run, count in with the click, and sing it back. Four notes to each click.
Sing runs lightly. Pushing more air makes them heavy and slow; a small, bright sound moves faster. Keep the jaw loose and let the vowel stay the same from the first note to the last.
Practice with the tempo ladder. At sixty percent every note should be clear and in tune. Move up only when it is; a run that smears at full speed was not clean when slow.
Pentatonic runs leave out the half steps, so they fall quickly and safely: the sound of soul and R and B. The blues run adds the flat five, a note to place on purpose, not to slide through.
A turn circles one note: the step above, the note, the step below, the note. In a gospel run it decorates the start; in Baroque music it ornaments a long note.
Tone colour and the vowel are not graded. What is graded: the right notes, each starting with the click, and smooth joins between them. The first levels are lenient on tuning; timing counts most.
To recap: one vowel, a light sound, clean at sixty percent before speed. Then the bebop lines at the top of this family put the same agility on swung eighths.
Every phrase gets a score — pitch, time, breath. The weakest one is looped slower until it passes, then the whole song again.
Every great jazz singer can sing a simple song perfectly. Start here: the band plays, the notes scroll, your voice is drawn on top.
A phrase is half pitch, a third time and a fifth breath: no gap inside it where the music has none.
The weakest phrase is looped a little slower. When it passes, try it at full tempo, then sing the whole song again.
Words are never graded — sing "la", numbers or names. With headphones the band stays out of the microphone.
The songs are ours, written for the app, or traditional tunes that belong to everyone — with a grown-up band: pop, bossa, ballad, rock.
The same five meters follow you from a folk song to a ballad: pitch, time, breath, dynamics and a steady tone.
Time is checked on clear notes only: those after a rest, and those that change pitch. Repeated notes on one vowel are not judged one by one.
Unaccompanied, from memory: you hear the key once, then sing alone. The app checks that you stay in the key to the end.
Our own songs have a verse and a chorus. Lift the chorus — the app wants it at least three decibels louder.
The performance take is one pass with no loops. It is scored and kept, like a recital card you can listen back to.
A common mistake is to sing the whole song again and again. Loop only the weak phrase, slower, until it passes — then put the song back together.
To recap: every phrase is scored on pitch, time and breath, the weakest is looped, and every phrase must pass for the level.
First the head as written; then move its rhythm — anticipate, delay, sit behind the beat — and keep its long notes.
A jazz head is a melody over chords. Singers rarely sing it as written: they phrase it.
Interpreting is graded honestly: the long notes must still be there, and a third of the onsets must move from the page.
A laid-back chorus sits a little behind the band, evenly — forty to a hundred and twenty milliseconds.
A ballad is long, steady notes and one breath per phrase. A bossa is soft, straight eighths, and no vibrato.
Our heads are written for the app, or are traditional tunes with our own jazz chords — no copied melodies.
Each level says what it measures: pitch per phrase, time, the long notes kept, the average lateness — never the words.
Three ways to move a melody: anticipate a note by an eighth, delay it, or hold it over the bar line.
Keep the shape: the long notes and the phrase endings are the skeleton of the song. Move what is between them.
Forms you will meet: the twelve-bar blues, the sixteen-bar spiritual, a minor two-five cycle, rhythm changes, a ballad and a bossa.
Behind the beat is judged as an average over eight notes or more, never note by note, because a phone onset wobbles a little.
Real titles of copyrighted standards appear only as chord charts. Their melodies wait for a licence — that is the law, and we respect it.
A common mistake is to change the notes instead of the rhythm. First move the timing; keep the pitches of the head until your phrasing is sure.
To recap: sing the head as written, then interpret it while keeping its long notes, sit behind the beat evenly, and shape ballads and bossas.
Scat is graded on rhythm and on landing chord tones — never on the syllables you choose.
Start with rhythm on one note: the app plays two bars, you answer with the same rhythm.
Guide tones are the 3rd and the 7th of each chord. Sing them through a two-five-one and you hear the changes move.
Then free lines — with a chord tone on beat one of every chord, and end on one.
A chromatic approach reaches a chord tone from a half step above or below — the sound of bebop.
Doo, bah, dee, dat — choose any syllables. Only the notes, their timing and where they land are counted.
Headphones keep the band out of the microphone, so only your line is heard and checked.
The order follows how jazz singers are taught: copy rhythms, then embellish a melody, then guide tones, then free lines that land.
Before guide tones you need the ear: the chord-tone levels of the singer's ear, and harmony singing.
Landing means beat one of each chord. Between the landings, anything goes — scale notes, chromatic notes, rests.
Leave space. A rest is part of a phrase, and short phrases with clear endings swing more than a stream of notes.
Over the blues, where C7 moves to F7, the 3rd of C7 (E) slides down a half step to the 7th of F7 (E♭) — a guide-tone line.
A common mistake is to fill every beat with notes. Fewer notes that land well sound better than many that wander.
To recap: copy the rhythm first, sing the guide tones through the changes, land a chord tone on every beat one, and approach it by a half step.
Read the melody while the band plays only the chords; on a lead sheet swing the eighths and hold the ties. Quarter tones are sung note by note.
Now the melody is never played to you. The band gives the chords and the count-in — the notes come from the page.
The trick: hear the first note against the first chord before you start. It is usually the root, the 3rd or the 5th.
A lead sheet is the jazz page: the melody, with chord symbols above. Eighth notes are swung, long-short.
A tie joins two notes into one: sing it once and hold it through. A note tied over the bar line is an anticipation.
And the notes between the piano keys: a quarter tone is half a semitone — the colour of the maqam.
Sing each of those notes on its own "da", so the microphone hears every one. The quarter tones must sit within fifteen cents.
Low voices read in the bass clef: the app switches by itself when your range starts at A2 or lower.
Look one bar ahead while you sing. Your eyes lead, your voice follows. Read the shape first — up by step, down by a leap — then the exact notes.
Each phrase is scored on pitch and on time against the written rhythm, exactly as with the songs.

Maqam players place quarter tones a little differently from town to town; the app takes the exact middle, so stay close to it. Listen: Bayati starts on a neutral step, between a half step and a whole step.
A common mistake is to stop when a note goes wrong. Keep going with the band, and fix it on the next take.
To recap: hear the first note in the chord, read a bar ahead, swing the eighths, hold the ties, and give each quarter tone its own syllable.
Develop a motif, embellish a head, accent the off-beats, trade twos and fours — and lead the band when it follows you.
A motif is a small idea of three notes. Repeat it, move it up a step, or start it later — the listener follows the story.
Embellishing a head keeps its long notes and adds neighbours around them. The melody stays recognisable.
Bebop syllables put the weight on the off-beat: doo-BAH, doo-BAH. The microphone hears that accent as loudness.
Trading: the band plays two or four bars, you answer in yours. Its next answer picks up your idea — pick up its idea too.
Colla voce means "with the voice": you sing freely and the band changes chords when you reach each bar.
In a blues call and response, sing the call, let its last note fall, and leave space for the band to answer.
Two different developments of the motif pass the level: a repeat and a sequence, or a sequence and a shift in time.
In trading, every turn must be used: at least three notes. Chord tones on the strong beats, and the eighths on the swing grid.
In the AABA chorus, the first three sections are sung as written; only the last A is yours to interpret.
In colla voce, take your time but keep each phrase in tune: only the notes you reach in tune count.
Your own song: open a recording of yourself, with the voice clear. The app finds its melody and scores you against it, phrase by phrase.
A common mistake is to start a new idea in every turn. Keep one idea and change it a little — that is a conversation.
To recap: develop one motif, keep the long notes when you embellish, accent the off-beats, use every turn, and let the band follow you in a ballad.
Keep the common tone, move the other voices to the nearest notes: C–E–G to C–F–A, not a jump to F–A–C.
Hi {name}! Play C major, then F major, both in root position. The whole hand jumps, and it sounds like blocks.
Now look for a note the two chords share. C is in both. Keep it where it is.
The other two voices move to the nearest notes of F: E up to F, G up to A. Three semitones in all, and F comes out in second inversion.
To G: C steps down to B, F down to D, A down to G. Then back home to C. Every voice moves by a step or stays.
Your turn: you see only the chord names and the first chord. Find the nearest inversion each time. The app counts how far your voices moved.
Why it matters: a pianist or guitarist who jumps block to block sounds like a beginner. Small moves make the chords sing like a choir, each voice its own line.
The rule of thumb: common tones stay, the other voices go to the nearest chord tone. C to A minor keeps two notes and moves one.
When no note is shared, like F to G, move all three voices by step, the opposite way from the bass. The bass goes up, the hand comes down.
Add the root in the left hand. The bass may leap, it is the floor. The right hand keeps moving by step above it.
On the guitar it is the same on three strings: the shapes change, the hand barely moves along the neck.
Try I, vi, IV, V the same way: C, then A minor keeps C and E, F keeps C and A, G moves everything by a step. Listen for one smooth line on top.
To keep: find what stays, step what moves, and let the bass do the leaping.
In ii–V–I the 7th of each chord falls a step to the 3rd of the next, and the 3rd stays as the next 7th.
Hi {name}! Two notes tell a 7th chord who it is: the 3rd and the 7th. D minor 7: F and C.
Move to G7. F stays: it is the 7th of G7. C falls a half step to B, the 3rd of G7.
Then C major 7: F, the 7th of G7, falls to E. B stays as the 7th of C. One note moves at each change.
That is the rule: when the root falls a fifth, the 7th steps down to the next 3rd. Two lines that hardly move, and the whole progression is there.
Your turn: the root in the left hand, the 3rd and 7th in the right. Start from the written pair and move one note at a time.
Start with the 7th below instead: C and F over D. Then B and F over G, then B and E over C. The same rule, the other shape.
Jazz players comp with just these two notes and a bass. It sounds full because the ear fills in the rest.
A common mistake: moving the 7th up. C up to D over G7 loses the pull. Let it fall.
In minor the same: D half-diminished, G7, C minor. The 7th falls to the 3rd, now E flat.
Why the 7th falls: it is the restless note of the chord. Over the next root it becomes the 3rd, the note that names the new chord. The tension leaves by the shortest road.
In a longer turnaround, I, vi, ii, V, the same two lines keep going. Every chord adds one small step, and the bass carries the roots underneath.
To keep: two notes, one moves, and the 7th always steps down.
Four notes inside an octave: ii–V–I alternates root position and second inversion, two voices moving each time.
Hi {name}! Now all four notes of the chord, close together. D minor 7 in root position: D, F, A, C.
To G7: D and F stay. A steps down to G, C falls to B. G7 comes out in second inversion: D, F, G, B.
To C major 7: G and B stay, D steps down to C, F to E. Root position again. Four semitones, then two.
Start from second inversion and the pattern flips: second, root, second. Either way, half the hand stays still.
Your turn, in every key. Then around the cycle of fifths: eight chords, each a short step down, the hand staying in one place.
Cmaj7 · Fmaj7 · Bm7♭5 · Em7 · Am7 · Dm7 · G7 · Cmaj7
