Around the cycle every root falls a fifth, so every 7th falls to the next 3rd. The voicings slowly sink: that is fine, start a little higher.
Count your motion: from D minor 7 to G7 the smallest move is three semitones. If you moved seven, one voice jumped.
A chain of two-fives down by whole steps works the same: D minor 7, G7, C minor 7, F7, and on. Each pair a new key.
Watch out for the 7th going up out of habit. Over the dominant it wants to fall.
You never have to think which inversion comes next. Keep the common tones, step the rest, and the right inversion appears by itself. The chord names are enough.
In minor, D half-diminished, G7 and C minor 6 move the same way. The flat 5 of the first chord, A flat, falls to G.
To keep: close position, two voices stay, two step, and the inversions take care of themselves.
Take a close voicing and drop its second (or third) voice from the top an octave: wider, warmer, and still led by step.
Hi {name}! C major 7 close: C, E, G, B. Take the second note from the top, G, and drop it an octave.
That is drop 2: G, C, E, B. On the piano the low note goes to the left hand. On the guitar it fits four neighbouring strings.
Lead it like close position: the top voice moves by step, the 7th falls to the 3rd. D minor 7, G7, C major 7, all in drop 2.
Drop 3 drops the third voice from the top instead: E, C, G, B. The bass sits low, on the guitar on strings six or five.
Your turn: the first voicing is written, its top note changes from item to item. Keep the top voice moving by step.
Each chord has four drop 2 voicings, one with each chord tone on top. Practice ii–V–I from all four.
On the guitar the app counts semitones, not frets. A shape far up the neck can still be the nearest voicing.
A common mistake: playing close position and calling it drop 2. If all four notes fit inside an octave, nothing was dropped.
Big bands voice saxes this way, and guitarists comp with it. The spread opens the sound without losing the line.
How to find the next drop 2 quickly: picture the close voicing you would play, lead it by step, then drop the same voice again. The hand learns the four shapes.
Drop 3 on the guitar puts the root on string six or five with a gap above it. It sounds like a small big band behind a singer.
To keep: drop the second voice for drop 2, the third for drop 3, then lead every voice as before.
Left hand root and 7th, right hand 3–5–9 led by step; with a melody, the melody note is always the top voice.
Hi {name}! A spread voicing uses both hands. Left hand: the root and the 7th. D and C for D minor 7.
Right hand: the 3rd, the 5th and the 9th. F, A and E. Together: a wide, open chord.
The left hand follows the root. The right hand moves by small steps: F, A, E, then B, E, A over G7, then E, G, D over C major 7.
With a melody the rule changes a little: the melody note must be on top. Build the chord below it, still by the smallest move.
Your turn: chord names, and a melody when there is one. Choose voicings that carry it.
On the dominant play the 13th instead of the 5th: B, E, A over G and F. It sounds richer and moves more smoothly.
In minor: D half-diminished with F, A flat, G on top, then G7 flat 9, then C minor 6. The right hand stays close.
Harmonising a melody: first find which chord tone the melody is, then fill in the others below by the nearest notes.
A common mistake: letting a chord note rise above the melody. Then the tune disappears inside the chord.
Practice the right hand alone first: three notes moving by step over the changes. Then add the left hand, which only follows the roots.
Listen to the top: in a good spread the highest note makes a small tune of its own, even with no written melody.
To keep: the left hand is the floor, the right hand sings, and the melody always sits on top.
Hear the key first, keep the tune in your head, then write it note by note: step or leap, up or down. Rhythm comes after the pitches.
Hi {name}! Writing a melody starts with the key. These four chords tell your ear where home is.
Now a short tune. Before writing anything, hum it back in your head.
The first note is given. For every next note ask two questions: a step or a leap? Up or down?
With rhythm, write the notes first, then their lengths: this one is long, short, short, long.

Stuck on a note? Sing the line from the start up to that note, then compare it with the home note: is it the tonic, the third, the fifth? Knowing the scale degree tells you exactly where to write it on the staff.
Your turn! Listen, hum, then write. Three replays are free.

Melodic dictation means hearing a melody and writing it in notation. It has three layers: the key (where home is), the pitches (which notes), and the rhythm (how long each one lasts). Solve them in that order.
Find the tonic first: after the melody ends, sing the note that feels like home. Most short dictation melodies end on 1, and most begin on 1, 3 or 5.
Memorize before you write. Listen to the whole melody, sing it back silently, and split it into chunks of three or four notes. Writing while it plays usually costs you the ending.
On the staff, a step moves to the next letter — line to space. A third skips one letter — line to line, or space to space. Size a leap by singing the notes in between: C to E passes through D.
Anchor leaps on the tonic triad. If you hear that a note is 5 in C major, it is G — on the second line of the treble staff. Degrees turn sound into position.
For rhythm, tap the beat and place each note against it: on the beat, between beats, or held through. Write beat by beat, then check that every bar adds up.
The usual mistakes: writing a step where there was a third, and losing track of the octave after a big leap. When you finish, sing back from your page — not from memory — and compare.
Practice tip: write down tunes you already know, such as a birthday song or a lullaby. You do not need to remember the sound, so all your attention goes to writing it correctly.
Recap: key, then pitches, then rhythm. Memorize first, think in degrees and steps, and always check by singing what you wrote.
Count the beats while you listen, then build the bars one beat at a time from blocks: a long note, two eighths, a dotted figure…
Two bars of rhythm over a click. Count one, two, three, four along with it.
Take it one beat at a time. One hit on a beat is a quarter note; two quick hits are two eighths.
A note that holds through two beats is a half note — nothing new happens on the second beat.
A dotted quarter followed by an eighth makes a long-short limp. The dot adds half the value, so the long note lasts one and a half beats and the short one fills the rest.
Now build both bars from the blocks, then play your version to check it.
Rhythmic dictation means hearing a rhythm and writing its note values. In 4/4 each bar holds four quarter-note beats, and every bar must add up to exactly four.
Values halve each time: a whole note lasts 4 beats, a half note 2, a quarter 1, an eighth ½, a sixteenth ¼. Two eighths fill one beat; so do four sixteenths.
Count with syllables: “1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &”. The number falls on the beat and “&” exactly halfway. A quarter takes one number; two eighths take the number and its “&”.
A dot adds half the value: a dotted half lasts 3 beats, a dotted quarter 1½. A tie joins two notes into one sound — often across a bar line, where a dot cannot reach.
Silence counts too. Every value has a matching rest: a quarter rest is one silent beat. Here beat 3 is empty — write a quarter rest there.
Syncopation puts a note off the beat and holds it across the next beat. Eighth, quarter, eighth sounds “short-LONG-short” and fills two beats.
A method: first mark four beats per bar, then note whether each hit lands on a number or on an “&”. Finally give each hit a value that reaches the next hit.
The common mistake is a bar that does not add up. After writing, count each bar aloud with the syllables. Three and a half beats means you missed a dot or an eighth.
Recap: know the values, count “1 & 2 &”, place every hit against the beat, and check that each bar adds up to the time signature.
In two-part music, follow one line at a time. Voices often move in opposite directions, and meet mostly in thirds, sixths and octaves.
Two lines at once, {name}. First just enjoy how they fit together.
Now only the top line. Hum it.
And the bottom line. Notice: when the top goes up, the bottom goes down. That is contrary motion.
Sometimes the lower voice copies the upper one a bar later. That is imitation — listen for the echo.
Where the voices meet, listen for the distance between them. Thirds and sixths sound sweet and full; octaves and fifths sound open and bare. The last note of a phrase usually meets on an octave.
Your turn! One voice is given — listen for the other one and write it.
Two-part writing means two independent melodic lines sounding together. Each must make sense on its own, and together they must form good intervals, especially on the strong beats.

There are four kinds of motion. Parallel: same direction, same interval. Similar: same direction, different intervals. Contrary: opposite directions. Oblique: one voice holds while the other moves. Here is contrary, then oblique.
Consonances: thirds and sixths are imperfect — full and sweet. Unison, fifth and octave are perfect — so bare that two in a row make the voices sound like one.
That is why parallel fifths and octaves are forbidden: the voices lose their independence. Parallel thirds and sixths are fine — but not too many in a row. First fifths, then thirds.
Hidden, or direct, fifths and octaves are a subtler fault: both voices move the same way into a perfect interval. Between the outer voices this is allowed only when the upper voice moves by step.

Start on a perfect consonance and end on an octave or unison. The usual approach is by contrary motion: one voice 2 to 1, the other 7 to 1 — a sixth opening to an octave, or a third closing to a unison.

Imitation: one voice repeats the other’s idea a little later, at the same pitch or another interval. When the imitation runs strictly all the way through, it is a canon; a round like “Frère Jacques” is a canon at the unison.
Listening and writing tip: give each line its own listen. Most people catch the top voice first; the lower one needs a separate, focused pass. Then check the interval on every strong beat.
Recap: two independent lines, mostly contrary or oblique motion, thirds and sixths in the middle, perfect consonances at the ends, and never parallel fifths or octaves.
The bass is the floor of the harmony. In root position it plays the chord’s root; in an inversion it moves by step; passing notes fill the gaps.
Listen to the lowest note under each chord, {name}. That is the bass line.
Alone, the bass already tells the story: home, away, tension, home.
In an inversion the bass takes another chord note, so it can move smoothly by step.
Passing notes walk between chord notes: do, re, mi.

A trick for the bass: hum the lowest note of every chord, quietly, under your breath. Then ask how far each step is from the one before — a step, a fourth up, a fifth down — and write that distance on the staff.
Your turn! Listen only to the bottom and write it in the bass clef.
Bass dictation means writing the lowest line of a progression. The bass fixes the inversion and most of the harmony, so a correct bass line is already half the chords.
In root position the bass plays roots, so it leaps often: up a fourth or down a fifth for V–I, a step for IV–V, down a third for I–vi. These are the sounds of strong progressions. Here: I vi IV V I.
Inversions smooth the line. With the third in the bass (figure 6) it can move by step: I – V6 – I is C – B – C. A 6/4 chord usually keeps the bass still or repeats it.
Listening strategy: sing the bass up an octave, in your own range, and name each note as a degree. A handful of patterns cover most basses: 1 7 1, 1 4 5 1, 1 6 4 5 1.
Phrase endings are landmarks. A bass going 5 to 1 is an authentic cadence; stopping on 5 is a half cadence; 4 to 1 is plagal. First a half cadence, then an authentic one.
Reading the bass clef: from the bottom, the lines are G, B, D, F, A. Middle C sits on one ledger line above the staff.
The common mistake is writing an upper voice instead of the bass. If your line jumps around strangely, you may be following the top — focus underneath everything.
Recap: roots leap, inversions step. Sing the bass in your range, name the degrees, use the cadences as landmarks, and write it in the bass clef.
Cadential 6/4: the tonic chord over the dominant bass, before V. Neapolitan: a major chord on the lowered 2nd. Augmented sixths: ♭6 and ♯4 pull apart to the dominant.
This chord sounds like home, but the bass is already on G. It is the cadential six-four: it leans into V.
The Neapolitan: a major chord on the lowered second degree — in C minor, D♭ major.
Augmented sixths: A♭ in the bass, F♯ on top. They move apart, out to the G octave. Italian has three notes, French adds D, German adds E♭.
It: A♭ C F♯ · Fr: A♭ C D F♯ · Ger: A♭ C E♭ F♯
Any chord can borrow a leading-note seventh: F♯ – A – C – E♭ is vii°7 of V in C.
Your turn! Read the notes, find the root and the special note, and name the chord.
Cadential 6/4 in C: G in the bass with C and E above, figured 6/4 then 5/3. Double the bass, G. The 6 falls to 5 (E to D) and the 4 to 3 (C to B). The 6/4 sits on the stronger beat, V on the weaker.

Neapolitan sixth: the major triad on ♭2, in first inversion. In C minor: D♭ F A♭ with F in the bass; double the bass. D♭ falls to the leading note B — a diminished third — and the chord moves to V, or to the cadential 6/4 first.

Augmented sixths in C: A♭ in the bass and F♯ above — ♭6 and ♯4, an augmented sixth apart. Both move outward by semitone to G. Italian: A♭ C F♯, with C doubled in four parts. French adds D; German adds E♭.
The German sixth has a trap: moving straight to V makes parallel fifths, A♭–E♭ to G–D. So it usually passes through the cadential 6/4. In major, E♭ is then spelled D♯, rising to E.
Secondary leading-note sevenths: vii°7/V in C is F♯ A C E♭, the leading-note chord of G, with E♭ borrowed from G minor. F♯ rises to G and E♭ falls to D.

How to identify on paper: stack the notes in thirds to find the root, then compare with the key. ♭2 as a major triad means Neapolitan. A chord that will not stack in thirds, with ♭6 and ♯4, is an augmented sixth.
Spelling mistakes to avoid: C♯ instead of D♭ in the Neapolitan, or G♭ instead of F♯ in an augmented sixth. A♭ up to F♯ is an augmented sixth; A♭ up to G♭ would be a minor seventh — a different chord.
Recap: each color chord has a fixed spelling and a fixed goal. Spell by letters, double the right note, and resolve the chromatic notes by semitone.
One letter per step, then fix the accidentals so the tones and semitones fall in the right places. Minor scales raise the 7th (harmonic) or the 6th and 7th going up (melodic).
A scale uses every letter once: D, E, F, G, A, B, C, D. Never two Fs!
Then the accidentals: major is tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. D major needs F♯ and C♯.
Harmonic minor raises the 7th: in A minor, G♯. Hear the wide step before the top.
Melodic minor raises the 6th and 7th going up, and comes down natural.
Modes start the same white notes from a different place. D to D on the white keys is Dorian; from another tonic, keep the same pattern of tones and semitones and add the accidentals it needs.
Your turn! Write the scale with accidentals — there is no key signature to help.

Scale spelling has two rules: use every letter exactly once, in order, and fit the scale’s pattern of tones (T) and semitones (S). The natural semitones are E–F and B–C; every other pair of neighboring letters is a tone apart.
Major is T T S T T T S. Write the letters from the tonic, then add sharps or flats until every gap fits. E major: E F♯ G♯ A B C♯ D♯ E — four sharps.
Flat keys work the same way. In F major, A to B would be a tone, but the pattern needs a semitone there, so B becomes B♭: F G A B♭ C D E F.
Natural minor is T S T T S T T. C minor: C D E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C — three flats, the same as E♭ major, its relative major.
Harmonic minor raises 7 by a semitone to make a leading note. Between 6 and 7 there is now an augmented second, three semitones — in A minor, F to G♯. Write G♯, never A♭: the letter G must appear.
Melodic minor raises 6 and 7 going up, smoothing that gap — in C minor, A♮ and B♮ — and comes down as natural minor. In jazz, the raised form is used in both directions.
Modes, compared with major or natural minor: Dorian is minor with a raised 6; Phrygian is minor with ♭2; Lydian is major with ♯4; Mixolydian is major with ♭7; Locrian has ♭2 and ♭5.

Common mistakes: skipping or repeating a letter (A♭ instead of G♯ in A minor skips G and repeats A), and mixing sharps with flats. Apart from the raised notes of minor, a scale uses only sharps or only flats.
Recap: letters first, then accidentals to fit the pattern. Major T T S T T T S, natural minor T S T T S T T, then raise 7 for harmonic, 6 and 7 for melodic going up.

Figures name the intervals above the bass: 5/3 root position, 6 first inversion, 6/4 second. In four parts: double the root, keep upper voices within an octave, avoid parallel fifths and octaves, resolve the 7th down.
Soprano, alto, tenor and bass: four voices, one chord. Here is C major with the root doubled.
Figures under the bass tell you the chord. E with a 6 means a sixth above E — that is C major, first inversion.
Two voices moving in parallel fifths sound hollow — the rule says avoid it. Listen.
In V7 to I the seventh falls by step and the leading note rises to the tonic.
Keep the upper three voices close: no more than an octave between soprano and alto, or alto and tenor. The bass may sit further away, down below.
Your turn! Read the figures, fill in the inner voices, and check the rules.

Four-part harmony writes every chord for soprano, alto, tenor and bass. Usual ranges: soprano C4–G5, alto G3–C5, tenor C3–G4, bass E2–C4. Voices must not cross: the alto stays below the soprano, and so on.
Spacing: at most an octave between soprano and alto, and between alto and tenor; tenor and bass may be further apart. This C major chord is well spaced.
Doubling: in a root-position triad, double the root. Never double the leading note or a chord’s seventh: both must resolve, and two of them would resolve in parallel octaves.

Figured bass gives intervals above the bass. 5/3, or nothing, is root position; 6 is first inversion; 6/4 is second. For sevenths: 7, 6/5, 4/3 and 4/2. An accidental alone applies to the third above the bass.

Parallel fifths and octaves are forbidden between any two voices — check all six pairs from chord to chord. IV to V is the classic trap: here everything moves up together, then the upper voices move down against the bass.
Smooth voice leading: keep common tones in the same voice, move the others to the nearest chord note, and prefer contrary motion to the bass.

Tendency tones: the leading note rises to the tonic, and a chord seventh falls by step. In V7 to I, B rises to C and F falls to E; a complete V7 then resolves to an incomplete I, with three roots and a third.
A working method: write the bass, then the soprano, then fill alto and tenor with the remaining chord notes. After each chord check range, spacing, doubling and parallels — in that order.
The most common errors: fifths hidden between inner voices, a doubled leading note in V, and a seventh that does not fall.
Recap: right ranges, close upper voices, root doubled, tendency tones resolved, no parallel fifths or octaves.
A new line against a cantus: consonances on strong beats, dissonance only as a passing note or a prepared suspension that resolves down, and never parallel fifths or octaves.
A slow given tune, the cantus, and a new line above it. Note against note: that is first species.
Thirds and sixths are sweet, fifths and octaves are open. A second or a seventh clashes.
Second species: two notes against one. The weak note may clash only as a passing note, walking by step.
Fourth species: a note is held over the bar and clashes, then steps down to resolve. That is a suspension.
Each line should also sing well on its own: mostly steps, a few leaps, and after a big leap a step back the other way.
Your turn! Read both lines and find what breaks the rules — or say it is correct.
Species counterpoint was set out by Johann Joseph Fux in Gradus ad Parnassum (1725). You write a line against a given cantus firmus in five stages, the species, each adding one rhythmic idea.
Perfect consonances: unison, fifth, octave. Imperfect: thirds and sixths. Dissonant: seconds, sevenths, the tritone — and the fourth, which counts as a dissonance in two parts.

First species, note against note, uses only consonances. Begin with a perfect consonance — a fifth only when the new line is above — end on an octave or unison, and favor thirds and sixths in between.

Never move into a perfect consonance by parallel or similar motion; approach it by contrary or oblique motion. Avoid long chains of parallel thirds or sixths. The cadence: a major sixth opening to the octave.
Second species: two half notes against each whole note. The downbeat must be consonant. The weak beat may be dissonant only as a passing note — approached and left by step in the same direction.
Third species: four quarter notes per cantus note. More passing notes, the neighbor note (a step away and back), and the cambiata, a traditional figure that leaps away from a dissonance.
Fourth species: syncopation. A note tied over the bar line clashes on the downbeat — a suspension — and must resolve down by step. Above the cantus: 7–6 and 4–3; below it: 2–3.

The line itself: mostly steps; leaps up to a fifth, a minor sixth upward, or an octave, but no sevenths and no augmented or diminished leaps. After a large leap, turn back by step. One clear high point.
Fifth species, florid counterpoint, mixes all the others. Fux modeled the method on the style of Palestrina, and here it starts to sound like real Renaissance music.
Recap: consonance on the strong beats, dissonance only as a passing note or a prepared suspension resolving down, perfect intervals reached by contrary or oblique motion.

Trill: fast alternation with the note above. Mordent: note, the one below, note. Upper mordent: note, the one above, note. Turn: above, note, below, note. Appoggiatura: a leaning note on the beat that resolves.
A trill shakes quickly between a note and the one above it.
A mordent is quick: the note, the one below, and back. The upper mordent goes above instead.
A turn circles the note: above, the note, below, the note.
An appoggiatura leans on the beat — a sigh — and then resolves to the real note.
On paper an ornament is often just a small sign above the note. Players read the sign and add the extra notes themselves, in the style of the music.
Your turn! Look at the notes written out, count how many there are, and name the ornament.
Ornaments decorate a main note. They are usually written as a small sign, not in full, and the player supplies the notes — so the exact execution depends on the period and the style.

Trill (tr): a fast alternation of the written note with the note above it in the key. In Baroque and Classical music it usually starts on the upper note; from the 19th century, usually on the main note. It often ends with a turn.
A small accidental above a trill sign alters the upper note. A trill on C with a flat above it alternates C with D♭.
Mordent (zigzag with a vertical stroke): note, the note below, note. Upper mordent, or Pralltriller (no stroke): note, the note above, note. Both are quick and, in Baroque music, start on the beat.
Turn (∽): above, note, below, note. Written over the note, it starts at once. Written after the note, the main note sounds first and the turn comes at its end.

Appoggiatura: a small note on the beat that takes time from the main note — usually half, or two-thirds of a dotted note — then resolves by step. Acciaccatura: a small note with a slash, crushed in as fast as possible.

Recognizing written-out ornaments: count the notes and check the direction. Many fast alternations: trill. Three notes, dipping below: mordent; rising above: upper mordent. Four notes circling: turn. One leaning note resolving by step: appoggiatura.
The usual mix-up is mordent versus upper mordent: the vertical stroke through the sign means the lower note. Signs also varied between composers, so check the edition’s table of ornaments.
Recap: trill alternates, mordents flick below or above, the turn circles, the appoggiatura leans and resolves. Read the sign, then play it in the style of the music.
Answer out loud or with a tap. No typing.
Right. It leapt up a fifth.

Practice by key adds the natural minor inside each major key, ladders for guitar and bass, and from the upper tiers melodic minor and the modes

Corrected Latin grooves: a true two-bar son clave you can hear, the bembe bell in 6/8, the tumbao kick and the songo hands; Brazilian items are played straight; the organ no longer reacts to touch and takes the swell pedal
Every lick runs in all 12 keys, in your language: a lick you play in many keys and use while improvising becomes yours
Each lick has two modes, from the page or by ear, and steps for the ear lead you from hearing to playing
Your takes are counted by how you played them: from the page, by ear or from memory; the progress page shows both sides
Notes fade as an item grows familiar, a short daily sight-reading dose, and two self-ratings when you pick an instrument
Practice has four places — Technique, Licks, Repertoire, Improvise — plus games and a tools strip; the menu reads Today, Practice, Path

Repertoire holds every piece: standards, songs, classical pieces, your charts, scores and recordings; add a piece from a lead sheet, a score or your own recording; each piece shows what you can do with it

One daily workout: new steps from the path, then technique and improvisation; the technique part comes from every key at your level, half from the key of the week; assignments from a teacher come first
Progress has an Over time tab: closed items per area, the ladder week by week, closeness to the target tempo, by ear and reading, the keys filling up, where the minutes go
One meaning of "closed" everywhere: three clean takes at the target tempo, on two different days
Your progress is saved as a daily summary, so charts of your progress over time can show your history
Practice by key shows every exercise in every key at your level, how many are closed, the time left and when you will finish at your minutes a day
Today's key workout: the next exercises in the order you choose (weakest first, by key or by exercise), filling today's time
Licks and Encore are one tile: the library, my phrases and the challenges; share a lick once you play it clean at a tempo
Approach licks now lead into every scale degree too, before the 3rds, triads and 7th chords, up and down, with each hand and then hands together
Lick 3 where the step above is only a half step (E and B in C): F D E♭ – E, C A B♭ – B

Practice in a key is a full workout: the scale at your level, 3rds, triads and 7th chords along the whole scale every time, the approach licks (lick 1, 2, 3 up and down the scale), contrary motion, Hanon, hand independence, octaves, leaps, a canon and a cadence, the ones you need most first
The coach knows your limit: three takes at the top without a faster clean take, it saves your best and moves on
The cursor over the notes follows the sound and stops on the last note

Continuous practice in a key is now the coach over a ladder: the scale at your level, then 3rds, triads and 7th chords along the whole scale, then a cadence — the tempo climbs as you play clean, and the basics are skipped when you are past them.
The areas map lives on Skills only, and it is clickable: tap an area to open its families; a tidier area card. “Practice” spelled the same everywhere.

Progress in an instrument course shows the course’s own areas (piano: technique, dynamics, time, harmony, comping, improvisation, by ear, reading): the map once on Overview, the areas with their families on Skills; no leftovers of the ear course.

Voicings keep every tension (a 7♭9 always has its ♭9, in drop 2, drop 3 and four-way close too); quartal So What ii–V–I in two versions; the Kenny Barron voicing on every minor 7 and in a ii–V–I; the harmonic minor formula pattern over four octaves; guitar shells for every cadence.

New technique: the jazz cadence library (37 cadences in nine voicings on piano, four on guitar, walking bass), colours of the diminished, every mode on a root (major, melodic and harmonic minor) and the symmetric scales as full scales, Hanon 2–20, minor octaves and double 3rds, contrary 7th arpeggios, guitar minor scales in five positions, bass diatonic 7ths. The coach: technique tiers set the timing tolerance, a short level check on a first session, a note at the end. Practice: Technique first, extras under More practice, Licks inside Encore. Swing tunes replace the children’s songs in the openers and the first repertoire.

Practice by key: a key of the week (your weakest key, or the next new one), Know the key (signature, chords, ii–V–I, 6th-diminished, the relative and parallel keys, three quick questions), dynamics as a lens on any scale, arpeggio or pattern (crescendo, accents, p, f, staccato), the circle of fifths on wide screens, the current level in each row, and key order by fingering.

Practice by key: the 12 keys as cards (major, minor, melodic / harmonic minor modes, symmetric), each key page opening with its continuous session and a row per kind of exercise — scales and modes, arpeggios, cadences, patterns, control and dynamics, Barry Harris, voicings, lines — with your best tempo, accuracy and timing; general technique below. By topic, a family splits the same way, and its card shows in how many of the 12 keys you play it well.
Continuous practice asks for the key order before it starts: circle of fifths up or down, chromatic up or down.

Continuous practice climbs: the tempo rises inside the session (faster after clean takes, two steps when it is easy), “almost” no longer counts as a miss, a slowed take never passes, and players past the basics (your course answers, the level test, or easy takes) skip free time and start hands together.
The narrator says abbreviations in words: “one octave, right hand, 66 beats a minute”, not “1 oct, RH”.
Fix: the metronome click during a take is now as loud as the count-in (it was lost under the keyboard).
Fix: “Turn sound on” now opens a fresh audio channel on the default output when the stuck one will not start.
Fix: when the browser kept the sound closed, Play, Listen and the coach’s demo waited for ever. Now they go on, Skip always works, and a small bar offers to turn the sound on.

Hands stay on the instrument between steps too: on an exercise’s opening page, a take waiting for Play, a result waiting for Next and the lesson summary, playing any note (or pressing any key) goes on.

Continuous practice in technique: one press starts a session that begins where you are and climbs — right hand, left hand, the next key, hands together, contrary motion … The next take starts by itself after a short note on the last one; pause or end any time. Every reading exercise has Listen beside Play, and a new step is played to you first.

Reading while you play: the score scrolls smoothly with the beat — the line you play near the top, the next lines below it, the scroll landing as the next line starts. Hands together: treble and bass of the same bars stay together and line up; on a computer the next system is in view.
On a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, the score’s cursor now waits for the click you actually hear (after the MIDI timing calibration), instead of running ahead of the sound.

With a MIDI keyboard connected, a speaker button at the top (and in lessons and technique) turns the app’s sound for your keys off or on, so a digital piano can play through its own speakers while you still hear the app. The first time a keyboard connects, the app asks.
Each course asks where you are in that course, by name ("Where are you in Piano?"), and a course picked at sign-up always asks its own question.

Jazz is now the top of every course instead of a course of its own: jazz ear and theory in Ear & theory, jazz playing in each instrument and the voice. It opens by your background, with jazz focus, or when you climb to mf.

Find my level now measures the whole course: harmony is asked in Ear & theory, and every instrument and the voice test cover every skill the course teaches. The Ear radar shows what the course teaches.

New in Ear & theory: a Symmetry unit (dividing the octave, P / L / R moves, interval vectors), Euclidean rhythms, and for the pro track the modes of Messiaen and the twelve-tone row. Negative harmony gains two listening levels.
Three new games: Mirror (negative harmony), Tonnetz (walk the triad grid) and Euclid (rhythms spread evenly).
Each rhythm lesson asks once to pick the written bar you heard — tap it, nothing to say — and once to play it back. Lessons now count “1 & 2 &” instead of “ta ti-ti”.
Rhythm questions: hear the rhythm, then play it back — tap the big pad, or say it in time on a short syllable like “dum”. No more “ta ti-ti” answers.
“About this course” is now a clear button on the Path page (and on Today before you start), so the course intro can be watched again any time — also after leaving it half-way.
A unit’s title on the path now matches what it teaches, as its intro does (unit 1 of the Ear course: “First steps for the ear”).

Phones: no more crackling. The sound now uses a slightly larger buffer on phones, so the piano, the band and the voice play clean even when a lot sounds at once; timing exercises still judge against the real sound. (Settings → live play latency → Low keeps the smallest buffer for MIDI.)
Testing round: everyone starts over. We reordered the steps in every course, so progress was cleared on purpose; your language, nickname, calibration and recordings were kept.

About seventy new lessons, so no step comes before its lesson: seventh chords, chords of the key and Roman numerals, scales, mode colours, the 6 chord and the diminished seventh, a welcome to jazz, walking lines, reading the staff on guitar and bass, pentatonic boxes, left-hand styles, and an opening lesson for every technique family.

Drums: note values and rests, accents and ghost notes, flams, shuffle and swing ride, bossa and clave, Middle-Eastern rhythms, fills, rolls and independence. Voice: swing and the blues form, guide tones, and the singer’s ear.
Every course, at every level: one new idea per unit, the rest of the unit practices what you just learned, and a topic climbs one level at a time.

No step comes before the lesson that teaches it: many topics now open with their lesson, and a lesson you skipped comes back as a quick check before anything that needs it. The Jazz path no longer runs out.
The first steps of each instrument are no longer skipped, and a step you passed in one course counts in the others.
One Hebrew term per idea across the app, and a fix to the upper-structures explanation (VI gives 13 with ♭9).
Every course now opens with a short animated tour of what awaits you, and each unit opens with a short intro the first time you enter it. Replay both from the course page.
Gentler pacing: each level gives you two or three questions before it climbs, and the first lessons teach one topic at a time.
The Ear course now starts with high and low, and a new lesson, “What is a chord?”, comes before major and minor. Games wait until their concept has been taught.
The language button now switches everything at once: the screens, the language you answer in and the voice that answers you.
Keep screen on: the screen no longer goes dark while the app is open (Settings → Display to turn it off).
The “home note” question now simply asks which note the tune would end on.

Shares now invite: every share (friend code, daily puzzle, daily challenge, new best tempo, rooms, challenges) carries a link to the app, and the link shows a preview card in WhatsApp and other chats. A friend’s link sends the friend request by itself — after signing in, if needed.
One look for the whole app: the earlier design is gone, along with its switch in Settings. A few screens were tightened so they still fit one phone screen.
A globe button in the top bar and on the welcome screen switches the whole app between English and Hebrew in one tap.
The games that still had the old look now open with the studio cover and play with the same top bar as the rest.
Guitar: rhythm stems under the tab, chord boxes mirrored for left-handed players, Encore guitar phrases checked like guitar drills, and MIDI guitars with a channel per string and pitch bend.

Measured touch goes further: accents in place, trills and repeated notes, leaps and octaves, sf and fp, the soft pedal, melody over accompaniment in pieces, and a touch section in the level test by microphone too. Settings cards have proper margins.
An "Install" button in the top bar and on the welcome screen, with the steps for iPhone and other browsers.

Guitar: a strum with a string that did not sound is no longer counted as full, and the app says which note and string; chord boxes show finger numbers and barres, with the current and next chord on chord drills and in Strum Changes; finger numbers sit in their own row under the tab; string names on the neck.
Piano: say "I use a different fingering" on any drill, a small keyboard strip shows the next key and finger, and a new best tempo gets its own moment. The new look now covers the remaining screens.

The new look reaches everything: a cleaner Today with one plan, a path of paper notes, game covers and one game frame, calmer practice tiles, new league, rank and badge art, new celebration screens, and a share card for challenges.

Measured touch on piano: crescendo and diminuendo as two clear lines, rolled chords, held notes and releases, speeding up, swing, voicing, pedal on every take, and a new touch section in the level test. Four new control exercises in all 12 keys. Wrong notes are now red, with small marks for early, late and wrong.
A new look: calmer cards, one clear main button per screen, cleaner type, a new logo, an opening animation, and Toni redrawn as a young musician with headphones.
Guitar: fairer timing by microphone, and no more keyboard-only advice on guitar takes.

Encore: suggested piano fingering you can change note by note, left-hand shells under a phrase, and 3/4, 5/4 and 6/8 phrases. Starred recordings can keep their notes (never the audio) on all your devices; turn it on in Settings.
When a friend masters a phrase you shared, you get 5 XP. A small card on Today shows a friend’s newest phrase to take on. New drawings for the gifts.
A new look for every icon and button: layered paper drawings in one language, with small, gentle motion when you tap (none if your device asks for reduced motion).

Encore challenges: share a phrase you mastered and challenge friends to beat your tempo. React with "Encore!" plus groove, sound or idea, and give a friend a fermata, dedicate a phrase, or invite them to practice together now.
Deeper content: harmonise, embellish and reharmonise a tune, more public-domain tunes, and a tune ladder. Fixes: profile saving, Community tabs on small screens, and bottom-bar labels.
Your measured practice time and your notes now travel with your results to every device you sign in on.

A teacher can attach their own playing to a phrase assignment, and longer phrases (up to 16 bars) travel whole. When a phrase becomes yours, friends see it in their feed — grade and tempo only, never its name.

Encore: keep any phrase you play — after an improvisation, an exercise or a free recording — trim up to 8 bars, set a target tempo and take it through all 12 keys until it is yours. On keys, guitar, bass and voice, by MIDI or microphone; a teacher can play a phrase and assign it.
My recordings: every take is kept on this device by date — rename, star, folders, playlists, loop a span, slow it down without changing pitch, compare two takes, and listen with the screen locked.

Grace notes and two voices in one hand in the notation; triad pairs in depth (patterns, voicings, lines, an ear level and a game); intros, endings, a ballad ladder and a whole tune in one take; two new harmony games; clearer drum and ear feedback.
A first game for every instrument, played on the real thing: Staff Runner (keys), Root Catcher (bass), Strum Changes (guitar), Rebound Ball (drums) and Sing It Back (voice).

Classical pieces from grade 1 to 8 — Burgmüller, Clementi, two Bach inventions and the C minor prelude join the list — each checked note for note against a public-domain edition. Ornaments are drawn as real signs, with a line saying how to play them.
All 12 keys across keys, guitar and bass; the level test now credits levels by difficulty; minor keys spell the raised 7th as a sharp; Hebrew durations read right to left.

More at every level: written theory from grade 1 (note values, interval numbers), ascending intervals first, counterpoint in the Ear course; jazz you play from the start on guitar, bass and voice; singers get first steps, improvising and pop and theatre style.

Piano: sight-reading to grade 8, a pop accompaniment ladder, pedalling, and classical pieces (Ode to Joy, Minuet in G, Für Elise, Bach’s Prelude in C) in our own engraving. Guitar modes from grade 5. Bass riffs, feels and all 12 keys. Drums: groove, develop, solo, and the rudiments where they belong.

Barry Harris, checked: the chromatic scale, the half-step rules from every degree, the ABCs in thirds, the two-voice chromatic scale and Echols’s shells are back, verified. Live marks now on two-hand pieces too, a velocity row and a “last take” overlay.

Nine new games: Guide-Tone Runner, Enclosure Target, Changes Crossword, Hold the Note, Border Control, Which Brother?, Run Catcher, Comp Caller and Elevator — each on the path, in the workout and in key mastery.
Live feedback while you play: each note marked early or late as it sounds, a pocket meter in place of “Go!”, and a clean chord chart for every jazz item.

A practice diary: real measured practice time, how clean your takes were over the weeks, a journal with notes and search, and a nudge when an item stops improving. Only measured practice keeps the streak.
Drums are out of beta. Material we could not verify against its sources is hidden until it is checked.
Games, cleaned up: every game fits one phone screen, setup extras moved into a small “More” sheet, flat readable colours, and the input check before every mic or MIDI game.
Games count more: ten games are now steps on the path, the workout rotates a game a day, and key-based games feed your per-key mastery; more games run in all 12 keys.
Hebrew everywhere in the games, a shared result card, per-note marks on the Highway, Rudiment Rush flams and drags, and Duel now records XP and a board.

Every take, clearer: the score is the hero (bigger notes and tab, look-ahead while you play), each note marked early or late, and a short review — one verdict, three chips (notes, time, evenness), one suggestion. Tap a bar under the score to loop just that spot slower until it’s clean.
Check your input first: before every exercise you see the mic level or your MIDI keys arrive, and a quiet banner tells you if nothing is heard during the take.

Singing: a vibrato readout, a note-by-note review after the take, sight-singing shows the score only while you sing, and one fair pass band everywhere (a note within 60 cents passes; 65 for beginners).
More of every course: first steps for keys, guitar, bass and drums; guitar grades 9–11; 49 drum levels; a top ladder for singers; three-voice and one-hearing ear training.

Singing, redesigned: a live pitch lane with the target notes, a big note name, a calm in-the-zone meter (no numbers while you’re on it; ▲ sharp, ▼ flat), steadiness bars, and a mic check before you start — you see your voice arrive before the take.
The path in every course now follows real difficulty, mapped to graded syllabi; Jazz has a true beginning (swing, the blues, shells, guide tones, a first solo you play); repertoire runs to the top.

Reharm and colour: one note, many chords; chromatic mediants; modal interchange; pedal, planing, sus and organ comping. Solo jazz piano after Jeremy Siskind: left-hand shells to stride, solo textures, comping vocabulary, improv habits.
Fixes: fresh sight-singing melodies every time, minor-key Roman numerals from natural minor, real agility levels for singers, and a correct minor cadence in the degrees exercise.

Barry Harris, from the sources: the 6th-diminished scale now goes up and down in its own scale; all four of Barry’s key scales (major 6, minor 6, dominant 7 and 7♭5 diminished); the scale of chords in moving inversions, drop 2, drop 3 and drop 2&4; borrowing with one, two and three voices; Thomas Echols’s nine-floor elevator; Harris’s named moves; the important minor and the tritone’s minor — eight ways to play one dominant.

Barry Harris lines: his chromatic scale, scale outlines of tunes in Chris Parks’s order, the 5-4-3-2 phrases, the three important arpeggios, seven down to the 3rd, the triplet and miscellaneous rules, and upbeat comping — on keys, guitar and bass.

Every scale and mode in every key, hands separate, together and in contrary motion, then harmonized: notes, 3rds, triads, 7ths, drop 2 and drop 3. Hand-independence studies for piano and a fuller guitar technique set.

Improvise as a path step, checked by 48 rule cards (Harris rules, enclosures, triad pairs, a lick you learned, rhythm and shape); write your own solo chorus and play it; comp and solo at once; the brothers, backdoor, Coltrane sub, intros and endings in context.
Heads: original tunes to harmonize (shells, close, drop 2, drop 3), chord-melody on guitar, a step-by-step comping ladder per tune, and a reharm studio that checks each choice against the melody.

The path teaches what’s new; today’s workout builds depth. A step is opened at 3 keys, 4★ at half the keys at tempo, mastered (gold) at all 12. Each step shows what’s missing, mastered units get a seal, and a step left alone for a month asks for a refresh. The checkpoint plays 4 random keys and only holds back your rank, never the path. “Path: guide me / I choose” in Settings.
Every standard in all 12 keys, and every jazz and theory level on keys, guitar and bass too.

Key changes: turnarounds, the rhythm-changes bridge, a pivot chord, ii–V of the new key, the common diminished (all three), the tritone sub, and 6-dim lines from key to key — plus “how did it modulate?” by ear.
Bebop vocabulary: approach notes and every kind of enclosure, the click on 2 and 4 and a silent bar, Barry Harris’s important minor, 3 to ♭9 and the triplet rules, and bebop lines on guitar and bass.

By ear: chord progressions you write bar by bar — root, quality, bass — with partial credit and a fix-it pass, up to a whole AABA; progressions and phrases played back on keys, guitar and bass; Play It Back on guitar and bass; a by-ear mode for licks.

The pivot (Barry Harris): the root on top, then drop to the next chord tone below and climb — Cmaj7 as C, then E G B. A lesson, an ear topic and drills on keys, guitar and bass in all 12 keys, on every chord type, from any chord tone, through ii–V–I, and combined with a scale line and with an enclosure. The old pivot lesson is now “Scale line with a pivot”.

Every key counts: for each skill on keys, guitar and bass the app now tracks which of the 12 keys you control and which are weak. Today, the workout and the path put weak keys first (a setting turns it off), each family shows a 12-key map — tap a key to practice it — and Insights has a Keys card. The AI teacher names your weak keys and builds the week around them.
Rhythm: polyrhythm taps 5:4, 5:3 and 7:4, metric modulation, hemiola, and new rhythm levels for keys, guitar (odd meters), drums, bass and singing.
Voice leading: new keys and guitar drills that grade how each voice moves — common tones held, smallest steps, drop 2 and spread voicings — with a score that shows every voice’s line.
Theory you play: triad pairs (C altered = F♯ + G♯ triads), pentatonic superimposition, polychords and their function, and reharmonizing a tune yourself.

Barry Harris, part 2: the three diminished collections, passing, auxiliary and dominant diminished, chords that move to chords, and m6 = m7♭5 = 9 over the bass. Harmony and ear: function by ear, modal cadences, borrowed extensions, form, negative harmony, jazz dictation and planing.
The path is now ordered by difficulty, with gentler first steps for beginners; jazz and Barry Harris are part of the default guitar path.

Singing: a note sung an octave away from the rest of the line is no longer counted right (moving the whole line by an octave is fine), and new sung intervals past the sixth — sevenths, the octave and ninths.

New ear topic “Hear the voices”: which voice moved, how many notes stayed, smooth or jumpy ii–V–I, close or drop 2. Bass gets 5 against 3; guitar odd meters join the level test, and guitar levels open in order of difficulty. The teacher’s hint now sits in the bottom bar.

Rubato first: a new technique item — scales too — starts in free time, with no count-in and no click: play the notes at your own pace while the marker waits for you; only the notes are graded. After two clean takes, once in quarter notes at ♩60, then the item’s own tempo and the tempo ladder. "Skip to tempo" for players who are ready.
A timed take with many wrong notes offers "Once in free time". Free-time takes earn a little XP but no stars — those still come only from measured tempo.

Theory check: arrows between chords read the right way in Hebrew (V → I), "parallel minor" is no longer called relative, and several jazz and Barry Harris demos play exactly the voicings they describe; small fixes in voice, drums and the Coltrane-cycle game.
An AI teacher where you need it: "Explain more" after a wrong answer explains this question by ear, with a few follow-up questions; the exercise page can explain the whole topic in depth.
"Ask for a hint" before answering, in practice (never in a level test or an exam): it points you to what to listen for without giving the answer — and the question then counts as "almost".
After a session, a short note from the coach on what was measured; on Insights, a weekly summary from your player profile.
These need you to be signed in; everything else works exactly as before without them.

Your player profile, at the top of Insights: your strengths, the patterns that keep coming back (with how many weeks in a row) and the ones that went away while you kept practicing — drawn from everything measured: technique, timing, the pairs you mix up, the Ear Index. A pattern shows only after it repeats, and each one opens the exercise that trains it.
After a lesson: when today’s tricky pair has come back for weeks, the summary says so.

The playhead on the staff sits on the notes: it glides through each note in the note’s own time (slowly through long notes, quickly through short ones) and stands on the notehead when the note is due — also triplets, dotted notes and swing, on wide screens and phones. A thin line instead of the wide column.
Voice level test: it sets up first (your range and the microphone delay), moves on by itself after each take, takes about 10 minutes, and continues where you left it.
With a MIDI keyboard: a theory question with note answers is answered by playing the note, and a rhythm to tap can be tapped on any key.

Voice course: Find my level is now its own test in sections — pitch, time, a song, the ear, sight-singing, scales and agility. One take per step, each in the real exercise (count-in, click, the now-cue); a good take moves you ahead, a miss moves the test on. Your voice path then starts where you are.
Notes on the keys: with a MIDI keyboard on, chord and note questions take the keys directly — no button; a whole chord, let go, answers by itself.
An unfinished level test from before no longer comes back in another course, and catching up asks only about the current course.

Find my level belongs to the course: in Ear & theory it measures pitch & harmony, rhythm & time, memory & structure and reading & theory only. Voice and instrument courses keep their own tests; Today’s button opens the course’s test.
B♯ and C (C♭ and B) are the same note: an answer that sounds the same counts, and spelling questions no longer offer the same sound as a decoy.
Sung questions always listen to the microphone, even with a MIDI keyboard connected (it used to wait for the keyboard).
Level test on a phone: the progress bar is a thin strip on top instead of a column covering the answers.

Singing in lessons: a sung melody or run gets a count-in, the click and the now-chip, and is graded on time too (half the grade, loosely). A sung note up to 60 cents off counts — you are told which way. After a second miss a sung item waits for Continue instead of rolling on.

Singing in Practice: more phrases are sung on the pulse (by ear, terraced, accents, arcs, breath phrases, vibrato on chosen notes). Up to the middle of the course a melody is graded mostly on the right notes and on time; intonation is shown and taught with gentler bands.

Guitar, bass and drums get the new level test in sections, like the piano: guitar — hands, chords, rhythm, lead, reading, ear (+ jazz comping); bass — hands, time and pocket, chord tones, walking, reading, ear; drums — hands, grooves, fills, reading, independence, ear. One take per step, a clean take jumps ahead, a miss moves on.

New piano level test, all on the keys: hands, chords, comping, reading, ear at the keys and (jazz) lines. One take per step in changing keys, at the step’s own tempo — a clean take jumps ahead, a miss moves straight on, "almost" gets one more try. About 8 minutes; every family gets its start level.
Guitar, bass and drum level tests no longer insist: at most two takes per step, a miss moves on.
"Again" starts right away everywhere: drills, licks, drum games, the transcribe coach, a lesson’s recap (no brief page again), and "Play again" in the games starts the first round.
In the piano, guitar, bass and drum courses, "Find my level" from the menu (and the catch-up card) now opens the playing test on your instrument, not the multiple-choice ear quiz.

Every timed take now says when: sung melodies get a count-in, a click (on/off) and the notes lighting up one by one; piano, guitar and bass drills, sight-singing, the guitar tab drill and rhythm reading show a moving highlight on the note that is due; Play It Back lights the due cell, Sing along keeps the click under the whole song, and the groove pad pulses on every click

Drum songs in the first levels are built up layer by layer, in Practice too: kick alone, then + snare, then + hi-hat, then the whole song with fills and crash; 85% opens the next layer, and the level opens on the whole song
Drum songs show whether the kit is connected, and each hit’s MIDI note and drum as you play, so a silent kit says why
Drum songs: pick the tempo before you play (slow, medium or full); a first-time song starts slow, and the level opens at full tempo
Drum songs: a metronome click through the whole song, and a drum-sound choice (your kit or the app)
Drum lanes say Hi-hat, Snare, Kick, Tom, Crash with a picture of each drum, never SN or BD; the notes are drum heads
Notes swell and light up as they come, and the drum pad glows the moment to hit
The first drum song is easier: kick and snare only, before the hi-hat joins
The narrator really speaks on phones now: old silent copies saved on the device are cleared and fetched again
The narrator is back on phones: every recorded line re-encoded so it plays as speech, not a click
Community: block and report a player, an activity feed from friends with one-tap cheers, quick messages in duels and rooms, challenge links, a weekly friend quest and a class board
Nine instrument games: Play It Back, Voicing Sprint, Chord Change Race, Walk the Changes, Roots by Ear, Harmony Hold, Sing the Interval Sprint, Kit Read Rush, Name That Groove
Chord & cadence builder; drum styles by ear; splash vs chick; speed records; 3–7 shells on bass; a model line after guitar trading
Upper structures and rootless voicings by ear, a whole 32-bar AABA; My song hears the chords; two-hand grand-staff reading; learn a solo phrase by ear
Serious badge titles and no emoji; smarter review spacing; finished pieces come back for review; more narrator lines
The narrator speaks again: the recorded lines were silent (only clicks on some phones); they are being re-recorded, and the rest are read until then
Rhythm exercises show a beating pulse, never a keyboard; the run screen names the key you are playing; no "Slower" button when you were ahead of the beat — it says so instead
Drums: mambo, songo and Mozambique (pending a teacher check), Rudiment Rush, Groove-off duels with friends, crash chokes

Drums, 91 → 133 levels: songs in sections (verse, chorus, road maps, your own chart), prog meters and polyrhythms, reading played on the kit, three new games, jazz with brushes

Ear & theory: an audit of every question, plus an advanced jazz ear (extensions, voicings, ii–V chains, reharmonisation, transcription) and prog rhythm (odd meters, polymeter, metric modulation)

Piano: a pianist’s ear (hear it, play it back, harmonise, transpose), reading both clefs, chords and scales as shapes
Piano: exam-grade target tempos, fingerings for every minor scale, cadences without parallel fifths, fairer timing at fast tempos

English narration with a natural on-device voice (Kokoro); Hebrew text types itself out.

Readable everywhere: no more yellow on white or pale-yellow behind icons; the recap comes as cards.

The opening shows the name and the slogan; the app opens in the light look
Bass: a full course of 14 technique families and 120 levels — plucking, time, chord tones, walking bass, pocket with the kick, ghost notes, slap and more — with 5- and 6-string and drop-D basses

Every technique session now counts for your streak, your teacher and the weekly league; bass is marked beta while its course grows

A new look across the whole app: light and dark (the colour themes are retired and their gems refunded; avatar frames take their place), Toni the eighth note who reacts as you play, note-head symbols instead of emoji, and a clearer path
Courses: ear & theory, voice, keys, guitar, bass, jazz and exam each have their own path, daily workout and practice — switch from the chip at the top
Shorter questions and one-line feedback ("Why?" only when you miss); answers move from names to the staff as you improve
Settings as a control centre with search, quick tune and sound cards you can listen to; a redrawn metronome, tuner and games (Flight, Highway, True or false)

The vibraphone, marimba and upright piano now have their recorded dynamics too — three each, soft to loud (the vibraphone on soft mallets when you play softly, hard ones when you play out)
Your best score on every improvisation challenge, shown in the challenge library; Practice counts the challenges you have mastered (85% and up)
The debrief asks for a whole chorus when there were too few notes, instead of slowing you down
Settings → Sound: clearer download note, organ and electric-piano options laid out for a phone, credits as a list

Read a lead sheet: a standard’s chords on the page — what key, where the ii–Vs are, what a chord does (dominant, secondary, tritone sub) — also in the jazz Bagrut, Jerusalem Academy jazz and Rimon mocks
Improvising on a MIDI keyboard now gets the musical report too (chord tones on strong beats, the ending, rhythm, range, approach notes)
Practice rows show where you stand: saved charts, the chords you know, today’s progression

The band plays like a band: a real walking bass (roots on the change, approach notes, lines that head somewhere) and comping with voice-led rootless voicings in rhythms that never repeat three bars running; ballads and slow swing on brushes
After every chorus under rules: what went well, the one thing to work on, the bars where it broke — and the next step (a harder challenge, again, or slower) in one tap
Lead sheets with the tune: a MusicXML file brings its melody — the head plays first, then you solo
Listen to your solo: the take over the same band (MIDI notes, or your own sound with a microphone)
For the exams: sing a line that changes key (5 levels), chorale analysis by ear (Roman numerals and inversions, 5 levels), swing rhythmic dictation (R8) — in the Bagrut and conservatory mocks

The band: a recorded jazz kit (4 dynamics, alternating strikes, ride, cross-stick, crash, toms) and a double bass with 3 dynamics and 4 plucks per note — and the drummer now plays like one: ride and hi-hat on 2 and 4 in swing, the clave on the rim in bossa, a jazz waltz
New keyboards: Wurlitzer (recorded), a tine electric piano and a tonewheel organ (modelled — drawbars, percussion, rotating speaker), with dynamics that follow your touch
Settings → Sound by category (pianos, electric pianos, organs, mallets and plucked), each instrument with its own options, and a Band card for the drums
Practice in four groups — Play, Train, Study and Tools — on the phone and in the side menu on a computer

A concert grand at full detail: all 16 recorded dynamics instead of 4, so every touch has its own color; full 48 kHz sound (the highs were cut before); the damper’s sound and the string’s ring when a key is let go; the top keys ring on as on a real grand; with a MIDI keyboard, the sustain pedal’s sound and the strings blooming while it is down
Settings → Sound: the grand’s detail — automatic (all layers on a computer, eight on a light phone), full or light

Improvising under rules, much bigger: 51 rules in four families (notes, intervals, rhythm and now phrases), and a library of 51 challenges by level — from one-note swing to the bebop test — with a random challenge. Each rule explains itself

Import a lead sheet: MusicXML or .mxl from MuseScore, Sibelius, Finale or Dorico, an iReal Pro link or playlist, or plain chords / ChordPro. The chords become a chart to play over, under rules — no teacher needed
Standards: 36 sets of changes (most as the whole form) in eight groups — blues, rhythm changes, swing, ballads, bossa, modal, bebop, Coltrane
Study programs and exams, and Improvise, now have their own place in the menu; teachers can assign an improvisation challenge over any level or standard; My pieces also opens .mxl files
A new first minute: the logo draws itself, one promise, a first taste (which note was higher?), three short questions, then your start
One serious, calm look everywhere: no cartoon art or emoji, flat answer buttons, a quieter path, calm celebrations, line icons

On a computer: search everything with Ctrl K, side panels beside exercises and Today, settings in two panes, dialogs in the middle of the screen, wider screens (two-column lists, a mixing desk), larger staves
Notation fixed: beamed eighths without flags, bar lines and time signatures, rests in gaps; after a take each note shows what you played — wrong pitch, early or late
Technique level test: your take marked on the staff, and an octave-shifted keyboard is detected with a one-tap fix
Sound output: choose where the sound plays (for MIDI keyboards and interfaces that take over the computer’s sound); or play with the computer keyboard (A–K, opt-in in Settings → MIDI)
Teachers: assign a topic level, a technique level, a chord chart with rules or a piece, with strictness, target tempo and a note; a grading inbox, a class map, and a parent link with a weekly summary
Progression games: Where is home?, What comes next?, Which chord changed?, Figure it out — and the Progression of the day, a daily puzzle to share
Improvisation studio: phrasing rules, vary a phrase, and trading fours with the app answering your idea developed
Exams: the music Bagrut by track and conservatory entrance exams (Jerusalem Academy, Tel Aviv, Bar-Ilan, Rimon) — every section to practice, and timed mock exams
Songbook by the chords you know: pick your chords and see the key each song fits — or the one new chord it needs
Plans: prices, sales and the free tier set from an admin panel; Voice Flight stays inside your range; American spelling and a full proofread

On a computer: a side menu instead of the phone tab bar — Today, Path, Practice (songs, technique, lessons, pieces, charts), Progress, Community, Tools, Find my level and Settings, with sections that open in place; on a tablet it is a rail of icons, and it collapses on request
Exercises on a computer: answer with the number keys, Space repeats, Enter continues, C compares, H hints, S skips, Esc pauses
A cleaner look: the leftover emoji and the big game-style buttons outside exercises are gone, the Find my level button no longer shows as a brown box, and path nodes are flat

Buttons mode answers quietly: a chime, the right answer in green and yours in red, one short line on what went wrong — no narration. Compare plays yours against the right one when you tap it, Continue moves on
Left in the middle? A phone that closed the app in the background now reopens the exercise where it stood (Find my level included), and five answers already count for today’s streak
The keyboard is a hint on degree and note-name questions: hidden until you ask for it, and asking costs a little XP. Find my level never shows it
MIDI keyboards: the sound now wakes up on the first tap and after the phone was in the background; a button in MIDI settings turns it on if the browser blocked it
Rhythm items (tempo, meter, downbeat, swing, syncopation, rhythm memory and building) now play on drums, not piano
Pause, Repeat and Skip now really stop everything: no metronome or drum pattern keeps playing, and replaying a comparison no longer mixes clips

Insights: one screen that reads all your practice — your Ear Index, the fingers, hands, keys and scales that need work, your groove, the answers you mix up, and your trouble bars, each with a button to practice it

Groove fingerprint: where your notes land against the beat — by subdivision, tempo, after rests, across a phrase — and how it changes week by week

Confusion map: the pairs you mix up most, with a boss fight that drills exactly that pair

My pieces (preview): bring a score (MusicXML or MIDI), set a target tempo, and the coach runs your practice — a few bars at a time, slow first, up a step after three clean takes, back to the bar with the mistake, then joining the parts until the whole piece is at tempo
Every lesson now has an "In depth" part: the whole topic — what it is, how to hear it and play it, the common mistake, where it lives in real music. The short version still plays before each exercise
The glossary grows from 30 to 137 music words, each with an example

Settings → Privacy & friends: one choice (Open / Friends only / Private), advanced options and a young-player mode
The path: short step names, your real unit number after the level test, every ✓ step on the road, and a quiet intro page before each exercise (with a quick refresher)
Progress in four tabs: Overview, Skill Map (areas you can open), Activity, Awards (only what you earned)
A calmer look for the games, the workout editor and the exercise buttons

A calmer, more grown-up look: the new Calm night theme, plus Studio, Paper (light), OLED black, High contrast and Classic arcade in Settings

Your areas and ranks moved to Progress, puzzles and the daily challenge to Play

Settings in tidy categories, and a MIDI keyboard section: devices, a key test, pedal and timing

The drill creator: tap a pattern on the keys or the neck, type it, or play it on MIDI — add rhythm, chords, a separate left hand — and run it through every key; share it with a code
A rank in every area, from Bronze to Master, leaderboards per area among friends, and a monthly area challenge
Hundreds of new badges with their own medals — and a celebration when you earn one
Find my level is about three times shorter: it jumps ahead while you are right, and your path keeps adjusting after every session
Refresh: unsure about a concept? Open its short lesson in the middle of an exercise and come back to the same question
Timing calibration for screen taps, MIDI keyboards and the microphone — never marked late when you were on time
Every exercise fits a phone screen: the Repeat / Skip buttons are always in view
Your path is rebuilt around you: choose a goal, leave out what you don’t want, and every unit mixes all your areas at your level — the level test and the questionnaire now change it right away
Steps you already know get a ✓ (from your answers, your speed and the level test), and any unit can be tested out
Play your instrument: find notes on the guitar neck and the keys, chord shapes and CAGED, scales, and play back what you hear — by microphone or MIDI
Write what you hear on the staff, build rhythms, two-voice and bass dictation, four-part harmony, counterpoint and scales on paper
New ear training: seventh chords and inversions, color chords, song form, style, inner hearing, intervals to sing, and a producer’s ear (EQ, reverb, panning, compression)
Time with the click: subdivide it, play through gaps, tap a tempo from memory, two hands, and read the drum kit
Today's workout comes first on Home: suggested from your goals, then yours — change the time, the minutes per topic, the order, add or remove — and it moves your path forward

New games: Chord Rush, Note Rush, Fretboard Sprint, Interval Sprint, Key Signature Rush, Progression Detective, Peak Hunter, Rhythm Highway, Voice Flight, Melody Puzzle, Name That Tune, Tune-up and Pitch Memory — by category, some inside your path units, and every game counts toward your levels
Read the chord: name chords drawn on the guitar, the keys or the staff

A new look: night colors, chunky game buttons, a new logo, and a tab bar at the bottom — Home, Path, Progress, Play and Friends

Right answers fly up as XP; phones give a light tap on right and wrong answers

Speed now counts — fairly: every answer scores up to 70 for being right the first time and up to 30 for answering within your own speed goal; each replay costs 10. A bar under the question shows the goal running down, a mark shows an answer within it, and the recap shows your score out of 100, stars from it, and exactly what was missing for 100. Real instruments: a recorded grand piano is the default sound, and every rhythm exercise plays on a recorded snare and kick

Preview: the Avatar studio — two 3D avatars to dress part by part, items to try (headphones, shades, beanie, a legendary guitar) and emotes, including a jam together

New practice: rhythm memory, chord memory, call & response (improvisation by ear), and deeper sight-reading (bass clef, minor, three versions)

Rhythm is tapped on a big pad everywhere (saying “ta” is optional in Settings)

More: quick lessons for every vocal track, sight-singing feedback per note, Barry Harris 6-chord and diminished notes and the chromatic scale in sections, secondary dominants and the blues turnaround, “in tune, sharp or flat” down to 10 cents

New skills — Tempo & pulse, Fine pitch, Sight-reading, Improvisation — with new topics (every interval by ear, minor & chromatic degrees); the Skill Map shows five domains; a cleaner home screen with today’s plan first
Every unit now starts with a quick lesson (about a minute): what it is, how it sounds, how to hear it — with examples. Skip any time
Hear a lesson to the end and the topic joins your collection: “Topics I learned”, by area — replay any card
Personal coaching: after a miss you hear what was off in *your* answer (“not 5 — this one is lower”, “the first 2 notes were right”), and the recap names the pair you mixed up most
Leagues become a chord: Root, Third, Fifth, Seventh, the Ninth, ♯11 and 13 — each league adds a note to your badge; the top ones are hard to reach. Your Skill Map shows your ear’s chord too

Barry Harris: the 6th-diminished scales, the diminished chord that becomes dominants and minor/major 6s, 6 chords over every chord, half-step rules, pivots, brother dominants — to hear and to sing (7 singing levels)
Singing feedback says how and where: “a bit flat”, “went sharp at the end”, “slid up into the note”, note by note in melodies
Notes shown your way everywhere: keyboard, staff, guitar tab or any mix — also in Echo Chain, vocal technique and sing-along
Sight-singing: read a melody with its rhythm and sing it from the tonic and a count-in

New practice topics: extensions & alterations, voicings, progressions, form, fine pitch, in tune?, two voices, trichords, maqamat with quarter tones, Middle-Eastern rhythms, polyrhythms, odd meters, swing feel, and written theory (key signatures, spelling, Roman numerals, circle of fifths, transposition, chord-scale, three clefs)
Play & improvise: backing tracks (ii–V–I, minor, blues), improvise with feedback, MIDI keyboard drills, guitar from tab; choir rooms where every phone sings its own part
Inner clock drill (the metronome drops out — keep the beat), sus4 / add9 / alt in extensions, a recorded organ drone, color themes for gems, a notification when a friend plays your duel
Leagues climb the overtone series: Fundamental → Octave → Fifth → Seventh → The Ninth; written theory now shows on your Skill Map
Instrument sounds: grand piano, upright, harpsichord, harp, marimba, vibraphone, organ (Settings → Sound)
Play together: every game in live rooms — and a big-screen mode (TV or laptop shows the game, phones answer); Echo Chain together, steadiest voice, true-or-false, modes, wrong notes
Advanced vibrato, harmony singing (intervals over a held note, missing chord notes, harmony lines), sing-along with songs you know
Spot the wrong note; blues, pentatonic, bebop and more in Modes by ear and in scales to sing
New lessons: slash chords & bass lines, melodic dictation, Jazz 2 (licks & melodic minor)
Today’s workout (5/10/20 min), achievements, weekly leagues, duels with friends, an optional absolute-pitch corner, instrument mode
Your answer next to the right one in the recap; synonyms understood (#11 = ♭5 = tritone, Δ = maj7 …); the drone is never mistaken for your voice

New: Vocal technique — 12 measured levels from one steady note to vibrato control, glides, leaps and fast passages: intonation, stability, drift, vibrato rate, width and evenness, transitions, timing. Live pitch trace, one tip per take, listen back
Your range: calibrate it once (glide on “ah”) — every sung exercise in the app now stays inside it
Scales & modes to sing: from Ionian up to “G Mixolydian up, altered down”
Modes by ear: hear a scale and name its mode — including the modes of harmonic and melodic minor
Find my level and True or false? are now in the menu, and Find my level sits under the main button on Home
New game — True or false?: three notes, two intervals: are both right? Solo 60-second runs or a duel on one device, four levels up to “by ear”
Aids while answering: the key or the note to sing is shown while a skill is still growing, and fades out as you reach Solid. Aided answers count a little easier, so the rating stays fair
After each answer, the notes you heard appear on every view you chose
Streak 2.0: a celebration when your streak grows, milestones with confetti, and a streak calendar
Streak freezes: one free every Monday, more with gems — a missed day no longer ends your streak
Gems: earned for good lessons, your daily goal, puzzles and milestones; spend them on freezes or a streak repair
Your overall rating: one number for your whole ear, next to your name, with your best and its trend on the Skill Map
After every session: how your rating moved — overall and in each skill — and when you reach a new level
Ratings next to names for friends (sort by rating), in online rooms, on the daily board and in class rosters

Find my level now covers every topic (degrees, notes, intervals, chords, cadences, melodies, rhythm, tapping, singing), adapts per topic, shows which topics are left, gives XP — and is the first step on a first visit
Your Skill Map sends you to the lesson that fits your level, opens the path up to it, and shows a trend chart for every skill
Topic progress bars on Home: lessons done out of how many, per topic
The keyboard no longer lights up the answer while you are still answering
Cleaner header: install and update buttons up top; language in Settings; “What’s new” in the menu
ToneTurn is now Ninth Sense — new name, new logo. Your progress, friends and account stay as they are.
Class mode: teachers create a class, students join with a code, the teacher assigns lessons and sees each student’s progress
Race your ghost: your best run comes back as an opponent that answers exactly when you did
Jazz 1 (lesson 21): major 7, dominant 7, minor 7 and half-diminished chords, and the ii–V–I family, voiced like a jazz pianist
Songs you know (lesson 22): famous public-domain openings — name the degrees, then find out which song it was
Review with spaced repetition: mistakes come back after 1, 3, 7, 16 and 35 days until they stick
Drone practice: sing every scale degree over a held tonic and see how in tune you are
MIDI keyboard: play instead of singing, and press a key to answer degree and note questions
Note sequences (lesson 20): hear notes and name them, turn names into degrees and back, sing from note names — the whole melodic matrix now works for sequences
Build the bar: in dictation, tap rhythm blocks to write what you heard
Riffs & runs (lesson 14): name a run’s scale or shape, then sing fast runs back — graded on pitch, clean separate notes and even timing
Runs workshop: each run at 60 %, 80 %, then full speed, at your level
Daily challenge leaderboard: see how many played today, your rank and top %, and your friends’ scores
Your first play is graded on the server — also when you played before signing in
Online rooms: create a room, share the code or link, and play friends on their own phones — same sound at the same moment, live leaderboard after every round, podium at the end
Daily challenge: 5 questions, the same for everyone today, scored on speed and accuracy, with a spoiler-free share card
Duel on this device: two players face to face on a split screen, same sound, fastest right answer wins
Rhythm 1–3: read rhythm notation and tap it on the metronome (or say “ta”)
New lesson: Sing it by name (echo a note, sing a named note)
Skill Map: rhythmic memory and rhythmic precision are now separate, like singing in tune and melodic memory
